# StockPulse — Claude Code Context

## What this is
A stock screener. Every symbol in the universe is measured the same way after every close — returns, trend, relative and volume readings, company fundamentals, and a mechanical Advice verdict that names the one rule that fired. State lives in **Turso** (hosted libSQL/SQLite). Price data comes from the Twelve Data API. The owner (admin) manages portfolios and refreshes data; the public sees a read-only cached snapshot.

The repo/folder is `StockPulse`; the app is branded **Tickr Lab** in the UI (`<title>` and the bar wordmark).

**93 symbols**, 14 of which are deliberate ballast — see **The universe, and the ballast that has been draining out of it**. **Read that section before trusting any number in this file**: the universe was 116 with 33 laggards until 2026-09-10, most measurements here were taken on that universe, and shrinking it moved them. Before designing any backtest, read **Does any of this predict anything? — the research log**: eleven framings have been tested and ten came back flat, and it records what is ruled out so the next attempt is a new one.

## Running the app
```
node --use-system-ca server.js
```
Runs on port 3000. Requires `.env` with `TWELVE_DATA_API_KEY`, `TURSO_DATABASE_URL`, `TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD`.

**Careful when running it just to look at the UI:** `computeStocks()` calls `ensureProfiles()`, which re-pulls any profile older than a day and rewrites the `profiles` and `snapshot` tables, burning API credits. To check frontend changes only, serve `public/` with a throwaway static server instead — the page falls back to admin-open mode when `/api/me` fails, so the whole chrome renders without touching the API.

## Persistence (Turso)
Everything goes through `db.js`. Tables: `portfolios`, `portfolio_tickers`, `names`, `profiles`, `snapshot`, `visitors`.

- **The accessor names are unchanged** from the flat-file era (`readPortfolios`, `writeProfiles`, …) and return the same shapes, so call sites only gained an `await`. `server.js` destructures them from `db.js`.
- **Writes are whole-collection replaces** — delete-then-insert inside one `db.batch`. That mirrors the old "rewrite the file" semantics and keeps `writeProfiles({})` working as the cache-clear `/api/refresh-all` depends on. Fine at tens of rows; revisit if the universe grows.
- **Portfolio order is an explicit `position` column.** The UI colours portfolios by index, so order has to survive the round trip — don't rely on insertion order.
- **`profiles.data` is a JSON blob** because it caches a third-party response whose shape we don't control. `fetched_at` is lifted into its own indexed column because the 24h TTL check runs against it every refresh.
- **`/api/visitors` aggregates in SQL** now (counts + `LIMIT 500`), instead of parsing the whole log into memory on every request.
- **`/api/refresh-all` expires profiles, it does not delete them** (`expireProfiles()` sets `fetched_at = 0`). Deleting them used to strip sector, market cap and fundamentals out of the shared snapshot for the ten-odd minutes the backfill ran, so every other viewer saw the holes. `readProfiles()` treats `0` as "keep the values, drop the timestamp": the row still renders, and `ensureProfiles()` still re-pulls it. **The blob also carries a `fetchedAt`, so the column has to override it** — otherwise the stale copy inside the JSON makes an expired profile look fresh.
- **Express 4 does not catch async handler rejections.** Every async route is wrapped in the `route()` helper near the top of `server.js`, which turns a database error into a 500 instead of a hung request. Any new async route must use it.
- **WHICH TURSO: the hosted libSQL service, not the Rust rewrite — probed against production 2026-10-05.** `select sqlite_version()` answers **3.47.0** and `libsql_version()` does not exist, so this is the SQLite **fork**; `@tursodatabase/serverless` 1.4.0 talks to it over HTTP at a `libsql://` URL. The two products share a brand and a version line, and **"Turso 0.8" is the ENGINE rewrite (formerly Limbo) whose release notes do not describe what this database runs** — worth knowing before reading a feature announcement as available here. What production already has, asked rather than assumed: window functions including `ntile`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST` and `jsonb`. Two things to watch if the hosting ever moves to that engine: `explain query plan` returns classic TEXT rows, which is the shape `query-plan-test.js` parses, and `BEGIN CONCURRENT` is irrelevant here either way — every write is one `db.batch` from a serverless function, so there is no connection contending with another.

### `init()` runs on EVERY cold start, and it is the floor under every response
**A schema statement added to `db.js` is not free — it is a round trip paid before the instance can answer anything (2026-09-18).** `init()` ran 46 `SCHEMA` statements and 36 `ADDED_COLUMNS` sequentially: measured against the live database, **46 sequential is 1.72s and the same 46 in one batch is 0.04s**. It is a batch now — safe because every schema statement is `if not exists`, which `init-test.js` asserts rather than assumes, since a batch is all-or-nothing and one "already exists" would sink the lot. The old per-statement tolerance stays as a fallback for the real race it was written for (2026-09-14, every instance that lost it cached its rejected init and served 500s until recycled).

- **The ALTERs cannot be batched.** `alter table add column` throws "duplicate column" on every boot after the first — 36 guaranteed failures a cold start. Ask what the columns ARE instead, in one read batch of `pragma_table_info`, and run only what is genuinely missing. Normally that is nothing.
- **How it showed: a long refresh makes every OTHER tab cold.** With a Fill missing running, `/api/stocks` on a second tab took 41.6s, 9.4s and 81.5s to first byte while `/api/status` stayed at 0.14-0.16s. The long run holds the warm instance for its whole duration, so everything else lands on a new one. Timing each read this path makes from a laptop against the same production database showed the database was never the bottleneck (`readSnapshot` 0.31s, the four smaller reads 0.05-0.07s each) — **an unexplained slowdown that a direct query cannot reproduce is a cold-start cost, not a query cost.**
- Two round trips per cold start now, against 82.

### A DROPPED CONNECTION IS RETRIED ONCE, AND ONLY ON A READ (2026-10-04, owner: "what is this error")
**Reported as a 500 on `/adjustedbacktest` and read as a bug in the backtest. It was the database.** The stack, pulled from the live Vercel log:

```
GET /api/adjusted-backtest?date=2021-01-04&... failed: LibsqlError: fetch failed
    at LibSQLClient.batch
    at async Object.readSecFactsSince (db.js:2279)
    at async Promise.all (index 1)
  cause: TypeError: fetch failed
    cause: SocketError: other side closed  (UND_ERR_SOCKET)
```

Turso closed the TLS socket part-way through one of that read's chunked batches. It is **one of six reads the adjusted backtest runs CONCURRENTLY**, so the `Promise.all` rejected and the whole **thirty-five-second** computation was thrown away. Measured by hammering production: **one failure in sixteen cold runs**, no pattern in the date or any control — the same query succeeded on the next two attempts, and ten other cold runs (including four at once) were clean.

#### WHY A RETRY IS SAFE HERE AND IS NOT SAFE IN GENERAL
`fetchJson`'s rule for Twelve Data is *retry only when the attempt provably did nothing*, because a charged call retried breaches the credit ceiling. The database question is whether the statement **may already have been applied** when the socket died — and for a `select` the answer cannot matter, because running it twice changes nothing. For a write it does matter and is unknowable from here, so **a write is never retried**: most of ours are idempotent upserts, but `chat_usage` and the signup throttle are `set n = n + 1`, and a silent double-count is exactly the kind of wrong nobody would ever notice.

- **THE TEST IS THE SQL, never a flag a caller passes** — every statement in the call must begin `select`, `pragma` or `with`. The same mechanical guard the production write-block harness used. A caller cannot forget to opt in, and cannot opt a write in by mistake. **Proved by reverting**: `readOnly = () => true` fails 3, including a mixed batch where one insert sits among selects.
- **AN EMPTY BATCH IS NOT A READ.** `every` on `[]` is true, so the obvious guard says yes to nothing — and there is nothing to re-run. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- **THE CAUSE CHAIN IS WALKED, because the code that names the drop is three levels down**: libSQL's `LibsqlError` wraps undici's `TypeError`, which wraps the `SocketError` carrying `UND_ERR_SOCKET`. A top-level message test finds nothing on the real error. Bounded at eight hops so a self-referential chain cannot spin. **Proved by reverting**: one hop fails 1.
- **ONE retry, deliberately.** A second drop inside a second is a database that is down rather than a blip, and the caller is better served by an error than by a page that takes another thirty-five seconds to fail. **Proved by reverting**: a loop fails 5.
- **`withDeadline`'s own throw must NOT match** — it reads *"… did not answer within 60s"*, and retrying a timeout would re-run the work the deadline exists to abandon. There is a check on that exact string.
- The retry is **logged, not swallowed**: a rising count is a database problem, and a retry nobody can see is a symptom hidden rather than fixed.

#### "Server error. Please try again." IS WHAT MADE IT READ AS A BUG
`route()` turns every exception into one sentence, so a reader cannot tell a network blip from a fault in the page — which is why this was reported rather than retried. It now says the connection dropped and that nothing is wrong with what was asked for. **The words are OURS, never the driver's**: an upstream message can restate the query, and the auth token travels in the same request. A check asserts no `libsql`, `UND_ERR`, `SocketError` or SQL reaches the body.

- **What reaches that catch now is a write, or a second drop** — the read retry handles the rest.
- **The exposure was never specific to this page.** `/api/stocks` makes six parallel reads too; the adjusted backtest is simply the most exposed, because its reads are by far the longest-lived.

- Verified: **23 checks**. The fixture is the REAL error shape — a `LibsqlError` wrapping a `TypeError` wrapping a `SocketError` — because a hand-made `new Error('fetch failed')` passes the message test and proves nothing about the walk, which is where the code actually lives. Drops are **counted at the stub client**, so a retry is counted rather than inferred from the result. **Proved by reverting seven times**, every one load-bearing.
  - **A ROUTE THAT IS BROKEN IN THE FIXTURE READS AS A BROKEN GUARD.** The end-to-end check first used `/api/stocks`, which 500s in `uni-boot` for its own reasons (no API key, empty snapshot) — so a working retry reported as a failure. Every such check now asserts a **baseline with nothing armed** first.
  - **TWO DROPS WERE NOT ENOUGH TO REACH `route()`, and that is a feature of the route.** `/api/portfolios` reads five times and **tolerates one read failing on purpose** — `serveStamps` catches per stamp so a slow auxiliary read costs one field rather than the page. The fixture has to take the database away entirely.
  - **AN UNGUARDED `await` IN THE SUITE TURNED A LOAD-BEARING REVERT INTO "0 failed".** With the retry removed the read THROWS, the run ended at check 5 of 23, and the harness reported the whole fix as not load-bearing. Every read in the suite is defensive now, and the harness prints `?? only N of 23 ran`.

## Deploys — one hard rule
**Production deploys happen via `git push` only.** On 2026-09-12 the site went down for an hour with no commit involved: `vercel` CLI deploys made from another folder replaced production with foreign code (its logs said "Legacy server listening…", a string not in this repo), and every database route 500'd while `/api/health` stayed green. Diagnosis path when "site down, no commit": check `npx vercel ls stock-pulse` for deployments that do not match the git log, and `npx vercel logs <deployment>` for a boot line that is not ours. Fix: `npx vercel promote <last git-built deployment>`. The Turso token was never the problem — `Turso: schema ready` in the logs clears the credentials immediately.

## Serving and the gate
**Two directories, and which one a file lives in decides whether a stranger can read it.**

| | `public/` | `private/` |
|---|---|---|
| holds | `login.html`, `reset.html`, `app.css`, `favicon.svg`, `logo.png` | every other page, the shared JS modules, every research JSON |
| served by | Vercel's CDN, without invoking the function | this Express app, behind `gateAssets` |
| reachable signed out | yes, deliberately | no |

- **`public/` is a Vercel static directory, and the CDN answers it before the function ever runs.** That is why `GATED_PAGES` — the redirect bouncing `/chat.html` to `/chat` — **had never once executed in production**. Every gated page answered 200 to anyone with the URL, as did `single-closes.json`, `lab-grid.json` and all sixteen `strategy-*.json` files: the whole price archive, with the portfolio names inside it. Locally it worked perfectly, which is exactly why it went unnoticed for so long. Confirmed by `X-Vercel-Cache: HIT` on `/single.html` against `MISS` on `/single`.
- **The fix is the directory, not the code.** Everything requiring a session moved to `private/`, which the CDN knows nothing about, so the request falls through to the function and the guard actually decides. URLs did not change — `private/` is mounted at the root, after `public/`.
- **Never put anything in `public/` that is not meant for a stranger.** There is no code path that can protect it.
- **`gateAssets` guards only what `private/` actually holds**, matching a filename set read at boot, and calls `next()` for everything else. This is load-bearing: `app.use()` sees every request that reaches it and **every API route is registered below that line**, so the first version — which refused outright — swallowed `POST /api/login` and made signing in impossible. Not just the gated pages; the entire site. Caught by testing the signed-**in** path, which is the half that is easy to skip.
- **A page request redirects to `/login`; an asset request answers 401 JSON.** Content negotiation cannot tell them apart — a browser's `fetch()` sends `Accept: */*` exactly like a navigation, so `req.accepts()` answered "html" for both and every data file got a redirect, which `fetch` follows, handing the page a login form and HTTP 200 where it expected JSON. `Sec-Fetch-Dest` is what a browser sets to say what a request is *for*; the file extension is the fallback for clients that omit it.
- **`GET /api/health` is deliberately open and returns a count, nothing else.** `private/` is not a Vercel static directory, so if the platform ever stopped bundling it with the function every gated page would 404 and it would look like a routing bug. `{"ok":true,"assets":35}` says which it is.
- **The offline builders write into `private/`** (`single-data.js`, `strategy-runs.js`, `lab-grid.js`), and `server.js`, `lab-grid.js` and `strategy-runs.js` all `require` the shared modules from there.
- **The APIs were never affected** — `/api/stocks` 401s, `/api/visitors` 403s, and the pages were empty shells without a session. No user data or credentials were exposed. What was readable was the derived market data and the page source.

## Auth model
The app is a **door**: the screener is shared, and accounts only decide who gets in.

- **Anonymous** → `/` redirects to `/login`; `/api/stocks` and `/api/portfolios` return 401.
- **`guest`** (2026-09-13) → the "Try as guest" button on the login page: a deterministic HMAC cookie (`st_guest`, 24h, `guest-access-v1` salted with ADMIN_PASSWORD — rotating the password revokes every guest cookie), **no account, no sessions row**. Guests see **`GUEST_SYMBOLS`** and nothing else — **twenty since 2026-09-26** (it was five: NVDA/JPM/PTON/JOBY/DELL). **Chosen for SPREAD rather than fame**, greedily against the live snapshot: all eleven sectors, all six verdicts, all six cap bands and five of the six trend states, every row with enough history to score. A preview whose rows are all mega-cap technology shows the product's range to nobody, and a row that renders blanks is worse than one row fewer. **The first cut WAS all mega-cap tech** — a pure size tiebreak filled nine of the last eleven slots with correlated names, so the fill is by least-represented sector instead, **enforced server-side on every route** — the CDN incident's lesson. Filtered: `/api/stocks` (+ portfolio names), sparklines, news/latest, the stock-page universe list. Symbol-guarded 403: history, stock, news, model, and the `/stock/:symbol` page redirects. Member-only (`requireMember`): portfolios, chat, contact, signal, lab APIs; the research pages redirect `/`; gateAssets 403s the research JSONs (`single-closes`, `strategy-*`, `lab-grid`) for guests. Prefs: **a guest must never touch the `'admin'` prefs key** (`prefsKey()` falls through to it) — GET returns `{}`, PUT 403s. `/api/me` carries `guest: true`; the screener hides the research menu and Ask button and rewords the read-only note.
  - **THREE PAGES CLAIMED A GUEST GETS “EVERY FEATURE” and none of them ever did** (found 2026-09-26, while widening the preview): the screener's own guest note, the landing page's FAQ and the login page's footer. A guest has never had the research pages, personal lists, the studio, the pivot, compare or alerts. The screener's note also still told guests the assistant *needs an account* — it needs **admin**. All three now say what a guest actually gets. This is the same error the Intro carousel carried, fixed the same morning: **a claim has to leave with the feature.** **Acceptance = the route walk as a guest AND as a member** — both were run on introduction: guest saw exactly 5 symbols everywhere and 403/redirects elsewhere; the member path was untouched (93 rows, all pages, research JSONs).
#### The read-only note was wrong in BOTH directions (2026-09-27, owner: "this is no longer correct")
**"The data updates when the site owner refreshes. You can sort, collapse column groups and keep your own themes."** Neither half had been true for a while, and the second is the *inverse* of the failure this file keeps recording — not a claim that outlived its feature, but **features that outlived the claim**.

- **The data has not waited on the owner since the intraday schedule went live (2026-09-24)**: prices refresh about every half hour through the US session and a full refresh runs after the close. A member reading that sentence would have had no idea the screen moves on its own.
- **"Sort, collapse column groups and keep your own themes" was three of a dozen things.** A member has column filters, screens (with starred favourites), personal column views, tiles, personal themes, alerts, the pivot, compare, the group pages, the promo studio, the research pages and the phone page. Named now: *your filters, views, themes, starred screens and alerts are your own.*
- **"STARRED screens", not "screens".** A member cannot write a screen — those are the owner's — only star one; claiming the screens would be the same overclaim in the other direction, which is what this fix is about. There is a check for the word.
- **`/help` §7 carried the same stale fact** and is fixed with it ("a full refresh runs on its own every evening" and no mention of intraday). `/about` and `/landing` were already correct, and `/alerts` already said it precisely — **four surfaces state this one fact, so check all four when the schedule changes.**
- **THE NOTE MUST STAY ONE LINE.** It is `flex: none` above a page that never scrolls, so a second line is taken from the table's rows. Measured with `getClientRects().length`, not guessed.
**AND IT CAN BE DISMISSED FOR GOOD (owner, the same day: "it is taking vertical space").** Measured: **69px** — 61 of note plus its 8px margin — off a page that never scrolls, so every one of those pixels was coming out of the table's rows. The × takes them back (783 → 852px of `.table-wrap`, two more rows on a 760px window).

- **`prefs.noteOff` for a member, `localStorage` for a guest.** The choice belongs to the person and should follow them to another machine — the rule `tickerOff` already follows — but **a guest has no prefs key at all** (`prefsKey()` would fall through to `'admin'`, which a guest must never touch, so GET returns `{}` and PUT 403s). One flag, two stores, decided by who is asking.
- **A hide with no way back is a trapdoor**, and this note is the only place that says what a member may and may not do. `⋯ → Read-only note` toggles it, labelled with the direction it will go — the news ticker's bargain exactly.
- **`paintNote()` HAS TO RUN AFTER `loadPrefs`, and the first cut did not.** `applyAdminUI()` draws the note during `checkAuth`, which runs *before* prefs land, so the stored flag arrived after the decision had been made: the dismissal worked and then came undone on every reload — the precise opposite of "for ever". Caught by the test, not by reading. **Proved by reverting**: dropping that one call fails 4, including the guest's.
- Every visibility change calls `paintWindow(true)` — the ticker's rule, the phone bar's and the announcement's: no resize event fires when a sibling goes, so without it the table keeps its old height and the reclaimed space is simply blank.
- Verified: **32 checks** — the member fixture is THREE steps (the first account registered becomes the admin, so registering once and calling it a member tests an admin, who sees no note at all), each dead phrase absent, each live one present, one line at 1600px with the table still filling what is left, the guest note untouched, and the admin still seeing none. **Proved by reverting**: the old sentence fails 10.

- **`member`** → sees the same shared screener, read-only (sort, collapse, personal portfolios). **Members and guests see an identity watermark** (2026-09-14): `private/wmark.js`, one script tag on each of the eight data pages, tiles the account email (guests: "Guest preview") across the viewport at 5% opacity — `.wmark` in app.css, fixed, `pointer-events: none`, z-index 70 so a capture of anything carries it. It prevents nothing (nothing in a browser stops a screenshot); it SIGNS captures, which is the honest version of "restrict screenshots". The owner is skipped, as is open mode. Copy-blocking was considered and rejected: `/api/stocks` hands any signed-in browser the whole table as JSON, so blocking Ctrl+C is friction dressed as security.
- **`admin`** → everything: add/remove tickers, Refresh, Refresh all, the forward-returns view, visitor log, user management.

### The privileged role is `admin`, and it was `owner` until 2026-09-26
**Renamed at the owner's instruction.** Seventeen occurrences across four files and ONE production row, which is why this was a real rename rather than the display-only treatment Action→Advice and Scores→`rank` got — those are keys in saved prefs, class names and column ids, where the blast radius is every stored preference. A role is one column value in a four-row table.

- **`ROLE_ADMIN` is the only value written; `isAdminRole()` accepts BOTH for ever.** The cost of accepting a word nothing writes any more is one comparison; the cost of not accepting it is an instance whose only privileged account has silently become a member. **A migration you can be locked out by is not worth its tidiness.** There is a test that authenticates a row still holding `'owner'` BEFORE any migration runs.
- **The migration lives in `init()`, batched with the universe backfill** — `update users set role='admin' where role='owner'`, idempotent, a no-op for ever after the first cold start. In `init()` so production, a fresh database and the test harness all converge with no manual step and no window in which an instance serves against the old value; **batched** because a cold start is paid before the instance can answer anything, and two independent idempotent writes have no business being two round trips. Exported as `runRoleMigration()` so it is testable as a thing rather than only as a side effect.
- **`ROLE_ADMIN_MIGRATION` can be deleted once no deployment predates it.** Left in place deliberately: it costs nothing inside a batch that already runs.
- **NOTE THE OVERLOAD.** `'admin'` was already a stored value — the fallback `user_key` in `prefs`, `chat_usage` and `user_portfolios`, and the actor in the activity log, for the legacy password cookie and open mode. Different table, different column, no collision; but the word now means two things and `who ? who.email : 'admin'` sits a few lines from `isAdminRole(u.role)`.
- `set-password.js --role owner` still works and stores `admin`, so an old note or muscle memory is not a trap.
- `ADMIN_PASSWORD` unset → fully open, everyone is admin (local dev). Set → sign-in required.

**Every account carries a NAME** since 2026-09-26 — asked for at registration, capped at 80 characters, **CR and LF stripped rather than escaped** (the contact form's rule: the name goes into the subject of the approval request, and a newline in a header is how a subject becomes extra headers). The column is NULLABLE because four accounts existed before it did, and a not-null default would have invented a name for each; everything that displays a user falls back to the email, which is what it showed before. It earns its place at the approval gate — deciding whether to let `kenjkatz@gmail.com` in is easier when the subject line says who that is.

### Sign in with Google — built 2026-09-26
**Authorization-code flow over plain `fetch`, no dependency**, the reasoning Resend already follows. Google answers *who is this, the first time*; the callback then mints the **same 32-byte `sessions` row** every other sign-in uses, so `getSessionUser`, the 30-day expiry and revocation are all untouched. That is why it is small. Routes: `/api/auth/google/start`, `/api/auth/google/callback`, `/api/auth/google/pending`, `/api/auth/google/finish`, plus the public page `/join`.

- **OFF IS THE DEFAULT.** `GOOGLE_READY` needs `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` **and** `ADMIN_PASSWORD` (which keys the HMAC below). Without all three every route answers 404 and `/api/me` reports `googleReady: false`, which is what keeps the button off the login page — **a button that leads to a 404 is worse than no button.**
- **THE ADMIN ACCOUNT IS NOT REACHABLE THIS WAY** (the owner's constraint, recorded before the code existed). A Google signup is **always a member**, and on an instance with **zero accounts it is refused outright** rather than bootstrapping the first (admin) account. `ADMIN_PASSWORD` and the password form stay the only way in there.
- **THE INVITE CODE IS ENFORCED ON THIS PATH TOO, and that is the whole reason the flow has four routes rather than two.** `SIGNUP_CODE` is checked in exactly one place — inside `POST /api/register` — which a callback never touches, and `REQUIRE_APPROVAL=false` makes "lands pending" a no-op. Shipped as originally scoped this would have been **an unlocked side door past the gate the invite code exists to be**. The owner chose *ask after Google comes back*: a returning user never sees a code field, and a new person proves who they are first, then gets `/join`. Same tolerant compare as the register route (trim + case-fold), because it is read off a phone.
- **The carrier between "Google says this is jo@" and "jo typed the code" is an HMAC-SIGNED COOKIE.** Unsigned, anyone could hand the finish route an arbitrary verified-looking address and mint an account for it. Keyed on `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, the guest cookie's trick; 15 minutes, so password rotation invalidating one in flight costs nothing. There is a test that posts a forged payload and is refused.
- **THE `id_token` SIGNATURE IS DELIBERATELY NOT VERIFIED.** Google's own docs sanction skipping it: the token arrives in the body of a server-to-server exchange we initiated, over TLS, authenticated with our client secret — no untrusted party is in the path, so JWKS/`kid`/RS256 would buy nothing and add the only fiddly part. **The CLAIMS are all checked**: `aud`, `iss`, `exp`, `nonce`, and `email_verified`.
- **`email_verified` is the one check standing between this and account takeover.** Linking to an existing password account on an email match is safe *only* while Google asserts the address; without it anyone could claim any address and inherit the account under it.
- **Match on `sub`, never email** — `sub` is stable, the address under it is not. `linkGoogleSub` is guarded on `google_sub is null`, so a sub can never be moved off an account by a later sign-in.
- **`password_hash` and `salt` are NOT NULL and SQLite cannot relax that** without rebuilding the table, so a Google-only account gets a **random unusable password**. Not a placeholder: it means `verifyPassword` can never accidentally succeed, and a password attempt against such an account returns the **same generic 401** as an unknown address — "this account uses Google" is a leak, and there is a test asserting the two responses are byte-identical.
- **Exactly the scopes `openid email profile`.** Non-sensitive, so the consent screen needs no verification review and there is no 100-login cap. Anything else changes both and is not a small decision — the test asserts the scope string exactly rather than loosely.
- `/join` is **public by necessity** (the person has no session yet) and is not a door: it can do nothing without the signed cookie, and with none it says *Nothing to finish* — **not worded as an error**, because opening the address directly or leaving it a quarter of an hour is the normal way to arrive there.
- Failures redirect to `/login?gerr=<slug>`. **The slug is ours, never the provider's words** — an upstream error body can restate the request and the client secret travels in the same exchange.
- `listUsers()` names its columns and allowlists its output, so the new `google_sub` is **not** exposed by `/api/users` — worth knowing if an admin badge for "uses Google" is ever wanted.
- Verified: **45 checks** on the real routes with Google stubbed at `fetch`, **every claim bent one at a time** (forged state, wrong nonce, wrong `aud`, wrong `iss`, expired, unverified email, no email — each asserted to make no account), the empty-instance refusal, the invite code refused and then accepted phone-typed, the member role, a second sign-in going straight in, linking to an existing password account and its password still working, the no-enumeration pair, and the forged carrier. Plus **14** on the default-off state (every route 404, no button drawn, `/join` calm and scroll-free at 390px).
- **A browser cannot walk this flow by navigating to Google.** `pg.goto` to `accounts.google.com` leaves the page on a dead cross-origin error page and the callback then reads as `gerr=state`. Do the handshake in Node, take the `sp_gflow` cookie off the 302, and hand it to the context with `addCookies`.

**Google must never be the only way into the `admin` account** (the owner's constraint). The admin keeps a password, and the `ADMIN_PASSWORD` escape hatch stays. The remaining design notes are in [docs/backlog.md](docs/backlog.md) entry 11.

Accounts live in Turso (`users`, `sessions`). Passwords are hashed with **`crypto.scrypt`** and a per-user random salt — no dependency needed. Sessions are random 32-byte tokens in the `sessions` table with a 30-day expiry, so a single session can be revoked; they are *not* the old deterministic HMAC cookie, which cannot work for more than one user.

- **The first account created becomes `owner`**, so a fresh install bootstraps itself. Everyone after is a `member` — and since 2026-09-14 **every member registration starts `pending` and cannot sign in until the owner approves it** (`users.status`, backfilled `'active'` for everyone existing). Enforced three ways: registration creates **no session** for a pending account, login answers 403 "awaiting approval" (only AFTER the password verifies, so the endpoint still cannot enumerate accounts — a wrong password gets the generic 401), and `getSessionUser` refuses pending rows outright. The sign-up notice to the operator IS the approval request ("Approval needed: Name <email>", button to `/users`); the **welcome email moves to approval time**, when it is true. `/users` shows a pending badge, an Approve button (`POST /api/users/:id/approve`, idempotent) and an Awaiting-approval stat; Delete is how a request is declined. The login page tells a registrant they are waiting rather than bouncing them to a page that would refuse them; approval is logged to the activity log (`account` / `approved:<email>`). Guests are unaffected — the preview stays the try-before-you-register door.
- **`SIGNUP_CODE`** (optional env var) gates registration. Without it anyone who finds the URL can sign themselves up — set it before making the site public.
- **Approval can be switched off: `REQUIRE_APPROVAL=false` (2026-09-26, before the public launch).** A gate somebody has to click is a gate people wait behind, and one registrant had already sat pending for days. With it off a member is `active` immediately, gets a session, and `SIGNUP_CODE` becomes the only door. **It DEFAULTS TO ON, so a deploy can never be the thing that opens registration** — only setting the variable is.
  - **THE ONE COMBINATION THAT MUST NOT HAPPEN BY ACCIDENT is approval off AND no code**, which hands a working account to anyone who finds `/login`. It is allowed — it is the owner's instance — but **never silently**: the server warns at boot in as many words, because the way you get there is setting one env var and forgetting the other.
  - The owner is still emailed on a signup with approval off; the notice reads **"New account"** rather than "Approval needed" and says the person is already in. Knowing who joined is worth an email even when there is nothing to decide.
- **`/api/register` is throttled per IP per day** (`SIGNUP_PER_IP_DAY`, 5). It was unthrottled, so a script could mint accounts and fire one email at the owner for each — the *data* was safe, since pending accounts cannot sign in, but the inbox and the Resend quota were not. **Counted only after every validation passes**, so a malformed body cannot burn the quota (the chat's rule), and keyed on the IP rather than the address, because the address is the thing being made up. Reuses `chat_usage` under a `signup:` prefix, as the contact form does.
- **`POST /api/login` with a password but no email still checks `ADMIN_PASSWORD`.** That escape hatch is deliberate: a broken `users` table can't lock you out of your own instance. **Do not change the HMAC salt `'stock-tracker-admin-v1'`** in `adminToken()` or every legacy admin cookie dies.
- Login failures are counted on the user row (`failed_count`, `locked_until`) and lock the account for 15 minutes after 8 tries. Tracked per user, not per IP, because an in-memory counter is useless on serverless.
- Wrong password and unknown email return the **same** error, so the endpoint can't enumerate accounts.
- **Password reset is by email**, via `POST /api/forgot` → a link to `/reset?token=…` → `POST /api/reset`. `set-password.js` remains the local fallback for when mail is unavailable or an account is locked out of its own inbox; it prompts rather than taking the password as an argument, which would leak it into shell history. `--role owner|member` changes a role, refusing to demote the last owner.
  - **The token is never stored — only its SHA-256**, for the same reason sessions and passwords are hashed: a database read must not hand anyone a working reset link.
  - **Single use and 30 minutes.** Valid tokens are deleted as they are read, so a link cannot be replayed even while unexpired, and issuing a new one deletes any older link for that account.
  - **`/api/forgot` answers identically whether or not the address exists** — the login endpoint already refuses to confirm which emails have accounts, and this one would otherwise give it away. It also refuses to issue more than one token a minute per account, or it becomes a way to flood someone's inbox.
  - **The password length is checked before the token is consumed**, so a typo does not burn the link.
  - `setPassword()` already drops every session and clears the lockout counter, which is what a reset should do.
- A signed-in user can change their own password via `POST /api/password` (needs the current one). Both paths drop that user's sessions, so a change signs other devices out.
- **`/users` is list-and-delete only, never create.** Accounts come from sign-up (gated by `SIGNUP_CODE`); an admin-created account would need a password set for it, which means either mailing a secret or inventing one — `set-password.js` already covers the rare case properly.
- **`deleteUser()` purges `prefs` and `chat_usage` too.** Those are keyed on email, not user id, so without it a new account registered at the same address would inherit the deleted one's saved column layout and its chat quota for the day.
- **Two guards, both enforced server-side and mirrored in the UI as a disabled button:** **an `admin` account cannot be deleted AT ALL** (2026-09-26, owner's instruction — change the role to member first), and nobody can delete the account they are signed in as — that would revoke their own session mid-request. The first was "not the LAST owner", which with a single admin was the same rule **by arithmetic only**, and would have stopped protecting the account the moment a second admin existed; the test promotes a second admin and asserts the deletion is still refused, which is the case the old rule allowed. `listUsers()` also returns active session count, last sign-in and any lockout, which is what makes the page worth opening.

#### Disable — the reversible half of this page (2026-10-01, owner's request)
**`POST /api/users/:id/status` with `active` or `disabled`, driven by a Disable/Enable button on `/users`.** Until this, the only way to stop somebody signing in was Delete, which destroys the row, their themes, their views, their saved layout and their chat usage and **cannot be undone**. A disable takes nothing: Enable puts the person back exactly where they were.

- **THE WHOLE FEATURE IS THE LIVE SESSION, and anything that only blocks `/login` does nothing you could see for a MONTH.** A session lasts 30 days, so a disabled account stays signed in and keeps reading every page until the cookie expires. `setUserStatus` therefore **deletes that user's sessions**, the rule `setPassword` already follows — and it is what makes the maintenance page's *Signed in now* truthful the moment the button is pressed (measured: 3 → 2 on the fixture).
- **`getSessionUser` IS AN ALLOWLIST NOW, NOT A DENYLIST.** It read `u.status <> 'pending'`, which **admits any status nobody has thought about** — so on the day `disabled` was added, every disabled account's live session would have kept working and the feature would have looked inert. It is `u.status = 'active'`. A gate should refuse what it does not recognise, and there is a check that a status this code has never heard of is refused too.
  - **REVERTING THAT CHANGE FAILED NOTHING AT FIRST, which is the lesson rather than a footnote.** Session deletion already covers the disable path, so the two were two fixes for one problem and only the revert said which — the Spotlight card's trap, met again. The gate is now proved on its own terms: the suite sets the status **directly in the database, leaving the session row in place**, and asserts the cookie stops working. That is not a contrived scenario — the status column is the invariant, and anything that sets it without dropping sessions (a direct edit, a future route, a restore) leaves a live cookie on a non-active account.
- **THE SAME TWO GUARDS DELETE HAS — an admin, and the account you are signed in as.** The owner asked for these in two steps and the second one matters: first *"You can disable any user except me"*, which took the admin-role guard off, and then **"Don't disable the admin"** once the gap below was reported. So the rule is the TARGET'S ROLE, not who is asking, and `/users` greys both buttons on an admin row.
  - **THE SELF-GUARD WAS NOT ENOUGH, AND THE REASON IS THE ESCAPE HATCH.** A session minted by the legacy `ADMIN_PASSWORD` login has no user row, so `currentUser` is null and the self-guard **cannot fire** — anyone on that hatch could have switched the admin row off. (Recoverable, since the hatch still works, but not something to be one click from.) A role guard does not depend on knowing who is asking, which is exactly why it closes this.
  - **THE SELF-GUARD IS NOW UNREACHABLE, and it is KEPT deliberately rather than deleted.** Everyone who can call the route is an admin (`requireAdmin`) and every admin is refused by the role guard above; the only other caller is the hatch, where it could not fire anyway. **Its revert proof therefore fails 0, which is recorded in the harness's own case name rather than left to look like a guard that never mattered.** It stays by the `CHAT_DAILY_LIMIT_MEMBER` rule — *keep what one guard flips back on, delete what can never be* — and here one guard really would: the owner's first instruction was the opposite of their second, inside an hour, and if the role guard ever comes off again the self-guard is the only thing left.
  - **The way through is DEMOTION, two deliberate steps**, exactly as for delete — and that is asserted as working rather than left implied: a demoted admin can be switched off.
- **A `pending` registration is refused, and that is NOT a restriction on who.** It already has Approve and Delete, and Enable on it would be **a silent second Approve that skips the welcome email** approval exists to send — while Disable would destroy the pending state with no way back to it. **The route cannot reach `pending` at all**: the status is validated against a two-value literal, so it can never be used to un-approve somebody and make the welcome send twice.
- **The login refusal is checked AFTER the password verifies**, exactly like the pending gate and for the same reason: a wrong password still gets the generic 401, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out which addresses have accounts. There is a check that a wrong password on a disabled account is **byte-identical** to the answer an unknown address gets. Telling somebody who HAS proved the password costs nothing and saves them guessing at a broken sign-in.
- **The page: a badge, a dimmed row, and a count.** `switched off` is **neutral, never amber** — amber means *notice this, something is wrong or old* everywhere in this app and is already spent on the pending count, which genuinely wants a decision; an account the owner deliberately turned off wants nothing. **The row is dimmed as a whole**, which is the part that reads down a list of twenty where a badge has to be looked for. Confirmed **only on the way off** — switching somebody back on restores what they had and needs no second thought.
- The activity log records `disabled:<email>` / `enabled:<email>` — facts, never content, and only when the status actually changed.
- Verified: **43 checks** against the real server, plus **22** driving the real page. The member is **signed in first and the cookie kept**, because that cookie is the thing every other assertion would pass over; and the page suite **promotes a member to admin and reloads**, asserting the button greys out, because a page that does not mirror the server offers a click that 409s. **Proved by reverting seven times, six of which bite**: the denylist fails 2, sessions left in place 2, the login gate 2, the admin-role guard 3, the pending guard 3, the status enum 4, and `requireAdmin` 3 — the seventh being the unreachable self-guard above.
  - **TWO ASSERTIONS HAD TO BE CORRECTED RATHER THAN WORKED AROUND when the role guard came back**, and both were asserting the previous instruction: the page suite claimed the admin row's Disable was *live*, and the API suite claimed another admin *could* be switched off. A third was subtler and is the better lesson — the self-guard check demanded the words *"signed in as"* in the refusal, and with the role guard in front it is now the ROLE guard answering, so **it was asserting which guard replied rather than what happened**. It asserts the outcome (409, nothing changed, your own session intact) instead.
  - **The self-guard revert needed a shadow rather than an anchor.** `if (me && me.id === id) {` is word-for-word the delete route's own guard so it cannot be anchored directly, and a multi-line anchor is refused because **server.js is CRLF on disk**. The revert shadows `currentUser` for that route's body instead, which makes `me` null and the guard stop firing — the same trick the `isCron` revert uses.
  - **`login-busy-test.js` fails 1 and it is PRE-EXISTING**, confirmed by stashing.
- Password hashing (`hashPassword`, `newSalt`, `verifyPassword`) lives in **db.js**, beside the users table — `server.js` and `set-password.js` both import it so scrypt parameters can't drift apart.
- `isAdmin(req)` and `isSignedIn(req)` are **async** now — always `await` them. `requireAdmin` / `requireAuth` are middleware built on the `route()` wrapper.

## Email
**Every message goes through one shell.** `emailShell()` and `textShell()` in `server.js` wrap a dark header carrying the wordmark, a white card, and a footer with the tagline, the site link and a one-line note saying why this particular message arrived — the question a reader asks first about mail they did not expect. Four messages use it: the welcome, the password reset, the contact form and the refresh report.

- **Tables and inline styles, not the app's CSS.** Outlook renders through Word, most clients strip `<style>` blocks, and neither flexbox nor grid is available. The wordmark is text rather than an image, because images are blocked by default in most clients and a logo would leave a broken box exactly where the brand should be.
- **The palette is for a light background**, not lifted from the app. Mail clients invert or ignore dark themes unpredictably, and a screenshot-black email arrives unreadable somewhere.
- **`mailButton()` wraps the pill in a table cell** — Outlook ignores `border-radius` on an `<a>`, so the radius goes on the cell.
- **The From display name comes from `BRAND`, not from `MAIL_FROM`.** `fromHeader()` keeps only the address out of that variable, so renaming the product cannot leave a stale name sitting in everyone's inbox — which is exactly what happened when Ticker Lab became Tickr Lab.
- **A hidden preheader repeats the intro**, so the grey line clients print beside the subject is the real first sentence rather than whatever markup happens to come first.
- **The Instagram handle is `BRAND_IG` (`tickr_lab`), on the tagline's bargain** (2026-09-26): defined once in server.js for the mail shells, restated as text on the five static public pages because they cannot read a server constant, and **`tagline-test.js` names any page that drifts** — the day the handle changes, four footers would otherwise point at a profile that no longer exists. Stored **without the `@`**, so the one place a URL is built cannot get it into the path; the `@` is display and every surface adds it. **Always an absolute `https://` link, never a bare handle** — a mail client will not linkify `@tickr_lab` and the reader will not type it, and the **plain-text half is the one that gets forgotten**, where a bare handle is simply a dead string. Every public anchor carries `rel="me noopener"`: `me` is what lets the site and the profile verify each other.
- **THE WELCOME EMAIL IS OFF (2026-09-26, the owner's call while opening registration).** `SEND_WELCOME=true` turns it back on; the shell, the copy and the owner/member split are all kept, so this is a switch rather than a deletion. Every account created is one more message from a young sending domain that a corporate gateway is already quarantining, and a welcome is the least necessary mail here — the person is looking at the screener a second after reading it. **Gated INSIDE `sendWelcome` rather than at the two call sites**, so neither registration nor approval can start sending again by being edited. The approval request to the owner is a different decision and still goes.
  - **The copy stopped promising it in the same commit**: the login page said *"you will get a welcome email when you are in"* and `/help` said the same. A promise of mail that is no longer sent is the "every feature live" error wearing different clothes.
  - **Consequence worth knowing**: with approval ON, an approved member now gets no notification at all — they find out by trying to sign in. With approval off (the current setting) nobody is waiting, so it does not arise.
- **Registration sends two notes to two people**, both after the response and both with their rejections swallowed — the account and session already exist by then, so a slow or failing mail provider can never hold up or fail a sign-up. `sendWelcome()` greets the new member; `sendSignupNotice()` tells the operator, with `Reply-To` set to the new member so a welcome reply reaches them directly.
- **The sign-up notice is skipped for the very first account**, which becomes the owner — otherwise it is an email telling you that you have joined your own site. It is skipped again when the destination *is* the address that just registered. Both guards are verified. **Since 2026-09-14 it is the approval request** — subject "Approval needed", button to `/users` — and the welcome is sent by the approve route instead of the register route (the owner's own welcome still goes at registration).
- **`operatorEmail()` (`REPORT_TO`, else the owner account) resolves the destination for both the refresh report and the sign-up notice**, so the two cannot drift apart. `contactDestination()` stays separate because `CONTACT_TO` is a deliberately different inbox.

Sent through **Resend** over plain `fetch` — a REST call does not justify a fourth dependency. Needs `RESEND_API_KEY`, `MAIL_FROM` and `APP_URL`; without all three `MAIL_READY` is false and `/api/forgot` still returns its normal reply while logging that mail is unconfigured, so the endpoint never reveals the difference.

- **Sending is scoped to `mail.tickrlab.com`**, a subdomain, so a reputation problem cannot reach the domain the site is served from. SPF, DKIM and an `MX` for bounce feedback live under it; **DMARC sits at the root** (`_dmarc`), where one policy covers every subdomain.
- **DMARC is at `p=quarantine`** (checked against live DNS 2026-09-25; this line said `p=none` long after it had been tightened, so re-read the record rather than trusting it). `sp=` is unset, so subdomains inherit the policy, and alignment is relaxed by default — which is why a second sending subdomain needs no DMARC change.
- **The live records, so the next session does not have to dig them out**: SPF and the bounce MX sit on `send.mail.tickrlab.com` (`v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all`, `feedback-smtp.us-east-1.amazonses.com`), DKIM on `resend._domainkey.mail.tickrlab.com`, DMARC on `_dmarc.tickrlab.com`. `mail.tickrlab.com` itself carries neither SPF nor MX, which is Resend's current scheme and not a gap.
- **The Resend API key is restricted to SENDING.** `GET /domains` answers `401 restricted_api_key`, so domains cannot be listed or created through it — adding one is dashboard work by the owner, deliberately. Worth keeping: a leaked key cannot reshape the account.
- **`APP_URL` is `https://www.tickrlab.com`**, the canonical host — the bare domain 308s to it, and a link in an email should not depend on a redirect.
- **Nothing receives mail at the sending address.** Set `MAIL_REPLY_TO` to a real inbox, or add a forwarder (ImprovMX or Forward Email work with Vercel DNS; Cloudflare Email Routing does not, since it needs Cloudflare as the DNS host).
- Upstream errors are logged by type only, never echoed to the client — the response body can restate the request, and the key travels in the same headers.
- **`/contact` is signed-in only**, which is what makes it safe without a captcha or a honeypot: every sender is a known account and the address comes off the session rather than a form field. That is also why the address can be used as `Reply-To` — replying in a mail client answers the person, not the server.
- **The subject has CR and LF stripped, not escaped.** A newline in a header is how a subject line becomes extra headers; the body is the only place free text belongs. The subject is prefixed `[Tickr Lab]` and capped at 120 characters, the body at 4,000.
- **Destination is `CONTACT_TO`, falling back to the owner account's email**, so the form works even if the variable is never set.
- The daily cap reuses `chat_usage` under a `contact:` key prefix — that table is a generic per-key-per-day counter that happens to be named for its first caller.

### The email log — every message, recorded where they all pass (2026-09-25, owner's request)
**`/emails` (admin, an Email log row in the console's People & logs section) lists every message this app has handed to Resend.** It exists because the list's first real broadcast produced a question nothing here could answer: the confirmation reached the reader and the post did not, and the only record of either was a line in a Vercel log that had already rolled off.

- **WRITTEN AT THE CHOKE POINT, not at the call sites.** `sendMailResult` is the one function all eleven senders funnel through, so the log cannot lose whichever send somebody forgets to annotate — the only thing a caller supplies is `kind`. A log with holes in it is worse than no log, because it is read as if it were complete. The test asserts this **statically**: it parses every `sendMail`/`sendMailResult` call out of server.js and fails if one names no kind.
- **FACTS, NEVER CONTENT — the activity log's rule.** `mail_log` is `at, kind, to_addr, subject, ok, status, provider_id, error, bytes`, and there is deliberately **no column a body could go in**: bodies would be a liability to hold, enormous to store, and are not what the table is asked. The size is kept, because *accepted and two megabytes* is the shape of a deliverability problem. A test drives a marker string through a real send and then searches the whole table for it.
- **A FAILURE IS RECORDED, and that is the half that matters.** The naive version logs on success and turns the log into a record of what worked — hiding exactly the sends anyone opens this page to find. All four return paths write, the unconfigured one included, so "nothing is sending" is a page full of failed rows rather than a page that is empty for no stated reason.
- **The write is AWAITED, not fire-and-forget.** Nothing may run after the response on this platform, so a detached write is simply lost. It is one small insert against a send that already costs a network round trip, and a failure to log never fails the send — the bars rule, with a test that breaks `logMail` and checks the message still goes.
- **Two reads, deliberately.** The tail is capped at 500, so a total derived from it would quietly understate the moment there is more mail than the cap; the counts are a SQL `group by` over the whole window. The page says which is which.
- **"Accepted" is not "delivered", and the page says so rather than printing a tick that means more than it should.** The provider taking a message is the last thing this app can observe, which is why `provider_id` is on screen: it is what you quote to Resend.
- Kept `MAIL_LOG_KEEP_DAYS` (90), pruned beside `pruneRuns()`. `mail_log` is not in the query-plan test's big-table list — the tail seeks on `idx_mail_at` and the rollup is bounded by the same 90 days, the reasoning the activity and news rollups already use.
- **The outcome is the THIRD column, before the address.** It is what the page is opened for, and on a phone the first three are all that fit before the table has to be scrolled inside its own box. **An email address and a message id are single unbroken tokens**: breaking them to fit gave one character a line and a row 300px tall, so they are clipped with the whole value on the cell's `title`. Measured as DRAWN — the markup was right in both versions. **Proved by reverting**: `word-break: break-all` takes the row from 39px to 55px and fails two checks.
- Verified: **57 checks** (the static choke-point scan, the table's own columns, a real send end to end, three failure modes, a broken log still sending, the cap against the counts, the window, pruning, and the page — cards, the kind filter over a fixture with two kinds *inside* the tail, failures-only, the long-address row height, the phone) plus **18** on the roles (anon, guest and member refused the page AND the API, with the address checked absent from every refusal body) and **4** proving the scan catches both a removed kind and a newly added send that names none.

#### It earned its place the next morning, and overturned two diagnoses (2026-09-26)
**Reported as "I sent a simple text message to the Investcorp account but it did not get delivered."** The log answered it in one read: two messages six seconds apart, both accepted — `post-list` to `cmandal@investcorp.com` (id `01a0dd43-73bb-715c-b319-8854e5e0a28e`, 10.7 KB) and `post-test` to Gmail. Resend's dashboard then showed a **Delivered** event for the Investcorp one.

- **"DELIVERED" AND "NOT IN THE INBOX" ARE CONSISTENT — read this before diagnosing the next one.** Delivered means the receiving MTA answered 250; where the message is filed afterwards is a second decision by a different system, and Proofpoint, Mimecast and Defender all accept at the edge and quarantine internally. A gateway that distrusted the sender would have refused at SMTP or bounced, so a Delivered event **rules out SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain reputation** — every one of which was the leading hypothesis an hour earlier, including mine.
- **It also killed the standing explanation for the FIRST failure.** That one was put down to 2 MB of images and 84 words of typo-laden placeholder; this message was 10.7 KB of clean prose and was filed the same way. **Content weight was never the cause**, and the note above this one used to imply it was.
- **`bytes` is why that could be settled in one glance**, which is the argument for keeping it: "accepted, and two megabytes" and "accepted, and ten kilobytes" are different stories and the column tells them apart without opening anything.
- **The provider id is what made the second half possible**, exactly as the column was built for — except that the **API key is send-only**, so `GET /emails/<id>` answers `401 restricted_api_key` and the delivery status is dashboard-only. Worth knowing before reaching for the API: the id is for a human to paste, not for this app to resolve.
- Two real defects surfaced and were **deferred by the owner** (Gmail delivers; a tenant's quarantine policy is not fixable from here) — the unset postal address and `MAIL_FROM` being `no-reply@`. Both are in [docs/backlog.md](docs/backlog.md) entry 10 with what each would take.

## Feature flags in .env
- `ENABLE_FUNDAMENTALS=true` — requires Twelve Data Pro+ plan

## Visitor logging
- Every `GET /` inserts a row into the `visitors` table (fire-and-forget, so a logging failure can't block the page)
- Fields: `ts`, `ip`, `ua` (user-agent), `ref` (referrer)
- Admin-only endpoint: `GET /api/visitors` — returns summary + last 500 entries
- Admin-only page: `/visitors` — same visual system as the screener

## Alerts — five per account, one stock each, in-app only (2026-09-26)
**`/alerts` (members and admin, guests refused): watch one stock for one thing, and see it the next time you open the site.** Every scope decision was the owner's: a single stock per alert (never a portfolio or the universe), **no email anywhere in the feature**, `ALERTS_MAX` **5**, a fixed list of types rather than the filter grammar, evaluated every intraday slot and the nightly.

- **THEY CANNOT BE REAL-TIME, and the page says so in an amber panel.** Prices land on a schedule, so an alert fires when new data arrives — up to ~30 minutes late in session, next morning outside it. Streaming is ruled out by the 610-credit/minute ceiling. This is a *what changed on my watchlist* feature; a screen implying otherwise disappoints someone at the moment they most trusted it.
- **`private/alerts.js` is the type registry, defined once** — `require`d by server.js for the pass and `<script>`-loaded by the page, which **draws its form from `fields`**, so a type added there appears in the UI with no edit. Six types: price level, moving-average cross, advice verdict change, RSI level, 52-week extreme, big day.
- **THE FIXED DROPDOWN IS A UI DECISION AND DELIBERATELY NOT A DATA-LAYER ONE.** Every type reads through `Filters.filterValue(row, key)`, so "price above 150" and the screener's `>150` in the Price column ask the same function the same question. The owner chose the dropdown over the grammar; this is what stops that choice becoming a second implementation of comparison, which is the drift `rowcard.js`, `action.js`, `cards.js` and `filters.js` all exist to prevent.
- **Never "price target".** `/terms` says *"No price targets — a target is a forecast wearing a decimal point."* The type is a **price level**.

### The whole feature is the edge detector
`Alerts.evaluate(alert, row)` returns `{side, fire, body}` and is shared by the pass and its tests. Five rules, each one a trap this codebase has met elsewhere:

- **A LEVEL IS NOT AN EVENT.** "Price above 150" is true every round once true, so firing on the level notifies every thirty minutes for ever. `alerts.last_side` remembers the previous reading and only a TRANSITION fires. It is a column on the alert row rather than a state table only because one alert watches one symbol.
- **`from === null` is ARMING, not a crossing.** An alert created while its condition is already true records the side silently and the row reads *"Arming — it will report the next change."* Announcing a crossing that did not happen is a false statement.
- **A NULL IS NOT A ZERO.** `Number(null)` is 0 and finite, so a missing price would trip every "below $150" alert at once. A null side means NOT EVALUABLE: it fires nothing, is counted as `skipped`, and **does not overwrite the remembered side** — otherwise the next real reading looks like a transition out of nothing. The `num()` / credits-header / `activity.ms` lesson, and this is where it does the most damage.
- **A gap counts.** 140 → 160 overnight never touched 150. The test is the **sign of `value − threshold`**, never equality.
- **Pausing forgets the side.** A resumed alert missed whatever happened while it was off, so it arms silently again rather than firing on a transition it never saw.
- The **event row is written BEFORE the side moves**. A crash between the two repeats one notification, which beats losing the only record that the thing the reader asked about happened.

### Where it runs, and where it must not
**`GET /api/cron/alerts`, bearer-authenticated, called by `intraday-ping.js` AFTER a slot's FULL round** — the light rounds write bars without rebuilding the snapshot, so there is nothing new to evaluate until the last one. **Never in the refresh tail**: the news top-up (2026-09-18), `techHistorySpan` (2026-09-19) and `archiveStats` (2026-09-20) were all work added there and all three surfaced as "the refresh failed" over data that was fine. The ping treats a failure here as non-fatal and a 404 as "an older server", so deploy order does not matter.

- **The pass re-scores the snapshot** (`scoreActionInto` + `stampCapDerived`) so an alert can never disagree with the screener about a verdict.
- **Delivery is a badge, never an interstitial.** The unread count rides `GET /api/prefs`, which every page already awaits before its first render — a second round trip per page load is the six-reads-in-series lesson. "Shown as soon as someone logs in" is satisfied by a badge you can ignore.
- **Scoping is in the SQL**, not the route: `delete … where id = ? and user_key = ?`. An admin cannot reach another account's alert, and there is a test for exactly that.
- **Admin review, on the same page** (2026-09-26, owner's request): an *Everyone's alerts* section appears for an admin, listing every alert on the instance with its owner, whether it is arming / watching / paused, when it was set and **whether it has ever fired**, plus every firing. `/users` already does this for member portfolios — nothing an account creates should be invisible to the person running the site. A row is drawn from the page's own type registry, so it reads as a sentence rather than a params blob.
  - **READ-ONLY, and that is the point.** The admin can SEE an alert and cannot pause or delete it: the mutating routes stay scoped to the owner in SQL, and reaching past that would make "your alerts" untrue for everybody else. Separate endpoint (`GET /api/admin/alerts`, `requireAdmin`) rather than more fields on the member response — a member must never be one changed boolean away from everyone else's alerts. `GET /api/alerts` carries only an `admin` flag, which is what tells the page to ask.
  - **`/privacy` says so.** It now states that the person running the site can see the lists and alerts an account creates. That was always true of anyone with database access; it is written down because there is now a screen for it.
- `alerts` and `alert_events` are in `SYMBOL_TABLES`, so a dropped ticker takes its alerts with it. Events pruned at 90 days beside the other logs.
- **`/privacy` was updated in the same commit** — it lists every table and its retention, and is written to match the software.
- Verified: **34 checks** on the edge detector driven through the real route with the snapshot rewritten between passes (arming, the gap, staying true, re-crossing, the null, one-shot, pause/resume, the cap, and that `ACTIONS` really runs worst-first so an upgrade is not labelled a downgrade) plus **20** on the roles (anon, guest, the cron secret, and one member unable to see, silence or delete another's alert even as admin).

## The admin announcement — a banner for when something is wrong (2026-09-26, owner's request)
**A message the owner types on `/admin` and every reader sees on the screener.** Stored in `app_meta` under `announcement` beside `hidden_columns` and the rest, because it is a site setting rather than anyone's preference.

- **THE SCREENER ONLY, and that was the owner's choice against my recommendation.** Offered "everywhere including signed-out" (which reaches people who cannot get in, when sign-in is the broken thing) and "signed-in pages only"; the owner took the smallest build. **It therefore rides `GET /api/prefs`** — the call the screener already awaits before its first render, the same channel `siteHidden` and `tileConfig` use — so there is **no new endpoint on the read path and no new script tag**. Worth knowing if it is ever widened: only `index.html` reads prefs, so any other page needs its own fetch, and `wmark.js` is the established one-tag-per-page pattern for that.
- **A GUEST SEES IT TOO.** If the data is wrong it is wrong on the preview as well, and somebody deciding whether to sign up should not be the only person not told.
- **`at` IS THE VERSION, and it is the whole reason the stored shape is not a bare string.** Dismissal is per device in `localStorage`, keyed on that timestamp — so an × hides it, and **editing the message brings it back for everyone**, which is what makes a follow-up ("fixed now") reach exactly the people who dismissed the first one. The owner picked this over both never-dismissible and dismissed-forever.
- **Clearing stores `null`, never an empty string.** *Nothing to say* and *something to say, which is blank* must not be two states a reader can land in.
- **The level IS the colour, and the colours already mean these things here**: accent is a fact, amber is *notice this* (the Price pulled column, the Turso bar, the stale status pill), red is the loud cell. The console's level chips are painted in the colour they will produce, so the choice is previewed rather than described.
- **Every visibility change calls `paintWindow(true)`** — the news ticker's and the phone bar's rule. The page never scrolls, the table sizes itself from `.table-wrap`, and **no resize event fires when a sibling appears**; without it the last rows fall off the bottom. Measured: the wrap goes 681 → 752px when the banner is dismissed.
- **Written only by `PUT /api/announcement` (admin), deliberately not through the prefs PUT** — that endpoint rebuilds a per-user row from an allowlist, and a site-wide message has no business travelling with somebody's collapsed columns. The activity log records the LEVEL, never the text: facts, not content.
- **The editor is inline at the top of `/admin`, above every section** — this is what you reach for when something is wrong, and a link to another page is a click paid at the worst moment. It also means the console's first line tells you whether a banner is up right now, which the textarea alone could not (a draft and a live message look identical).
- Verified: **45 checks** — the store (whitespace collapsed so a pasted newline is not a layout bug, the cap, an unknown level falling back, clearing leaving nothing), member/guest/stranger all refused on both routes, a member AND a guest receiving it through prefs, the banner drawn at the right colour measured off the icon, **dismissal surviving a reload and then an edit bringing it back**, markup in the message rendered as text, the table reclaiming its height, and the console panel saving, reporting and clearing.
- **`esc` does not exist in `admin.html`** — the first cut of the panel called it and would have shipped a `ReferenceError`. The status line is built with `textContent` and `append` instead, rather than inventing a second escaper on a page that has none.

## Activity logging
**Who did what, fact-only — the `activity` table** (`ts`, `user`, `kind`, `detail`, `ip`), separate from `visitors` on purpose: that one is the anonymous front-door knock, this one is a known account doing a thing. Facts, never content — a chat row says `asked`, not the question. Viewed at **`/activity`** (admin only, linked from the bar and from `/visitors`), which shows per-user and per-kind rollups plus the filterable 500-row tail, and carries a **Clear log** button (`DELETE /api/activity`, confirm-with-count like the visitor one). Pruned to `ACTIVITY_KEEP_DAYS` (60) during every refresh, fire-and-forget.

- **Two halves.** Server routes call `logAct(req, kind, detail)` (fire-and-forget, never blocks the action): `page` (every gated page, symbol included), `login` (password / account / signup / guest), `chat` `asked`, `refresh` (plain / all / as-of — a Refresh All logs ONCE at its POST; its `?refresh=1` rounds are skipped via `opts.running`), `portfolio` CRUD, `model`, `contact`, `account` (logout / password-changed / reset). The client half is **`private/track.js`** (`window.track(kind, detail)`), loaded by the screener and the stock page for what the server never sees: `sort`, `tab`, `picker` (columns / weights / past / rules), `export` (the CSV is fully client-side), `panel` (ladder opens), `chart` (ranges, MA / RSI / Mom / Trend toggles, why-card).
- **The beacon batches** — events queue and flush as one `sendBeacon('/api/activity')` every ~20s, on a full queue and on `pagehide` — so a sorting session is one Turso write, not thirty. `POST /api/activity` (any signed-in user, guests included) allowlists the six client kinds (`CLIENT_ACT_KINDS`), clamps details to 80 printable chars and caps a batch at 50, so it cannot become free-form storage — the prefs-PUT rule.
- **Guests are the point.** The shared `st_guest` token cannot tell two guests apart, so the guest door also sets **`st_gid`** — a random id used ONLY as the log key (`guest-<id>`), kept if already present so a returning guest stays one trail. Deliberately noise-free: no `/api/status` polls, no sparkline/news fetches, no hovers, no refresh-all rounds, no cron.
- Verified on introduction with an admin walk + guest walk against a local boot: junk kinds dropped, oversize details clamped, guest 403 on GET/DELETE, anonymous 401, clear removed all rows.

### How long each operation took — `activity.ms` (2026-09-20)
**Every row can carry a duration, and `/activity` reports the spread per kind.** Asked for after a day spent finding slow paths blind; the summary is the half that earns its place, since a column of milliseconds down a 500-row tail is not something anyone reads.

- **WHOSE CLOCK depends on the kind, and there is deliberately no second column saying so.** The client kinds (`sort`, `tab`, `picker`, `panel`, `chart`, and the new `load`) are measured in the browser and are **what the person actually waited** — network and paint included. Every other kind is the server's own elapsed time, from a `req._t0` stamped by the first middleware. One rule read off the kind, in db.js and on the page, rather than a flag that can drift from it.
- **`page` is deliberately untimed, and the page says so.** Those rows are written at the TOP of their route, which then serves a static file, so the elapsed time is ~1ms every time: true, useless, and enough to drag the whole summary into nonsense. A page's real cost arrives separately as a browser-measured **`load`** row. `window.trackLoad(name)` reports it, and **the page decides when it is usable** — the screener calls it after its first render, not on `window.load`, which fires while `/api/stocks` is still in flight.
- **The duration rides on the EVENT, not the flush.** A beacon carries up to fifty events and the server stamps them all with ONE timestamp, so nothing downstream could ever recover how long a single interaction took. `track(kind, detail, ms)` is the only place that knows.
- **Reject the empty before coercing — the third time this codebase has needed that sentence.** `Number(null)` and `Number('')` are both `0` and finite, so the obvious ordering stores a fabricated `0ms` for every untimed event and puts a floor of zeros under every percentile, flattering it. Untimed is `null`; a *genuine* zero is kept and renders as `0ms`, distinct from the `—` of untimed. Browser input is clamped to `0…ACT_MS_MAX` (10 min) like any other untrusted field.
- **Exact sample percentiles in JS, not SQL**: one bounded read of `(kind, ms)` over a table already pruned to 60 days, the same reasoning the other `/activity` rollups use. **A p95 at n=5 lands on the fourth value** — that is what the statistic means, not a bug, which is why `n`, a `thin` marker and the slowest all sit beside it and the note says a p95 needs a few dozen observations.
- Verified: 33 checks against the real server and the real page — every coercion trap above, the cap and the clamp, an un-allowlisted kind refused, the rollup's median against a skewed sample where a mean would disagree, `page` untimed, and **the Took cells measured by `getBoundingClientRect()` rather than by their markup** (the `/quality` lesson: a style attribute can be perfect while nothing is drawn).
- **Two of the three failures in the first run were the test's own**: a p95 asserted against fixture noise from an earlier block, and a case-sensitive regex against headers that CSS upper-cases. The third was real — a lost backslash in a patch script left `a page's` terminating a JS string, which took the whole page down. **`node --check` on the extracted `<script>` block is how to catch that in an HTML file.**
- **It exposed one pre-existing layout bug**: `.island` is a single non-wrapping flex pill whose buttons already overran it by ~10px at 390px, invisible until the new panel made the page tall enough for a scrollbar to claim that width. The Clear log label takes `hide-sm` like its neighbours.
- **Unrelated and pre-existing, found while regressing this**: `views-test.js` and `screens-test.js` in the scratchpad both die with `window is not defined` — confirmed identical at HEAD with these changes reverted. `filter-test.js` was broken the same way and is fixed here: `visibleStocks` was split into `scopedStocks` / `prefilterStocks` / `activeColFilters` by the filter-row commit (2bc163a) and the harness was never told.

## Frontend layout
Everything above the table is **one bar**. There is no separate masthead, no tab rail, no chip row — they were merged to reclaim vertical space (the table used to start ~685px down; it now starts ~91px down).

```
.page (100dvh flex column, never scrolls)
├── header.bezel.bar          ← wordmark · portfolio picker · columns picker
│                               · add-ticker field · as-of field · status
│                               · Refresh · Export · ⋯ more menu
├── #readonlyNote / #fwdViewBar / .error    (flex: none, shown conditionally)
└── .table-bezel (flex: 1, min-height: 0)
    └── .table-wrap           ← the only scroll container on the page
```

- **The page itself does not scroll.** `body` is `height: 100dvh; overflow: hidden`; the table bezel is the flexible row and `.table-wrap` scrolls inside it. Never reintroduce a `max-height: calc(100dvh - Npx)` on the table — its height is derived from the flex column, so adding a notice steals from the table instead of pushing the page taller.
- **`.deck`** (add-ticker field, as-of field, status, Refresh) is `display: contents` on desktop, so its children join the bar's flex row directly. Below 768px it becomes a fixed full-screen glass sheet toggled by `#menuBtn` (a hamburger that morphs into an X, fixed to the top-right corner).
- **`.status`** uses `flex: 1 1 0` — a zero flex-basis makes it invisible to flex line-breaking, so it can never wrap a button onto a second line; it absorbs the slack instead. It's a **block** with `text-align: right`, not a flex row: a flex row justified to the end clips its *start* with no ellipsis.
- **The readout is a PILL, and the box is on a child (2026-09-26, owner: "the small green blink is hard to see sometimes").** It was 12px `--muted` text with a 6px pulsing dot, at the far right of a bar full of buttons. **The background cannot go on `.status` itself**: `flex: 1 1 0` means it is as wide as whatever the bar has left, so a background there paints a band across the slack rather than a pill round the words. `setStatus` builds a `<span class="pill">` inside it instead — inline-block, so the box is the size of the text, with its own `max-width: 100%` and ellipsis since the parent's cannot reach a child.
  - **STILL `textContent`, NEVER `innerHTML`.** Portfolio and theme names reach this function as free text (`added to "<name>".`), so an interpolated pill would turn the one status line into an injection point. The span is created and its `textContent` set; there is a test that drives a portfolio named `<img src=x onerror=…>` through it.
  - **AMBER IS SPENT, NOT DECORATIVE — which is why the badge is not permanently yellow.** In this app amber already means *notice this, it is old*: the Price pulled column past a day, the Turso usage bar past its threshold, the studio's freshness line past 26 hours, the alerts real-time panel. A badge that is always lit stops being read within a day and would leave nothing to say a reading is genuinely stale.
