Beside a debt or preferred word it is decisive; the three notes also carry `due <year>`.
- **TWO INDEPENDENT TESTS, and neither alone was enough.** The name scan graded by tell; the cross-check asked the orthogonal question — **which rows can the app not SCORE**, since `classify()` types a row ETF when it has neither Quality nor a P/E, which is a heuristic for *we hold no fundamentals for this thing*. They agreed on the three notes (typed ETF, `rev=0`, no Quality, all carrying an **Avoid verdict**). **BMNP was caught by the name test ALONE** — and that is the point of running both.
- **BMNP IS WORSE THAN A BLANK ROW, which is why the scorability test missed it.** It is typed **Early with Quality 9 and a Hold verdict** on the PARENT's fundamentals wrongly attached — the pattern the September pass recorded when 8 of the 29 carried a parent's market cap. A preferred scored as though it were a company is a wrong answer wearing a verdict, not an empty cell.
- **THE NEAR-MISS IS A NEW SHAPE: `BNS` — "Bank Nova Scotia Halifax Pfd 3".** The name says `Pfd`, and it is **Scotiabank's COMMON stock** — $25.2B revenue, $6.8B net income, ROE 11.5, P/E 13.9 forward / 17.2 trailing, Quality 8, 1.22B shares outstanding, $112.2B cap, NYSE, Banks – Diversified. September's near-misses were instruments whose names *legitimately* read like a preferred (ADRs, tracking stocks, an MLP's "Common Units"); **this one is simply a wrong name from the provider.** So the rule generalises: **a name is evidence and fundamentals are proof — a preferred series has no revenue, no ROE and no earnings.** Nothing but checking the numbers would have saved it.
- **Spared and named in the script so a later reader sees the decision**: BNS, AZN (ADS on common) and ET (an MLP common unit is real equity).
  - **`SKF` was raised separately and the owner removed it the same day** ("I removed SKF"). It was **not** a non-equity — a genuine ProShares leveraged inverse ETF, so a fund, and funds are kept here on purpose — which is exactly why it was reported rather than swept up with the four. The objection to it was never its instrument type but that **a −2x inverse fund in a stock screener draws an all-technical verdict off a rulebook written for companies**. Universe 1,188 → 1,187, purged clean: no bars, no profile, no name, no theme held it, nothing stranded.
  - **The rule this keeps: report the judgement call, remove only what the instruction covers.** "Remove the non equities" did not cover a fund, and deleting one on my own reading of the phrase would have destroyed something the owner had deliberately added.
- **Nothing was stranded**: none of the four sat in a theme, so no theme lost a member, and `fundamentals_history` — the one thing a purge destroys irrecoverably — held only the parent's figures wrongly attached, which is worth nothing for a note.
- Verified against the DATABASE rather than the route's 200: **0 bars, no profile and no name** for all four; BNS/AZN/ET intact with 4,434–5,008 bars each (SKF was intact here too and went separately, above); universe table 1,188; **no theme member outside the universe**; Sector Benchmark still 11. The route's own reply prints as `[object Object]` through my logging — cosmetic, and the reason the check is the data.

### Site-wide hidden columns (the owner's floor)
**`/columns` (admin, its own page, linked from the console's Screener section) hides columns for EVERYONE (2026-09-15).** It was a panel on `/admin` for an hour; the owner moved it out rather than grow that page — the console stays a door. The page carries search, a per-group tick with an n/total count, Show all, **Undo changes** (back to what the server last confirmed) and a Save that is disabled until something differs. 85 columns is more than most accounts want as a default, and a view is a per-person choice; this is the floor under all of them.

- The console's **Scoring** section became **Screener** (what the table shows, and how it scores) and carries the row that opens it.
- **The catalogue is parsed out of `private/index.html`'s own header row** by `columnCatalogue()` in server.js (cached per instance): id from `data-col` / `data-fkey` / `data-key`, group and group label from the banner, label from the cell's text with `<br>` and entities resolved. **78 columns** — Symbol, Name and the four forward-returns columns are excluded (the anchors, and the as-of view's own). Restating the list anywhere else would drift the first time a column was added; adding a column needs no edit here.
- **Stored in `app_meta` under `hidden_columns`** as a JSON id array (`readHiddenColumns` / `writeHiddenColumns`) — a site setting, so deliberately not in `prefs`. `GET`/`PUT /api/columns` are admin; the PUT keeps only ids the catalogue knows, so it cannot rot or become free storage.
- **Delivered to every page in `GET /api/prefs`** as `siteHidden`, which the screener already awaits before its first render — a second request would paint the full table and then visibly drop columns. Guests get it too.
- **Enforced in `applyView()` for Standard, views AND screens**: the `#viewStyle` nth-child rules are now built from `siteShows(c.id) && (!view || view.columns.includes(c.id))`, so a view or a screen cannot bring back what the site hid. Banners span what is actually shown; `hideCollapsedCells()` hides a group with nothing left. The view EDITOR does not offer a hidden column — listing one would look like the tick did nothing.
- Nothing is deleted: the data keeps being recorded, and unticking restores the column. An open screener tab keeps the old set until it reloads, which the admin note says.
- Verified end to end against the real server and pages in headless Chrome (20 checks — catalogue size and labels, unknown ids dropped, malformed PUT refused, `siteHidden` on prefs, the admin list/count/search/group tick, the column gone from header and body, a fully hidden group losing its banner, the neighbouring banner's span, a view unable to show a hidden column, the editor not offering one), plus the 42-check column suite re-run to prove the nothing-hidden case is unchanged.

### Tiles — the same rows, drawn as cards
**A Table / Tiles toggle beside View (2026-09-16).** A short selection — a portfolio, a screen, a filter — leaves two-thirds of the screen empty as a table; the owner asked for a nicer shape for exactly that case (the Mag 7 view, 7 rows). **One selection, two shapes**: `render()` builds the same `sorted` rows and then either `paintWindow()` or `paintTiles()`, so the sort, the portfolio, the sector/industry/advice/advice-move pickers, the screens and every column filter apply identically. `body.tiling` hides the table bezel and shows `#tileWrap`.

- **A tile shows**: symbol, display name, price and today's move, the 90-day sparkline (the SAME `sparkCache` markup the table's column uses — not a second drawing), the Balanced verdict with its fired rule and the trend word, four returns (1W / 1M / 1Y / 5Y) and chips for Overall / Mom / Qual and the sector. Nothing is re-derived: every value comes off the row the table would have drawn.
- **The whole tile is one link** to `/stock/<SYMBOL>` in a new tab, so tabbing moves tile to tile and Enter opens — no mouse-only targets.
- **A return of 100% or more drops its decimal** (`+850%`, not `+849.7%`), and **the name line is omitted when the display name has collapsed to the ticker**, which would otherwise print the symbol twice.
- **Tile setup is one SITE-WIDE setting, admin-only** (2026-09-16, owner's call — the tiles are what gets shared on social media, so "a member choosing their own would make the same screenshot mean different things"). `Tile setup` appears beside the toggle for the owner in tiles mode and opens a dialog: the **chart period** (none / 1M / 3M / 90d / 6M / 1Y), five toggles (verdict, the rule that fired, trend state, score chips, sector chip) and **up to 6 detail fields** (8 at first; six reads as a tile, eight reads as a table cell). Stored in `app_meta` under `tile_config` (`readTileConfig` / `writeTileConfig`), delivered to every page in `GET /api/prefs` beside `siteHidden` so the first render has it, cached a minute server-side.
- **The dialog IS the view editor's** — same grouped, searchable, three-column field list with the group colours and the count beside the search box, at the same 640px. The `.vd-*` styles were scoped to `#viewDialog`; they are shared now, **with a `dialog.modal` prefix on the label rules** because `dialog.modal label` (small caps, block) is more specific than a bare class and was winning — the first attempt rendered every field name as an uppercase caption above a floating checkbox. Both dialogs were screenshotted to check.
- **The fields are rowcard's own** — `RowCard.fieldCatalogue()` and `fieldValues()`, added for this, list FIELD_SPEC as `group|label` keys and return one row's values under the same keys. So a tile field is formatted exactly as the hover card formats it, and adding a field to FIELD_SPEC offers it here with no further edit. The server shape-checks the key (`TILE_FIELD_RE`) against the known groups and caps the list; the browser ignores a key it no longer knows.
- **Two escaping traps, both caught by tests.** `TILE_FIELD_RE` was built with `new RegExp(\`...\${groups}\|...\`)`, and inside a template literal `\|` collapses to a bare pipe — the pattern became "one of the groups, OR anything at all" and stored a field key of `evil|drop table`. It is a literal now. And the dialog **repainted its whole list on every tick**, which dropped the checkbox under the cursor and most of a bulk change; it updates the count in place instead, disabling the unticked boxes at the cap.
- **The tile's chart is drawn for the tile, at a chosen height** — Short 44px / Medium 72 / Tall 110, beside the period in the setup. `sparkSVG(closes, {w, h, pad, area})` takes a size now: **the viewBox height IS the pixel height**, so a tall chart is a taller drawing rather than the table's 32-unit box stretched, which thickens the stroke unevenly under `preserveAspectRatio="none"`. `opts.area` closes the path to the floor for a soft fill, and the tile's line is **coloured by its own period's move** — green up, red down — where the table's column stays deliberately neutral: a tile is a picture of one stock and the line is the biggest thing on it.
- **The tile's chart is fetched separately whenever it is not 90 days** (`tileSparkCache`), since the table's 90d column owns that cache. **`/api/sparklines` is now cached server-side per (days, guest) for 10 minutes** — a year of closes is ~68,000 bar rows and every signed-in page load was asking for its own copy.
- **A `Per row` control sits beside the toggle** (2026-09-16, shown only in tiles): Auto, or a fixed 2-6. Auto is `auto-fill minmax(290px, 1fr)`; a fixed count is `repeat(N, minmax(0, 1fr))` — a width floor there would wrap the row at the first long name instead of honouring the count. **Below 1100px the window decides regardless**, so six across on a monitor is not six across on a laptop. Saved as `prefs.tileCols`.
- **Capped at 60 with a More button**: a tile is markup and 271 of them is not free. The windowed table's own budget is untouched.
- **Saved per account** (`prefs.layout`, `'tiles'` only — table is the default and stores nothing), so it opens the way it was left; the PUT whitelist takes the one value.
- Verified in a browser over a 7-stock portfolio: 16 checks — the toggle, table hidden / tiles shown and back, one tile per row, the fields on a tile, the new-tab link, the 100% rounding, the name-line rule, tiles following the table's sort, the preference saved and re-read on the next load, the empty state, no console errors. The column-structure and changed-chip suites were re-run unchanged.

### The stock card — one renderer, two surfaces
**`RowCard.stockCard()` draws the card the screener's Tiles view shows and the card the phone page shows (2026-09-16).** The owner asked for "each stock tile to look like these", holding up the Apple Stocks and Google Finance cards, and chose one renderer for both rather than a second implementation: the quote on top, a chart with real gridlines and price labels, then a small grid of whichever fields the owner picked.

- **The contract is already-formatted data**, not a snapshot row: `{symbol, name, price, change, up, fields:[{k,t,c}], closes, from, to, rangeLabel, verdict, chips}`. The desktop hands it `RowCard.fieldValues()` output, the server hands it what `mobileRow()` already built — so the function knows how to lay a card out and nothing else, and it renders identically in Node and the browser. Styles are `.sc-*` in **app.css**, for the same reason the markup is in one function.
- **Gridlines come from `chartSVG(closes, {ticks, area})`**, not a third chart implementation. Two things were added to it: `area`, a tint drawn as its OWN path (never a `fill` on `.ln`, which closes the line back to its start and paints a wedge), and **`tick.drawn`** — it already skipped a gridline outside the price band but still returned the tick, so a caller labelling every tick hung a price beside nothing. On a card that label landed on top of the header; `stock.html` had the same latent bug and now filters the same way.
- **Price labels are HTML in a 36px gutter**, positioned by each tick's viewBox fraction. HTML because `preserveAspectRatio="none"` would distort SVG text; a gutter because a label over the plot has the line running under it.
- **The x axis is the window the chart actually drew** — that symbol's own first and last session, not a shared calendar. Symbols do not share one (Samsung misses US sessions, a recent listing starts late), so one date axis for everybody would mislabel some of them. `readCloseSeries()` returns the dates the query was already selecting and discarding; `sparkSeries()` trims to the range and takes the two ends **after** the trim, or a 3-month card would be labelled with the date its wider query happened to reach back to. The rest of the date list is dropped server-side — only the two ends are ever shown.
- **The middle of that axis carries the move over the window**, named ("3 months +22.5%"), because the header's change is today's and two unlabelled percentages on one card is a trap.
- **`CARD_RANGES` is 1W/1M/3M/6M/1Y and lives in server.js**, delivered to every page on `/api/prefs` and to the phone on `/api/m/config`, so neither surface restates it. **No 1D**: the archive is daily bars, so a single session is a single point. **No 2Y**: a year is 253 sessions ≈ 68k rows a fetch, and Turso meters rows read.
- **One range control for the whole view, not one per card** (owner's call): every chart on screen then covers the same window, which is what makes a grid of them comparable and what makes it one fetch instead of one per card. On the screener it is a `Range` select beside `Per row`; on the phone a strip under the title, shown only where there are charts to change. Both remember the choice in `localStorage`. **The admin's Tile setup period is still the default**, snapped to the nearest offered window, and `spark: 0` there still means no chart at all — so "no chart" stays a setting rather than a sixth range.
- **The tiles cache the DATA now, not the markup** (`{closes, from, to}` per symbol): the card draws its own chart, so one series serves it whatever it does with it.
- Verified: 30 checks over the card and the ranges inside the mobile suite — the quote, the gridlines, labels clear of the plot and none reading "88.0", the axis naming its own dates and its own move, the fields grid, the thinning, the compressed cost, a shorter range redrawing every card with a first date inside the window, an unknown range falling back; on the screener, a tile being the same card, still one link to the stock, chips intact, the control appearing only in Tiles and moving every tile together, the table still aligned after; plus the stock page's axis (one label per gridline, all inside the chart).

### Column views
**Named column sets per account, switched from the `View` menu (the former Columns button), 2026-09-15.** The column half of what personal portfolios are for rows. **Standard** is the full grouped table and keeps the group toggles; a view shows Symbol, Name and exactly its own columns, **in the table's existing order (v1 — the owner chose this over drag-to-reorder)**.

- **Storage: `column_views`** (`id`, `scope`, `name`, `position`, `columns` JSON). `scope` is `'shared'` for **starter views** — seen by every account, edited only by the owner, shown with a lock to everyone else, with a `+` to copy one into your own — or the account key (email, else `'admin'`) for personal ones, up to `VIEWS_MAX` 10. Own table, not prefs, for the user_portfolios reason; `deleteUser()` purges them. The active view is `prefs.activeView` (`standard` or an 8-char id), validated against the loaded views on boot.
- **Starter views are seeded once**, on the first `GET /api/views`, guarded by an `app_meta` marker (`views_seeded`) so one the owner deletes does not come back. Three: Trend & returns, Fundamentals, Advice — each leads with Market cap, so the default sort is never hidden in them.
- **Routes**: `GET /api/views` (any signed-in; guests get shared only), `PUT /api/views/mine` (member), `PUT /api/views/shared` (admin). Whole-collection replace, rebuilt by `cleanViews()`: names trimmed, unique case-insensitively, columns deduped and **shape-checked only** (`VIEW_COL_RE`) — the server does not know the screener's column list, and the page ignores ids it does not recognise, so adding a column needs no server edit. An id that would shadow a shared view's is reissued.
- **Column ids** come from the row-2 headers: `data-col` (the 90d chart: `spark90`), else `data-fkey` (Portfolios), else `data-key`. `buildViewCols()` reads them once; forward returns are excluded (they follow the as-of mode, not a view).
- **Hiding is CSS, not per-cell work**: `applyView()` writes `nth-child` rules into `#viewStyle` for the header (index + 1), the body (index + 3 — Symbol and Name come first; `.padrow` and `.errrow` excluded, since those rows span) and the filter row (index + 3, built in body order). So the windowed repaint and the filter row need nothing new. Group banners get `colSpan` = the view's columns in that group; a group with none is hidden through `hideCollapsedCells()`, which in a view ignores the saved collapse state (except forward returns).
- **`filterHidden()` treats a column outside the view as hidden** (the dashed chip); **`#sortNote`** says "Sorted by X — not in this view" when the sort column is hidden.
- **The editor** is `#viewDialog`: name, search, every column under its group with a group tick, a count; it starts from what is on screen. Saves adopt the server's cleaned answer and switch to the saved view.
- Verified: headlessly as member (48 checks), owner (48) and guest (32) against a stub — exact columns shown, header-over-cell alignment for every column, banners spanning exactly the visible columns, filter row aligned, deep scroll, sort note, hidden-filter chip, create / validate / edit / copy / delete, owner editing a starter view, Standard's group collapse unchanged; the real server locally — seeding, guest 403s on both PUTs, anon 401, `cleanViews` on junk (bad id, duplicate and unsafe columns, duplicate/empty names, empty column list, shadowing id), and the owner's list restored after.

### The filter row
**A filter box under every column, behind the `Filter` button in the bar (2026-09-15)** — built for a 1,000-symbol universe, and only possible because rendering is windowed (see `paintWindow`): a keystroke re-sorts and repaints ~40 rows, not 1,000.

- **Built once from the header, not hand-written.** `buildFilterRow()` walks row 1: a `rowspan` cell is one column, a group banner stands for the row-2 cells carrying its `grp-<id>` class (by class, not `colspan`, because `applyAdviceCols()` rewrites the Advice banner's span). **Every filter cell copies its header's classes**, which is the whole trick: `hideCollapsedCells()`, the `body.hide-av-*` rules and the frozen `.frz` offsets treat it like any other cell in that column with no new code. A header cell with no `data-key` gets an empty filter cell; Portfolios opts in with `data-fkey`. Adding a column therefore needs nothing here unless it wants a non-numeric filter.
- **A third sticky header row**, `top: calc(--h1 + --h2)`; `updateStickyOffsets()` measures both. `size=1` and `min-width: 0` on the inputs are load-bearing — measured, the table width does not move by a pixel when the row opens.
- **Filters read what the cell SHOWS** (`filterValue()`): the 1-10 rating rather than the score behind it, days to earnings rather than a date, the MA cross as its word, name as short + legal, portfolios as shared + personal. Kind comes from the key: `TEXT_KEYS`, `CAT_KEYS` + `av:*` (dropdowns ordered by the ActionRules ladders, with counts over the tab), `BOUND_KEYS` (sector/industry — **they write `sectorFilter`/`industryFilter`, the bar pickers' own state**, so the two can never disagree and they are not counted as column filters), everything else numeric.
- **Grammar**: bare number = at least; `> >= < <= = !=`; `a..b`, `..b`, `a..`; K/M/B/T; `%`, `$`, commas ignored; `=` matches at the precision typed (`=61` finds 61.2). **Blanks never match a number filter in either direction.** Text: contains · `=exact` · `!not` · `a|b`. Input that does not parse is marked red and **ignored rather than emptying the table**.
- **AND across columns. Filters are not saved** — a filter surviving a reload is a table missing rows for no visible reason — but **whether the row is open is** (`prefs.filterRow`, boolean-only in the PUT whitelist). `/analysis` now hands back the whole prefs row it read; it used to drop `advices`, a pre-existing instance of the hand-back rule.
- **A filter on a column that is then hidden keeps applying**, and `#fltBar` (chips with ×, `N of M rows`, Clear filters, and Show filter row when it is closed) marks it dashed "hidden column". The bar is redrawn from `applyAdviceCols()`, which every render and every column toggle reaches — the first cut drew it from `render()` only, and collapsing a group left it stale.
- **A filter change scrolls to the top**, and `paintWindow()` clamps its first row so a list that got shorter can never open on the blank spacer.
- Verified by a headless harness on the real page (400 synthetic rows): 58 filter cells aligned to 58 body cells by group, grammar units, counts against independent filters over the payload, AND, hidden-column persistence, bound sector, Escape, empty state, deep-scroll-then-narrow, clear, sort still working, prefs PUT carrying `filterRow`.

### Turso meters ROWS READ — the anchor query was the lesson
**Turso sent a 75%-of-quota warning hours after the archive was deepened to 1.08M rows (2026-09-15).** The cause was `closesBefore()`, which the new 5Y column calls **on every refresh round**: it joined against `select symbol, max(d) from bars where d < ? group by symbol`, and at a five-year boundary that reads **748,859 rows** — about 35 times a day across the nightly rounds and the intraday runs, so tens of millions of rows a day for 254 numbers. Rewritten to seek per symbol on the `(symbol, d)` primary key, batched and chunked at 250: **254 rows and 80ms, against 748,859 rows and 231ms**. Same answers, verified against the old query.

**Two more of the same shape were found and fixed in the same hour**, both on the refresh path, both reading the whole bars table every round: `barsMaxDates()` (`select symbol, max(d), count(*) ... group by symbol` — 1.08M rows, 133ms; now one `order by d desc limit 1` seek per symbol, 271 rows, 57ms, and the `count` it also returned was never read by anything) and `barsOn()` for the split probe (`where d in (...)`, which the `(symbol, d)` primary key cannot seek on a date alone — 1.08M rows, 261ms; now one seek per (symbol, date) pair, 271 rows, 62ms). **A refresh round went from ~2.2M rows read to ~800.**

**Being over quota SLOWS the database, it does not only bill for it.** The same evening a plain refresh went 15s → 143s → 187s with identical API usage (272 credits, no profiles), and came back to **25-39s** once the plan was upgraded and the scans were gone. So an unexplained, uniform slowdown on every database call is worth checking against the Turso usage page before it is debugged as a code problem.

**`phaseTimer()` exists because that was invisible.** Every round now logs and returns `phases` on the payload — `profiles 0.1s · prices 3.0s · score 0.5s · trend-bars 5.4s · persist-bars 2.4s` — since Vercel's log view does not show a function's stdout. **`trend-bars` is the one to watch**: it is `readBarsFor(universe, 650 days)`, 118,671 rows at 271 symbols and ~440k at 1,000.

**The usage itself is on `/database` now** — a tile above the tables showing rows read, rows written and storage for the billing period, from **Turso's own platform API** (`GET /api/turso-usage`, admin, cached an hour, `?fresh=1` to force). It has to come from Turso: the client reports rows RETURNED, and for a scan that is a tiny fraction of what is billed. Needs `TURSO_API_TOKEN` (a platform token from Settings → API Tokens, **not** the database auth token) and `TURSO_ORG`; the optional `TURSO_ROWS_READ_LIMIT`, `TURSO_ROWS_WRITTEN_LIMIT` and `TURSO_STORAGE_LIMIT_GB` draw the percentage bars, since the API does not report the plan's allowance. Unconfigured, the tile explains what to set. **The daily watchdog cron checks it too** and mails once the worst of the three passes `TURSO_ALERT_AT` (0.7) — the same pass that watches for a missed nightly run, because both are "only worth hearing about when wrong". A Turso outage never breaks the page or the watchdog. Verified with the platform call stubbed: 11 checks (numbers, limits, the hour cache, `fresh=1`, a 500 handled, the watchdog still answering, the tile's text, GB formatting, the amber bar past the threshold, the bar's width, no page errors).

**`query-plan-test.js` now enforces the rule** (2026-09-15): it lifts `SCHEMA` + `ADDED_COLUMNS` out of db.js into an in-memory `node:sqlite`, pulls every SQL literal out of the same file, runs `explain query plan` on each, and fails if anything plans as `SCAN` over a big table (`bars`, `fundamentals_history`, `earnings_history`, `news`, `activity`, `visitors`, `snapshot`). **No network, no data, under a second** — run it after touching db.js. Deliberate scans live in `ALLOWED` with the reason written beside them (the `/database` counts, whole-collection reads of small tables, the two log tails — which say SCAN but walk the primary key backwards to a LIMIT — and the pruned `activity` / `news` rollups). Proved to work by re-introducing the offending `group by` and watching it fail.

**It found three things on its first run.** Two queries got an index — `news (published_at)` for the ticker's 12-hour read and `fundamentals_history (d)` for the report's day-pair lookup — and, more seriously, **the `news` and `news_state` tables had no `create table` in the schema at all**: a scoring cleanup (`ca2efed`) deleted them, production already had them so nothing broke, and a fresh database would have failed every news write. Restored verbatim from the live `sqlite_master`. **The test also enforces statement ORDER**, since an index that precedes its table throws at boot.

**The rule this leaves: on this database, a `group by` over a whole table is a quota event, not a slow query.** Prefer N indexed seeks — they are cheaper in rows AND in time. Measured read sizes to budget against (271 symbols, 1.08M bars):

| path | rows read | when |
|---|---|---|
| a refresh round's 650-day window (`readBarsFullFor`) | **118,671** | every round — the dominant cost |
| sparklines (`readCloses`, ~90 sessions) | 25,914 | every screener load, after the table paints |
| the 5Y anchor, before / after | 748,859 → **254** | every round |
| `/database`'s counts | 1.08M+ | that page only, cached 5 min; `?fresh=1` always counts |

At 1,000 symbols the 650-day window becomes ~440k rows a round, which is what to design against next (a shorter window for intraday rounds, or fewer intraday runs).

### The Price pulled column
**When each stock's price was last fetched, per symbol, first in the Short-term group (2026-09-17, owner's request).** It exists because the day the batched price call started failing made the question urgent, and because the snapshot's single `updatedAt` cannot answer it.

- **It is a per-SYMBOL clock, and that is the whole point.** `price_state` (`symbol`, `pulled_at`) is written with exactly the symbols a live pull actually served — `Object.keys(liveSeries)`, not the ones we asked for, so a chunk that failed cannot claim to have been priced. Same table shape as `news_state`, same reason: a fetch clock belongs beside the data it describes, not inside it. In `SYMBOL_TABLES`, so a dropped ticker takes it along.
- **Why per-symbol rather than the refresh time.** Price rounds are **paced**: past ~529 stocks a round prices only the slice that fits inside the minute and reads the rest from the archive, so "when was this priced" genuinely differs row to row. A Fill missing run prices nothing at all. Today, at 271, most rows share a timestamp — the column earns its keep as the universe grows.
- **"We asked" and "something came back" are different facts, and the column is deliberately only the first.** Measured on 2026-09-17: ten stocks were pulled on time and were not on the day's bar, **AVB carrying a close from 24 August**. So the tooltip names the newest bar beside the pull time and says so in as many words; read the two together. A column that conflated them would have hidden exactly the staleness it was asked for.
- **The refresh response is stamped where the clock is WRITTEN, not on the read path.** `/api/stocks?refresh=1` returns the computed payload directly and never reaches the snapshot stamp, so the first cut left the column blank for the one person who had just clicked Refresh and populated for everyone else — caught by fetching the refresh's own response rather than a later read, which is the only way to see it.
- **Stamped on the way out** (`stampPricedAt`, beside `stampShortNames` and `stampAdviceAge`, at all three read paths) so a snapshot written before the column existed still carries it, and the value is current rather than frozen at whenever the snapshot was built.
- **The cell shows the time alone when the pull was today** — the common case and the narrow one — and gains the date as soon as that stops being true, **amber past a day**. `—` means no pull recorded rather than a fabricated time. `.warn` is colour-only (`span.warn` scoping, the Cushion incident), so an amber cell is still a table cell; there is a test for exactly that.
- **The FILTER reads an age, not a timestamp.** A raw epoch value is nothing anyone can type against, so `filterValue` returns **hours since the pull** — the treatment `nextEarningsDate` already gets — and `>24` means "not refreshed for a day". Hours rather than days because most pulls are hours old and day resolution would put the whole table in one bucket. The filter strip says so.
- Row width is 90 cells (`PAD_SPAN`), the error row spans 85, the empty row 87, and the Short-term banner spans 6. **The banner still reads "Short-term %" though one of its six columns is not a percentage** — left alone deliberately, since renaming it means mirroring `GROUP_LABELS` in two files for a cosmetic gain.
- **Nothing else needed editing**: `/columns` parses the header row, so the column is hideable site-wide on its own; column views key on ids; the filter row is built from the header; and `RowCard.FIELD_SPEC` gained one entry, which is what puts it in the hover card, the tiles and the phone at once.
- Verified: 28 checks in a browser over fresh / two-day-old / never-pulled stocks (the store round-trip and that a second pull MOVES the row rather than adding one, placement immediately before Today and first in its group, **90 headers against 90 body cells**, every banner spanning its own columns, the three cell states with their tooltips, amber still being a table cell, sort putting the most recent first and the never-pulled last, the filter's hint / parse / `>24` / clear) plus 6 more in the refresh suite (a real refresh writing the clock for every symbol it served, the benchmark absent from it, a later refresh moving it forward, and the served row carrying `pricedAt`).

### The 5Y column
**Long-term gained a 5Y column after 1Y (2026-09-15, shown to everyone).** It is the one return column that does NOT come from the refresh window: a refresh fetches ~300 bars and an archive round reads 650 days, so `pctChange(values, 1260)` would be null for every stock. Instead `computeStocks` takes **one `closesBefore()` query for the whole universe** — the last close before today minus five years, the same anchor mechanism the promo studio's week/month windows use — and divides today's price by it. An anchor more than **30 days** earlier than the boundary is refused, so a hole in the bars cannot quietly stretch the window; a stock with no bar that far back stays blank. A failed query logs and leaves the column empty, the bars rule.

**It is blank for most of the universe until the archive is deepened**: measured 2026-09-15, **82 of 271 symbols have five years of bars** (the 2021 deep backfill covered the universe as it was then), 182 have one to two years — those arrived through refreshes, which keep ~300 bars. `backfill-bars.js --commit --depth 1300` fills the rest at **1 credit a symbol**; the cost is rows written to Turso, not credits.

### YTD — the one return a bar COUNT cannot express (2026-10-01, owner's request)
**A `YTD` column in the Long-term group between 6M and 1Y, and the same row in `FIELD_SPEC`, so it reaches the hover card, the stock page, the tiles, the phone and `/compare` at once.** The owner's words: *"in screener and everywhere else we should add a new column for Year to date (YTD) between 6M and 1Y"*.

**EVERY OTHER RETURN HERE IS AN OFFSET, AND THAT IS WHY THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT.** `pctChange(values, daysAgo)` counts bars back, and a count of sessions is not a calendar boundary on any date but one — two stocks with the same close on 31 December and the same close today have the same YTD however many times they traded in between, and an offset read gives them different numbers. So it is an **anchored** read: the last close before 1 January, through the `closesBefore` mechanism the 5Y column already uses, which is N indexed seeks on the `(symbol, d)` primary key rather than a `group by` over the whole table.

- **BOTH ANCHORS COME BACK IN ONE CALL.** `closesBefore([fiveBound, ytdBound], symbols)` already takes a list of boundaries, so the 5Y anchor was not duplicated and YTD costs **one extra seek per symbol** on a path that was already making one. Turso meters rows read; at 1,181 symbols that is ~1,181 single-row reads, not a second scan.
- **THE GRACE PERIODS DIFFER, deliberately: 30 days for 5Y and 10 for YTD.** A hole five years back is ordinary and that window is approximate anyway; the last close before 1 January is **31 December or the trading day before it**, so anything older means the stock stopped trading in December and calling that "year to date" would be wrong by weeks. Probed at **10 days (accepted) and 11 (refused)** — a threshold is a step function and every bug lives on its edge.
- **A STOCK THAT LISTED THIS YEAR IS BLANK, NEVER ZERO.** There is nothing to measure from, and `0.0%` would read as *it is flat this year* about a company that did not exist in January. The blank-versus-zero rule this file keeps meeting.
- **`MIN_CLOSE` guards BOTH ends**, through one shared `anchored(a, px)` helper rather than the arithmetic written twice. A sub-cent reading at either end is a bad bar: SOLS printed **+56,129,902%** on a live page off exactly this shape, and the revert proof reproduces it in miniature (`+50,504,950%` with the floor removed).
- **`price` IS PASSED INTO the helper rather than read from scope.** It is a per-row variable inside the `.map()` and the helper lives outside it, so reaching for it resolves to nothing — the `payload` / `secData` / `baseStocks` trap, caught during the edit this time.
- **THE BOUNDARY IS THE LOCAL YEAR, not `toISOString`'s.** On 1 January the two disagree west of Greenwich and UTC would ask for *last* year's boundary — the card-dating lesson. It cannot be told behaviourally on any other day, so it is asserted **statically**, the treatment `PAD_SPAN` already gets, and the revert says so.
- **Blank in the as-of view**, like 5Y: "this year" there would mean the as-of date's year, which is not the question the header asks.
- **The cell takes `cacheTitle`, not `liveTitle`** — it is an archive anchor like the 5Y beside it, not a window over the freshly-pulled series, so the live timestamp would make it claim a freshness it does not have.
- **Deliberately NOT added, each with a reason**: `techrow.js` (`back(n)` is a bar offset, it feeds `tech_history`'s 891k rows and the eighteen-year replays, and no rule reads YTD — adding it would mean a rebuild for nothing); `basket.html`'s `RANGE_FIELD` (it maps chart range BUTTONS, which are bar windows); and `STARTER_VIEWS` / the starter screens, which are seeded once behind an `app_meta` marker and so would reach only a fresh database — YTD is available there through the view editor.
  - **`cards.js`'s `CHART_WINDOWS` was on that list and is not any more (2026-10-02)** — see **…and on the Chart card, as a date-anchored slice** below. The reasoning held (a bar count cannot express a calendar boundary); what changed is that the card now slices the date axis instead of counting bars. **Two of the three claims in the sentence above were also wrong**: it said "all four are asserted" and only `techrow.js` and `RANGE_FIELD` ever were.
- **`/api/stocks` serves the cached snapshot, so the column is blank until the next FULL round rebuilds it** — about half an hour. Judge a new row field after a refresh, never immediately after the deploy; the `instrumentType` entry records the same arithmetic.
- Constants after the change: the Long-term banner **5**, `PAD_SPAN` **99**, the error row **94**, the empty row **96**. `/columns`, column views and the filter row needed nothing — they parse the header.
- Verified: **45 checks**. The fixture's load-bearing half is a **dense/sparse PAIR** — same anchor, same price today, 196 sessions this year against 28 — which a calendar read must answer identically and an offset read cannot; the suite also computes what an offset read WOULD give (+6.6% against +56.3%) so the equality is a property of the code rather than of a flat fixture. **Proved by reverting eleven times**, every one load-bearing: the offset read fails 7, the floor 2, the grace 1, the local year 1 (the static check, as recorded), the banner at 4 fails 2, **the header moved with the body cell left behind fails 9** — including both value cells reading `+11.0%`, the 1Y number sliding one column left — `PAD_SPAN` 1, the error row 1, the empty row 1, `liveTitle` 1, and the `FIELD_SPEC` row 3.
  - **`regroup-test.js` carried a literal `=== 98` for the row width** and went stale the moment a column was added. **Corrected, not worked around**: it is derived from the header plus its three anchor cells now, which is strictly stronger and cannot date — the same rot `reported-test.js`'s `=== 19` had.
  - **A test fault worth keeping: the provider stub's own `/stocks` branch matched `http://localhost:3999/api/stocks`**, so the route under test answered with the stub's `"stubbed off"` body and every refresh assertion failed over a server that was working perfectly. Pass our own origin through FIRST — and by literal, not by the `B` const, which is declared after `uni-boot` and would be in its temporal dead zone.

### % from record — how far below its own best close a stock sits (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**A `% from record` column last in the Relative group, and a `New record closes` section in the nightly refresh email.** Asked as *"How best to show stocks that hit all time highs"*, answered with a measurement, then *"Add column and include in nightly email"*.

#### IT IS NOT "ALL-TIME", AND THAT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN CAUTION
**718 of the 1,282 archives begin in 2006** — the provider's 5,000-bar ceiling, not a listing date — so for most of the universe "all-time" would be a claim about a window that merely happens to be where our data starts. Every surface therefore says **record close**, the cell's tooltip names the window (*"highest since 2006-11-08, where this archive begins"*), and the email says it too. There is a check that the word *all-time* appears on neither the column nor the mail.

- **A CLOSE, NEVER AN INTRADAY HIGH.** Measured on the live archive: on closes, 5 stocks sat at a record that session; on intraday highs, **0** — a high set years ago in a spike nobody could have sold into is not a level the screener should rank against. It is also the number every other column here is computed from, so the two cannot disagree.
- **The first full reading**: median **−30.6%** below its own record, p10 −72.8, p90 −7.7; **43 stocks within 2% of a record and 345 more than 50% below**; 23 records set on the day it shipped. (Measured across a session, the median is ~32 new records a session.)

#### A RUNNING MAX ONLY EVER GOES UP, WHICH DECIDES THE WHOLE DESIGN
`price_extremes` (symbol, ath_close, ath_d, first_d, through_d) is one row per symbol, maintained incrementally by `noteRecordCloses` beside `noteTechMark` on the Refresh-all gate. Everything awkward about it follows from that one property: a max cannot be corrected downward by a later close, so anything wrong that gets in stays for ever.

- **A PROVISIONAL BAR MUST NOT BE FOLDED.** Twelve Data serves a bar for today whose close is the current price, and bars self-heal through the overlap re-upsert — **a stored max does not.** So the fold tests `settled`: the session is before today in New York, or the bell has gone. Before it, nothing is folded and `through` does not advance. **Proved by reverting**: forcing the flag off fails 21.
  - **The gate alone was not enough, which is why the test is `settled` and not the gate.** Refresh all is run after the close, but **Fill missing is run by hand mid-session** and rides the same gate — so my own comment claiming today is never stored was false about my own code. Asserted against the clock either way, so it proves the guard is consulted without depending on the hour the suite runs.
- **A MISSED SESSION IS LOST FOR EVER WITHOUT THE GAP REPAIR.** A nightly that does not run leaves a stretch nothing has folded, and no later close recovers a high inside it — the page would quietly understate the drawdown with nothing to show it. Each symbol carries `through`, and the fold asks `maxCloseBetween` for the highest close strictly between `through` and the session being folded. Self-pacing, so it heals after any number of missed nights — `noteTechMark`'s rule. **Proved by reverting**: fails 5.
- **THE FIRST FOLD MUST ANNOUNCE NOTHING.** There is no stored record to beat, so without a guard the first nightly after this shipped would have mailed **1,282 new records**. `isNew` requires a stored record above the floor. **Proved by reverting**: fails 25.
- **A symbol with no usable bars is left ALONE, never written zero** — the `backfill-instrument-type` rule: a stored zero reads as *checked, and it has no high*, where absent correctly reads as *not known yet*. 20 symbols, all with no bars at all.
- **`MIN_CLOSE` guards both ends**, the same floor `pctChange` takes. A sub-cent close is a bad bar, and SOLS printed **+56,129,902%** on a live page off exactly that shape.

#### TODAY IS COMPARED LIVE, SO THE SCREEN IS RIGHT BETWEEN FOLDS
`stampAthDistance` takes `Math.max(stored, price)`, so a stock closing above its record **reads as a record the moment the price arrives** rather than waiting for the night. That is the whole reason the stored table may lag: mid-session, and on any instance whose nightly has not run, the record is behind the price.

- **A NULL IS NOT A ZERO, and on this column that is the worst failure available** — `0.0%` MEANS *at a record*, so a symbol with no stored record would claim one. Blank, with a tooltip saying why. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- **The window start is READ, never guessed.** `firstDate` comes from the archive (`firstBarDates` for a symbol no fold has seen); defaulting it to today would have every record claiming a window that began this morning. **Proved by reverting**: fails 2.
- **It is the fifth READ-PATH STAMP, and they are a SET.** `stampShortNames`, `stampAdviceAge`, `stampPricedAt`, `stampCapDerived` and now this, across four read paths. *(SIX since 2026-10-03 — `stampSpMember` joined them. The set is the thing to keep in step: a new read path applies all of them or it has a blank column nobody notices, which is how `pricedAt` and `adviceDays` were missing from `/stock` for weeks.)* **Adding one broke every row on the page**: both callers of `serveStamps` destructure its array **positionally**, so a fourth stamp shifted `pf` and `membershipOf` got the refresh flag — `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object`, a 500 on every row. The existing comment there guarded against a *missing* stamp and not against the array's LENGTH. `serveStamps` returns ONE `Promise.all` now, so a stamp can be added without re-counting at two call sites.

#### The nightly's records section
Between the movers and the fundamentals, capped at `REPORT_RECORD_CAP` (25), **biggest company first** — a record at a $3T company is a different event from one at a $300M shell, and sorting by price would have ranked by share price, which means nothing across companies. `records: null` means *not computed* and `[]` means *none*, which the section words differently: **"None — no stock closed above its own record"** is a fact about the session and is worth printing.

- **Computed in `finishLiveRefresh` where the fold happens**, so the mail reports what was actually stored rather than re-deriving it.
- Verified: **39 checks** against the real server on an in-memory database, over a fixture of four stocks that separate every mechanism — one climbing to a genuine record, one printing an intraday spike **four times its own close**, one that peaked long ago, and one whose archive starts late. Plus a session **no fold ever saw**, a session dated today asserted against the New York clock either way, and a stored record **lowered below the live price** to exercise the live comparison at any hour. **Proved by reverting eight times**, every one load-bearing.
  - **TWO OF THOSE REVERTS FIRST REPORTED 0 FAILED, and both were the test rather than residue.** The live comparison's own check ran **after the close**, by which time the fold had already stored today — so the stored record EQUALLED the price, `Math.max` was a no-op on every row, and the assertion passed with the comparison removed. It now lowers a stored record directly, which is every mid-session moment made reproducible. And the null-default revert was written as a guard that let a missing record reach `e.athClose`, which **threw** — swallowed by the stamp's own catch, leaving the null the line above had already set. **A revert has to simulate the bug, not an impossible state.**
  - **A REVERT THAT ABORTS THE SUITE REPORTS A HANDFUL OF FAILURES INSTEAD OF TWENTY.** Two of them left the table empty and the fixture dereferenced `ex.RISE.athClose` in a detail string, so 16 of 39 checks ran and a load-bearing guard read as a marginal one. Every stored-record read goes through one safe accessor now: missing is a legitimate state here and must fail a check, not end the run.
  - **A `\n` IN A PATCH ANCHOR MATCHES NOTHING AND THE PATCH IS SILENTLY SKIPPED.** `server.js`, `index.html` and `db.js` were CRLF on disk this session, so three python patch scripts reported success and changed nothing — the lesson written into this file the same morning, met the same afternoon. Detect per file, at the moment the harness runs.

#### `backfill-ath.js` — the one-off load, and it reads no bulk data
The column is blank for everyone until this runs. **Two indexed seeks per symbol on the `(symbol, d)` primary key** — 2,604 single-row reads, the `closesBefore` shape — never `max(close) group by symbol`, which is 4.58M rows and the scan that caused the 75%-of-quota warning. Measured against production: **1,282 of 1,302 symbols in 8.1 seconds**, read back and counted matching.

- **It applies the fold's OWN `settled` test** rather than a rule of its own, so the two cannot disagree about what a finished session is. Before the bell the boundary steps back a calendar day: `through` landing *earlier* than the true last session only makes the nightly re-scan a day, which is an idempotent upsert, where claiming a session was folded when it was not loses a record for ever.
- **`store.barsThrough` ALREADY REDUCES to the newest date across the symbols — it is a string, not a per-symbol map.** The first cut spread it with `Object.values` and reduced the characters, which picked the largest DIGIT (`'6'`) and threw `Invalid time value` one line later. *A field's shape is something to read, not to guess at* — the same mistake that once reported `0 pts` on three benchmark series.
- **Worth reporting separately: `MDI.TO` is in the universe** — a Toronto listing, which the standing US-listed-only rule refuses. It has no bars at all, which is consistent with the provider refusing it, so it is one more permanently unfillable gap of the `BBX` / `PXD` / `BF` kind. Not acted on; removing a ticker is the owner's call.


#### The `At a record high` screen (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**A starter screen in Market movers, beside Recent 52-week highs: `pctFromAth >= 0`, sorted by market cap.** Live on the day it shipped: **23 of 1,282**.

- **THE OWNER ASKED FOR "All time high" AND CHOSE "At a record high" when the measurement was put to them.** The column refuses that word for a reason — 718 of the 1,282 archives begin in 2006 at the provider's ceiling — and a screen is the most prominent surface the claim could sit on, so the name in the menu would have outrun the data behind it. **A screen name is a claim**, and this is the one place the overclaim would have been read first and checked last.
- **`>= 0` IS EXACTLY THE RECORD-SETTERS, with no epsilon to get wrong.** `pctFromAth` is `px / max(stored, px)`, so a stock at OR above its record reads a true `0` and everything else reads negative — the comparison is exact rather than tolerant. The owner took this over a 2% band (43 rows) knowing the cost.
- **IT CAN BE EMPTY, AND THE DESCRIPTION SAYS SO.** Measured: 23 the day it shipped, ~32 a session typically, and **a sharp week takes it to nothing**. That is the failure the `/analysis` thresholds were tuned to avoid — *a screen returning 0 names is a dead box* — so the cost is paid in copy instead: *"Empty on a falling week, which is the answer rather than a fault."* The screener's own empty state then reads *"Nothing matches the column filters"*, which is honest rather than broken.
- **SORTED BY MARKET CAP, NOT BY THE FILTER COLUMN.** Every row reads `+0.0%` from its record **by construction**, so sorting on `pctFromAth` orders 23 identical values and hands the reader an arbitrary order dressed as a ranking. **Proved by reverting**: it comes back `ABOVE,EQUAL` against the market-cap order's `EQUAL,ABOVE` on the fixture.
- **A SCREEN'S COLUMN LIST IS A SET, NOT AN ORDER, and I wrote that down wrongly first.** The note here claimed the filter column "leads the columns, because it is the screen's claim made visible" — true of the `def.columns` array and **false on screen**: a screen shows its columns in the TABLE's own order (v1, the owner's choice over drag-to-reorder), so `% from record` draws LAST, after Market cap and Advice. Measured on the live page: 6 columns drawn, `marketCap | av:Balanced | todayPct | oneMonthPct | oneYearPct | pctFromAth`. What matters is that the evidence column is INCLUDED, which it is.
  - **The probe that nearly hid this read `textContent` off the first row's cells and reported the FULL table.** Hiding is CSS (`#viewStyle` nth-child rules), so every `td` still exists in the DOM and reads back its text whether drawn or not — the `/quality` lesson in a new place. **Ask `getBoundingClientRect().width > 0`**, never presence.
- **A NEW STARTER SCREEN NEVER REACHES AN EXISTING DATABASE** — `seedScreensOnce` is marker-guarded so a screen the owner deletes does not come back. Inserted with the existing `add-starter-screens.js`, which needed no edit: it diffs defined against stored and appends what is missing. **Targeted INSERT, never the PUT endpoint and never `writeScreens`** — both rebuild the list through `cleanScreens()`, and a filter reading `>=0` would be walking into the 2026-09-15 door that stripped `<` and `>` out of thirteen screens. Measured: 29 defined, 28 stored, 1 inserted, read back through `readScreens()` with the definition matching.
- Verified: **21 checks**. The fixture's load-bearing property is that **`pctFromAth` is never written into it** — it is stamped by the read path from `price_extremes`, as production does it, so a screen that could not see the column at all would fail rather than pass over a hand-written field. Six stocks separate every case: above its record, exactly at it, 0.4% below (**out — near is not at**), far below, no stored record (out, and never as a 0), and at a record but sub-cent (out on `MIN_CLOSE`). Plus the menu's live count, the applied table, and **the empty week driven by lifting every stored record above today's price**. **Proved by reverting three times**: the 2% band fails 5, the all-time name 8, the filter-column sort 3.
  - **A VACUOUS ASSERTION CAUGHT BY ITS OWN FIRST RUN.** "Biggest company first" read `syms[0] === 'EQUAL'` and **passed while the screen was not being applied at all** — the table's default sort is market cap too, so EQUAL led either way. It is guarded on the row COUNT now.
  - **`screenRows(def, rows)` takes the DEFINITION first**, read off `filters.js` rather than guessed at; the other order throws on `.filter` and says nothing about the screen.
  - The screener's Screens trigger is **`#scrBtn`** (inside `#scrPicker`, menu `#scrMenu`). A guessed `#scrTrigger` clicks nothing, the menu never opens, and the row reads as *absent* — which looks like a missing screen rather than a wrong selector.

### Period — what the fundamentals actually describe, on the screener (2026-10-04, owner's request)

**A `Period` column in the Fundamentals group between Payout and Reported: the trailing-twelve-month END every figure in that group covers.** Asked as *"I don't think we show the last reported period for financials, can you bring that from API and show it"* — and the screener really did not: `Reported` is the ANNOUNCEMENT, and **its own tooltip has said so since the day it shipped** (*"It is NOT the period they cover"*). This is the half that sentence was pointing at.

#### NOTHING WAS BROUGHT FROM THE API — IT WAS ALREADY THERE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK
`most_recent_quarter` rides on the `/statistics` call already charged at 50 credits, `fetchProfile` has stored it since 2026-09-30, and **`computeStocks` already named it on the row** for `/stock`'s caption. So the request cost **no credit, no endpoint, no backfill and no rotation wait** — it is display only. *Before costing a field, grep for it: this one was two lines from being drawn.*

- **Measured rather than assumed: 1,254 of 1,278 rows (98.1%) already carry it**, the rotation having filled it over the four days since it was stored. The 24 blanks are **every one an ETF**, which files no statements — so the group's existing NA rule covers them with no new code.

#### IT IS A DIFFERENT FACT FROM `Reported`, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS WHAT PROVES IT
A second date column beside an existing one has to earn its width. Over the 1,250 rows carrying both: the announcement lands a **median 30 days after the period** (p10 22, p90 43) and **the two are NEVER the same day — zero rows of 1,250**. The figures belong to the earlier date and were spoken about on the later one.

- **The fixture is built on that property**: every stock's period differs from its own announcement, and there is a check that no row anywhere has the two columns equal. A fixture where they coincided would pass with the cell wired to `lastEarningsDate` and prove nothing. **Proved by reverting**: the body cell left behind fails 10, the header never added 18.
- **Placed BETWEEN Payout and Reported**, so the three date columns read left to right as the events happen: the quarter ends → the company announces → the 8-K reaches EDGAR.

#### NO COLOUR, AND THAT IS A MEASUREMENT THAT REVERSED MY OWN FIRST READING
I set out to amber a stale period and had a draft justification for it — *6 of the 15 rows with a period over 150 days are invisible to the Reported column's own amber*. **That was computed at the wrong threshold and does not survive looking at the distribution.** These dates are month ends, so the ages are discrete: **35, 66, 97, 127, 158, 188 — and then nothing at all until 278.** The only defensible line sits in that 90-day empty run, and at it:

| | |
|---|---|
| rows with a period ≥ 200 days old | **8 of 1,278** |
| of those NOT already ambered by `Reported` | **1** (FIG) |

**A third staleness colour on a column adjacent to two that already carry one, to flag a single row, is noise.** The 188-day group I had counted as stale is mostly **semi-annual filers** (VOD, HDB and other ADRs) reporting exactly as they should — the `SEC_BEHIND_DAYS` lesson, where a threshold set below the empty bucket flags normal behaviour. The cell states the fact and the column beside it does the warning: the `instrumentType` rule.

- **Proved by reverting**: colouring it by age fails 3, including a check that reads the DRAWN colour rather than the class name. There is also a check that `Reported` **still** ambers a stale announcement, or the warning would have been lost rather than deliberately placed.

#### The rest
- **The fiscal year end is named in the tooltip ONLY when it is not December** — measured, **291 of 1,254**. For everyone else it says nothing; for those 291 it is the one clause that changes how every other figure in the group should be read. **Proved by reverting**: printing it unconditionally fails 1.
- **Days since, never the date string.** `filterValue` converts, exactly as `lastEarningsDate` does and through the same local-noon parse, because an ISO string is nothing a reader can type a comparison against. **Proved by reverting**: fails 2.
- **Local noon.** `new Date('2026-06-29')` is UTC midnight, so west of Greenwich every age here comes out a day high — and here that is **behavioural rather than static**, because the tooltip prints the count: the revert reads *98 days ago* against a true 97. The card-dating lesson, in a place a test can see it.
- **One `FIELD_SPEC` row carries it to the hover card, the tiles, the phone and `/compare`** — and it **LEADS the `fund` group**, ahead of `Reported`, which serves that group's existing intent better: a reader should see what period the figures cover before seeing when they were announced.
- **`/stock` SKIPPED the row until 2026-10-04, when the owner asked for it back** — see **PEG leads the P/E columns** below. The reasoning here was that the caption already opens *"Trailing twelve months to 29 Jun 2026"* off the same field, so the row printed a byte-identical string a screen lower. It is drawn now, and the caption keeps its clause deliberately: it is the only place that says these figures are a trailing **twelve months**, which `Period: Jun 29` alone does not.
- **THE BOUNDARY NEEDED NO CHECK, which is worth saying rather than leaving implied.** `mostRecentQuarter` was already on the row before this change, so adding a *column* cannot reach the Advice engine; there is no new field for a rule to read. The three-way scoring proof the `instrumentType` and S&P columns needed does not apply.
- Constants after the change: the Fundamentals banner **21**, `PAD_SPAN` **103**, the error row **98**, the empty row **100**. `/columns` picked the column up on its own, **95 → 96**, as designed.

- Verified: **41 checks** over a fixture of five stocks that separate every case — the modal 97-day period, a 188-day semi-annual filer, an 827-day one (DRQ's real age, carrying its year), a company with no period, and a fund. **Proved by reverting twelve times, every one load-bearing**: the header 18, the body cell 10, PAD_SPAN 3, amber 3, the banner 2, the filter 2, the FIELD_SPEC row 2, and the error row, the empty row, the fiscal clause, the UTC parse and the `/stock` skip 1 each.
  - **TWO SORT CHECKS WERE VACUOUS AND THE FIXTURE'S OWN COMMENT CLAIMED OTHERWISE.** It said symbol order disagreed with period order; it did not — `ANOR BSEM COLD` was both the alphabet and the period order, so a sort that never ran passed both. The stocks are `ZNOR BSEM ACOL` now and the market caps are a **third** order again, so neither the alphabet nor the table's own default sort can stand in for the period, and there is a check that the drawn order is neither of them.
  - **THE THREE STATIC SPANS ARE DERIVED, NOT WRITTEN DOWN.** None is on screen in a five-row fixture, so no behavioural check reaches them; they are read off the source and compared against the DRAWN header (`PAD_SPAN === headers + 3`, the two short rows 5 and 3 below it), which cannot date the way `PAD_SPAN` once sat at 51 with nothing noticing.
  - **AN ABORTED REVERT REPORTED 14 FAILURES WHERE THERE ARE 18.** With the header reverted away every period cell is null, and `P(s).title.slice(...)` — in a check's **detail argument**, not its condition — threw and ended the run at 25 of 41. The accessor is total now (`Object.assign({}, BLANK, …)`) and the sort click is guarded. *A read in the detail argument aborts a suite just as surely as one in the assertion.*
  - **`reported-test.js` asserted the OLD arrangement twice and was CORRECTED, not worked around**: *"it sits immediately after payout"* (Period is between them now) and *"it leads the Fundamentals group"* (Period does). Both behaviours it describes are still right, so each now pins **both** neighbours, which is strictly stronger than what it had.
  - **Two test faults worth keeping.** A fund legitimately reads `NA` in **both** date columns — it files no statements — so the never-equal check had to exempt it rather than report a defect. And the `/stock` caption is `.rc-cap`, read off `buildSections`; a speculative `p, div, span` sweep matched the page's own cards and reported the caption missing on a page that was correct.
  - **`sitecols-test.js` fails 4 and it is PRE-EXISTING** — confirmed by stashing: 95 at HEAD against its hardcoded 83, 96 after. That the catalogue grew by exactly one is itself the evidence `/columns` registered the column with no edit.
  - **A `git stash` / `pop` rewrote all four touched files from LF to CRLF mid-session**, the documented hazard met again. Git stores LF either way, so the diff is unaffected — but a patch harness carrying a hardcoded ending would have gone silently inert from that moment.

### PEG leads the P/E columns, and the three dates reach `/stock` (2026-10-04, owner's request)

**Two asks in one message: *"Move PEG ratio before forward P/E that way all the P/E ratios will be together"*, and *"make sure Period, Reported and Announced (SEC) fields are present on the individual stock page"*.** The first is a column move; the second turned out to be the interesting one.

#### Moving a column WITHIN a group is free, and the check is header-over-cell
The Fundamentals group ran `Fwd P/E · PEG · Trail P/E · Live P/E`, so the one ratio that is not a P/E sat in the middle of the three that are. It is `PEG · Fwd P/E · Trail P/E · Live P/E` now.

- **No span moved** — the banner stays at 21, `PAD_SPAN` at 103, the error row at 98 and the empty row at 100. A move is not an addition, and all four are asserted anyway, because a static span is the thing that goes stale when nobody is watching.
- **THE LOAD-BEARING CHECK IS THE BODY CELL, NOT THE HEADER.** A header moved without its body cell does not throw and leaves no gap — it slides every later value one column over and the table still looks perfectly well formed. So the fixture gives **every Fundamentals column a value nothing else on the row holds**, and each check reads the cell under a named header and demands that column's own number. **Proved by reverting**: the header moved alone fails 2 and prints `1.66` under Fwd P/E.
- **`FIELD_SPEC` moved with it**, so the hover card, `/stock`, the tiles, the phone and `/compare` read the same order. Order is not part of a stored key — tiles and mobile fields key on `group|label`, views and screens on column ids — so reordering costs nothing.
- The `Trail P/E` tooltip says *"unlike the Fwd P/E beside it"*, which is still true: Fwd P/E is now immediately before it.

#### A caption is not a field list, and the owner was looking at the field list
`/stock` carried **no** Period row, **no** Reported row and **no** Announced (SEC) row. The first two were deliberately skipped — the Fundamentals caption states both — and the third had never existed on that page at all.

- **THE RECORDED REASON FOR SKIPPING `Reported` WAS MEASURED AND IS WRONG.** `buildSections`'s own comment said the caption reads `earnings_history` while the row reads the PROFILE's copy, *"so the two could disagree by up to the 7-day rotation"*. Checked against production over **95 symbols including the 40 oldest reporters on the screen: they agreed 95 times and differed none.** Both come out of the **same `/earnings` pull in the same `ensureProfiles` round**, so they are written together and cannot drift. The comment is corrected rather than left.
- **So the cost was duplication, and the duplication is now DELIBERATE.** The caption keeps both clauses because it is the only place that says these figures are a trailing **twelve months** — `Period: Jun 29` alone reads as the quarter that ended then — and the only place carrying the **time of day** and the **SEC-behind** warning, whose *"reported X **but** the company filed…"* construction needs the date in front of it. A field list is where a reader looks a value **up**; a caption is a sentence that qualifies the group. **Both halves are asserted**, so a later edit cannot quietly trim either.

#### `announcedSec` — one decision, two surfaces
The Announced (SEC) column's whole rule moved into `rowcard.js` the moment a second page wanted it. It returns `{t, c, title}` and the caller wraps it in whatever a cell or a row is on its page.

- **THE WRONG-CHANNEL REFUSAL IS WHY IT HAD TO BE SHARED RATHER THAN RESTATED.** 51 of 1,062 companies have a 2.02 date that predates the feed's own by more than a quarter — Energy Fuels announces under Items 7.01 and 8.01 and has exactly one 2.02 ever, from 2016 — so a second implementation on `/stock` would have printed **"2016"** beside a current Reported value. **Proved by reverting**: dropping that branch fails 2 and does exactly that.
- **`ANN_AHEAD_DAYS` moved with it**, beside `SEC_BEHIND_DAYS` and for its reason: two copies drift the first time one is tuned. Its measured justification (the distribution with the empty bucket at 36–45 days) moved too, since a constant and the measurement that set it belong together. **Probed at exactly 40 and 41 in both directions** — a threshold is a step function.
- **It is NOT a `FIELD_SPEC` row**, and that is the standing rule rather than a detail: `secLastResults` is stamped client-side from a separate endpoint and is never on the snapshot, so a FIELD_SPEC entry would print an em-dash on the tiles, the phone and `/compare`. `extra` exists for exactly this.
- **`extra` can now name the row it sits beside** (`after: 'Reported'`). Appended, this value would land **twenty-five rows below the only number it can be compared with** — it is marked when it runs *ahead of Reported*. Named-but-not-found appends, which is what every row without an `after` does. The same pass fixed a latent throw: the group filter admits a group holding **only** extras, where `byGroup[g]` is undefined and `.concat` threw.

#### THE DATE IS STAMPED BEFORE THE NO-FILINGS RETURN, and that ordering is the subtle part
`loadSec` removes the whole SEC card when companyfacts carries no statements — the right answer for a fund, and also what the **~64 IFRS filers** get, who answer 404 on companyfacts **and still file an Item 2.02 8-K**. A stamp after that `return` leaves their row reading *"still reading the filings"* for ever. The card is the statements; the row is a date, and they are different facts. **Proved by reverting**: fails 2, and the fixture carries that exact shape (`sec_state` with a 2.02, `sec_facts` empty).

- **A refused fetch settles the row too**, or it sits on the pending text for the session.
- **`pending` is a state, not a default.** A dash is right either way, but *"no Item 2.02 recorded"* is a false statement about a company that has one, so the first paint says it is still reading. A **fund answers NA before `pending` is consulted** — it needs no fetch. **Proved by reverting**: the other order fails 1.

#### Worth knowing
- **`lastResults` rides `/api/sec`'s existing read.** `readSecState()` already reads the whole ~1,200-row `sec_state` table on that route, so the column was one more field on a query that was already happening — never a second whole-table query, and never from `sec_facts`, where **we hold zero 8-K rows for anyone** (companyfacts carries only XBRL-tagged facts and an earnings 8-K generally has none).
- **An extra row may carry a plain `title`** now, which is where the screener puts the same explanation — on the cell. Only an extra row can have one, so the hover card is unchanged: a tooltip inside a tooltip helps nobody.
- Verified: **49 checks**, over a fixture whose six stocks separate every state the renderer can return — ahead of the feed, in sync, the wrong-channel shape, checked-and-nothing, a fund, and the IFRS filer — and whose period, announcement and 2.02 dates are three **different** days on every row, so a row wired to the wrong field comes out at a different value rather than coinciding. **Proved by reverting fourteen times, every one load-bearing**: the Announced row never added fails 10, Period and Reported skipped again 5, the ahead-of-the-feed mark 5, the pending/fund order 4, the store and the route 4 each, the wrong-channel refusal 3, the threshold at 10 fails 3, the PEG header moved alone 3, PEG moved back 2, `after` ignored 2, and the appended row, the late stamp and the title 1 each.
  - **ONE GUARD REPORTED 0 AND IT WAS THE CHECK, NOT RESIDUE.** `paintAnnRow` sets the row's `title` a second later on every path, so an assertion taken after the filings land passes whether or not the MARKUP carries one — two mechanisms for one attribute, and only the module can say which is being tested. It is asserted against `buildSections`'s output directly now, which is what the first paint actually has, and the revert then fails 1.
  - **`reported-test.js` ASSERTED THE OLD BEHAVIOUR and was CORRECTED, not worked around** — it checked that `/stock` draws NO Reported row. It asserts the row IS drawn now, plus the thing that makes stating it twice acceptable rather than a page arguing with itself: **the row's day must appear in the caption's own sentence**.
  - **`pelive-test.js` carried a literal Fundamentals width that has now gone stale TWICE** — 19 before Live P/E, 20 before Period. Corrected to what that check is really for (Live P/E is inside the group and the banner counts it), which is derived and cannot date; the general header-over-cell check beside it is what catches a miscounted banner. Confirmed pre-existing by stashing.
  - **Two test faults worth keeping.** A `<br>` contributes no whitespace to `textContent`, so the drawn label is `FwdP/E` and a check on the words failed over a header that was perfectly correct — the order is asserted by `data-key` instead. And **`peLive` is DERIVED by the read path** (`price / dilutedEpsTtm`), so the fixture's own value is overwritten: the expectation is the stamped number, which is the column working rather than a fault.
  - **A `cat` heredoc refused to close** on this suite and wrote no file at all — the documented escape hazard, met from the other side. Written with the Write tool instead.
  - **Pre-converting a block and then letting the patch helper convert again gave `\r\r\n` on 69 lines.** `node --check` passes a file like that, and the only visible symptom was `cat -A`. Convert the newline once, at the moment of writing.

### Live P/E — the trailing multiple, struck at today's price (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**A `Live P/E` column in the Fundamentals group immediately after the provider's `Trail P/E`: today's Price divided by the EPS TTM column, both of which are already on the row.** Asked as *"we show Forward P/E and trailing P/E, can you show the actual P/E"* — which reads as a misunderstanding (a trailing P/E **is** the actual P/E) and turned out to be a real defect when it was measured.

#### THE PROVIDER'S FIGURE IS STRUCK AT A PRICE THAT IS NOT THE ONE ON THE ROW
`trailingPe` arrives with the **profile**, which rotates on `FUND_ROTATION_DAYS` (7), while the price refreshes every half hour — so the two cells sit side by side disagreeing and nothing says so. **Measured rather than asserted**: back out the price each stored ratio implies (`trailingPe × dilutedEpsTtm`) and compare it with the row's own price. The gap correlates with each stock's **own 1-week return at r = 0.565**, decaying to 0.439 at a fortnight and 0.391 at a month — the signature of a figure struck a few days ago, not of noise. Median gap **1.21%**, 961 of 1,040 within 5%, **6 past 20%**. NVDA read **28.9** beside a price/EPS of **29.8**: the vendor's was struck at $227.21 while the row said $233.95.

- **THE READER COULD NOT SEE THE INCONSISTENCY**, which is why it went unreported for so long: `dilutedEpsTtm` is one of the **19 columns hidden site-wide**, so the two numbers that fail to divide were never both on screen.
- **The owner was offered three readings** — replace the vendor's column, add a third beside it, or leave it and fix the tooltip — and **chose the third column**. So `forwardPe` and `trailingPe` are **byte-identical to what they were**; this is an addition, and there is a check on every row that neither moved.

#### IT IS STAMPED, NEVER STORED
`stampCapDerived` already derives from fields on the row and runs at **all seven read paths**, so a snapshot written before the column existed carries it and the value is current rather than frozen at whenever the snapshot was built — the `capBand` / `capChangeToday` bargain. It reads `price` and `dilutedEpsTtm` and nothing else, so it costs no query and no credit.
- **The function's name is now slightly narrow for what it does** and was deliberately NOT renamed: 7 call sites plus 7 mentions in this file is 14 touchpoints of churn for a display change. The field is documented in the comment above it.

#### A MULTIPLE OFF A LOSS IS A DASH, and on a SORTED column that is the whole point
`px / eps` on a loss-maker is a confident negative number, and **ascending by P/E then puts every loss-making company at the top as the cheapest thing on screen** — the Size card's rule, the Bubble card's and the peer table's, met a fourth time and in the place it does most damage. The test is `px > 0 && eps > 0`, which **rejects the empty before coercing** in the same expression: `Number(null)` is `0` and finite, so a zero EPS and a missing one are both refused rather than producing `Infinity`. **Proved by reverting three times**: the naive division fails 5, relaxing the guard to `Number.isFinite(eps)` fails 5, and dropping the stamp fails 5.

#### NO CURRENCY GUARD, AND THAT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED
Price is the **trading** currency and every absolute is the company's **reporting** currency, so `price / EPS` looks exactly like the documented ADR trap (the share count is the ordinary count against an ADR price, and the two disagree by 2,921% on CX). **It is not**: checked against the vendor's own ratio, depositary receipts agree at a **2.24% median against 1.17%** for everything else, and the single non-USD row (SKX, in EUR) agrees too — the vendor's `diluted_eps_ttm` is already per **traded** share. A guard here would have withheld the column from exactly the rows it is correct for.

#### Worth knowing
- **The cell takes `liveTitle`, not `cacheTitle`** — it is recomputed on every read, where its neighbour is struck whenever the profile was pulled. A live figure claiming a cached one's timestamp is a small lie on a column that exists to fix a staleness problem. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- **NA for a fund**, which is the one way it is harsher than the column beside it: the vendor's weighted figure for an ETF's holdings is real and cannot be reproduced from a single EPS, so this is **deliberately not in `FUND_HAS`** while `trailingPe` stays. The fund's NA run goes 8 → 9; **proved by reverting**, a miscount is not an error, it is a row one cell short.
- **The Trail P/E tooltip was rewritten in the same commit** to say it is the data provider's, re-pulled about weekly, and struck at a close up to seven days old — *"that is what the Live P/E beside it is for"*. A column whose staleness is now documented elsewhere must say so itself.
- **THE BOUNDARY HOLDS, and it was checked rather than assumed**: nothing in the Advice engine reads `trailingPe` — only `forwardPe`, at [action.js:305](private/action.js#L305) — so adding a second trailing multiple cannot reach a verdict. Asserted **behaviourally**, not by grep: every row is scored three ways (field absent, present, and **lying**) and the verdicts must be identical.
- **IT FIXES THE PRICE HALF OF THE STALENESS AND INHERITS THE EPS HALF, which is the right trade and has one failure case.** EPS moves quarterly and the price moves every half hour, so a cached EPS against a live price is strictly better than two cached numbers — **except after a SPLIT**. *(That clause used to end "where the archive is re-priced by `persistBars` within one refresh and the stored per-share EPS is not" — **the first half is FALSE and was corrected on 2026-10-05**: CTVA's archive still carries the raw step 77.65 → 12.57 on 2026-10-01 four days later, because the PROVIDER serves it unadjusted and `persistBars` detects a split by disagreeing with a re-fetch. So both halves are stale after a split, not one, and it does not self-heal — see the entry below.)* Measured live the day it shipped: `CTVA` split **6.18x on 2026-10-01** and the column read **7.2 against a true ~44**, while the vendor's 47.1 was right (both halves of its ratio are pre-split, and a split does not move a ratio). **One row of 1,278, and it does NOT self-heal** (see below). The column did not create it — `bookValuePerShare` is wrong over the same window — it is the first surface that divides a per-share figure by a price and so makes it visible. The fix is one call on the path that already detects the split; it is [docs/backlog.md](docs/backlog.md) entry 21, not done, because it touches the refresh path on the back of a display change.
