**Since 2026-09-15 the stocks the screener tracks live in their own `universe` table (`symbol`, `added_at`); portfolios only group them.** Before, the universe was the union of the admin portfolios, so deleting a portfolio silently removed every stock only it held and purged their data — measured before the change: deleting Fin, Chips, Software and the industry-style lists would have taken ~150 of 271 stocks out. The owner wanted to delete those portfolios now that Sector and Industry cover them.

- **`store.readUniverse()` is the only source** — server (`readUniverse`), `purge-orphans.js`, `backfill-bars.js`. It returns the table **plus any portfolio member not in it** (belt and braces), ordered by `added_at`.
- **Filling it**: `init()` runs `insert or ignore into universe select distinct symbol from portfolio_tickers` on every cold start (idempotent, no marker — that is how the 271 arrived), and **`writePortfolios()` runs the same insert before it deletes the memberships**, so no portfolio write can drop a stock.
- **Routes**: deleting a portfolio and taking a ticker out of one never purge. `DELETE /api/tickers/:symbol` (the × in the All view) is the only way out: `removeFromUniverse()` deletes the universe row and every membership in one batch, then `purgeSymbol()`. `POST /api/universe {symbol, portfolio?}` adds a stock with an optional portfolio (the console's Add a ticker, "No portfolio — screener only" by default); adding to a portfolio still adds to the universe. Every portfolio answer (`portfolioAnswer()`) carries `{portfolios, universe}`, and the screener's `applyPortfolioMap(map, universe)` keeps a row for every universe stock.
- **Snapshot memberships are stamped on the way out** (`membershipOf` per row, `snap.portfolios` from the table) — a deleted portfolio would otherwise linger on every row until the next refresh.
- Verified against the real server on an in-memory node:sqlite in place of Turso (27 checks: delete a portfolio keeps stocks and data, remove-from-portfolio keeps, remove-from-screener purges and removes memberships and is not brought back by a later write, the add route's 409/404/400s, snapshot stamping) and the screener's reconciliation (5 checks).

### The Sector Benchmark theme — the eleven Select Sector SPDRs (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**XLK, XLF, XLV, XLE, XLI, XLY, XLP, XLU, XLRE, XLB, XLC, in a theme called `Sector Benchmark`.** Universe **1,181 → 1,192**. One fund per GICS sector, which is a **complete set rather than a sample**: our sector names map one-to-one onto GICS at sector level, checked when the industry column was built, so every sector the screener knows has exactly one fund standing for it.

- **US-listed, all eleven** — the standing rule, and the test is the listing. NYSE Arca.
- **THEY POLLUTE NO TAXONOMY AGGREGATE, and that was measured before the add rather than hoped for.** A fund that IS a sector sitting INSIDE that sector's aggregate double-counts it — the trap the four index ETFs are excluded for on the day card. Measured across all **17 funds the screener already held: 0 carry a sector and 0 carry an industry**, because the provider files a fund under neither. **Re-measured once all eleven profiles had landed: still 0 and 0**, so the sector and industry aggregates really are safe, and that is the half that mattered.

##### I ALSO CLAIMED THEY CARRY NO MARKET CAP, AND THAT WAS WRONG (corrected 2026-09-30)
**The sentence used to end "…no size band (no market cap — a fund reports AUM), and below the day card's $1B mover floor. That holds after their profiles land." It does not.** A fund reports AUM and the provider returns it in `market_capitalization`, so the moment a profile lands the cap is populated. Measured after the Fill missing: **9 of the 11 carry one** — XLF $46.0B, XLK $43.7B, XLV $28.3B, XLI $23.6B, XLP $17.3B, XLY $14.3B, XLE $10.8B, XLU $7.5B, XLB $3.7B (XLC and XLRE not yet).

- **The error was measuring the wrong field.** The pre-add check read `sector` and `industry` on the 17 existing funds and found none; I extrapolated to the cap without checking it, and every fund I looked at happened to have no profile yet. **An extrapolation across fields is not a measurement**, and the giveaway was available: this file already says in the Size-band section that *"seven symbols legitimately have no market cap — all ETFs"*, which is a statement about symbols with no profile, not about funds.
- **What it actually costs, measured rather than feared**: the eleven are now **banded** (Mid-Large and Mid), so they appear in `/size/<band>`, in the pivot's Size dimension and in `/consolidated` grouped by Size; and nine of them clear the **day card's $1B mover floor**, so they can take a mover slot against real companies.
- **IT IS NOT NEW BEHAVIOUR, WHICH IS THE ONE MITIGATING FACT.** `SMH`, `SOXX` and `GLD` already did exactly this before the eleven existed — funds carrying a cap, banded, and eligible for a mover slot. The eleven take that from **3 to 12**. So this is a pre-existing wrinkle the addition made larger, not one it created.
- **`BENCHMARKS` still does not fix it and is still the wrong tool**: that list exists for the delete guard and the day card, and it would put a 409 on eleven rows the owner may want to prune.
- **The principled fix is now AVAILABLE and is deliberately not built**: `instrumentType === 'ETF'` identifies a fund directly, so the day card's movers and the size bands could exclude funds by what they ARE rather than by a hardcoded symbol list. Both are display decisions and both change what is on screen, so they are the owner's call. Noted here rather than done.
- **The general rule this leaves: when a claim rests on "the provider has none of X for this kind of instrument", check X itself, on rows that actually have a profile.** Every fund in the pre-add sample was unprofiled, which made the sample agree with the claim for the wrong reason.
- **SO THEY GET NO `BENCHMARKS` TREATMENT, and the asymmetry is the point.** That list does two jobs — the **delete guard** (409, because every group page draws the S&P and Dow lines, so dropping one would take the comparison off pages that have nothing to do with that row) and **removal from the day card's pool**. Neither applies: nothing draws an XLK line, so deleting one damages no other page, and the arithmetic above already keeps them out of every aggregate. Adding them would be a guard against nothing, and a delete guard on eleven rows the owner may well want to prune is a cost rather than a safety.
- **The point of the theme is `/theme/Sector Benchmark` and `/consolidated` grouped by Theme** — eleven rows, one per sector, read against each other and against the index. That is the reading the four index ETFs cannot give.
- **Backfilled BEFORE the next price refresh, which is the documented hazard and not optional.** `backfill-bars.js --commit --rate 100 --only …` wrote **49,842 bars in 0.2 min** (archive 4,582,378 → 4,632,220 rows, 1,181 → 1,192 symbols), finishing **20 minutes** before the next intraday slot. Without it the first refresh would try to build eleven archives inside one request, which is exactly the 504 of 2026-09-22. Every one now clears `LIGHT_MIN_ARCHIVE` (300) and is pulled shallow. **`--rate 100`, not the default 580**, so the throttle cannot starve a live price round.
  - **XLRE reaches back only to 2015-10-08 and XLC to 2018-06-19** — their real inception dates, Real Estate and Communication Services being the two sectors GICS created late. The other nine reach 2006-11-13, the 5,000-bar API ceiling. A short archive here is the market's, not the backfill's.
- **A ROW DOES NOT EXIST UNTIL A FULL ROUND REBUILDS THE SNAPSHOT.** `/api/stocks` serves the cached blob, so immediately after the add it still carried **1,181** rows and the eleven had none — which reads as a failed add and is not one. The screener page itself reconciles (`applyPortfolioMap`) and shows the documented `No data yet` placeholder meanwhile. Judge a bulk add by the universe table and the bar count, never by the snapshot.
- **Names arrive with the PROFILE, and nothing else writes one** — `ensureProfiles` backfills from the provider's own `providerName` for any symbol with no name, and never overwrites an existing one. `POST /api/universe/check` was **vacuous here**, and I recorded the wrong reason: it answered `listingRows: 0` and I read that as the table being empty. **It counts the ASKED symbols found, not the table** — which holds 7,136 rows (measured 2026-10-03). Zero was correct and expected: the listing is a STOCKS file and all eleven of these are ETFs. The field is `listingHits` now. The consequence stands — the warning could not fire and **no names were derived at add time** — so this is still not a clean bill of health, just not for the reason given.
  - **So a bulk add lands eleven nameless rows, and they stay nameless until a profile is pulled.** The owner reported it from the screener seven hours later — four named (the four whose profiles had landed) and seven blank. **A blank NAME column is the visible symptom of a missing profile**, which is worth recognising rather than diagnosing as a name bug.
  - **Fill missing is the fix and it is one round**: 7 gaps, all `reason: none`, **~561 credits, 23 seconds**, and it filled the name, the profile and the instrument type together. Names 11/11 afterwards, gaps 0. Waiting for the nightly would also have worked (it fills gaps first) at the cost of a day.
  - **Run it clear of a slot.** A Fill missing raises the refresh flag, and the intraday route stands aside while another refresh is running — so a run still open at :15 or :45 costs that slot. The driver refuses to start inside the ten minutes before one.
- Verified live: all eleven in the universe, the theme holding exactly the eleven, every bar count clear of the floor, and `/theme/Sector Benchmark` drawing **11 of 11 with history at the window start** plus both benchmark lines at 180 non-null points — **measured against Mag 7 and `sector:Technology` as controls**, since the three must agree on the two index lines and disagree on the basket.
  - **The benchmark series is `bench[].index`, and guessing `series` reported `0 pts` on all three** — a defect that was not there. A field name read off a hunch is not a measurement; the controls are what showed it.
- **THE FIRST SLOT AFTER THE ADD CAME BACK CLEAN, which is the confirmation the backfill was for**: 11:45 ET, **3 rounds, `complete`, 1,276 credits**, snapshot 1,181 → **1,192 rows**, all eleven priced. No 504 on the round that would have produced one.
  - **`loaded: 1182/1192` is PROFILE coverage, not prices**, and it reconciles exactly — 1,181 plus XLB, the one of the eleven that picked up a name that round. The 1,276 credits against the usual 1,185 is ~+91: one cold profile at 80 plus eleven extra price credits. The other ten names arrive with the rotation.
  - **A WAIT THAT WATCHES THE WRONG FIELD REPORTS A FAILURE THAT IS NOT THERE.** My first poller exited on `total === 1192`, which appears **4 seconds** into a slot — round 1 of 3, still `running` — and printed "NOT CLEAN" over a slot that was working. A slot is 2 light rounds and one full one, ~2m34s of which 130s is the two mandatory 62s gaps, and **only the full round rebuilds the snapshot**. The condition is the run's own STATUS leaving `running`.
  - All eleven carry Advice verdicts from the all-technical rulebook, as every fund here does — they file no statements, so there is nothing else to score them on.

## Dropping a symbol
**A ticker removed from the screener (the All view's ×) takes its data with it** — `bars`, `fundamentals_history`, `profiles`, `names` and headlines, via `purgeSymbol()`. *Before 2026-09-15 this happened when a ticker left its last portfolio; see the universe table above.* `purge-orphans.js` sweeps up anything left, comparing against the universe.

- **Two of those come back, one does not.** Bars cost a single API credit to re-pull at any depth and every technical is recomputed from bars, but **`fundamentals_history` cannot be rebuilt** — the API only ever returns today's numbers, so a deleted row is gone and re-adding the ticker starts that series from zero. Every surface says so: the confirm dialog, the dry run, and the comment on `purgeSymbol()`.
- **The decision is made from the universe before and after the edit, not from the route.** A symbol still in another portfolio is untouched — verified: removing AAPL from one of two lists purged nothing, deleting the last portfolio holding SPY removed all 9,739 of its rows.
- **`snapshot` is deliberately not in `SYMBOL_TABLES`.** It is one JSON row rewritten wholesale on the next refresh, so it heals itself.
- **A failed purge never fails the edit.** Losing the portfolio change because the cleanup broke would be worse than leaving rows behind, and the sweep exists to collect them.
- **The UI confirms only when data will actually be destroyed.** `lastHome()` asks whether this removal leaves the symbol in no portfolio, so removing it from one of several still passes without a dialog — that really is trivially undone. Deleting a portfolio names the symbols that will lose their history. Both then report the row count through `setStatus()`, because a silent ten-thousand-row delete is not something to discover later.
- Swept on introduction: **SPY 9,739 rows, XLF 5,009, BTC 1** — the database now holds data for exactly the 83 symbols in the portfolios.

## Editing portfolios does not pull
**Adding or removing a ticker, and creating, renaming or deleting a portfolio, no longer refresh from the API.** Every one of them used to call `refresh()`, which sets `?refresh=1` and recomputes the entire universe from Twelve Data — roughly **560 credits and a ten-second wait** to reflect a change the server had already made and had already told the client about. Refresh is a button; it stays one.

- **`applyPortfolioMap(map)` reconciles the table from the response.** All five endpoints answer with the fresh `name -> symbols` map, and membership, badges, tab counts, the portfolio picker and the purge warning all derive from it. Only the price and fundamental columns need a pull.
- **A symbol with no row yet gets a placeholder**, reusing the `s.error` branch the row renderer already has: `No data yet — click ↻ Refresh to pull it.` It is in the portfolio, so it belongs in the table and in the count — silently not appearing looks like the add failed. `applyLens()` already skips error rows, so nothing downstream needed changing.
- **A symbol left in no portfolio loses its row**, because the server has just purged its stored data.
- **`activeTab` falls back to `All`** when the portfolio it names stops existing. `renamePortfolio()` sets the new name *before* reconciling, so a rename keeps you where you were.
- **The add route returns the company name it resolves** (1 credit, cached, and it was already being fetched). That lookup is now the only thing that touches the symbol before the next Refresh, so a name coming back empty is the earliest hint of a typo and the page says so. Without it a mistyped ticker would sit as a placeholder until the next refresh turned it into an error row.
- **The as-of date still pulls**, both setting and clearing it — a forward-returns view is computed live by definition.
- Verified against the extracted function with eight cases: a new ticker, a ticker already in the universe added to a second portfolio, removal from one of two holders, removal of the last holder, rename, delete with one orphan and one survivor, a null map, and a placeholder being replaced by real data.

## Saved column layout
Which column groups a user has collapsed — and which starter screens they have starred — is stored per account in the `prefs` table (`user_key`, JSON `data`), read by `GET /api/prefs` and written by `PUT /api/prefs`.

- **Server-side, not `localStorage`.** The choice belongs to the person, so it follows them to another browser or machine rather than belonging to a device and being shared by whoever sits at it.
- **Keyed on the signed-in email**, falling back to `'admin'` for the legacy password cookie and for open mode, where there is no user row — the same convention `chat_usage` uses.
- **`fwd` is never persisted.** It is derived state: `refresh()` sets it from whether an as-of date is set, so saving it would only store a value the next load overwrites.
- **Prefs are awaited before the first render**, in the boot chain `checkAuth().then(loadPrefs).then(refresh)`. Applying them afterwards would paint the default layout and then visibly rearrange it.
- **Writes are debounced 600ms** — the columns menu stays open while toggling, so changes arrive in bursts — and are suppressed until the load lands, or the defaults would be written back over the values being fetched.
- **The server stores only what it understands.** `PUT` rebuilds the `collapsed` map from scratch against `/^[a-z]{1,16}$/`, so the endpoint cannot be used as free per-user storage and `__proto__` cannot get in.

## Member portfolios
**A member's own lists — named FILTERS over the shared snapshot, never new data (2026-09-14).** The load-bearing invariant, enforced server-side: `PUT /api/my/portfolios` validates every symbol against the live universe and silently drops the rest, so a member can never add a stock to the system. Everything heavy (bars, profiles, scoring, refreshes, the snapshot, chat) is untouched — a personal portfolio costs nothing.

- **Storage: `user_portfolios`** (`user_key`, `name`, `position`, `symbols` as a JSON array per row) — deliberately NOT in `prefs`: three pages debounce-write prefs under the hand-back rule, and a page bug there must not be able to wipe someone's portfolios. Keyed on email (else `'admin'`, the prefs convention); `deleteUser()` purges them; `purgeSymbol()` sweeps a dropped ticker out of every member list and reads filter to the universe anyway (belt and braces). Caps: 10 portfolios, 40-char names, whole-collection replace rebuilt from scratch on write (the prefs-PUT rule).
- **Routes**: `GET`/`PUT /api/my/portfolios`, both `requireMember` — guests 403 and have no key. The PUT logs the **diff** to the activity log (`myportfolio` kind: `create:Name +2`, `Name +NVDA -MU`, `delete:Name`), capped at 10 rows per save, never the blob.
- **UI (screener)**: personal tabs live under the **`my:` prefix** in `activeTab` so names can never collide with shared portfolios (`tabExists()` guards the three fallback sites). The portfolio picker grows a personal section — green tint, each row with rename/delete as `.pick-row` siblings (a button cannot nest in a button) — plus "New personal portfolio". Membership is toggled from the **star on each row** (`.mypf` in the symbol cell, hidden for guests), which opens the `#myPop` fixed popover: tick portfolios in and out, menu stays open while toggling (the Rules-menu pattern), saves debounced 600ms and **adopts the server's cleaned answer** so the UI cannot drift from what was stored. Personal memberships render as **dashed badges** (`.badge.mine`) beside the shared solid ones. The ⋯ menu's Rename/Delete stay shared-only (`isMyTab` guard); loaded in the boot chain beside prefs, before the first render.
- **Admin review**: `/api/users` attaches each account's portfolios (name + symbols, shown as a summary cell with the full lists in the tooltip on `/users`), plus `otherPortfolios` for keys with no account row (the legacy `'admin'` key), so nothing escapes review. The activity log carries the edit stream.
- Verified on introduction: junk/duplicate/lowercase symbols cleaned, the 10-portfolio cap, guest 403s, diff rows in the activity log, the review shape, and the purge sweep (2 rows edited, symbol gone, other symbols kept).

## The refresh budget — pacing and rotation
**Two changes on 2026-09-14 took the nightly job from "breaks at 530 symbols" to "1,000 in 24 minutes", on the same Pro plan.** Both were prompted by costing an upgrade and finding it was not worth buying: 987 credits/minute is a slider inside Pro at $149 — no `/market_cap`, no forward estimates, no analyst data, all of which need Ultra at $999 — and it would have bought **nine minutes on an unattended midnight job**, while removing not one required fix. 1,001 price credits do not fit a 987 ceiling either.

**Prices are paced across rounds.** They cost 1 credit a symbol and the whole universe was pulled in one round, so above **529 symbols** the round asked for more than the minute allows and was refused — and a Refresh All could never get past its first round. A price round now takes the next slice that fits, anything outside it is read from the archive so the snapshot stays complete, and only the round reaching the last symbol stamps `prices_at`. `refresh_state.priced` is how a stateless function knows where it got to; `notePriceRound()` is the one place that advances it, so the cron route and `/api/stocks` cannot drift. Only freshly-priced symbols go to `persistBars` — re-persisting archive-sourced bars is a no-op upsert of the overlap window for every unpriced symbol, every round.

**Fundamentals rotate instead of being re-pulled nightly.** `PROFILE_TTL_MS` is now `FUND_ROTATION_DAYS` (env, default **7**) rather than 24 hours, and the cron's `?start=1` expires the **oldest** `ceil(N/7)` profiles (`expireOldestProfiles`) instead of all of them. The justification is measured and already in this file: the twelve tracked fundamental fields move on **1-5% of nights**, and when they move it is a step, not a wobble. A symbol with no profile at all is never waiting its turn — `ensureProfiles` treats a missing one as stale. `?full=1` on the cron, and the console's **Refresh all**, still sweep everything.

| universe | nightly before | nightly now | credits before → now |
|---|---|---|---|
| 270 (today) | 39 rounds, 40 min | **6 rounds, 6 min** | 21,909 → **3,396** |
| 500 | 73 rounds, 75 min | 12 rounds, 12 min | 40,573 → 6,272 |
| 1,000 | *impossible* | **23 rounds, 24 min** | 81,145 → 12,463 |

- **`MAX_ROUNDS=60` and `timeout-minutes: 45` did not need raising** — 23 rounds and 24 minutes at 1,000 symbols sit inside both. They would bind on a full sweep, which the nightly job no longer runs.
- **A plain Refresh above ~609 symbols prices what fits and leaves the rest on their archived close.** Honest but partial; Refresh All is what walks the whole list.
- Verified by simulating whole runs against the real `liveRefreshOpts()` at nine universe sizes from 93 to 1,500: **no round anywhere exceeds 610 credits and every profile is still pulled**. The load-bearing half of that is the bottom — 93 and 270 reproduce today's 14 and 39 rounds exactly, because below 529 the slice is the whole universe and the new path is never taken. The rotation SQL is unit-checked against a throwaway in-memory SQLite: oldest-first, the limit respected, never-fetched rows not counted against it.
- **What none of this fixes**, and what will bind next: the assistant's ~700-stock context wall, and `readBarsFor`'s 650-day window across the universe (3.5s at 85 symbols, so ~41s at 1,000) on every round.

## A live price pull is SHALLOW — the archive carries the history
**On 2026-09-17 Twelve Data's batched `time_series` started failing, and the fix was to stop asking it for data we already had.** Every refresh was fetching `outputsize=300` per symbol — **9.56 MB across 271 symbols** — to compute a window the `bars` table already holds. A live pull now asks for **`LIGHT_BARS` (12)** and the scoring window is joined on from the archive. Credits are unchanged (1 a symbol whatever the depth, measured), so this was free all along.

**The incident, because the symptom pointed the wrong way.** Three refreshes failed with three different messages — `terminated` at 194s and 133s (both having spent 120 credits), then `Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "...` at 77s with 0 credits. All one cause. Measured from two vantage points (a laptop and Vercel), the SAME 120-symbol request returned in 12s, in 375s, as an HTML gateway page and as a dropped socket, within one hour. Seconds apart: **300 bars → HTTP 524 after 125s; 12 bars → 200 OK in 33s.**

- **Smaller batches were tried first and are WORSE — measured, on the real universe.** 3x120 took 62.3s; **9x30 took 719.2s, dropped two sockets and lost 58 of 271 symbols**; 30 symbols at 12 bars did the lot in 12.2s. **The stalls are per-request, not per-byte**, so splitting a pull multiplies the exposure instead of reducing it. Do not reach for a smaller `CHUNK` next time this happens; reach for a smaller payload.
- **Three guards make the shallow pull safe, and each one exists because without it the archive silently loses history.**
  - **A symbol whose archive does not REACH the live window is re-pulled deep.** `persistBars()` treats "the fetched window does not overlap what we hold" as "rebuild this symbol from the fetch" — which from a 12-bar pull would replace years of bars with twelve. The overlap is checked (`archive newest >= oldest live bar`) and anything that fails is re-pulled at full depth.
  - **`persistBars` is handed the LIVE bars, not the joined window.** It detects a split by comparing an old fetched bar against the stored one; every bar in the joined window came OUT of the store, so a joined series agrees with itself and no split is ever seen. The probe is shallower now (about 11 sessions rather than 60), which is sufficient because it runs on every refresh — a split is caught the day it appears.
  - **A thin archive (under `LIGHT_MIN_ARCHIVE`, 300 bars) is pulled deep**, since the join could not supply the ~260 sessions the long-window returns need. **SPY is always deep**: the benchmark is deliberately never archived.
- **The as-of view is untouched and still deep.** It reads a range the archive may not cover at all.
- **Verified against production's own numbers, and the first comparison was wrong in an instructive way.** Long-window fields looked off by up to 51 points against production's morning snapshot. They were not: the window is a **bar COUNT**, so a run that has today's session anchors one bar further back than one that does not. Reproduced from the archive by hand, both sides land exactly — BE's 1Y is 302.89% against `bars[252]` and 281.02% against `bars[251]`, each matching what that run reported to the decimal. **Compare returns between two runs only after checking they saw the same newest bar.**
- Measured after: **267 shallow + 5 deep, ~4,704 bars against 81,600, a full universe refresh in 30.8s** while the provider was still failing deep pulls outright.

### Reaching the provider: a deadline, one retry, and the real reason
**`fetchJson` had no timeout, did not check `res.ok`, and discarded `err.cause`.** All three turned a provider wobble into a long hang ending in an unactionable word.

- **A deadline per attempt (`TD_TIMEOUT_MS`, 120s) and a ceiling on the whole price phase (`TD_PRICE_PHASE_MS`, 210s).** A serverless function is killed at the platform's ceiling, so an unbounded wait does not fail — it vanishes, taking the round's credits with it. The per-call budget alone was not enough: three chunks could each take it.
- **The retry is conditional on NOT having been charged.** Credits are the binding constraint and the round's profile budget is sized against a known price cost, so a blind retry could breach 610/minute. An attempt whose `Api-Credits-Request` header never arrived was never served. Both `terminated` failures and the gateway page fit that exactly — and a live run since has been seen to recover: *"attempt 1 failed after 120013ms (aborted due to timeout) — nothing was charged, 78s of budget left, retrying"*, then completed.
- **Two coercion traps, both caught by tests rather than by reading.** `Number(null)` is `0` and `Number.isFinite(0)` is true, so a missing credits header read as **"we were charged"** and suppressed every retry — the `num()` lesson again: **reject the empty before coercing, not after**. And `netReason` preferred `err.code`, which for a `DOMException` is the legacy NUMBER (a timeout is 23), so a real timeout reported `Failed to reach Twelve Data: 23 — 23`. Only a non-numeric code is a name worth printing.
- **A gateway failure is an HTML page, not JSON.** `res.json()` on it produced the `Unexpected token '<'` that read like a bug in here rather than a failure over there. `res.ok` is checked first, a JSON error body keeps the provider's own words, and an HTML one says so.
- Verified: 21 checks on `fetchJson` (each of the three real failures replayed, the charged/uncharged rule, the budget, the message shapes) and 16 on the shallow pull against the real server on an in-memory database (who is pulled shallow vs deep, the stale-archive re-pull, history NOT replaced, a split still rewriting, the as-of path unchanged), plus live full-universe refreshes.

## Fast refresh — the same sweep without the per-round rebuild
**A Refresh all re-pulls every profile AND rebuilds the whole table on every round** — a 650-day window of bars for the entire universe, rescored, advice re-run, snapshot rewritten — to fold in the seven profiles that round fetched. Measured 2026-09-16 at 271 stocks: **40 rounds, 72.4 minutes, 21,837 credits**, of which 62s a round is the deliberate wait and **~46s is that rebuild**. **Fast refresh (2026-09-16) keeps the sweep and drops the repetition**: its rounds fetch profiles and nothing else, and the table is rebuilt **once, at the end**.

- **Why it matters at 1,000 stocks**, which the owner is heading for: the round count is fixed by the API (80 credits a profile against 610 a minute = 7 a minute = 143 rounds ≈ 2.4 hours, which nothing can beat), but the per-round work is not. Estimated at 1,000: **Refresh all 5-7 hours and ~63M rows read; Fast refresh ~2.5 hours and under 1M**. A five-hour run driven from a browser tab does not finish — two runs were already `abandoned` at 134/271 on 2026-09-16.
- **`GET /api/refresh-profiles`** is the round: `ensureProfiles(universe, 7)`, `noteRefreshProgress`, `recordRound`, and a stopped-run check — no bars read, nothing scored, no snapshot written. It **deliberately does not close the run** when coverage completes; the rebuild does.
- **The rebuild is the ordinary round.** `RefreshLoop.run('fast', …)` calls `/api/refresh-profiles` until every stock has a profile, then **one** `/api/stocks?refresh=1&run=…`, which is where scores, advice, the snapshot, `fundamentals_history`, the report and the email all come from — the same ending a Refresh all has, so none of that is duplicated. The hook fires `onWait('rebuild')` so the page can say what is happening.
- **Stopping loses nothing**: the profiles fetched so far are stored, and the next refresh of any kind picks them up. A stopped or stalled run does NOT rebuild.
- **The trade-off, and it is the reason Refresh all stays**: the screener shows the previous numbers until the final round. Refresh all remains the manual "everything, visibly" sweep; Fast refresh is the one to use as the universe grows.
- **`Fill missing` is a different axis and they multiply**: it narrows WHICH stocks get pulled (fewer rounds), this narrows what a round COSTS. Measured the same night: Fill missing 20 rounds / 137 profiles / 31.2 min ≈ 93s a round against Refresh all's 108s — halving the rounds did not make a round cheaper.
- Verified: the loop against a fake server (12 checks — the fast start, profile-only rounds, exactly one rebuild and it is last, the run named on it, progress from the round counts, a stop ending it without rebuilding, a refusal retried, a stall giving up without rebuilding) and the round endpoint against the real server on an in-memory database with the provider stubbed (11 checks — the flag's mode, the run's kind, seven profiles a round really fetched, the round recorded, progress written, NO snapshot until the end, the run still open after full coverage, a stopped run refusing).

## Fill missing — the incremental refresh
**`Fill missing` on the admin console's Data section re-pulls only the stocks whose company data is missing (2026-09-15).** Same round loop, banner and report as Refresh all; the difference is which profiles are expired at the start.

- **What counts as missing — `profileGaps()`**, in order: no stored profile (`none`, a new ticker); a stored profile **lacking a key** the app now writes (`fields`); a pull refused or never finished (`failed`, fetched_at 0). **Old is not missing** — that is the rotation's job and Refresh all's.
- **Absent, not null, is the test, and it is load-bearing.** `emptyProfile()` is the literal `fetchProfile()` starts from, and `PROFILE_FIELDS = Object.keys(emptyProfile())`, so every pull since a field was added carries its key even when the provider has no value. A fund pulled since 2026-09-14 has `industry: null` and is left alone; a naive "industry is blank" test would re-pull SMH, XLF, KRE and CYBR on every run and buy the same null. Measured before building: 115 profiles lacked the `industry` key (Cisco and Netflix among them — pulled the morning of the 14th, before the field shipped), 4 had it null. Adding a field to `emptyProfile()` is therefore all it takes to make the next Fill missing backfill it.
- **Prices**: none by default — `POST /api/refresh-all?mode=missing` stamps `prices_at` at once and every round is an archive round (7 profiles, 561 credits). The exception is a stock with **no bars at all**: `liveRefreshOpts()` gives a `mode: 'missing'` run one price round of exactly those symbols, then `notePriceRound` stamps `prices_at`.
- **State**: `refresh_state.mode` (`'missing'` or null). **`beginRefresh()` now also resets `prices_at` and `priced`** — it upserts onto a possibly stale row, and before this a row left by an abandoned run could tell the next run its prices were already pulled.
- **`GET /api/refresh-missing`** (admin) is the costed preview and changes nothing: the console shows it under the button ("115 of 271 stocks — 115 pulled before a field existed (industry). About 17 rounds, ~17 min, ~9,217 credits") and repeats it in a confirm; with nothing missing the button says so and does not navigate. The POST answers `{nothing: true}` in that case and the screener says so instead of starting.
- **The nightly job fills gaps first**: on a rotation night the cron `?start=1` expires the gaps before `expireOldestProfiles()`, which only picks among fetched_at > 0, so gaps are not counted against the rotation. A new ticker or a new field fills the next night.
- **The report** is titled *Fill missing* and adds "Still missing" (a fresh `profileGaps()` after the run) and "No industry from the provider (expected for funds)".
- **Credits are a pacing unit, not a budget**: Pro has no daily cap (`/api_usage` returns only `plan_limit: 610` per minute — a Basic key also returns a daily limit).
- Verified: the preview on live data (115 gaps, 17 rounds); a vm simulation of the real `profileGaps` / `missingPlan` / `liveRefreshOpts` / `notePriceRound` over an in-memory store (17 checks — only the 115 gaps re-pulled, 17 rounds, max 561 credits/round, a new ticker priced alone in round one, a normal Refresh all and a plain Refresh unchanged, null industry not a gap); headless page runs of the console preview + confirm, the screener's `?do=refreshmissing` run, and the nothing-missing path.

## Intraday price refreshes
**Prices refresh every 30 minutes through the US session, 9:40 AM to 3:40 PM New York time, on trading days (2026-09-15).** An external scheduler (**cron-job.org**, owner's choice over GitHub Actions, whose schedule can run 5-30 minutes late or skip under load) calls `GET /api/cron/intraday` with `Authorization: Bearer $CRON_SECRET`, set in New York time at minutes 10 and 40 of hours 9-15, Monday-Friday. **The server decides whether to act**, so the schedule can be broad and daylight saving needs no thought:

1. **Weekday, 9:38 AM-4:00 PM New York** (`nyClock`, two minutes of scheduler slack). Outside it the call returns without logging — the 9:10 call lands there every day by design.
2. **Nothing else running** — a Refresh all, Fill missing or nightly run in `refresh_state`; two jobs in one minute breach the 610 credits. Logged as a `skipped` run.
3. **NYSE open** by Twelve Data's `market_state` (`XNYS.is_market_open`, **1 credit**, verified on this plan 2026-09-15) — it knows holidays and early closes, so there is no holiday list to maintain. Logged as `skipped` when closed. An unreadable answer proceeds (a holiday run costs 272 credits and harms nothing).
4. One plain price refresh through the same `computeStocks` → `finishLiveRefresh` path as the Refresh button: snapshot rewritten, bars upserted (today's provisional bar, healed by the overlap), 12 stocks' headlines topped up, **no email**, logged as an `intraday` run with measured credits (~273 a run, ~3,550 a trading day; no daily cap on Pro).

- `?dry=1` runs every check and reports the decision without refreshing or logging. Measured: 13 runs on a summer day and on the Monday after the clocks change; boundaries at 9:37/9:38 and 16:00.
- **Open screener tabs follow the data**: every five minutes a visible tab calls `/api/status`, which now carries `updatedAt` from the snapshot's own column (`snapshotUpdatedAt()` — the ~1MB payload is not read), and reloads in place when it is newer. Sort, filters, tab and scroll survive (page state the reload does not touch); it waits while pulling, in a forward-returns view, and while the ladder panel or the star popover is open. Verified headlessly: 8 checks.
- **Advice is intraday too**: mid-session the Advice columns and the Advice move picker read "so far today" against a provisional bar. The status line shows the update time.
- `/refreshes` shows the kind as *Intraday prices*, `skipped` runs with their reason, and a line in the Last nightly tile: today's intraday runs, the last one, failures and skips.
- **Setting it up is on cron-job.org, not in this repo** — nothing runs until that job exists.

#### A single-round refresh re-priced the same 500 stocks for ever (2026-09-24)
**The owner asked why only 500 of 1,165 stocks were being refreshed, and the answer was worse than the slice size: it was the same 500 every time.** Measured on production after the first scheduled intraday run:

| | |
|---|---|
| freshly priced | **500 of 1,164 (43%)** |
| of the FIRST 500 in universe order | **500** |
| of the remaining 665 | **0** |
| the tail's price age | **90 to 119 minutes, and climbing all session** |

**The pacing worked; its cursor did not exist outside a run.** `liveRefreshOpts` took the offset from `refresh_state.priced`, and that row is only written by a MULTI-ROUND run. A plain Refresh and the intraday schedule deliberately write no such row -- one there raises the "refreshing" banner for every viewer, thirteen times a trading day -- so `done` was always 0. `notePriceRound` opened with `if (!opts.running) return`, and **the intraday route never called it at all**.

- **The cursor lives in `app_meta` under `price_cursor`**, not in `refresh_state`: one integer, no flag, no banner, and it survives the cold start a process variable would not. `readPriceCursor` / `writePriceCursor` follow the `hidden_columns` pattern.
- **It wraps**, so the universe rotates. At 1,165 symbols against a 500 slice that is three rounds -- 500, 500, 165 -- and with the schedule at 30 minutes every stock is priced about every 90 minutes instead of never.
- **A cursor past the end restarts** rather than slicing nothing, which is what happens the first time the universe shrinks below where the cursor had reached.
- **Inside a run the cursor is ignored.** A Refresh all inheriting whatever offset the schedule happened to leave would skip every stock before it and still report itself complete.
- **`PRICE_SLICE` is not the problem and was not touched.** 500 is measured: at 609 a round took 170s on a good day and 423s on a bad one and produced two 504s, so 500 holds a round near 155s against the platform's 300s kill.

Verified: 10 checks driving the REAL endpoint with the provider stubbed, reading who got priced out of `price_state` -- the per-symbol clock the Price pulled column uses -- rather than recomputing the slice arithmetic, which would only prove the same sum can be done twice. The fixture is 12 symbols against a slice of 5, so a cycle is 5 + 5 + 2 and **the wrap lands on a short round**, the case an even division would hide. **Proved by reverting**: the old line gives S00-S04 three times and 5 of 12 covered, which is the production symptom in miniature.

#### ...and then one dead ticker took the whole refresh down (2026-09-24)
**The cursor fix immediately produced two 502s in a row, and the cursor stuck at 1000 meant NOTHING was being refreshed — worse than the 500 it replaced.** Both read `Failed to reach Twelve Data: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')`, which is why the diagnosis went at the provider for an afternoon. It was ours.

- **`BF` is not a symbol Twelve Data knows** -- Brown-Forman trades as BF.A and BF.B -- and **a batched `time_series` reply carries a PER-SYMBOL error object under that key, with no `values` at all**: `{status:'error', code:404, message:'**symbol** not found: BF.'}`. That is NOT the top-level `{status:'error'}` `pullPricesFor` tests for. The call succeeded; 164 of 165 symbols came back fine.
- **Every field on the row guards a missing series except two.** `volume` and `dollarVolume` were inline IIFEs testing `values[0]` rather than `values`, so a series that is UNDEFINED rather than empty threw a TypeError out of `stocks.map`, out of `computeStocks`, and left 1,164 stocks unrefreshed. Note the shape: `error: ok ? null : (s.message || …)` two lines below ALREADY expected this payload — the row was designed for it and two siblings had not been told.
- **The cursor did not cause this, it REACHED it.** BF sits past position 1000, a slice a single-round refresh had never once pulled live, so the bug had been latent since the day BF was added.
- **A catch that names the wrong culprit costs more than no message.** `computeStocks`'s wrapped every failure as "Failed to reach Twelve Data" and **discarded the stack**. A network failure IS a TypeError too (undici's `fetch failed`), so the test is the CAUSE CHAIN — undici hangs the reason off `err.cause`, our own faults have none. It now says "Refresh failed inside the app (not the provider)" and `console.error`s the stack, since Vercel does not show a function's stdout any other way.
- **Reproduced against production with every write blocked at the libSQL client**, which is how the stack was obtained without a deploy-and-wait cycle: `createClient` is wrapped before db.js requires it, and any statement that is not a `select`/`pragma`/`create … if not exists` is logged and skipped (2,327 blocked, nothing mutated). That is the general tool for "it only fails on production data" — the local server talks to the live database, so the guard has to be mechanical rather than careful.
- **A ruled-out hypothesis worth not re-testing**: the failing round reads 1,000 symbols off the archive against 665 for the rounds that worked, so `readBarsFullFor` binds 1,001 parameters. Probed against production at 665 / 900 / 998 / 999 / 1000 / 1001 — **all fine**. There is no variable-count ceiling here.
- Verified: 16 checks with the dead symbol in the MIDDLE of the slice, so a round that merely stops early still fails — the round completes, the dead row carries the provider's own words and no fabricated price or volume, the other eleven are priced, **the price clock refuses to claim the dead one**, and the cursor still advances. **Proved by reverting**: the old expressions fail with production's exact error at the same line. Live after the deploy, the 12:45 slot: `REFRESHED in 21.9s`, positions 1000-1163 all priced, cursor wrapped to 0.
- **BF was removed from the universe** (owner), the same ending `BBX` and `PXD` got: a permanently unfillable ticker is a gap every future Fill missing re-attempts forever.

### Running the intraday schedule from a laptop (2026-09-24, owner's request)
**The intraday refresh had never once fired.** `GET /api/cron/intraday` shipped on 2026-09-15 with the note *"Setting it up is on cron-job.org, not in this repo -- nothing runs until that job exists"*, and that job was never created: on 2026-09-24 the run history held **95 runs, every one `trigger=manual`, and zero of kind `intraday`.** The owner asked for the schedule to run from their laptop instead.

- **`intraday-ping.js` is an HTTP call, not a refresh.** It reads `CRON_SECRET` and `APP_URL` out of `.env` and asks the deployed app to do the work. **It must never become `node server.js`**: booting a local server against the production database to do the same job is the documented way to burn credits and fight the live instance for the same rows.
- **The secret comes from `.env`, not from the command line or the task definition.** A scheduled task inherits almost none of a shell's environment, and a secret passed as an argument lands in the task XML and in history.
- **The server decides whether to act, which is what makes a dumb scheduler safe.** The route refuses at weekends, outside **9:38 AM - 4:00 PM New York** (`INTRADAY_START_MIN` / `INTRADAY_END_MIN`), while another refresh is running, and when the NYSE is shut for a holiday or an early close. A schedule that is broad, slightly early, or firing on Christmas morning costs one credit and changes nothing, and daylight saving needs no thought at either end.
- **Exit 0 on a skip, 1 only on unreachable or refused.** A skip is the design working; a task that goes red every weekend teaches its owner to ignore it.
- **`intraday-task.ps1` registers the Windows task**: weekdays, 09:45, repeating every 30 minutes for six hours -- thirteen firings, last at 15:45. There is deliberately no 16:00 slot: the 4:15 PM nightly is what records the settled close.

**A LAPTOP IS A WEAK CRON HOST, and three Task Scheduler defaults make it weaker.** `AllowStartIfOnBatteries` and `DontStopIfGoingOnBatteries` are set because **Task Scheduler refuses to start a task on battery by default** -- an unplugged laptop would silently skip every slot. `StartWhenAvailable` runs a missed slot when the lid opens, and `WakeToRun` asks the machine to wake for one, **which does not work on Modern Standby (S0) machines** -- `powercfg /a` says which. None of that makes a laptop reliable; it makes it tolerable. An always-on scheduler (cron-job.org, as originally chosen, or a Vercel cron) is still the better host, and the endpoint is identical for all three.

- **The schedule is in LOCAL time and this machine is on Eastern**, so 09:45 here is 09:45 in New York. If the laptop moves timezone the trigger moves with it and the server refuses whatever lands outside its window -- which is the argument for the window living on the server rather than in the schedule.
- **Both files are ASCII only.** Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a `.ps1` as ANSI unless it carries a BOM, so an em-dash in a comment is a parse error at a line nowhere near it; and `Get-Content` decodes the log as ANSI, so a UTF-8 dash in a message arrives as mojibake. Verified: registered, inspected (`DaysOfWeek 62` = Mon-Fri, `PT30M for PT6H`, battery start allowed, wake on, run-if-missed on), triggered once end to end, and the log read back clean.

### A SLOT is several rounds, and only the last one is expensive (2026-09-24, owner's request)
**"Why are we not refreshing the entire universe every 30 minutes?"** Because one round cannot: prices are 1 credit a symbol against a hard **610/minute** ceiling, so a round takes `PRICE_SLICE` (500) and no more, and a lap of 1,164 stocks took three slots — **90 minutes**. The 500 is also what keeps a round inside the platform's 300s kill (at 609 a round took 170s good, 423s bad, and produced two 504s).

**Nothing about the CADENCE forbids it — the scheduler was firing once per slot, and one call was one round.** So the fix is in the ping, not the pacing.

- **THE NAIVE VERSION IS THREE FULL ROUNDS AND IT TRIPLES THE DATABASE READ FOR NO EXTRA PRICES.** An ordinary round re-reads the ~470-day archive window for everything it did not price live, rescores, and rewrites the snapshot — **work that is identical whether the round priced 500 symbols or 5**. Measured in the test: 6 window reads against 2.
- **So a slot is `rounds - 1` LIGHT rounds and one FULL one.** The light round is the body that already existed behind `/api/refresh-prices` — next slice, archive it, move the cursor, no window, no scoring, no snapshot — **extracted as `runPriceSlice()` rather than copied**, and reached at `/api/cron/intraday?light=1` so it sits behind the same four gates (weekday, 9:38-16:00 New York, nothing else running, NYSE open) as every other intraday call. A separate route would have needed its own copy of those or it would price on Christmas.
- **THE FULL ROUND MUST BE LAST, and that ordering IS the feature.** It reads its unpriced remainder off the archive, which by then holds the bars the light rounds just wrote — so the closing snapshot is fresh for **every** stock, not just its own slice. Nothing in `computeStocks` needed changing for that; it falls out of the archive being the join.
- **A slot is ONE run of N rounds, not N runs.** The first call opens it, `?run=` attaches the rest, and only the full round closes it — so `/refreshes` reads "3 rounds, 1,164 priced" rather than 39 runs a day that each look like a whole refresh. A slot abandoned half way is swept like any other run that stopped reporting; `startRun` writes no `refresh_state`, so there is still no banner and no stand-aside.
- **The SERVER plans the slot.** `?dry=1` now reports `total`, `slice` and `rounds`, because both of the first two move and a copy of that arithmetic in a scheduler goes stale in silence. **An older server answers neither and the ping falls back to one full round** — exactly the previous behaviour, which is what makes the deploy order not matter. The Windows task is unchanged.
- **Measured on the first real slot, and the light rounds are far cheaper than estimated**: `500 symbols in 4.0s`, `500 in 3.5s`, then the rebuild in `21.2s` — **2m34s wall clock, of which 130s is the two mandatory 62s gaps**. Afterwards all 1,164 carried a price under three minutes old. Roughly 1,250 credits a slot (~16k a trading day, and Pro has no daily cap), no minute anywhere near 610.

| | rounds/slot | coverage | 470-day window reads/slot |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 1 full | every 90 min | 2 |
| three full rounds | 3 full | every 30 min | **6** |
| **2 light + 1 full** | 3 | **every 30 min** | **2** |

- Verified: **26 checks** driving the real routes with the provider stubbed and **`Date.now` OFFSET (not frozen) to a Wednesday mid-session**, so the gate is exercised rather than dodged and elapsed-time code still works. The load-bearing check compares the slot against a **measured baseline** rather than a hardcoded number — three rounds cost the same two window reads as one ordinary round — because hardcoding it would make the test a statement about today's call sites instead of about the saving. **Proved by reverting**: disabling the light branch gives 6 against 2, the exact 3x this avoids. Plus the closing snapshot fresh for all twelve fixture stocks including the ten only a light round touched, the cursor wrapping, one run of three rounds, and `/api/refresh-prices` still working after the extraction.
- **The provider's closes move with an `EPOCH` counter in that fixture**, which is the only way to tell a price refreshed by this slot from one left over from the seed. A fixture with static prices would have passed whether or not the light rounds' work reached the snapshot.

## Refresh runs — the history page
**`/refreshes` (admin only, linked from the console's Data section) tracks every refresh run, manual or scheduled (2026-09-15).** `refresh_state` is the live flag and is deleted when a run ends; `refresh_runs` (one row per run) and `refresh_rounds` (one per round) are what is left afterwards. Kinds: `refresh` (plain price Refresh, a run of one round), `all`, `missing` (Fill missing), `nightly`, `nightly-full`, `nasdaq` (the three exchange pulls as one run). As-of views are lookups, not refreshes, and are not recorded.

- **Linking a stateless round to its run**: `refresh_state.run_id`. The browser loop passes `&run=<id>` on every `/api/stocks?refresh=1`, the workflow passes `runId` in its body, the NASDAQ page passes it between its three calls. A round lands on `running.runId`, else the id it was given — so a round whose 4-minute flag aged out still lands on the run that started it.
- **Credits are MEASURED**: `fetchJson` adds each response's `Api-Credits-Request` header to an `AsyncLocalStorage` meter (`creditMeter`) that `metered()` opens around each round's `computeStocks`; `fetchProfile` counts pulls and refusals into the same meter. Outside a metered round the store is undefined and nothing is counted.
- **Outcomes**: `complete` (finishLiveRefresh's covered branch), `incomplete` (the client's or the job's DELETE — gave up), `stopped`, `failed` (a plain Refresh or NASDAQ pull that errored), `abandoned` (still `running` with no update for `RUN_ABANDON_MS`, 6 min — swept lazily by every read, so no job has to), `running`. **`finishRun` only closes a run still running**, so the client's give-up arriving after a Stop cannot overwrite it.
- **Stop** (`POST /api/refresh-runs/stop`): clears the flag, marks the run `stopped`, sends the report. The loop driving it is told on its next round — `/api/stocks?refresh=1&run=<stopped id>` answers `{stopped:true}` and computes nothing (measured 0.4s, no round written), the cron route answers `{done:true, stopped:true}` and the workflow exits 0. **Without the run id the loop would have carried on as plain refreshes**, which is why every caller passes it.
- **Reports are stored on the run** (`report_html`, whether or not mail went out — `sendRefreshReport` now builds for a tracked run even without `MAIL_READY`), with failed and still-missing symbol lists; the page shows the report in a sandboxed iframe.
- **The missed-night alarm is a Vercel cron, not GitHub** (`vercel.json`, `GET /api/cron/watchdog` at 23:30 UTC — 7:30 PM EDT / 6:30 PM EST; Hobby crons fire somewhere in the hour). The failure it exists for is GitHub's scheduler not firing, and a watchdog on the same scheduler would miss the same night. It mails only for `missed`, `failed`, `abandoned`, `incomplete` or `stopped` on today's New York date; `running`, `pending` and `untracked` stay quiet. Vercel sends `Authorization: Bearer $CRON_SECRET`, which `isCron` already checks. `?dry=1` returns the verdict without mailing.
- **`nightVerdicts()`** judges each New York day by the newest nightly-kind run started that day (any trigger — a workflow_dispatch counts): ok / running / missed / pending (today before 5 PM) / untracked (before the first recorded run) / the run's own status.
- **The workflow** now sends `trigger` (`manual` for workflow_dispatch), the Actions `runUrl` (stored as the run's link, GitHub URLs only), and the `runId` from its start call on every round; it exits 0 on `stopped`.
- **Retention**: `pruneRuns()` rides every finishLiveRefresh — 90 days of runs, 30 of rounds. **Tracking never fails a refresh** (`trackSafe`), the bars rule.
- **The page**: the live run (progress against the run's own targets, rounds, ETA at 7 profiles a round, credits so far, last round vs 610, GitHub link, Stop), a health strip (last nightly, 14 New York nights, company-data age buckets + the Fill missing count + prices-through), trends (nightly run time over 30 runs coloured by outcome, credits per day stacked by kind), filterable history (type / trigger / outcome), and a run dialog (round chart with the 610 line, refused rounds in red, the coverage curve, a round table, the stored report). Polls every 10s while a run is live, 60s otherwise.
- Verified: db functions against the real tables with test rows removed afterwards (13 checks — round numbering, aggregates through an error round, Stop not overwritten, abandonment sweep, report storage); a local route walk (anon/guest 302 and 403, admin 200, 404 for an unknown run, the stopped short-circuit, watchdog 401 without the secret); the workflow's jq payloads; headless page runs over synthetic history (live card, Stop, 14 nights, trends, filters, dialog with rounds and report).

## Refresh state
**One Refresh All pulls prices ONCE (2026-09-13).** Its first round fetches prices live (chunked, 1 credit/symbol), archives them via `persistBars`, and stamps `prices_at` on `refresh_state`; every later round sees the stamp and rebuilds all rows **from the archive** (`readBarsFullFor`, zero price credits, SPY alone re-fetched live for 1 credit since the benchmark is deliberately never archived — the orphan sweep would collect it). An archive round therefore affords **7 profiles** (7×80 = 560 of the 610/min, `PROFILE_CAP_ARCHIVE_ROUND`), while any pass that also pulls prices sizes its profile batch down via `liveRefreshOpts()` so prices + profiles fit one minute — at 93 symbols that is 6, at 300 it is 3. Rounds run 62s apart; the browser budget is `ceil(total/7)+6` and the workflow's `MAX_ROUNDS` is 60 (~400-symbol headroom). At 300 symbols a full run is ~44 rounds ≈ 46 minutes. A Refresh All re-pulls only that round budget of profiles per call, 62s apart, so it runs for several minutes. The `refresh_state` table (at most one row; absent = idle) lets every instance know — a process variable cannot work, since Vercel shares nothing between them.

- `POST /api/refresh-all` expires the cache and calls `beginRefresh()`; `DELETE /api/refresh-all` ends it when the client's loop finishes or gives up.
- Each `?refresh=1` round calls `noteRefreshProgress()`, which **only updates a refresh that is already running** — that is what stops an ordinary price Refresh (seconds long) from raising the banner. It closes the flag itself once every row has a profile.
- `readRefreshState()` returns `null` once `updated_at` is older than `REFRESH_STALE_MS` (4 min), so an admin closing the tab mid-backfill can't pin the notice up forever.
- **The browser loop's round budget scales with the universe**: `ceil(total / 6) + 4`, where `total` comes from the `POST /api/refresh-all` response. It was a flat 15, which at 84 symbols left one round of slack — so a single refused round ended a run early and it stopped at 78/84. Refused rounds now have their own allowance (`REFUSALS_ALLOWED`) instead of spending the budget of a round that would have fetched something.
- **`DELETE /api/refresh-all` reports too**, like the cron job's equivalent. That is the give-up path — the loop ran out of rounds, or the tab was closed — and a run that stopped short has to say so. It discarded `endRefresh()`'s return before, so an incomplete run went silent, which is indistinguishable from success.
- **`endRefresh()` returns the run it cleared, or `null`.** Both the natural finish and the client's `DELETE` land there, and only the caller whose `delete` actually removed a row gets the state back — that is what stops one run sending two report emails. Anything hung off completion must go through its return value, not just call it.
- `GET /api/status` is a cheap poll for viewers — every open page hits it every 30s while a refresh runs, so it deliberately does not return the snapshot. When the flag clears the page pulls the finished data on its own.

## Similar stocks — the peer table at the foot of `/stock` (2026-09-26, owner's request)
**Up to six companies in the same industry, closest by market cap, with price / today / 1Y / market cap / forward P/E / the Balanced verdict and a `vs` pill into `/compare`.** The stock page was a dead end: you arrive from the screener and the only way sideways is a picker listing 1,185 names alphabetically.

- **FORWARD P/E IS THE ONE COLUMN THAT DOES NOT TAKE `FIELD_SPEC`'s ANSWER** (added 2026-09-26, owner's request). `['fund','Fwd P/E', V.num(s.forwardPe)]` prints a loss-maker's **-41.7** verbatim, which is tolerable in a labelled row on one stock and actively misleading **down a column of six**, where the eye reads the most negative number as the cheapest. Live, **73 of 1,167** companies carry one, and the first real screenshot found one in the top six: APTV's Auto Parts peers read 10.4 / 18.0 / 7.2 / **Aurora at -13.5** / 10.7 / 7.5. A non-positive one is a dash and the note says why — **a multiple off a loss is arithmetic, not cheapness**, the Size card's rule and the Bubble card's, met a third time. `> 0` rejects the empty before coercing in the same expression, since `Number(null)` is 0. **Proved by reverting**: without the guard four checks fail and the column prints `-41.7`.
  - **This is a deliberate divergence from the hover card, `/stock`'s own field list and `/compare`, which all still print the negative.** Left alone rather than fixed globally: in a labelled single-stock row "Fwd P/E −41.7" reads as *this company loses money*, and changing `FIELD_SPEC` would move five surfaces for a request about one. Worth revisiting as its own decision.

#### The stock itself is the first row (2026-09-29, owner's request)
**"I want to see a line for Bristol-Myers on top in the similar stock section."** Without it the reader compares six companies against a seventh they have to hold in their head, scrolling back up the page for each number — which is most of the work this table exists to save.

- **ONE ROW BUILDER, and that is the whole value of the row.** `peerRow` was extracted from the `rows` map and is used for the anchor and the peers both. Formatting the anchor separately would leave the one comparison this table exists for running between two different formatters — the drift `RowCard.fieldValues` is here to prevent — and it would look perfectly correct on screen. The **Fwd P/E guard therefore reaches the anchor too**, which is the sharpest place for it yet: a loss-maker reading `-41.7` at the head of the column it is meant to be compared against is worse than the same number anywhere else.
- **It is NOT a peer and is counted as one nowhere.** `total` already excluded the anchor's own display name, `seen` already held it before the pick loop, and the caption still reads *"Others in Drug Manufacturers - General … 12 in the industry"* — which stays true because the extra row is visibly *this stock* rather than another one.
- **Three differences from a peer row, and no fourth**: the tint, a name that is **not a link to the page you are already on**, and **no `vs` pill** — a stock cannot be compared with itself. The cell is still emitted so the columns line up; reverting that produces `/compare/ANCH/ANCH`, which is the argument.
- **A TINT, nothing louder.** Every colour on this page already means something — green and red are direction, amber is *notice this*, the accent is a link — and "this is the stock you are looking at" is not a reading about the data. It is the hovered-row treatment, held on, plus a `this stock` chip.
- **THE CHIP COST THE PHONE ITS NUMBERS, and the existing suite caught it.** It is ~70px of a 390px screen, and it pushed Today off the visible box — the exact fault the 116px name truncation was written for. Hidden under 620px, where the tint says which row it is anyway. `.self` also takes the same `max-width` box as `.namelink`, or the one row that is not a link is the one row that breaks the column.
- **An older server sends no `self`** and the table simply opens with the peers, so deploy order is not a thing to think about.
- Verified inside the existing 56-check peers suite rather than beside it — it is that table's own property. **Four of its checks had to CHANGE rather than be worked around**: "the six the API chose" now skips `tr.me`, the Fwd P/E column carries seven values, the loss-maker moved a row down, and the phone draws seven. **Proved by reverting four times**: dropping `self` fails 9, the page not drawing it fails 9, keeping the `vs` pill fails 2, and not hiding the chip on a phone fails 2 — including Today back off the screen at 353px against a 333px box.
  - **A test fault worth keeping**: the new checks first compared the drawn name against `p.self.name`, but `p` had been reassigned by the cases above, so ANCH's row was being checked against the no-cap anchor's name. A variable reused across cases is not a payload.

- **IT COSTS NOTHING, which is what settled it.** `/api/stock` already holds the whole snapshot in memory to find the stock and build that picker, so peers are a filter over rows in hand. Asserted rather than claimed: the test wraps `global.__client` and counts round trips, and a request that builds a group makes **exactly as many as one that does not** (2 vs 2).
- **"Similar" is defined and the page SAYS which definition it used.** Same industry, ranked by the **log ratio** of market cap — caps here span six orders of magnitude, so a linear distance means "the other trillion-dollar companies" for a mega-cap and "everything under a billion" for a small one. Measured on the live 1,185: **909 stocks have 6+ industry peers, 174 have 3-5, 66 have 1-2, 14 are alone**, so the `PEER_MIN_INDUSTRY` floor of 3 widens **80 stocks (7%)** to their sector and leaves 93% on the finer cut. A widened group prints *"Only 1 other in Uranium, so this is Energy instead"* rather than silently answering a different question.
- **A FUND IS NOT A COMPANY, AND THE REFUSAL HAS TO RUN BOTH WAYS** (owner: "no peer group needed for etfs"). Refusing it only as an ANCHOR is the bug that shipped in the first run: a sector fund is classified into the industry it tracks, so `FUND1` sat fifth in the fixture's Semiconductors group at a "$6B market cap" that is really **AUM**. `companyType === 'ETF'` now excludes it from the pool as well. Live, that is SMH, SOXX, QQQ and fifteen others.
- **No peer table for a GUEST** (owner's call). The preview is twenty stocks, so a filtered group would be nought to two rows of a table whose whole claim is *here is the rest of the industry* — and one more route that has to remember to narrow.
- **Formatted through `RowCard.fieldValues()` server-side**, the `mobileRow()` pattern, so a number cannot read one way here and another on the row it came from — and the payload is ~1KB rather than the ~18KB six whole snapshot rows would cost.
- **IT MUST NOT BECOME A RECOMMENDATION.** No ordering by return, no tick on a "winner", and the note says so: *"not a ranking, and not a list of better alternatives"*. That is the line the rest of the product declines to cross, and a peer table is the easiest place to cross it by accident.
- 22 rows carry no industry yet and four of those carry no sector either; they simply draw no section. **A heading with an empty table would be worse than no heading.**
- Verified: **56 checks**. The fixture anchors at a MID-SIZED $50B with the industry's biggest company five rows down, so **alphabetical, largest-first and same-sector-ignoring-industry each fail**; plus the sector fallback, an anchor with no cap of its own (largest first, and the payload says so), the round-trip count, the formatter against `fieldValues` directly, and the page at 1500px and 390px. **Proved by reverting** three times — the unfiltered pool puts the fund fifth, and dropping the phone rule fails all three phone checks.
  - **A screenshot found both layout faults, as usual here**: `.rng` never resets `text-decoration`, so the `vs` pill arrived underlined; and at 390px a full legal name took the whole viewport with every number off-screen. Below 620px the name link truncates to 116px and the compare column stands aside.
  - **A short fixture name made two of those assertions vacuous.** With `Near One` in place of a real 39-character legal name they passed with the truncation reverted — caught only because the revert-proof was run. **A width assertion needs input at the length the provider actually returns.**

## Which dates the fundamentals actually describe (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**A caption under the Fundamentals heading on `/stock`, naming every date that gives those figures a period:** the trailing-twelve-month period they cover, the fiscal year end where it is not December, when the company last reported, when it reports next, and when we pulled the profile. Plus two rows — **Dividend paid** and **Last split**. The owner's words were *"we don't show the Fundamental reporting date"* and then *"show all the dates that are meaningful"*; **"Keep Edgar out of this"** scoped it to the vendor's own fields, so the SEC card is untouched.

> Trailing twelve months to 31 May 2026 · fiscal year ends 28 Aug · reported 24 Jun 2026, after hours · next due 12 Nov 2026 · pulled 2 days ago

- **EVERY FIELD IS FREE.** `most_recent_quarter` and `fiscal_year_ends` ride on the `/statistics` call `fetchProfile` already makes and already pays 50 credits for; `dividend_date` and `last_split_date` sit beside the `ex_dividend_date` that was already being kept. **A day not recorded is gone for good** — the API only ever returns today's numbers — which is the same argument that took the profile from 16 stored fields to 58.
- **THE FOUR NEW FIELDS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT IN `emptyProfile()`, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DECISION.** `PROFILE_FIELDS = Object.keys(emptyProfile())` and `profileGaps()` flags any stored profile MISSING one — so declaring them would make **all 1,188 profiles a `fields` gap at once**, and the nightly expires gaps before it rotates: ~170 rounds, ~2.9 hours against a 90-minute timeout, **~96,000 credits**, and a failed run. The `earningsRows` precedent exactly, and the `instrumentType` entry records the same arithmetic. The cost is that they are **null on every existing profile and fill over the ordinary 7-day rotation** — until then the caption shows only *reported / next due / pulled*, with no TTM period. **Proved by reverting**: declaring them fails 5.
- **A PROFILE FIELD DOES NOT REACH THE ROW UNLESS `computeStocks` NAMES IT.** It copies profile fields one by one rather than spreading, which shipped `instrumentType` blank for ever once already. All five are named explicitly, and the suite asserts it. **Proved by reverting**: dropping one line fails 1.
- **`most_recent_quarter` IS A PERIOD, NOT A FILING DATE** — measured before it was wired to anything: the announcement lands **23-29 days after** the vendor's date across the universe, so labelling it "reported" would be wrong by a month. It is *Trailing twelve months to <date>*, which is also what the figures beside it actually are. The announcement is a different fact and comes from `earnings_history`.
- **The vendor rounds a 52/53-week fiscal calendar to month-end** — MU and NVDA differ from their filings by 2-5 days. Harmless as a period label, and the reason the caption never claims to be a filing date.
- **The fiscal year end is shown only when it is NOT December**, since for most companies it says nothing. That is the one line that changes how every other figure should be read for the ~15% it applies to.
- **`readEarnings` RENAMES ON THE WAY OUT** — the table's `d` and `reported` become `date` and `time` on the payload. Reading the stored names gives `undefined`, and the announcement clause then **silently vanishes** rather than erroring. **Proved by reverting**: fails 3.
- **Dates are parsed at LOCAL NOON** (`+'T12:00:00'`), because `new Date('2026-05-31')` is UTC midnight and renders as the 30th west of Greenwich — the card-dating lesson, met again.
- **`captions` is a new `buildSections` option**, so a caption belongs to the page that knows the dates rather than to `FIELD_SPEC`. Opt-in: only `/stock` passes it, and the hover card and the tiles are unchanged.
- Verified: **32 checks** — the caption's clauses present and absent (a December year end omitted, a stock with no quarter showing no TTM clause), both new rows, the five fields on the row, and the four absent from `PROFILE_FIELDS`. **Proved by reverting four times**, every one load-bearing.
  - **A FIELD_SPEC row always renders with an em-dash; only an `extra` row is omitted.** An assertion that a missing dividend date draws nothing was testing the wrong contract.
  - **`period_type` is `'Q'`, not `'quarterly'`** — a probe filtering on the long word returned 0 rows and briefly read as empty data over a healthy 269,597.

### The same date on the SCREENER — a Reported column and a Reported row (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**"Can we show that date … on the screener as well in the fundamental section."** Both, at the owner's choice when asked: a **`Reported` column last in the Fundamentals group** (96 → 97 columns) and a **`Reported` row leading the `fund` group in `FIELD_SPEC`**, which puts it in the hover card, the tiles, the phone and `/compare` at once.

- **NO BACKFILL AND NO ROTATION WAIT, unlike the four fields shipped that morning.** `lastEarningsDate` has been in `emptyProfile()` all along, so every stored profile carries it, and **`computeStocks` already named it** — it was simply never displayed, surfacing only inside the Next Earn cell's *tooltip* (`· last 2026-06-24, …`) and as the screen-only `daysSinceEarnings` key. The whole feature is display.
- **It is in FUNDAMENTALS rather than beside Next Earn in Info, and that is the point of the request.** The two are a pair of dates, but this one is a **property of the numbers it stands with**: it says when the margins, growth and multiples beside it were struck. That is also why the `FIELD_SPEC` row LEADS its group rather than joining the dividend dates at the foot — a reader should see how old the figures are before reading them.
- **AMBER PAST 100 DAYS**, where the company has missed a normal quarterly cadence and everything in the group is a quarter stale — the colour's existing meaning here (*notice this, it is old*), the Price pulled column's rule. `.warn` is colour-only, so the cell stays a table cell; there is a check on that and the threshold is **probed at 100 AND 101**, since a threshold is a step function.
- **THE YEAR JOINS THE LABEL ONLY WHEN IT IS NOT THIS ONE** (`Jul 27 '25`). A two-year-old date reading `Jun 24` beside one from this quarter is exactly the kind of thing nobody notices is wrong — the Price pulled cell's same bargain with the time of day.
- **THE FILTER COUNTS DAYS SINCE, mirroring Next Earn's days-to**: a raw date string is nothing anyone can type against, the `pricedAt` rule. **TWO NAMES, ONE EXPRESSION** — `daysSinceEarnings` is the screen-only key the starter screens already filter on and `lastEarningsDate` is the column's, so a second copy of that arithmetic would be the drift `filters.js` exists to prevent.
- **SORTING NEEDED NO SPECIAL CASE, and that is luck worth asserting.** `valueFor` falls through to the raw field and an ISO date sorts lexically, so descending really is most-recent-first — the News column needed a branch only because `newsAge` is not a field. There is a check, because the day the stored format changes that silently inverts.

#### `/stock` STATES IT BETTER, SO THE ROW STANDS ASIDE THERE — `buildSections({ skip })`
A `FIELD_SPEC` row reaches `/stock` too, where the Fundamentals caption **already** says `reported 24 Jun 2026, after hours` — so the first cut printed the same date twice, six lines apart. Worse than untidy: **the two can genuinely disagree.** The caption reads `earnings_history`, rewritten every refresh round and carrying the time of day; the row reads the PROFILE's copy, which lags by up to the **7-day rotation**. Two different dates under one label is worse than either alone.

- **`skip` is a new `buildSections` option** — a list of `group|label` keys a page drops because it states the same fact better elsewhere. Only `/stock` passes it, for `fund|Reported`, the way only `/stock` passes `extra` and `captions`.
- **The caption was NOT trimmed instead.** That was the other candidate and it is the worse one: it would have left the page's single statement coming from the *staler* of two sources, and lost the time of day with it.
- **Proved by reverting**: dropping the `skip` draws `ReportedSep 20` directly under a caption already saying it.

#### "NEXT DUE 8 SEPT 2026" THREE WEEKS AFTER IT (2026-09-30, owner, from a screenshot of Loews)
**`/stock/L` read `reported 9 Jun 2026, after hours · next due 8 Sept 2026 · pulled 4 days ago` on 30 September.** Two faults in the caption, both mine, and the second only possible because of the first.

- **`8 Sept 2026` WAS NEVER A VENDOR DATE — it is our own arithmetic.** `fetchProfile` falls back to `last report + 91 days` when `/earnings` offers no upcoming one, and 2026-06-09 + 91 is exactly 2026-09-08. The row carries `nextEarningsEstimated: true` and **the Next Earn column has always marked that with a leading `~`** (`~Sep 8`, visible in the same screenshot, four inches to the left). The caption dropped the distinction and stated the estimate as fact.
- **AND A DATE IN THE PAST CANNOT BE "NEXT DUE".** Measured on the live screen the same evening: **51 of 1,188 rows carry a next-earnings date that has already passed, and EVERY ONE of them is an estimate — 0 confirmed.** That is the whole diagnosis in one number: a vendor-confirmed date never goes stale, our +91 guess lapses the moment the real report slips past it. 42 rows also last reported over 100 days ago, so the new amber column was already flagging most of them.
- **The replacement clause is about OUR RECORD, not about the company**, which may well have reported without the vendor telling us: `due about 8 Sept 2026, not yet recorded`. A future estimate keeps "next due" and gains the same hedge — `next due about 19 Oct 2099`. A confirmed date is not hedged, and there is a check for that, or the word would spread to every row.
- **THE ESTIMATE ITSELF IS DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED, and that is a boundary rather than laziness.** `nextEarningsDate` is read by the Advice engine's earnings guard, by the Next Earn column and by the "Reporting in 14 days" screen — suppressing a lapsed one at source would move verdicts. **New data may feed display surfaces but must never feed the live Advice calculation**, and the inverse holds too: a display fault is fixed on the display. Worth raising separately; several of the 51 are **funds** (DRAM, ITA, KWEB, SOXX, BUG), which file no earnings at all and should arguably never have been given a date.
- **The vendor's record for L is independently thin** — 2026-06-09, 2026-04-30, then a **three-year hole back to 2023-04-30** — and the profile was pulled 3 days before the report, so this is the vendor's own gap rather than our staleness. Nothing to fix here; worth knowing before reading a long "not yet recorded" as a bug in the app.
- Verified inside `funddate-test.js`, that caption's own suite, which went 32 → **39 checks**: two new fixtures, a LAPSED estimate carrying the Loews shape exactly and a FUTURE one, plus a check that the confirmed date is not hedged. **Proved by reverting twice**: restoring the unconditional `next due` fails 2, and dropping the estimate hedge fails 2.
  - **The heredoc ate a backslash level for the FOURTH time on this project** — `'\n-- …'` in a patch script became a real newline inside a JS string literal and the file would not parse. Use Write/Edit for anything carrying an escape.

#### THE VENDOR'S EARNINGS FEED GOES STALE, AND OUR OWN FILINGS PROVE IT (2026-10-01, owner, from a Google Finance screenshot of VNO)
**"Our system says last reported 4-May-2026 whereas Google Finance says 3-Aug-2026."** Correct, and it is the vendor rather than us.
