It is the file everyone reaches for and it is **not loaded**. The **bi-weekly** consolidated file (`cdn.finra.org/equity/otcmarket/biweekly/shrt<date>.csv`, 2.75MB, 22,595 symbols) is the real position, and that is this.

**THE PAID FIELD IS THIS NUMBER.** `fetchProfile` computes `shortPctFloat = shares_short / float_shares × 100`; doing the same arithmetic with FINRA's position and our stored `floatShares` reproduces it to **0.00pt on NVDA, PTON, MU and JPM** (AAPL −0.08pt). So the provider adds nothing here, and the free source adds the **~8 years of history it does not sell at all** — 2017-12-29 onward, 210 readings for a long-listed name.

- **ONE CALL PER SYMBOL, not one per settlement date.** A symbol's whole history comes back in a single request — NVDA is 210 rows and **8.9KB**. The other shape, ~190 bulk files at 2.7MB, is 513MB to extract the same ~10MB. The API (`api.finra.org/data/group/otcMarket/name/consolidatedShortInterest`, keyless, POST) is **partitioned by `settlementDate`**, which its own 400 error tells you — so sorting needs that key, and the bulk file stays the right tool for the fortnightly top-up, where one file covers everyone.
- **`shortint-load.js` is local**, the `insider-load.js` precedent: dry run by default, `--commit`, `--only`, `--missing`, `--rate`. Measured: **10 symbols, 1,947 readings, 0.3 min**, so the universe is ~230k readings and ~35 minutes.

##### THE FIRST FULL RUN DIED AT 65% AND REPORTED SUCCESS (2026-09-28)
**Turso answered one batch write with an `HTTP 404`** — transient, the database was healthy a minute later — and the run stopped at **769 of 1,181 symbols, 142,682 readings**. Two separate faults, and the second is the one that hides the first.

- **THE WRITE SAT OUTSIDE THE TRY/CATCH.** Only the FETCH was guarded, so a database blip threw clean out of the loop and abandoned the remaining 412 symbols. It has its own catch now: a blip costs ONE symbol, never the run, and the symbol is left **unrecorded rather than marked checked**, so `--missing` picks it up — the insider walk's rule, where a day that fails does not advance the cursor. `ok`/`rows` are also incremented AFTER the write lands, or the receipt overstates what is actually stored.
- **`node script.js | tail` REPORTS `tail`'s EXIT CODE, NOT NODE'S.** The crash dump was right there in the output above a cheerful `[exited with code 0]`. This is the *inverse* of the lesson this file already carries for backfills — there, a batch succeeded and exited 1; here it failed and exited 0. **The rule that covers both: judge a load by the rows it stored, never by how it exited.** `readShortState()` answers that in one small read and is what was used to find the real figure.
- **The rate was also 3x my estimate**, and for the reason this file already records: the ten-symbol trial wrote into an EMPTY table at ~33 symbols/min; against a filling one it settled at ~10/min. **Budget a backfill by the archive it is writing INTO, not by the symbol count.**

#### It tops itself up now, and the cadence is DAILY because the data is fortnightly (2026-10-01, owner: "how best to schedule this")
**`GET /api/cron/shortint`, bearer-authenticated, run as its own phase by `nightly-ping.js` after the rotation completes — beside `secRotate()` and for the same reasons.** Until this, picking up a new settlement date meant remembering to run the local loader.

**THE CADENCE QUESTION WAS ASKED AS "why not weekly", AND THE DATA ANSWERS IT.** Measured off NVDA's 210 stored settlement dates rather than recalled: **exactly 24 a year, every year since 2018**, with gaps of 13–19 calendar days (85 at 15 days, 57 at 14, 25 at 16) and **not one of 7**. FINRA publishes the consolidated position twice a month — the 15th and the month end — so half of a weekly job would find nothing, and under the old tool that half was not free (see below).

- **DAILY, and that is not a contradiction.** A fortnightly *calendar* cannot line up with a gap that varies by six days: a fixed cron drifts off the real dates, sometimes firing before publication and sometimes twice for one settlement. A daily self-pacing check needs no calendar, catches a date within hours of publication, and **heals after any number of missed runs** — `noteTechMark`'s rule, which exists for exactly this.
- **THE DATE IS DISCOVERED BY ASKING FINRA, NEVER BY COMPUTING IT.** Settlement dates are the 15th and month end *rolled back over weekends AND market holidays*, which is where the 13–19 day spread comes from — so deriving them means maintaining a holiday list, and this project already refused that once: the intraday gate asks the provider whether the NYSE is open precisely so *"there is no holiday list to maintain"*. One POST for one liquid symbol (`SHORTINT_PROBE`, default NVDA) answers it exactly and cannot drift.
- **So a run writes nothing on almost every day, by design**: one `max(newest)` read, one POST, done. **Proved by reverting**: dropping the cutoff fails 2 and fetches the bulk file on a day with nothing new.
- **THE API CAN KNOW A DATE BEFORE THE BULK FILE IS POSTED**, so that is a reported state rather than a failure — `{pending: '2026-09-30'}`, and tomorrow's run collects it. An unreachable FINRA is the same: `{done, error}`, non-fatal, nothing written. This data is already **eight business days old** when it appears and nothing downstream reads it, so being a day late costs nothing.
- **ONE FILE COVERS EVERY SYMBOL.** The bi-weekly bulk file is 2.75MB and ~22,595 symbols against **1,192 per-symbol calls for the same ~1,192 rows**. The per-symbol API stays the right tool for a cold load of nine years; this is the right tool for one fortnight. `ShortInt.parse` already reads both shapes — it sniffs the delimiter and takes the bulk file's own date field — so **the split guard comes along for free**, which is the point of going through the parser rather than round it: FINRA does not restate for splits and ships a `changePercent` anyway (NVDA's 10:1 reads **+978.77%**), and `normalise` withholds it wherever `stockSplitFlag` is set.

##### `appendShortInterest` is the other half of a PAIR, and confusing the two would destroy the archive
`writeShortInterest` opens with `delete from short_interest where symbol = ?` — correct for a full per-symbol load, and catastrophic as a top-up: picking up one new fortnight would rewrite all **220,386** stored readings, ~2 hours at the measured ~10 symbols/min against a filling table. **The screens-incident rule, which cost thirteen screens their filters: a restore or a top-up must not pass through a transforming path.**

- **IDEMPOTENT BY CONSTRUCTION**, which is what makes a daily check safe to run as often as it likes: the primary key is `(symbol, d)`, so the same date twice writes the same rows twice and changes nothing.
- **`rows` is RECOUNTED, never incremented.** An increment drifts upward every time a date is re-applied, and a receipt that overstates what is stored is the exact failure this loader's own history records. The recount is a correlated `count(*)` per symbol **inside one statement per 200-symbol chunk** — on this database the cost is per STATEMENT rather than per row (measured 23x on `tech_history`), so 1,192 single updates would be the slowest part of a job whose data write is six statements.
- **`newest` only ever moves FORWARD.** Re-applying an older date must not drag a symbol's clock backwards and make it read as stale.
- **`shortNewest()` takes the MAX, not the min**, and it is one small read of `short_state` (1,192 rows) rather than `max(d)` over the 220k-row readings table. **Two symbols lag for ever for real reasons** — SQ stopped reporting when Block renamed its ticker (last reading 2025-01-15) and FI stands at 2025-10-31 — so the minimum would report us a year behind while 1,190 of 1,192 are current, and the job would fetch on every single run. **Proved by reverting**: the min fails 5.
- **MAP FINRA'S SPELLING BACK TO OURS, preferring the one that WORKED.** FINRA strips separators (`BRKB` for our `BRK.B`), but a handful of symbols matched on our own spelling instead and the loader recorded which in `short_state.finra_sym` — so this is a lookup rather than a second guess at the rule, with the derived rule as the fallback. **Proved by reverting twice**: no map-back fails 2, and preferring the rule over the record fails 3.
- **Only our universe, and only the date we came for.** The file carries ~21,000 symbols we do not track, and a stray row for another date must not overwrite a settled reading. **Proved by reverting**: no universe filter fails 3 (junk symbols stored), no date filter fails 2.
- **The route answers 401 and `requireAdmin` answers 403**, so the status code says which bundle is live — a 403 moments after a push is deploy lag, not an auth failure, which cost an hour once on the SEC route. An admin session also satisfies it, so `?dry=1` in a browser is the manual check; there is no `/admin` panel, deliberately, because there is nothing to drive.
- Verified: **32 checks** with FINRA stubbed at `fetch` BEFORE the server loads, so nothing reaches either address. Each case sets the API's newest date and the file's availability **independently**, because that is the feature's shape — the date is discovered from one and fetched from the other, and either can be ahead. **The load-bearing check is that HISTORY SURVIVES**: the fixture seeds four older settlement dates per symbol and counts them after, because routing the top-up through the replace stores the new date correctly and every other assertion still passes. **Proved by reverting ten times**, every one load-bearing — the replace fails 4 and leaves NVDA with one reading where it had five.
  - **The plan for the recount is asserted in this suite rather than in `query-plan-test.js`.** That test pulls SQL literals out of db.js, and the statement carrying the subquery is built with a variable placeholder count — so it lands among the 11 it reports as "could not be prepared" and is never looked at. It is the one read inside a write path, so it is checked by hand: `SEARCH short_interest USING COVERING INDEX`.
  - **A PATCH THAT MATCHES NOTHING IS WORSE THAN A WRONG PATCH, and it happened in this session.** A `python` replace adding an assertion silently hit zero times (an escaping mismatch), and the only reason it was caught is that the stale assertion beside it failed loudly. The revert harness therefore **asserts every anchor hits exactly once before applying it** and prints `PATCH DID NOT APPLY` otherwise — which is what it did for the one anchor that spanned lines, since **server.js is CRLF on disk**. The guard line is word-for-word the one on `/api/cron/alerts`, so it cannot be anchored directly; the revert shadows `isCron` for that route's body instead, which is what "the guard dropped" means behaviourally.

#### The three traps, each measured
1. **FINRA DOES NOT RESTATE FOR SPLITS, AND SHIPS A CHANGE FIGURE ANYWAY.** Measured on NVDA's 10:1 of June 2024: `current 315,033,985 | previous 29,202,972 | stockSplitFlag S | changePercent **978.77**`. The 4:1 of 2021 does the same, 7.2M → 30.0M. So a raw shares-short chart back to 2017 draws a **40× build-up in bearish bets that never happened**, and the change figure is nonsense twice a decade. The flag is what makes it safe: `changePct` is **withheld** where it is set, and **the strip draws days to cover** — a ratio, so both halves scale and NVDA rides through both splits at ~1.0.
2. **PERCENT OF FLOAT IS THE LATEST READING ONLY.** Float history is not stored (`fundamentals_history` began 2026-08-30), so dividing a 2019 position by today's float would invent a series. Shown where today's float is genuinely contemporaneous, and nowhere else — the card says so.
3. **A THIRD SPELLING OF ONE SYMBOL.** We write `BRK.B`, SEC and Yahoo write `BRK-B`, **FINRA strips the separator entirely: `BRKB`, `HEIA`** — zero dots and zero spaces across all 22,595 symbols. The failure is a silent miss, never a 404, so the loader tries our own spelling when the stripped one finds nothing.
   - **And the file format changed under us**: 2024-06-14 is unquoted pipe-delimited, 2026-09-15 is quoted, the API is comma-delimited. The parser sniffs the delimiter and treats quotes as optional, or it silently stops reading one of the three.

**THE BOUNDARY, and it matters more here than it did for the filings card.** `shortPctFloat` is **already an Advice input** — [action.js:360](private/action.js#L360) makes an Early company above 25% of float an Avoid, and 379/382 are the weak/ok fundamentals split. The live verdict keeps taking it from the profile; this table exists so the number has a HISTORY, which is the research question and a separate one. `shortint-test.js` reads the real `/api/stocks` and the real rendered screener header and fails on a leak.

- Verified: **43 checks** — all three file shapes parsed, the split's +978.77% dropped, an absent field null rather than a coerced zero, the route, the p90 ceiling ignoring a 9.0 spike, the boundary, and the card measured as drawn. **The strip's encoding is proved by a RATIO**: two fortnights either side of the split whose share counts differ ~10× and whose days-to-cover differ 1.2× must draw 1.21× apart. **Proved by reverting** three times — letting the split's change through fails 1, drawing the share count instead gives **10.75×** and fails 4, and the long header label fails 2.
  - **"The tallest bar is the spike" was the first assertion and it was wrong**: with the ceiling at p90, three bars already sit at full height, so `reduce` returned the first of them. That is the capping working as designed, and a test that asserts a unique maximum is asserting something the design does not promise.

#### And it is a CHART LAYER too, on the rug's bargain (2026-09-28, owner: "show this data in the graph section as an optional similar to what we did for Earning")
**A `SHORT` button beside `EARN`, and a strip under the plot.** Aligned by the rug's own trick — the same `margin-right: 52px` to clear the price axis, children placed by percentage — so the bars, the crosshair and the price cannot disagree. Remembered per device in `localStorage`, self-gating twice over: nothing where FINRA has no history for the company, nothing where no settlement falls in the window.

- **A LEVEL, NOT AN EVENT, which is the one way it differs from the rug.** A short position stands until the next settlement, so it is drawn as a **step line**, flat until the next reading; the rug's point-ticks would say the position existed for a single day, and a sloped line would claim it drifted day by day, which is not what is filed. **The reading BEFORE the window is carried in at the left edge** for the same reason — dropping it leaves the first fortnight of every chart blank and implies the shorts arrived later than they did.

##### IT WAS ZERO-BASED BARS FIRST, AND DOUBLING THE HEIGHT IS WHAT EXPOSED THAT (2026-09-28)
**Days to cover sits in a NARROW BAND on most stocks, so a zero-based bar spends most of the strip on empty space.** Measured across four the day it shipped:

| | days to cover over a year | lowest bar sat at |
|---|---|---|
| MU | 1.00 – 1.22 | **50% of the track** |
| NVDA | 1.00 – 2.55 | 40% |
| JPM | 1.57 – 4.60 | 43% |
| PTON | 2.74 – 11.52 | 31% |

MU's entire year lived between 50% and 61% of the height and read as a solid grey block. Doubling the strip doubled the dead space along with the signal.

- **The bars could NOT simply be given a floor.** Truncating a bar axis is the classic misleading chart: a bar is read as a quantity measured from zero. **A line carries no such claim** — it is read as a shape — so the range becomes the data's own and the variation fills the strip. **The note says the baseline is not zero**, because that is the one thing a reader could otherwise get wrong, and it prints the range the line is drawn against.
- **`preserveAspectRatio="none"` is what keeps the line aligned with the price above it**, and is exactly why the stroke carries **`vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke`** — without it the flat runs and the vertical steps draw at different weights. No `<text>` inside for the same reason; the tooltips live on transparent HTML hit areas over the line, since a path cannot carry one per segment.
- **A flat series would divide by zero** and is drawn down the middle, which is what "it did not move" looks like.
- **Proved by reverting**: forcing the baseline back to zero puts the 1.00–1.22 fixture's line at **8.7px of 56** and fails the check. The fixture carries MU's real measured range for exactly that reason — a wide-range fixture would have passed either way.
- **NEUTRAL, deliberately.** Green and red are the price's direction on this chart, and *short interest rose* is not a direction the price went. The rug can colour by the reaction because that IS the price's move; this cannot. Amber marks a split, which is the "notice this" colour and the one thing about the series that is not comparable across.
- **It rides the card's fetch.** `/api/shortint` is a separate route so the price never waits on it, so the series lands AFTER the first paint — `loadShortInt` stores it at script scope and repaints **the strip alone**. Toggling repaints the strip alone too: a full `paintChart()` would rebuild the plot, the ribbon and every overlay to switch one layer underneath them.
- **The strip is 56px, doubled from 28 at the owner's request** — under a ~500px plot the first cut was a squat band and the shape was hard to read. **The CSS height and `H` in `sintStripHtml` are ONE measurement in two places**: let them drift and the bars either float short of the top or overflow, neither of which looks broken enough to notice. There is a check that a bar at the ceiling really fills the track, and it fails on 26-of-56.
- Verified: **+24 checks** (67 total) — drawn under the plot, inset by the gutter, the split marked, nothing in the price colours, the note, the toggle surviving a reload, a one-week window self-gating, and the carried level. **Proved by reverting** twice more: dropping the carry fails 1, and drawing ticks instead of steps fails 2.
  - **THREE OF THESE ASSERTIONS WERE WRONG FIRST AND ALL THREE WERE THE FIXTURE OR THE THRESHOLD.** The alignment check compared against the earnings rug, which is **hidden on a fixture with no earnings** — and a hidden element's rect is all zeros, so it asserted `1391 vs 0` and would have passed the day the rug broke; it measures against the plot's own right edge minus the gutter now. The bars ran **200 calendar days**, ending before the last three readings, so "the split is marked" failed over a window that never contained it. And "every bar has some width" **passed against ticks**, because the threshold I chose was the same 0.35 the code uses as its floor — the real claim is that the bars **TILE**, which is what a level held until the next reading means.

##### `getClientRects().length` COUNTS LINES ON AN INLINE ELEMENT AND NOTHING ON A BLOCK ONE
**The header read `210 readings since 2017-12-29` beside the title, and at 390px both wrapped to two lines — a cramped 42px header.** Found by eye on the live page; every check in the suite passed over it. What makes it worth recording is the two wrong measurements it took to reach:

- **An ELEMENT screenshot paints whatever covers that region.** `element.screenshot()` on the card caught the **sticky nav island** sitting over its header, which read as the two texts overlapping. It is not a picture of the element alone — scroll to it and shoot the VIEWPORT when the question is what a reader sees.
- **So the first assertion checked for overlapping boxes, and there was never an overlap.** It passed against the broken version, which is the failure this file already names: *an assertion written after a layout bug found by eye must be checked against the broken version, or it records the wrong symptom.*
- **The real defect was a WRAP, and `h2.getClientRects().length` cannot see one.** On a **block** element that returns a single border box however the text flows inside it — the give-away is the box HEIGHT (36px against ~18px a line). One rect per rendered line only comes from a **Range over the contents**, which is what the check uses now: 1 line fixed, 2 lines reverted.
- **`readonly-note-test.js` is NOT affected, checked rather than assumed** — it measures the note's inner `<span>`, an inline element, where `getClientRects()` really does return a rect per line. The trap is specific to blocks.
- Fixed by dropping the date from the count (the axis below already carries `from` and `to`, so it was a repetition as well as too long) and a **scoped** `#sint .sec-h { flex-wrap: wrap }` — `.sec-h` is shared with `#sec` and `#ins`, and this project has nine unscoped classes that captured later markup.

### The Check button refuses what the provider cannot price (2026-10-03, owner's request)
**`providerCheck()` asks Twelve Data directly — one batched `/quote` per 120 symbols, 1 credit each, PINNED to the United States — and both add routes refuse a symbol it cannot serve.** Asked for the morning after twenty-four unservable tickers were deleted: *"can you enhance the button so that while adding a ticker it does not allow me to add if the data is not available on Twelve data"*.

- **THE OLD CHECK WAS ADVISORY, AND ITS ONE WARNING FIRES ON THE WRONG THING.** It consults the stored NASDAQ listing, which is **a stocks file of 7,136 rows loaded 2026-09-14 and never refreshed since** — so it is silent on every ETF, share class and new listing, and nineteen days stale on everything else. That is how the twenty-four got in, sat producing nothing, and stalled the nightly rotation behind them for days.
  - **I FIRST WROTE THAT THE TABLE WAS EMPTY, HERE AND IN TWO OTHER PLACES, AND IT IS NOT (corrected 2026-10-03).** `listingRows: 0` is `known.size` — **how many of the ASKED symbols were found** — and the eleven sector SPDRs returned zero because a stocks file holds no ETFs. The field is **`listingHits`** now, since the name is what produced the misreading; nothing reads it, so the rename was free. **A field named for a table and holding a match count will be read as the table**, and the measurement is one `count(*)` away.
- **BATCHING IS FREE AND PINNING IS THE WHOLE POINT.** Measured: `/quote` takes a comma-separated batch, charges **1 credit a SYMBOL** (4 symbols cost 4), and applies `country` per symbol inside the batch — so a batch costs exactly what asking one at a time costs and takes one round trip. Unpinned, the provider resolves a ticker to whatever listing it prefers: **ARCH comes back as Arch Biopartners on the TSXV, APLS as a London inverse-Apple ETP, CEQP as a Toronto asset-allocation fund, VRTU as a Swedish crypto ETP** — four tickers that had been in the screener since July carrying a foreign instrument's prices under a US company's name. Every one is refused once `country=United States` is set. It is also the first time the standing **US-listed-only** rule has been mechanically enforceable.
- **"THE PROVIDER SAYS NO" AND "WE COULD NOT ASK" ARE DIFFERENT ANSWERS**, and conflating them is the expensive direction — `fetchProfile`'s `fetchOk` rule. A rate limit, a dropped socket or an HTML gateway page read as *unavailable* would lock an admin out of adding **anything** for as long as the provider wobbles. Only a definite per-symbol refusal blocks; everything else is `unchecked` and is let through. An unservable ticker is recoverable; a blocked afternoon is not.
- **ENFORCED SERVER-SIDE ON BOTH ADD ROUTES, not only in the page** — the CDN incident's rule applied to a write. The single add answers **422 and writes nothing**; the bulk add **drops the refused ones and names them**, the way it already handles `invalid`. The page blocks first as a courtesy and offers a one-click **Remove the N unavailable** that strips exactly those tickers and re-checks, because a block with no way forward is a dead end.
- **An already-tracked symbol is never re-asked** — a credit spent confirming a stock the screener already holds is a credit spent on nothing. The response reports `credits` so the preview can say what the check cost.
- **`fetchName` was ALSO unpinned**, which is how a London ETP could have supplied the display name for a US company. It goes through the pinned helper now, and the single add reuses the name the check already paid for rather than asking twice.

#### A BATCH OF ONE IS THE ODD CASE, and it let a dead ticker straight through
**The gate shipped, held on the bulk add, and let `PSTG` into the universe through the single add — found by driving the live route with the exact tickers deleted that morning, not by the suite.** Measured against the provider:

| asked | answer |
|---|---|
| ONE unknown symbol | **HTTP 404**, top-level body, `**symbol** … invalid` |
| TWO OR MORE, any unknown | **HTTP 200**, the refusal reported per symbol |
| ONE known symbol | HTTP 200, the quote object itself, **unkeyed** |
| a bad key | HTTP 401, `**apikey** …` |

`fetchJson` turns a 404 into a throw, and the catch was reading **every** throw as an outage — which is deliberately let through. So the refusal became an approval on exactly the path a person uses to add one ticker.

- **The discriminator is narrow on purpose**: a 404 naming the SYMBOL parameter, **on a single-symbol ask**. A 401 names `**apikey**` and a rate limit names credits; neither is a statement about a ticker. A 404 on a multi-symbol ask is unexplained and stays `unknown` rather than condemning the whole slice.
- **THE STUB WAS WRONG ABOUT THE PROVIDER, and that is why 34 checks passed over a live hole.** It answered 200 for the single-symbol case because the shape was assumed rather than measured. Both stubs carry the real 404 now, and the suite gained a **bad-key** case so the discriminator is proved not to over-reach. *A fixture that does not match the provider is not a test of the provider.*
- The unkeyed single-symbol success is the same asymmetry from the other side: reading only the keyed shape makes every single-symbol check look unavailable.

- Verified: **37 checks** on the real routes with the provider stubbed, plus **23** driving the real page. **The fixture is the test** — `FOREIGNY` is the ARCH shape, served unpinned and refused pinned, so a check that forgets the pin admits the exact class of ticker this exists to refuse while every other assertion still passes. **Proved by reverting seven times**: the pin fails 10, an outage treated as a refusal 7, the single-symbol 404 read as an outage 11, no bulk guard 7, no single-add guard 11, the unkeyed shape 1, re-asking tracked symbols 2.
  - **A `\b` INSIDE A JS DOUBLE-QUOTED ANCHOR IS A BACKSPACE, not backslash-b**, so a revert anchored on a line carrying a regex matched nothing and the case was SKIPPED — which reads exactly like a guard that does not bite. Anchor on a line with no escape, or neuter the body instead of the condition.
  - Live: all six of the deleted tickers refused on the single add with the universe unchanged at 1,278, `SPLG` and a junk string refused, and eight real new ETFs accepted with their correct US exchanges and names.
  - `bulk-test.js` and `universe-server.js` fail at HEAD too, confirmed by stashing.

### Index membership — the issuer's own daily holdings file (2026-10-03, owner's request)
**`GET /api/cron/holdings`, bearer-authenticated, run as its own phase by `nightly-ping.js` after the rotation — beside `secRotate()` and `shortRotate()` and for their reasons.** Asked as *"is there a way to figure out if the stock is part of s&p 500"*, answered with a measurement, then *"first thing is the importing of this data on a scheduled basis"*. **This is the IMPORT only: nothing displays it yet.**

#### EVERY OTHER SOURCE WAS MEASURED AND REFUSED, and two of the refusals are the useful part

| source | what it actually does |
|---|---|
| Twelve Data `/stocks` | carries `type`, `figi_code`, `cfi_code` — **no index field** |
| `/indices?symbol=GSPC` | **200 with `data: []`** — answers, and says nothing |
| `/index`, `/indices/composition`, `/index_constituents` | 404, none exist |
| `/etfs/world/composition` | **403, Ultra or Enterprise only** — the same wall as `/market_cap`, the forward estimates and the analyst data |
| iShares IVV holdings | **200, `content-type: text/csv`, and 2.26MB of HTML in the body** |
| slickcharts | 403 behind Cloudflare |
| the datahub CSV (a bot's mirror of the Wikipedia table) | 503 rows, **eleven days stale** |

- **THE iSHARES SHAPE IS WHY `parse` VALIDATES WHAT IT READ RATHER THAN THE STATUS CODE.** A 200 with a declared csv type and a page of markup in it is the silent failure this project has met before (`/api/news` through a redirect, a gated asset answering 200 with a login form). `Holdings.parse` throws unless the bytes unzip, carry a `Ticker` column, carry an `As of` date and yield at least the fund's floor — and **a throw writes NOTHING**, because the file is a full snapshot and a short one applies as hundreds of removals.
- **RE-CHECKED 2026-10-03 WHEN THE MIRROR WAS PROPOSED AGAIN**, since a stale reading is worth nothing: still 503 rows, still last touched 2026-09-21 (twelve days), **still missing VYLR**. Its four extra columns (GICS Sector, GICS Sub-Industry, Date added, CIK) are real and are the only free GICS this project has found — and were still declined: the licensing question is SHARPER for GICS than for membership (no "the issuer publishes this for its own fund" argument), coverage would be 503 of 1,302 so the column would be blank for 800 rows, and as a cross-check it is 12 days behind BY DESIGN, so it would disagree on every index change and be right to — an alarm that always fires says nothing.
- **THE MIRROR WAS MISSING A REAL NAME, which is what settled the source.** `VYLR` — Vylor Inc., NYSE, common stock, **0.070% of the index** — is in SSGA's file and absent from the mirror. Every other one of its 503 agreed, so the staleness is small and **not zero**. A maintained list is wrong by one name eleven days after a change; the issuer's file is wrong by none.
- **AND IT WRITES OUR OWN SPELLING: `BRK.B`, `BF.B`.** No translation table, unlike SEC (hyphens) and FINRA (separators stripped entirely). Checked rather than assumed.
- **IT DOES NOT CLOSE THE GICS GAP.** The workbook has a Sector column and **it is `-` on every row** — SSGA publishes it empty for SPY. I was about to report free GICS sectors as a bonus; checking the column is what stopped that.

#### NO DEPENDENCY, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A CRON PHASE AND NOT A LOCAL LOADER
An xlsx is a ZIP of DEFLATE entries and node ships `zlib`, so `holdings.js` reads the workbook in ~40 lines of `inflateRawSync`. That is the whole reason it runs in the function like `shortint` rather than locally like `insider-load.js`, which shells out to PowerShell's `Expand-Archive` and is Windows-only by design.

- **THE CENTRAL DIRECTORY, NEVER THE LOCAL HEADERS — and on this file that is the difference between working and not working at all.** Measured: every local header in SSGA's workbook sets the **data-descriptor flag (0x08) and a compressed size of ZERO**, with the real size in a trailer after the data. **A reader that walks the file from the front finds zero entries.** So this is not defensive style. **Proved by reverting**: the suite cannot even start.
- `Expand-Archive` refuses a `.xlsx` extension outright (*".zip is the only supported archive file format"*), which is worth knowing before reaching for it to inspect one by hand — copy it to `.zip` first.

#### Two tables, and the history is the point
`fund_holdings (fund, symbol, d, weight, shares)` keyed on all three, plus `fund_state` for the per-fund clock — the `short_interest` / `short_state` shape exactly.

- **KEYED ON `d`, so it is the HISTORY rather than a current state, and that is deliberate.** SSGA publishes today's file and only today's: **yesterday's weights are not retrievable at any price.** `fundamentals_history` exists for precisely that reason, and this project has already recorded what discarding an irrecoverable daily reading costs. ~504 rows a session, so ~126k a year against 4.6M bars.
- **`fund` IS THERE FROM THE FIRST DAY though only SPY is wired.** Measured 2026-10-02: **SPY, DIA, MDY, XLK, XLF and XLV all answer 200 with a real xlsx at the same URL shape** — the sector SPDRs being the eleven we already hold as the Sector Benchmark theme. A second index is a config entry rather than a migration.
- **NOT in `SYMBOL_TABLES`**, the `insider_trans` reasoning: this records what the INDEX held, not what we track, so dropping a ticker from our universe must not delete the index's own history of it.
- **`fund_holdings` is on `query-plan-test`'s big-table list FROM THE DAY IT SHIPPED**, which is what `insider_trans` had to learn the hard way (its quarter-delete ranged on an unindexed `filed` — a full walk the guard could not see). `idx_fund_holdings_d (fund, d)` is what makes "everything the index held on date X" a seek; the primary key leads on symbol and cannot answer it. The recount inside the write path is checked by hand, since it is built with a variable placeholder count and lands among the twelve the plan test cannot prepare.
- **EVERY HOLDING IS STORED, not only the ones in our universe.** The insider walk filters before fetching because that is what makes ~9,000 document fetches affordable, and it pays with a permanent hole for any ticker added afterwards. Here the file is complete and 54KB, so narrowing buys nothing — and a stock added to the universe tomorrow already has its membership and its weight. Asserted over an EMPTY universe table, so a route that filtered would store nothing.

#### DAILY, because the weights move daily even though membership does not
Membership changes perhaps 20-25 times a year (the quarterly rebalance plus ad-hoc for M&A), which argues for a weekly check. **Weights move every session**, and the file is published daily and only for today, which argues for daily. Daily also needs no calendar, catches a change within hours, and **heals after any number of missed runs** — `noteTechMark`'s rule. On a day when the file's as-of date has not moved it writes nothing.

- **A FAILURE MUST NOT BLANK A SINGLE HOLDING, and here that matters more than anywhere this rule has applied before.** `noteSecMiss` made this mistake once with the CIK and silently broke the insider card for 64 filers; a membership flag emptied by a transient refusal would look like **504 deletions**, with nothing on screen to say otherwise. `noteFundMiss` records the miss and **carries `as_of` and `holdings` forward**, so the clock keeps saying how old the data genuinely is.
- **THE TRUNCATION FLOOR (450) IS THE GUARD THAT MATTERS MOST.** S&P targets 500 names and the count has sat between 500 and 505 for decades, so no real file lands under 450 — which makes a short one a partial download, an error page or a changed layout, never news. **Probed at exactly 450 and 449**, since a threshold is a step function. **Proved by reverting**: the floor removed, a 12-holding file applies and fails 10.
- **An honest User-Agent, CHECKED rather than copied.** The NASDAQ loader needs a browser-shaped one because that endpoint answers a bot-shaped agent by **never replying at all**. Measured here: SSGA serves this file identically with an honest agent, a browser one, and none at all — so there is no reason to impersonate anything, and `SSGA_UA` reuses `SEC_UA`'s fallback.
- **A ticker has to LOOK like one.** The file carries two non-equity rows — a cash line whose ticker is `-` at 0.269% and `2602335D` at 0.000003% — so a digit anywhere is refused while dots are kept. **Proved by reverting**: the cash-equivalent row becomes a holding, 504 goes to 505, and 13 checks fail.
- **The as-of date is parsed COMPONENT BY COMPONENT, never through `new Date()`**, which reads a bare date as UTC midnight and renders a day early west of Greenwich — the card-dating trap, met in both the earnings and the fundamentals captions. There is no Date object in that function, so it cannot apply.

#### A REVERT PROOF THAT PREDICTED ZERO FOUND A REAL BUG
The route's as-of cutoff was written off as an efficiency guard — the write is idempotent on `(fund, symbol, d)`, so a repeat stores identical rows — and the revert was expected to cost nothing. **It failed 3.** `appendFundHoldings` guarded `as_of` to move forward only and wrote `holdings` **unconditionally**, so re-applying an older file left the clock reading *"2026-10-02, 504 holdings"* on a date that had 501. **The two fields now move together or not at all**, and only then does the cutoff revert settle at the 2 failures it should have: both assertions about the `already` response it exists to produce, with no data check failing.

#### THE FIRST LIVE IMPORT'S RECEIPT WAS WRONG, AND THE SUITE PASSED OVER IT
**504 holdings stored and the response read `"rows": 0`.** `rows` is recounted in the `on conflict do update` branch — and **a fund's FIRST insert has no conflict**, so the literal in the `values` clause is what lands, and it was 0. Self-healing on the next run, which is exactly why it could sit there unnoticed.

- **The suite asserted `rows` only after a SECOND run**, where the conflict branch does recount (`504 + 501 = 1005`), so 63 checks passed straight over a receipt that understated what was stored by 504. **A receipt that misreports what is held is a failure this project has already recorded** — on `shortint-load.js`, where the fix was to increment after the write landed rather than before.
- **Found by READING THE LIVE RESPONSE, not by the tests.** The same division the `instrumentType` entry records: a fixture proves the display surface, and only production proves the flow. There is a check on the first run now, and the revert fails 3.
- The count is correct in either branch because the holdings inserts are earlier statements in the same batch, and a batch is one sequential transaction.

- Verified: **63 checks**. The parser is validated against the **real workbook**, frozen as a fixture — the `secfacts` rule, since a hand-made one would carry none of the traps: the two non-equity rows, the dotted spellings, the 100.23 weight sum and VYLR are all properties of SSGA's actual file. The guards get **synthetic workbooks built by a real store-only zip writer with true CRC32s**, so they are genuine xlsx files rather than something shaped to satisfy the reader under test. **The load-bearing check is that HISTORY SURVIVES**: a newer file must leave the earlier day intact, because routing a top-up through a wholesale replace stores the new day perfectly and every other assertion still passes — the screens incident and the `writeShortInterest` trap. Plus a removal absent on the new date and still present on the old, an addition, an unreachable source, an HTTP 500, a 200 carrying HTML, and a dry run writing nothing. **Proved by reverting seven times**: the floor fails 10, the digit guard 15, the central-directory walk stops the suite dead, `noteFundMiss` 4, the forward-only clock 2, the first-run recount 3, and the route cutoff 2.
  - **THE FORWARD-ONLY CLOCK IS PROVED ON ITS OWN TERMS, by calling the store DIRECTLY.** The route's cutoff means an older file never reaches `appendFundHoldings` through it, so a revert of that guard would be shielded and read as costing nothing — two fixes for one problem, the `getSessionUser` allowlist trap. Not contrived either: a backfill loading historical files is exactly a caller that arrives out of order.
  - **A REVERT HAS TO SIMULATE THE BUG, NOT AN IMPOSSIBLE STATE — the third time this project has recorded that.** The `noteFundMiss` case first changed `insert into` to `insert or replace into` and **left the `on conflict do update` clause behind**, and SQLite then applies the UPSERT: the row was preserved, the revert simulated nothing, and it reported a load-bearing guard as costing nothing. With the clause removed too it fails 4.
  - **AN ABORTED SUITE REPORTS `0 failed`**, which is indistinguishable from a guard that never mattered. The harness carries the check count and tags a run that threw or stopped short separately — the central-directory case reads *"the suite cannot even START"* rather than *"not load-bearing"*.
  - **A BACKTICK IN A SQL COMMENT TOOK db.js DOWN — the `Cards.STYLE` trap, in SQL this time.** The statement is a JS template literal, so `` `as_of` `` inside a `--` comment ended the string. **`node --check` would have caught it and was not run after that edit**; the revert harness caught it instead by refusing to report against a baseline that would not boot.
  - **The shell ate `` `insider_trans` `` out of a comment** while patching `query-plan-test.js` — a backtick inside a double-quoted `node -e` string is command substitution, the documented trap, met again. Single-quote the expression or use a file.

#### `/holdings` — the page (2026-10-03, owner's request)
**Admin only, an `Index membership` row in the console's Data section.** The import had no surface at all, so "did it run, and what did it get" could only be answered by querying Turso by hand.

- **ADMIN RATHER THAN MEMBER, and that is the licensing question rather than a permission one.** A reconstructed constituent list *with its weights* is exactly what the GICS decision already declined to republish. A page behind `requireAdmin` does not raise it; a member-facing column would. **Every refusal is checked to carry no symbol and no weight in its body**, not merely the right status code.
  - **A MEMBER-FACING BOOLEAN DID FOLLOW, and the line held where it matters (2026-10-03).** The owner asked for membership on the screener and took the boolean when offered both — so *is this stock in the index* is now a column everyone sees, while **the weight never leaves this page**. That is the distinction the licensing question actually turns on: a Yes/No for the stocks we happen to track is derivable from any financial website, a weighted constituent list is the dataset. See **…and on the SCREENER as a boolean column** below.
- **The clock is the top of the page**, because that is what it is opened for: data as-of, last checked, status, and rows stored. **Amber past 6 days on the as-of date and 4 on the check** — reasoned rather than measured, and said so in the code: the file is published daily with the prior session's date and NOT at weekends, so on a Monday morning the newest available is Thursday's, about four days old through no fault of ours. **Probed at 7 and at 6**, since a threshold is a step function.
- **A FAILED ATTEMPT IS PRINTED IN WORDS.** `unreachable` alone does not say whether the host was down or the file was refused, and those want different responses. Writing that check is what found that **`fundNewest` never returned `error` at all** — so the page could have reported that something failed and never why.
- **`tracked` is the cross-reference the page exists for.** The import deliberately stores every holding rather than only our universe, so the two genuinely differ — 498 of 504 today — and a member we do not hold reads `not tracked` rather than leaving a blank that looks like missing data. A tracked symbol with no name row still reads as tracked; those are different facts.
- **`readFundDates` is a `group by` over a growing table and is still a SEEK**, because `(fund, d)` is a COVERING index: SQLite walks it in order and never touches the table. Bounded at 60 besides. Checked against the plan rather than assumed.
- The footnote says the weights are **the fund's, which tracks the index rather than being it** — the distinction the whole source rests on, and the one a reader would otherwise never be told.

##### Which members the screener is MISSING, and adding them (2026-10-03, owner: "the aim is to figure out if my app has all the s&p tickers")
**A panel above the table names every member not in the screener, each with its index weight, and adds them through the existing `POST /api/universe/bulk`.** The page could say *498 of 504* and not which six, or do anything about it — which is the whole question it is opened for.

- **THE BACKFILL COMMAND IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS**, handed over naming exactly the symbols just added and paced at `--rate 100`. A ticker with no bars is pulled DEEP inside the next price refresh's own request, and on 2026-09-22 a bulk add did precisely that and answered **HTTP 504 after 300s, leaving the whole universe unrefreshed**. The `/quality` precedent: report the fix, not just the diagnosis.
- **With nothing missing it says so in green rather than going blank.** *"You have all of them"* is the answer somebody opens this to find; an empty panel is not.
- **Ticked by default**, because adding all of them is the common case, and `Select all` toggles rather than only selects.
- The weight rides on each chip, so **the size of what is missing is visible** — `GOOG` at 2.409% is a different omission from `BF.B` at 0.007%.
- Verified: the add is asserted to reach the UNIVERSE TABLE, not merely to return 200 — and the roles suite checks a member, a guest and a stranger are each refused the add route **and that none of them got a symbol in**. That route is the one thing on this page that changes the screener for everybody.

##### The six were added, and the index is complete (2026-10-03, owner: "Can you add the missing ones")
**Universe 1,278 → 1,284, tracked 504 of 504.** GOOG (2.409% of the index), TEL (0.095), VYLR (0.070), CBOE (0.044), ERIE (0.009), BF.B (0.007).

- **THE MISSING LIST WAS RECOMPUTED RATHER THAN TAKEN FROM THIS FILE.** The holdings file is daily and the index moves, so the six were read off `/api/fund-holdings` at the moment of the add — the same read the panel makes — not from the six recorded here hours earlier. They happened to agree.
- **`BF.B` IS PERFECTLY SERVABLE, AND ONLY THE BARE `BF` WAS NOT.** That ticker was removed on 2026-09-24 as permanently unfillable, and the provider's own message said why: *"symbol not found: BF."* — Brown-Forman trades as BF.A and BF.B. **A removed parent says nothing about its share classes**, and the gate answered in one credit rather than leaving it to judgement: `BF.B  NYSE  Brown-Forman Corp. Class B Common Stock`. All six came back `ok` with their real US exchanges, 6 credits.
- **THE BARS WERE BACKFILLED BEFORE ANYTHING COULD PRICE THEM**, which is the documented hazard and the reason this is not just an add. Six symbols with no archive are six DEEP pulls inside one refresh request, and on 2026-09-22 that answered **HTTP 504 after 300s and left the whole universe unrefreshed**. Measured: **23,960 bars in 0.1 min**, archive 4,653,253 → **4,677,213** rows, 1,284 symbols — finishing **2h17m** before the 19:30 nightly, with the market shut and no intraday slot to contend with.
- **`VYLR` HOLDS TWO BARS AND ALWAYS WILL FOR A WHILE.** It listed on 2026-10-01, so it sits under `LIGHT_MIN_ARCHIVE` (300) and is pulled deep on every refresh — which costs nothing, because *thin is only expensive when the provider HAS history to send*. The other five reach 2006-2010 at the 5,000-bar ceiling.
- **The screener still reads 1,278 rows until the next FULL round rebuilds the snapshot** (~30 minutes), and the six carry no name until a profile is pulled. **A blank NAME column is the visible symptom of a missing profile**, not a name bug — the Sector Benchmark add recorded the same thing seven hours after the fact. Fill missing fetches name, profile and instrument type together in one round.

##### Two faults the fixture found, both the "a null is not a zero" family
- **A NULL WEIGHT CRASHED THE WHOLE PAGE.** `r.weight.toFixed(3)` is unguarded, the throw happened inside the row map, and the fetch's own `.catch` then rendered **the entire table as one error row** — a single absent number taking the page with it. It draws an em-dash and **no bar** now: a zero-width bar would read as *held at no weight*, which is a different claim from *not reported*. The schema allows a null, so this is reachable rather than theoretical.
- **THE BAR FLOOR WAS ONE PERCENT, WHICH IS 0.9 PIXELS.** `Math.max(1, …)` on an 86px track is sub-pixel and draws as nothing — so the smallest holdings looked absent. It is `min-width: 2px` in CSS now: the Size card's rule, that a small thing drawn at its honest size still has to be visible. **Measured off `getBoundingClientRect()`**, never the style attribute, which was perfectly correct in both versions — the `/quality` lesson.

- Verified: **48 checks** driving the real page plus **22** on the roles. The fixture is dated in OFFSETS FROM TODAY so the staleness checks cannot rot, and every row separates one mechanism: tracked and untracked, a name present and absent, a weight at the top of the bar scale and one on its floor, and a null that must sort last whichever way the column goes. Plus the amber measured as a drawn colour, the dates listed newest-first with the newest marked, sorting opening on the interesting end, the finder matching a symbol prefix and a company name, and no sideways scroll at 1500px or 390px with the table scrolling inside its own box.

#### …and on the SCREENER as a boolean column (2026-10-03, owner: "Yes add Boolean column")
**An `S&P 500` column in the Info group, immediately after Instrument: Yes, No, or an em-dash.** Asked for after "Are you showing if a stock is part of S&P on the screener", to which the answer was no — the import had been running for a day and the only surface was this admin page.

- **BOOLEAN ONLY, NEVER THE WEIGHT — the owner's call when offered both, and it is the same line the page above draws.** A reconstructed constituent list *with its weights* is exactly what the GICS decision declined to republish, twice; `/holdings` is behind `requireAdmin` for that reason and this column is member-facing. **Membership is a fact about the stock; the weight is the issuer's dataset.** There are three checks that no weight and no share count reaches a row.
- **IT COSTS NO REFRESH AND NO ENDPOINT.** `stampSpMember` is the sixth read-path stamp (the fifth inside `serveStamps`; `stampCapDerived` is the synchronous one), so the column populated **the moment the deploy landed** rather than waiting ~30 minutes for a full round to rebuild the snapshot — which is the arithmetic the `instrumentType` and YTD entries both record paying. Measured live within a minute of the push: **498 Yes, 780 No, 0 unknown, as of 2026-10-01**.
- **CACHED A MINUTE**, because `/api/stocks` is the hot path and this is two reads — the `groupIndex` and `tile_config` reasoning. A minute stale means a stock that joined the index overnight, which does not happen between two page loads.
- **A NULL IS NOT A FALSE, and this is the sharpest place that rule has landed.** With no holdings file ever imported, `false` on every row is **the screener stating that no stock is in the S&P 500** — a confident, universal, wrong answer. It is unknown until there is a file: the cell draws an em-dash, the tooltip says *this is not the same as No*, and `filterValue` returns `''` so the dropdown cannot silently filter those rows away. **Proved by reverting twice**: `!!(set && set.has(…))` fails 5, and `filterValue` reading unknown as No fails 1.
- **THE SOURCE IS NAMED ON THE CELL.** It is SPY's own daily holdings file — *the fund that tracks the index, not the index* — so the tooltip says which and the cell carries the as-of date. That is the same distinction the page above already makes in its footnote, and it is the one thing a reader could otherwise never be told.
- **NO COLOUR.** Membership is not a direction and not a verdict; green and red mean up and down on every row here. `Yes` reads at full strength and `No` takes `.na`, so the eye finds members without the cell making a claim. **No hover card** either (`.nocard`), the rule Sector, Industry, Size and Instrument already follow.
- **THE DROPDOWN IS ORDERED Yes-THEN-No**, which the alphabet gets backwards. Every other `CAT_KEYS` dropdown is alphabetical and nobody minds, but a reader scanning a two-value boolean expects Yes first — one clause in `ladder()`. **Proved by reverting**: fails 3.
- **THE BOUNDARY IS UNTOUCHED, and it is asserted BEHAVIOURALLY rather than by a grep** — a grep passes if the engine reads the field under another name. Every row is scored three ways (absent, present, and **lying**) and the verdicts must be identical.
- One `FIELD_SPEC` row carries it to the hover card, `/stock`, the tiles, the phone and `/compare` at once; it renders as text, so it has no `n` and `/compare` correctly withholds a difference. `TILE_FIELD_RE` needed nothing — it is `[^|]{1,32}`, so the ampersand passes. `/columns` picked the column up on its own, **93 → 94**, as designed — measured against the live route, not off `sitecols-test`, whose `86` is the count of columns still SHOWING after the site-hidden ones are taken out and is a different quantity.
- Constants after the change: the Info banner **11**, `PAD_SPAN` **101**, the error row **96**, the empty row **98**.

##### `readFundHoldings` RETURNS AN OBJECT, AND THE ONLY SYMPTOM WAS AN ABSENT COLUMN
It is `{ fund, asOf, holdings }`, not a bare array. Mapping the return value directly throws — and **`serveStamps` catches per stamp**, which is correct policy (a slow auxiliary read should cost one field, not 500 rows) and here meant the field was simply never set on any row. No error, no blank cell, no 500: the column was absent from the payload and the page drew its em-dash on every row exactly as the no-file case does.

- **A field's shape is something to READ, not to guess at** — the `store.barsThrough` trap (reduced over the characters of a string) and the `bench[].index` one (reported `0 pts` on three healthy series), met a third time.
- The suite caught it, but only because it asserts the **values**. A check that the column exists, or that the cell renders, passes in both worlds.
- **Proved by reverting**: the shipped bug fails 17, and dropping the stamp entirely fails 18.

- Verified: **41 checks**. The fixture's load-bearing property is that **the biggest company on it is NOT a member**, so "in the index" cannot be confused with "big", and **every neighbour's value is unique on the row** — the load-bearing check is header-over-cell, since a header added without its body cell slides every later value one column over and the table still looks perfectly well formed. **Proved by reverting nine times**, every one load-bearing: the accessor shape 17, the stamp dropped 18, a null read as false 5, **the body cell left behind 6** (the market cap sliding under the S&P header), the banner at 10 fails 2, `PAD_SPAN` 1, the Yes-first ladder 3, `CAT_KEYS` 6, and `filterValue` 1.
  - **`PAD_SPAN` IS DELIBERATELY STATIC and no behavioural check can reach it** — it is the colspan of the Refresh-all progress line and the windowed spacer, neither of which is on screen in a four-row fixture, so its revert cost nothing and it would have sat unproven. It is **derived** from the drawn row (header count plus the three anchor cells) rather than written down, which is what the literal that went stale at 51 could not do.
  - **A COARSE BOUNDARY CHECK CRIES WOLF AGAINST PRODUCTION, for the second time on this project.** `/"weight"/` over the serialised rows reported a leak that was not there: **every production row carries `qualityBreakdown[].weight`**, the Quality score's own factor weights. It reads the row's TOP-LEVEL KEYS now, which is the only place a stamp can put one. The first correction then false-alarmed on its own fixture (`price: 100` against a share count of 100), so the fixture's share counts are deliberately values nothing else on it holds.
  - **NEVER `page.selectOption` ON A DROPDOWN A REVERT CAN REMOVE.** On a value the select does not carry it waits 30s and **throws**, so three of the nine reverts aborted the suite and reported a handful of failures instead of eighteen — indistinguishable from a guard that never mattered. Set `.value` and dispatch the page's own `change` event. **The documented trap, met for the fourth time in a fortnight.**
  - **A row's `textContent` opens with the markup's own indentation**, so `startsWith(sym)` matches nothing and the row finder silently returns `[]` — which read as an off-by-six offset and eight alignment failures over a table that was correct. Trim first.
  - `sitecols-test.js` fails 5 and it is **PRE-EXISTING** — it hardcodes a catalogue of 83 against the live 94. `/columns` parses the header row, so the catalogue grows on its own, as designed.

### A filed fundamental as a chart layer (2026-09-29, owner's request)
**A `FUND` button and a metric picker: revenue or net income, trailing twelve months, from the company's own SEC filings, drawn as a step in its own strip beneath the chart — the FIRST of the three optional layers there.** The owner asked for "a line on the individual stock chart on fundamental, maybe a different axis, using the data from SEC EDGAR", chose the pane when the axis was argued against, and then moved the pane out of the svg and set the order of all three layers.

**A SECOND Y-AXIS WAS THE THING TO REFUSE, and that is the design decision worth keeping.** Two independent scales can be slid against each other until any two series appear to track, and the "divergence" a reader then sees is an artefact of where each zero was put. This chart had settled that once already: the stock overlay is **rebased** rather than given its own axis, and `/compare` follows the same rule.

**IT WAS A PANE INSIDE THE SVG FOR AN HOUR, and the strip is better twice over.** The owner's instruction was *"Fundamental panel should come first and it should appear below the chart, Earning should be right below fundamental, and short can be where it is"*. As a strip the three layers read as **one stack in one place** rather than one being inside the chart and two outside — and it drops the four-way coupling a pane forced between `rowcard.js`'s bands and this page's box heights, which this file already names as a trap. The chart is back to its two documented heights, and there is a check that handing `chartSVG` a `fund` option now changes nothing at all.

- **ORDER, in the toolbar and under the chart, and they match**: FUND, EARN, SHORT. The metric picker travels WITH the toggle it configures — the tile controls' rule — and is hidden while the strip is off, since a control that can change nothing reads as broken.
- **ALL THREE DEFAULT TO OFF (the owner, the same day).** The rug and the short strip used to arrive switched on. `=== '1'` rather than `!== '0'`, so someone who deliberately switched one ON keeps it while someone who never touched it starts clean. That chart carries the price, two moving averages, up to five overlays, the trend ribbon, an RSI pane and a volume pane before any of these three.
- **IT COSTS NO ENDPOINT AND NO READ.** `/api/sec` is already fetched on that page after the chart, so the series rides it — `ttmSeries` is one more field on a response the page was already waiting for. The earnings rug's bargain exactly.
- **Repainted ALONE**, the short strip's rule: a full `paintChart()` would rebuild the plot, the ribbon and every overlay to switch one layer beneath them. That is the other thing the strip bought — as a pane it could not be.

#### The four decisions that make it honest
- **TRAILING TWELVE MONTHS, never raw quarterly.** A quarterly line is a seasonal sawtooth that says nothing about trajectory. `SecFacts.ttmSeries` rolls the identical four-quarter window `ttm()` already uses back down the trail, so the newest step IS the TTM row on the card below it.
- **FROM `latestFilled`, NOT `latestPerPeriod`, AND THE TWO CAN NEVER DISAGREE ABOUT A NUMBER.** Filling only ever supplies a figure the winning filing left BLANK, so where the card's TTM row exists the strip equals it, and where that row is absent the strip still has a line. Coverage 65% → 90%. That property is what makes two different bases safe on one page, and there is a check on it in both directions.
- **`periodEnd` WITH THE LATEST RESTATEMENT, matching the card immediately above it.** The other coherent pairing is `filed` with as-first-reported — `visibleAsOf` already does exactly that, and it is what `/adjustedbacktest` uses. **Mixing them is the worst option**: a point plotted at a 2024 filing date carrying a 2026 restatement is incoherent. The cost is that the step lands some weeks before the figure was public, **so the note says in as many words that this cannot be read for lead or lag** — that is a timing claim, and the backtest is where timing claims get tested.
- **A STEP, NEVER A SLOPE, WITH A BOUNDED CARRY.** A filed figure stands until the next filing replaces it; a slope between two quarters would claim it drifted day by day. `RowCard.stepSeries` lays the quarterly points onto the session axis and stops carrying after **400 days** — without a bound a company that stopped filing draws a flat line to today, which reads as *revenue held* rather than *the record stops here*.

#### Its own range, not zero — and the zero line that follows
The short-interest strip's rule and its reason: a trailing year sits in a narrow band over a short window, so a zero base spends the whole strip on empty space. **A line carries no measured-from-zero claim the way a bar does**, which is what makes that legitimate — and the note says the baseline is not zero and prints the range. **Where the DATA spans zero the zero line is drawn**, which is the whole difference between a revenue line and a net-income one: profitable or not is the reading, and a line with no zero on it cannot say which side it is on.

- **THE TEST IS THE DATA, NEVER A PADDED BOUND, and PRODUCTION is what caught that.** While it was still a pane the axis carried 12% of value padding, and MU's trailing revenue runs **$8.0B to $90.3B** — so the padded floor landed at **-$1.9B** and a zero line was drawn on a REVENUE chart, implying a crossing that cannot happen. A fixture with a narrow range passes either way; the check needs a wide positive series. The strip pads in PIXELS instead, so the value range is exactly the data's and the hazard is gone by construction.
- **TWO MORE FOUND BY SCREENSHOT while it was a pane, both about printing a padded bound.** The gutter labels read `$10.2B` at the top of a series whose highest filed figure was `$9.0B` — a number no company ever reported — and fixing that put the label exactly on the run that reaches the maximum, which on a rising series is the run at the right edge where the labels are. The strip carries no gutter labels at all: the range goes in the note, as the short strip's does.
- **NEUTRAL, deliberately** — `--text`, the short strip's colour. Green and red are the PRICE's direction on this chart, and *revenue rose* is not a direction the price went.

#### Worth knowing
- **ONE PATH COMMAND PER CHANGE OF LEVEL, not one per session.** A step holds its value for a quarter, so writing a segment at every bar put ~5,200 of them in a Max chart — about 42KB of markup for a line with forty levels. Measured live on MU at Max: **64 levels in a 774-character path**.
- **`preserveAspectRatio="none"` is what keeps the steps aligned with the price above**, and is exactly why the stroke carries `vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke` — without it the flat runs and the vertical risers draw at different weights. No `<text>` inside, for the same reason.
- **A pre-revenue company gets no line at all**, because `ttm()` refuses a sum whose revenue is under its floor and that floor is load-bearing where `ttm` feeds the margin comparison. Measured: 3 of 1,181 symbols. A second summation here would be the drift `secfacts.js` exists to prevent.
- **THE BOUNDARY IS UNTOUCHED**: no `FIELD_SPEC` entry, no snapshot stamping, no screener column. A chart layer is squarely on the display side of the line the SEC card's own condition drew, and there is a check that no filings series reaches a screener row.
- Verified: **50 checks** — the rolling window against hand-computed sums, a gap refusing every window that spanned it, either concept null on its own, the `latestFilled` coverage claim proved BOTH ways (the same fixture loses the newest window under `latestPerPeriod` and keeps it under `latestFilled`, at the same number), the carry and its bound, the drawn strip measured below the chart and inside the same 52px gutter as the other two, the chart's own height unmoved, **every path segment flat or vertical**, the zero line present and absent, the note's four claims, the order of the buttons and of the strips, and the self-gating. **Proved by reverting four times**: the strip drawn second puts the rug above it, defaults back to on fails 4, a slope gives 3 diagonal segments of 5, and a strip that never paints fails 2.
  - **TWO EXISTING SUITES ASSUMED THEIR LAYER ARRIVED ON** and had to be told, not worked around: `around-test.js` and `shortint-test.js` both measured a layer that is now off. They seed the remembered choice in an `addInitScript` — **but only where nothing is stored yet**, because setting it on every navigation puts the layer back after the suite switches it off and silently defeats the two checks that it is remembered per device. That cost two failures before it was noticed.
  - **`rowcard.js` ASSIGNS TO `globalThis`, NOT `module.exports`** — one file for the browser and Node, and server.js requires it for the side effect. `const RowCard = require(...)` returns `{}`, and every call on it is a TypeError.
  - **A fixture whose quarter-ends are 91-DAY STEPS does not land on calendar quarter-ends.** The gap check filtered `2025-06-30`, which the generator never produced, removed nothing, and passed over an intact fixture.
  - **A REVERT PROOF THAT DOES NOT RUN THE TEST REPORTS ZERO FAILURES**, which reads exactly like guards that were never load-bearing — all four did on the first attempt, because the harness built a `node` path out of `sys.executable`. It counts PASSes now and refuses to report on a run that did not happen.

### Around earnings — how one stock behaves around its own reports (2026-09-28, owner's request)
**Inside the earnings card on `/stock`: one faint line per quarter rebased to its report-day close, the median over them, an interquartile band, and four figures.** The owner asked for the aggregate rather than markers on the price chart — *"how does this stock typically behave around earnings"* — and explicitly ruled out drawing on the chart itself.

- **`earnstudy.js` is pure** (bars + events → the aggregate), the `news.js` / `secfacts.js` / `insider.js` shape, which is what lets every statistic be tested with no server. `/api/stock` gains one `readBars(symbol, 2600)` in the Promise.all it already runs, and ships ~2-8KB of aggregate rather than ten years of closes for the browser to re-derive.
- **THE REACTION IS t → t+1, and that single choice decides whether the card is true.** Measured on the live table: **34,499 of 34,754 events are After Hours** (235 pre-market, 20 unspecified), so the session a report lands on does not contain the market's answer. Verified against NVDA rather than assumed — `t → t+1` gives +8.7 / −1.8 / −5.5 / −0.6 / −3.2 / −0.8 while `t−1 → t` is small. **The drift is measured FROM the reaction**, so the jump is never counted twice.
- **`POST` is 42 sessions, which is not a round number.** A quarter is ~63 trading days, so a longer window runs into the NEXT report and starts measuring that instead.
- **THE BEAT/MISS SPLIT IS DEGENERATE ON REAL DATA and is withheld rather than printed.** NVDA has **24 beats against 2 misses**, AAPL 24 against 1 — companies beat nearly every quarter, so "the median move after a miss" is routinely a median of one, set in the same type as a median of twenty-four. `MIN_SPLIT` (4) counts the thin side and withholds its median, and the note says misses are rare, which is the useful fact.
- **Two numbers, because one describes it wrongly.** NVDA's signed median reaction is **−0.22%** and its median ABSOLUTE reaction is **2.34%**: it moves hard and not predictably in one direction, and either figure alone misleads.
- **The hit rate carries the stock's own base rate** — "44% against 49.3% on an ordinary session". A stock that rises most days hands a flattering number to a signal that knows nothing; the research log's rule, and it costs no second source.
- **A FILTER I NEARLY BUILT AND THE MEASUREMENT KILLED.** 9.56% of consecutive events sit under 45 days apart (Alcoa has a pair 8 days apart; NVDA has one 33 days before the next), so I assumed those were non-report rows diluting the medians toward an ordinary day. **Measured: they move MORE, not less** — NVDA's crowded pair has a 3.05% median absolute reaction against 2.34% for the spaced ones, MU's 5.42%, and dropping them moves NVDA's median by 0.27 points. They are real events. No filter, and the hypothesis is recorded so it is not rebuilt.
- **HTML labels, never SVG text** — the box is stretched to the page width — and every stroke carries `vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke`, or a horizontal line and a vertical one draw at different weights. There is a check that the svg contains no `<text>` at all.
- **Hidden with a per-device toggle** (`localStorage`, the `/compare` and `/m` call) rather than a prefs flag: a prefs flag follows the account but would cost this page a round trip it does not currently make, and a guest has no prefs key. **The button is always visible and labelled with the direction it will go** — a hide with no way back is a trapdoor.
- **It is DESCRIPTION, not a signal**, and the note says so: drift after earnings is untested here (backlog entry 1) and ten of eleven framings in the research log came back flat.
**AND THE RUG — when, in price context (the same day, once the aggregate was in).** One tick per report **under** the plot, never on it: the owner ruled out drawing on the chart, and a tick beneath a gap answers *"was that earnings?"* without fighting the price line. An `EARN` button sits with the other chart layers, remembered per device.

- **It costs nothing.** `earnRows` is already on the page for the earnings card, so the rug is a second reading of data in hand — no fetch, no query, no endpoint.
- **SELF-GATING rather than range-gated.** It draws whatever falls inside the window and hides when nothing does, so a 1W chart is clean with no rule about which ranges may have it, and a report that *did* land in a short window is still shown. Measured on the fixture: 3 ticks at 1Y, 0 at 1M, 9 at Max.
- **Aligned by the ribbon's own trick** — `margin-right: 52px` to clear the price axis, children placed by percentage — so the ticks, the crosshair and the plot cannot disagree.
- **IT WAS A ROW OF NEUTRAL TICKS FOR AN HOUR, AND THAT WAS THE OWNER'S NEXT MESSAGE** — *"the marker is not showing how good or bad the earning was, can't you do something to make it visually intelligent"*. A tick answers *when* and says nothing about *what happened*, which is most of why anyone looks. It is a **signed bar chart** now: **colour is the direction of the next session's move, height is its magnitude**, growing from a centre baseline, the strip at 38px (the owner offered the room — "you can also increase the height as this is just optional").
  - **I HAD ARGUED AGAINST COLOURING IT AND THE ARGUMENT WAS ONLY HALF RIGHT.** Green and red mean up and down on this chart, so a green **beat** tick beside a red session really would make a different claim from the one the colour carries everywhere else — but colouring by the **reaction** makes *exactly* the same claim as the price line above it. The objection was to the beat/miss encoding, and I had generalised it to colour as such. Beat or miss stays in the tooltip, where it costs nothing and claims nothing.
  - **THE CEILING IS THE 90th PERCENTILE OF WHAT IS IN VIEW, floored at 3%** — `rugScale()`, the `earnScale()` precedent from the surprise strip on the same page, and for the same reason: a single +40% reaction would flatten every ordinary quarter to a hairline. A bar past the ceiling is drawn full height, marked `.capped` and **says so on hover** rather than being silently clipped.
  - **A REPORT WITH NO NEXT SESSION YET IS A NEUTRAL STUB, NOT A ZERO-HEIGHT BAR.** The newest report has no t+1 until tomorrow, and a bar of no height in a chart where height is magnitude reads as *it did nothing* — which is a statement, and a false one. `.pending` is drawn as the old tick.
  - **Every bar keeps a 2px floor**, so a 0.1% reaction is a mark rather than a vanishing act — the Size card's `·` rule: a small thing drawn at its honest size still has to be visible.
- **THE EMPTY STRETCH IS EXPLAINED.** The bar archive reaches back twenty years and the earnings record does not, so the note says where the stored record starts — on a Max chart the absence is most of the picture and would otherwise read as "no reports happened".
- **`payload` IS NOT IN SCOPE INSIDE `paintChart`, and reaching for it killed the whole chart.** It is a local of the boot IIFE; `paintChart` lives at script scope. The first cut threw a ReferenceError, the chart never drew, and the page still *looked* half-alive because the earnings card is rendered by the page template. Use `earnRows`, which is the page's own script-scope copy.
- Verified: **+24 checks** — ticks positioned by date rather than by DOM order (`earnRows` is newest-first, so "ascending across the width" tests the emission order and nothing a reader sees), the unclassified quarter claiming no verdict, the count per range, the record-start note present on Max and correctly absent at 1Y, the toggle surviving a reload, and five on the encoding: direction, **colour MEASURED as drawn** (`getComputedStyle`, not the class name — a check on `.up` would pass against a stylesheet that painted both the same), heights in proportion, the 2px floor, and the note naming the scale.
  - **THE HEIGHT ASSERTION WAS WRITTEN WEAK AND CAUGHT BY ITS OWN REVERT-PROOF.** `h <= previous + tolerance` passes if every bar is the **same** height, which is the exact regression worth catching — the encoding would be decoration and nothing would say so. It is strictly taller now, with a real gap between the largest and smallest; flattening every bar to a constant fails it (8%/6%/4% all at 10px).
  - **Five of the earlier checks failed first and every one was the test, not the page**: it expected 9 ticks on a 1Y window that holds 3, asserted DOM order, and read the verdict off the newest event — which is deliberately the one with no estimate.

- Verified: **29 checks** on the statistics with no server (the fixture jumps on t+1, so anything reading the report day reads zero; it straddles the beat/miss floor with six beats and two misses so both branches run) plus **52** driving the real page.
  - **A screenshot found what the assertions did not**, twice: the bottom axis figure sat under the first x label, and zero rendered as "+0%".

### Six fields that were collected and never shown (2026-09-23)
**Audited by running the real renderer over a Proxy of a live row and recording every property it touched** — not by reading the source, which got it wrong the first time. 89 of 119 row fields reach the page; of the 30 that did not, most are shown another way (`ma50`/`ma200` are chart overlays, `volume` has its own pane, `realisedVol` feeds the Cushion figure) or are internal (`prevTech`, `trendTimeline`, `maCrossRank`).

Six were real and are now card rows, so they reach the stock page, the hover card and the tile/mobile field pickers at once: **enterprise value** (Size), **FCF yield**, **net cash %**, **dividend rate** (Fundamentals), and **MACD line / signal** (Trend, beside the histogram that is their difference). They are offered UNTICKED — nothing was added to any default tile or mobile view, and no screener column was created.

- **The dividend rate does not use `V.money`**, which abbreviates for market caps and renders a .48 dividend as "". It takes the Price row's treatment: currency symbol plus two decimals.
- FCF yield and net cash % are **price-divided**, so they move every day — the same reason the refresh email excluded them from its moved-fields list, back when it had one. Fine to read, misleading to watch for changes.

### Three sets that were computed and read by nothing — removed the same day
- **`mom12_1`** (the 12-1 return) and **`posMonths`** (the consistency factor) were residue from the momentum removal: still computed on every row of every refresh, stored in every snapshot, read by nothing. **`posMonths` was still in `CHAT_FIELDS`**, so the chatbot was being handed a momentum factor months after the owner pulled that family from it. Their helpers `windowReturn()` and `positiveMonths()` went too; `indicators.js` has its own `windowReturn` and is untouched.
- **The whole analyst path.** `analystConsensus`/`Score`/`Total`/`Counts`, `targetMean`/`High`/`Low`/`Upside`, the `analystConsensus()` helper, the `/recommendations` + `/price_target` fetch and the `ENABLE_ANALYST` flag. **They were null for every symbol and always would be**: the endpoints need Ultra and 403 on Pro for everything but the AAPL demo. A flag that cannot usefully be switched on is residue, not scaffolding — git has it if the plan ever changes.
  - The flag also sized the credit budget (`MAX_PROFILE_FETCHES_PER_CALL` and `PROFILE_CAP_ARCHIVE_ROUND` were `ANALYST_ENABLED ? 4 : …`), so removing it collapses those to 6 and 7 — the values every real run has used.
  - **REMOVING a key from `emptyProfile()` is safe in a way adding one is not**: `profileGaps()` looks for profiles MISSING a key the app writes, so extra keys in stored blobs are ignored rather than triggering a re-pull of the universe.
- Verified: 25 checks driving a real refresh and the real page — each removed field absent from the row, the analyst endpoints never called, `posMonths` out of the glossary, and all six new fields rendering both in `fieldValues()` and on `/stock`.

## Adjusted Advice — the same rules, read off the filings (2026-09-29)

**`/adjusted` (admin, a Research row on the console): one line per ticker carrying every field the Advice engine reads, with each technical taken from Twelve Data's price bars and each fundamental from the company's own SEC filings, and the verdict `action.js` produces from that.** The owner's framing: *"a new sheet showing the tickers and all the fields used in the advice calculation, Twelve data for Price and Edgar for fundamental, the rules remain the same"* — and explicitly **not** a backtest yet; see the design note in [docs/backlog.md](docs/backlog.md) entry 17 for where that goes next.

**IT IS NOT A NEW RULE SET.** No rule, threshold or ordering is touched, which is the whole point: the only variable is where the numbers came from, so a difference between the two verdict columns is a difference of SOURCE and nothing else. Inventing rules tuned to filings-native metrics was the alternative and was refused — it would mean fitting thresholds against the same data a backtest would then test on.

**Deliberately plain, at the owner's instruction** ("Nothing fancy, No hover etc."): no hover card, no score tooltip, no ladder panel, no chart. There are checks asserting `#rowcard` and `#tip` do not exist on the page, because "no hover" is a property worth keeping rather than a preference that quietly erodes.

- **`adjusted.js` is pure** — no network, no database, no `store` — the `secfacts.js` / `insider.js` / `news.js` shape, which is what lets every substitution below be tested without a server.
