- **The house rule, applied**: only a wide table may run past the edge, and it gets `overflow-x: auto` on **its own container** so the page body never scrolls sideways. `#abWrap` already does exactly this for the picks table.
- **`overflow-wrap: anywhere` on the name cell**, because a name is a sentence now: at ~76 characters it would otherwise hold the column open. It wraps, which costs row height and nothing else.
- **THE CHECK IS THAT DELETE CAN BE REACHED**, not that the table is narrower: the box is scrolled to its end and the button's own rect is asked whether it is inside the viewport. A width assertion would pass on a table that is merely a bit smaller and still clipped. **Proved by reverting**: without the container it fails 2, reporting `inView: false` and **81px** of page overflow — the production symptom in miniature.
- The page itself is asserted still not to scroll sideways, which is the half the container could have broken.

- Verified: **20 checks** on the formula with no server and no browser — it is pure, so the budget, the collapse and the two shapes are all reachable that way — plus **17** driving the real page and the real save route. **Proved by reverting nine times, every one load-bearing**: a default spelled out fails 4, the placeholder never set 3, Save reading the controls 3, the subline repeating the name 2, the old cadence 2, the row read with the payload's names 2, and the verdict collapse and the empty-field fallback 1 each.
  - **ONE OF THEM FIRST REPORTED 0 AND IT WAS THE REVERT, NOT RESIDUE.** The DATA-not-controls guard was reverted on the PLACEHOLDER line, which is written once per run -- so neither version re-runs when a control moves afterwards and the two are indistinguishable. The guard is load-bearing on the SAVE path, where the divergence is actually stored, and it fails 3 there. *A revert has to be put where the bug would do its damage, not where the same words appear.*

### It wears `/backtest`'s chrome now (2026-10-05, owner: "make the Adjusted Backtest page look nice similar to Backtest")
**The controls moved into a bezel panel, the labels, inputs and verdict pills took `/backtest`'s treatment, and the stat cards became cards.** Nothing about what the page computes changed — this is the skin, and the skin was the whole of the ask.

- **THE DIFFERENCE WAS THE CARD, not the colours.** `/backtest` puts its controls in `<section class="bezel panel"><div class="core panel">`; this page had them bare on the page background, which reads as debug chrome rather than as the instrument. One wrapper is most of the fix.
- **THE VERDICT PILLS ARE THE OTHER HALF, and they are a legibility fix rather than decoration.** They were grey-on-grey when pressed, so *which* verdicts were selected could not be read without going along all six; `/backtest` paints the ladder — green, light green, amber, grey, rose, red — and `data-t` was already on the button, so this is six CSS rules and no JS.
- **The cards put the KEY ABOVE THE VALUE**, which is `/backtest`'s order and the right one: the label is what you scan for and the number is what you stop on. `#abCards` is a `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(170px, 1fr))` grid, so they share one width and read as a set instead of as boxes sized by whatever text they happened to hold.
- **A FLOOR AND A CEILING ON THE SELECTS (150/250px), because this page has TEN against `/backtest`'s eight** and they are wildly uneven on their own: `1Y` is three characters and a theme name is forty. Without the floor the row reads as ragged offcuts; without the ceiling one long option sets a 360px control and pushes the verdicts onto a line of their own.
- **One rule for every control in the panel, `#abName` included.** It had its own lighter surface (`--surface`/`--hair` against the rest's `--surface-2`/`--hair-2`) and sat visibly apart from its neighbours.

#### TWO ELEMENTS SHARED `id="abBar"`, and wrapping them is what ended it
`getElementById` returns the first and CSS matches both, so `body.frozen #abBar` really did hide both rows and **nothing was visibly wrong** — which is why it survived. The rows are `.abrow` inside one `#abPanel` now, and the frozen rule hides the panel, so every control inside it goes with one selector rather than relying on a duplicate id to do the work of two.

- **`btruns-test` asserts the frozen view by MEASURING `#abGo`, `#abSave`, `#abDate` and `#abRunsBox` at zero height**, not by naming the container — so hiding the panel instead satisfies it unchanged, and that is the check doing its job rather than luck.

#### Two dead hooks found and NOT shipped
- **`btn-accent` IS NOT DEFINED ANYWHERE** — not in `app.css`, not in any page's own styles — and **`/backtest`, `/trend-backtest` and nothing else have carried it on their Run buttons all along**, so all three render as a plain `.btn`. It was added here for a few minutes and taken out again: residue reads as intent, and *defining* it would make this page diverge from the one it is meant to match. Worth deciding across all three if a primary action should ever look like one.
- **`.stb` was a class hook nothing styled.** The bezel does the work on its own.
- **`.st` IS ON THE CORE ONLY, deliberately.** The `/quality` lesson: that page put `.card` on the bezel AND the core, `querySelectorAll` matched two per card, and one click toggled its filter twice. `#abCards .st` is what `adjbt-test` counts, so it must stay one node per card.

#### THE PANEL'S DEAD FOOT IS THE ONE THING ABOUT `/backtest` NOT WORTH COPYING
`.panel { padding: 18px 20px; margin-bottom: 18px }` is applied there to **both** the shell and the core, so the core's margin lands *inside* the card — measured here as **18px of empty space under the last control** before it was scoped. `section.abpanel` takes the margin, `.abpanel` takes the padding. The doubled *padding* is kept, because that inset is what gives the reference card its weight.

- **Found by looking at the rendered page**, as every layout fault on this project has been. No assertion would have seen it: the markup was correct and the numbers were right.

#### Worth knowing
- **The phone keeps one control per row and that is a choice, not an oversight.** Two-up fits at ~134px, which truncates `Never — buy and hold` and `Cushion (room to the exit)` — and **truncating a control's label is worse than truncating a display name**, because the reader cannot tell what is selected. The page scrolls; legibility wins.
- **The shot harness now phones the LIVE view too.** `btruns-shot.js` only ever phoned the frozen one, where the panel is hidden by design — so the new markup was the half it could not see.
- Verified: **adjbt (all), abdefaults 30, btruns 83, rebalaxis 24, period 41 and bookname 29 all pass unchanged**, which is the point — a skin that moved a selector any of them reads would have said so.

## Price as of — how old the stock page is (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**A quiet line under the price in `/stock`'s masthead: `Price as of Oct 2, 2:09 PM`, amber once the pull is over a day old.** Asked for after the owner reported ASML reading **$1857.6 / +2.7%** on the stock page against **$1865.5 / +3.2%** on the screener, with the verdict differing too (Strong Buy against Hold).

**NEITHER PAGE WAS WRONG AND NOTHING DISAGREED.** Measured before changing anything: `/api/stock?symbol=ASML` and the screener's `/api/stocks` returned **byte-identical values on every field** — price, all seven returns, the verdict. The two screenshots were one or two intraday slots apart. **The cause is an asymmetry rather than a bug**: a visible screener tab polls `/api/status` every five minutes and reloads when the snapshot moves, and **`/stock` has no poller at all**, so two tabs left open across a slot drift. The verdict moving with them is Advice behaving intraday, as designed.

- **THE SCREENER COULD ANSWER THE QUESTION AND THIS PAGE COULD NOT** — it has the Price pulled column and the status pill; `/stock` had nothing. That is the whole gap this closes. Every other data surface here already states its own freshness (the status pill, the Price pulled column, the studio's amber 26-hour line, the phone's "data as of"); `/stock` was the omission.

#### The route applied ONE of the four read-path stamps
**`/api/stock` called `stampCapDerived` and not `stampPricedAt` or `stampAdviceAge`**, so `pricedAt` and `adviceDays` were undefined on every stock page — confirmed on production across ASML, BRK.B and MU — and **Price pulled and Days held each drew a label with an em-dash**. `/compare` withheld both for the same reason.

- **The comment directly above the fix records this exact class of bug being found once already** (`capBand`, found by `/compare` putting an empty cell next to a full one) and it did not stop the next two. *The stamps are a SET; a read path applies all four or it has a blank row nobody notices.*
- **The irony worth keeping: the field that would have answered the owner's question in one glance was the blank one.**
- Applied **in parallel, each with its own catch** — the screener's rule: independent single-row reads, and a slow auxiliary read should cost one row rather than 500 the page.

#### The decisions
- **THE VALUE COMES FROM `FIELD_SPEC`'s OWN FORMATTER** (`RowCard.fieldValues(s)['short|Price pulled']`), never a second copy of the rule, so the masthead and the screener's column cannot drift on what counts as stale or how a time is written. **Proved by reverting**: a hand-rolled `toLocaleTimeString` loses the amber and fails 1.
- **THE DATE IS KEPT EVEN WHEN THE PULL WAS TODAY, deliberately differing from the screener's column.** That column drops it to save width in a 90-column table; a masthead has no such constraint, and this element exists precisely for the reader who left the tab open overnight — for whom a bare `2:09 PM` is the ambiguity the feature was built to remove.
- **ASKING IS NOT RECEIVING, and the tooltip carries it**: the pull time, the newest stored bar, and that the two are different facts. Ten stocks were once pulled on time and were not on the day's bar, AVB carrying a close from five weeks earlier — so a fresh clock must not be read as a fresh price. **Proved by reverting twice**: 1 each.
- **Never pulled is a different fact from pulled long ago** — `Price as of —` with a tooltip saying why, never a fabricated time. **Proved by reverting**: fails 3, and the page throws (`Cannot read properties of null`), which is what the guard is for.
- **Amber past a day**, the colour's existing meaning here (*notice this, it is old*), taking `.warn` for colour only — all `.warn` does in app.css. Scoped `.px .asof`: nine unscoped class names on this project have captured later markup.
- **THE DUPLICATE ROW STANDS ASIDE** — `short|Price pulled` joins `fund|Reported` in `buildSections({ skip })`. Reading the field's own formatter means the row below would print a **byte-identical** string a screen further down. Unlike Reported the two cannot disagree (they are one value), so this is purely duplication and the masthead states it better. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1, printing the clock twice.
- **It costs 20px and wraps nothing.** Measured as an A/B on the same page.
- Verified: **25 checks** over a fixture whose three stocks differ ONLY in the price clock — fresh, **23 hours and 25 hours** (a threshold is a step function, so it is probed either side of the field's own 24-hour line), and never pulled. **Proved by reverting nine times**: the two stamps 6, the price stamp alone 5, the readout 18, the bar tooltip 1, the asking-caveat 1, the amber 1, the never-pulled guard 3, the duplicate row 1, a second copy of the formatter 1.
  - **CLUSTERING CHILD TOPS IS THE WRONG WRAP TEST ON THIS MASTHEAD, and it failed first over a layout that was fine.** That heuristic comes from the screener's bar where every control is roughly one height; `.head` is **baseline-aligned** with a 46px `h1` beside a 26px chip, so their tops legitimately differ by ~16px **on one line** and any threshold near that flips when the line's height changes. The honest measure is how far each item MOVES between the two states: a wrap is a whole line, and the only thing that moved was `.outs` by **10px of the 20px growth** — exactly half, because those pills are `align-self: center` and a taller line re-centres them. Arithmetic, not a wrap.
  - **TWO REVERTS ABORTED RATHER THAN FAILED on the first run, one of them reporting "0 failed"** — indistinguishable from a guard that never mattered. A revert that breaks the render makes `waitForSelector` throw, and the A/B block touched `el.style` on an element that was no longer there. Both waits swallow their timeout and every read is defensive now.
  - **A relative `fetch` has no base URL on `about:blank`** — the API probe has to run after a navigation.

## Charts and the stock page

### The jump bar — the console's chips, on a page whose sections come and go (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**A row of chips under the masthead, one per card: Price · News · All fields · Earnings · About · Similar stocks · SEC EDGAR · Insiders · Short interest.** Asked for as *"the menus that you have on Admin page, can you add something similar to individual stock page"* — same `.jump` chips, same glyphs out of the same house sprite, nine of which `/stock` did not carry and now does.

- **IT IS BUILT FROM THE PAGE, NEVER FROM A LIST WRITTEN BESIDE IT, and that is the one real difference from `/admin`'s eight fixed sections.** Three cards are only rendered when there is something to render (Earnings, About, Similar stocks) and three more ship `hidden` and are either revealed or **removed** by their own fetches long after the first paint (SEC EDGAR, Insiders, Short interest). A written list would offer a fund chips for filings it never makes. A card opts in with **`data-jump`** — its label, allowed to be shorter than its heading, which is how *"Everything the screener knows"* becomes **All fields** — and `data-icon`.
- **ONE `MutationObserver`, not a call at the end of each loader.** That would be three call sites to keep in step and a fourth card later would be the one somebody forgets. It watches **`childList` as well as the attribute**, because those loaders also call `card.remove()` — every early return removes a card that was still hidden, but **the catch at the end of each can fire after it has been shown**, which would leave a chip pointing at nothing.
- **THE SIGNATURE GUARD IS NOT AN OPTIMISATION — it is what stops the observer feeding itself.** The bar lives inside the subtree being watched, so rewriting its markup is itself a mutation. **Measured by reverting: the page never reaches `networkidle` and the navigation times out.** My own comment first called it a performance measure, which was true and understated it; the revert is recorded in the harness as *expect a HANG* rather than as an ambiguous abort.
- **`section.card` takes a `scroll-margin-top`**, or a chip parks its card under the sticky island — the `/help` lesson. Measured as drawn rather than asserted off the href: every chip is clicked and the card's top compared against the island's bottom (76 against 57). **Proved by reverting**: at 0 the card lands at 0, under an island ending at 57.
- **On a phone the chips are ONE ROW that scrolls sideways in its own box**, not four wrapped rows — a screen of furniture in front of the thing being read. The page itself still cannot be panned. **Proved by reverting**: 3 rows and 130px.
- **One chip is not a bar**, so with fewer than two cards nothing is drawn. Unreachable as the page stands (Price, News and All fields are unconditional), so it is **driven directly** rather than left unproven — hide the rest, assert the bar goes, put them back.
- Verified: **26 checks against the drawn page**, every one comparing the chips against the cards that are **actually there** rather than against a literal — in both directions, so neither a missing chip nor an extra one passes. **Proved by reverting eight times.**
  - **THE HIDDEN-CARD FILTER COULD NOT BE SEEN TO DO ANYTHING at first, and the window is the reason.** Those three cards are hidden only until their fetches land, and `waitForSelector` already resolves after that — so by the time anything was measured the hidden ones had removed themselves and the revert failed on an unrelated check. It is now checked on a page whose three requests are **held open**, which is the state a reader genuinely sees for the first second or two of every load.
  - **PRODUCTION CORRECTED MY FIXTURE'S IDEA OF A FUND.** It assumed a fund has no earnings, no description and no short interest; **SPY has all three and draws six chips, not three.** The mechanism was right and the label overclaimed, so the label was narrowed to what the fixture actually shows. The claim that survives is *the bar equals the page*, which is what the live check measured on MU (9 chips, 9 cards, none orphaned) and SPY (6 and 6).
  - **`$` DOES NOT EXIST ON THIS PAGE** — it uses `document.getElementById` throughout, 49 times. The painter was written with the console's `$` and threw on every load; the nav was in the DOM and empty, so the first failure read as *"there is no bar"*. `pageerror` is what named it.

Charts are hand-rolled inline SVG in `rowcard.js` — no library, no build step. `chartSVG(closes)` returns `{ svg, log }`.

- **The y-axis goes logarithmic above a 4× range.** MU ran from $1.69 to $932, so on a linear axis nineteen of twenty years flatten onto the floor and only the last month is visible. The caption says "log scale" when it happens, because an unmarked log axis misleads. A single year rarely trips it, so the default view stays linear.
- **The chart window is 253 bars, not 252.** A change is measured across the *gaps* between bars, so matching `pctChange(values, ONE_YEAR)` — bar 0 against bar 252 — needs one bar more than there are intervals. One short and the headline disagreed with the card's own 1Y row by 27 points on a name that gapped on earnings a year ago.
- **`/api/history` reads the archive only** — no API call, so it costs nothing and works for members. It returns `dates`, `closes` and `volumes`; ~1.9 KB for a year of closes. Fetched per symbol on hover and cached by `symbol|days`, so the card never waits on the network to appear. **The `days` floor is 2**, because the stock page's shortest range is a trading week — it was 20, which silently returned 20 bars for a 1W request.
- **No area fill — the price is a stroked line only.** Keep `fill` off `.ln`: the stroke and fill rules are deliberately *not* grouped, because setting `fill` on the line path closes it back to its start and paints a filled wedge. The area path masked that for a while.
- **`chartSVG(closes, { volumes, ticks })` draws volume bars and price gridlines**; without them it is a plain line. It returns `{ svg, log, ticks }`, each tick carrying `top` as a fraction of the viewBox so the caller can place an HTML label at the same height.
- **The price axis replaced the floating high/low captions** on the stock page — with real gridlines the two said the same thing twice. Ticks are evenly spaced along whichever scale is in use and rounded to significant figures; even spacing beats round numbers, because on a log axis round values land unevenly and the gridlines look accidental. The hover card passes none — at 104px there is no room — so the two surfaces share one function without the card becoming cramped. Bars are scaled to the largest in view, not an absolute, so a quiet stretch still shows its own shape, and each is green or red by whether that session closed above the one before it.
- **Axis labels are HTML, not SVG text.** The chart stretches with `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, which would distort any glyph inside it. The same reason the price captions are absolutely-positioned spans, anchored by percentage to the bands they describe rather than to the box.
- **Stock page ranges are 1W/2W/1M/3M/6M/1Y/5Y/Max** in trading days (5/10/21/63/126/253/1260/5200).
- **The symbol in the masthead is the stock picker.** Clicking it opens a filtered list of the whole universe, alphabetically, matching on symbol *or* company name. It is styled as the heading it replaced — only the caret says it opens — so the page gained navigation without gaining a control or a row.
  - **The list comes from `universe` on `/api/stock`**, `[{symbol, name}]`. That route already holds the whole snapshot in memory to work out the rank, so the field costs a `map` and ~3 KB rather than a query or a second request.
  - **Selecting navigates (`location.href`) rather than swapping in place**: back and forward keep working, and the per-symbol history fetch dominates the timing anyway.
  - Arrow keys move, Enter goes, Escape and an outside click close. On open the current symbol is the active row and is scrolled to **`center`**; arrowing uses `nearest`, so the list moves as little as possible.
- **Employees, website and the company description come from `/profile`, which `fetchProfile()` already calls for the sector** — the call costs the same whether one field is read or five, so these were free and were simply being discarded.
  - **They are deliberately absent from the snapshot**, and therefore from `/api/stocks` and from the chatbot. Eighty-odd descriptions is ~70 KB on every screener load and ~20k tokens of prose that answers none of the numeric questions the bot is asked. `/api/stock` reads them from the profile row instead, via `readProfile(symbol)` — a single-row read added for exactly this, since `readProfiles()` would pull 84 blobs to render one page.
  - **`buildSections(s, { extra: { info: [...] } })` appends rows to a named group.** Opt-in, and only `stock.html` passes it: these values are not in the snapshot, so putting them in `FIELD_SPEC` would print an em-dash in the hover card on every other page. A row with `href` renders as a link (`.rc-link`).
  - **A row with no value is omitted, not shown empty.** A profile last pulled before these fields existed simply has fewer rows, which reads better than a column of dashes — they fill in as each profile refreshes.
  - **`.about` carries NO max-width (owner, 2026-09-26).** It was `1100px` — a reading measure, which is the right default for prose and made the description **the only constrained block on the page**: the earnings note, the peers note and the closing line all run the full card, so on a wide monitor it stopped ~800px short of everything above and below it and read as a layout fault rather than as a measure. At 2400px the same text goes from six lines to two. The cost is a long line on a very wide window; a cap can come back as a number nearer the card if that ever bites.
  - **A `max-width` is invisible until the container is wider than it**, so a check at one comfortable laptop width passes either way — `about-width-test.js` measures at **2400px and 1500px**, and measures **the text's own client rects, not the paragraph's box**: a block fills its parent whatever `max-width` says, so the box was 2286px wide while the ink stopped at 1100. The tolerance is **the widest word, measured in the page**, since a full line can only fall short by the word that would not fit on it — a fixed 40px tolerance failed on a legitimately-wrapped line. **Proved by reverting**: the cap back fails 6 of 13.
- **The sector/portfolio/rank chips sit inside `.head`, not on a row of their own.** A separate band cost 26px plus 30px of margins and pushed the chart 265px down the page; inline they cost nothing above ~900px wide and simply wrap below it.
- **Indicators stack as panes below the price, in the order RSI then volume** — RSI is 0–100 and price is in currency, so it cannot share the price axis. Turning a pane on **grows the chart** rather than squeezing the price panel: the svg stretches with `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, so a taller viewBox alone would just squash every band.
  - **WHAT MUST STAY CONSTANT IS PIXELS PER VIEWBOX UNIT**, and that couples two files. The bands live in `rowcard.js` (`PRICE_H`, `PANE_GAP` 13, `RSI_H` 58, volume `PANE_H` 44) and the box heights in `stock.html`; the 18px of bottom padding is the date axis and is *not* part of the svg, so a height is `viewBox H × px-per-unit + 18`. Change one without the other and the bands silently shrink instead of the price growing — which looks subtly wrong rather than broken.
  - **The price panel grew TWICE on 2026-09-21**, each step 30% on the one before, at the owner's request (taller chart, *not* taller bands). `PRICE_H` **150 → 195 → 254**, so the viewBox is **317** with volume alone and **388** with RSI too, and the boxes are **468px / 577px** (were 320/427). Measured through both steps: the price panel went **213 → 277 → 359px** and **216 → 281 → 365px**, while **volume stayed 62/63px and RSI stayed 83px** throughout — which is the whole point, and only holds because px-per-unit was held constant each time.
  - **Only the paned case moved.** `PRICE_H` is `anyPane ? 195 : 104`, and the 104 branch is the hover card and the tile/phone stock card, which pass no panes.
  - Verified: 13 checks measuring **bands in PIXELS** off `getBoundingClientRect()` and each pane's reported viewBox fraction — never the viewBox numbers that produced them — in both RSI states, plus the RSI threshold labels still landing inside their own band and the unpaned chart still 104 units. **RSI defaults ON**: the first cut of the test assumed off, swapped its two phases and compared every reading against the wrong baseline.
- **`chartSVG` returns `panes`**, each with `top`/`bottom` as fractions of the viewBox, so the caller positions HTML labels against real geometry. The volume label moves down on its own when RSI appears — an earlier hardcoded percentage had to be fixed once already.
- **Those fractions are of the viewBox, and the svg does not fill the box** — 18px at the bottom is reserved for the date axis. Every pane label therefore goes through `atY()`, which converts with `calc(f * (100% - 18px))`. A raw `top: %` lands things progressively low and pushed the oversold label clean out of its pane.
- **The chart has a hover crosshair** — a dotted line, a dot on the price, a date pill on the axis, and a readout of price, day change, volume and RSI. All of it is HTML overlaid on the svg, never drawn inside it: `preserveAspectRatio="none"` would stretch the dot into an ellipse and distort any text. `panes.price.at(v)` exists so the dot can sit on the line without the caller knowing whether the scale is log or linear. The static change caption and MA legend fade while hovering, so the top-left says one thing at a time.
- **`priceTicks()` returns low-to-high**, so in the DOM the *first* axis label is the bottom of the scale and the *last* is the top — the reverse of reading order. The end-clamping rules were briefly backwards and pushed the top label 6px above the chart, where `overflow: hidden` ate it.
- **The RSI band is taller than the volume band** (58 vs 44 viewBox units) because it carries threshold lines with words above and below them, where volume only needs bars. It also paints its own `.pane-bg`, a shade off the chart's ground, so the indicator reads as a separate instrument. 70 is red and 30 is green — the colours mean overbought and oversold; 50 stays neutral because it is only an anchor for the eye.
- **`RowCard.rsiSeries()` uses Wilder smoothing**, matching `rsi()` in server.js. Wilder is an exponential average and converges slowly, so it is computed over the padded window and sliced. Cross-checked against the screener's own RSI column for six symbols: **gap 0.000**, at both 300- and 453-bar warm-ups.
- MACD is the obvious next pane and is already computed per row (`macdLine`, `macdSignal`, `macdHist`); adding it is a pane entry rather than a rewrite.
- **Another stock can be overlaid on the chart, from a picker beside the index toggles (2026-09-20, owner's request).** It is NOT a new mechanism: the page already overlaid four index ETFs (SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA) as toggles, so this is a fifth entry in the list `paintChart` builds, whose symbol happens to be chosen. `benchSeries` does the alignment, `chartSVG` draws the path, and the legend already lists whatever is drawn.
  - **REBASED, not a second price line.** The overlay is scaled to this stock's close at the first date the two share, so it answers "what would that have done from the same starting point" and the **gap between the lines is the relative performance**. Two raw prices on one axis is the misleading version — NVDA at $180 against KSS at $12 flattens one into the floor and the chart says nothing. The test builds its fixture at a **100x price difference** in opposite directions precisely so a raw overlay could not pass it.
  - **The picker never offers this stock, nor the four indices** — those have their own buttons, and offering SPY twice is two controls for one line. It labels by the **display name**, for which `/api/stock`'s universe now carries `short` beside `name`: "NVIDIA" beats "NVIDIA Corporation" beside a line, and `shortName` is already stamped on every row so it costs nothing. The legal name stays, so the symbol picker's filter matches what it always matched.
  - **The toolbar is rendered once** (`#page`'s innerHTML) and `paintChart()` only replaces `#chart`, which is why the select's options and its listener survive every repaint. Worth checking before adding a control there.
  - Verified: 16 checks on the real page — the picker's contents, the line appearing and clearing, the legend naming it, survival across a range change, and the rebasing read back out of the **drawn SVG path**: both lines start within 2px of each other, then diverge by 130px. Two fixture traps: `innerText` on `#chart` returns **empty** (the captions are absolutely positioned — read `textContent` on the caption itself), and an assertion that the overlay is not pinned to the axis floor is meaningless against a **monotonically rising** stock, whose first point IS the floor. It measures the overlay's own vertical span now.
- **Moving averages are a list (`MAS` in stock.html), 50-day and 200-day.** Adding another is one entry there plus a colour in `app.css`.
  - **The page fetches `range.days + MA_PAD`**, padded by the *longest* average rather than by whichever are switched on, so toggling redraws from the cache instead of refetching. Without the run-up a line would start 200 sessions late and leave a gap at the left edge; with it, even the 1M view draws both averages as unbroken paths.
  - **Overlays are folded into the y-scale.** An average sits above a falling price and below a rising one, so scaling to the price alone clips it. A `null` breaks the path rather than joining across the gap.
  - `RowCard.sma()` is exported for it. Cross-checked against the screener's own `vs50ma` and `vs200ma` for six symbols: exact agreement, gap 0.000 on both.
- **NO HOVER CARD AND NO SCORE TOOLTIP ON A TOUCH DEVICE (2026-09-26, owner's request).** A touch browser **synthesises `mouseover` on tap**, so the card ambushed the finger reaching for the link underneath it and the first tap was spent dismissing it. `RowCard.canHover()` is the one place the question is asked — `attach()` returns a no-op `{hide(){}}` before wiring anything, and the screener's `.rating` listeners are gated on the same call, so the card and the tooltip cannot disagree. **Nothing is wired, rather than wired-and-suppressed.**
  - **WIDTH IS THE WRONG TEST and would have failed the exact device it was asked for.** Measured in the suite: **an iPad Pro 11 in landscape reports `innerWidth` 1340**, so a breakpoint at 768 or 1024 leaves hover switched ON there — while a 900px laptop window holding a mouse would lose it. `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` asks directly: a touch screen answers `hover: none, pointer: coarse`; a laptop answers fine even when its screen is also a touch screen, which is correct, because that person has a mouse.
  - Read **once at boot** (`const HOVERS` on the screener), not per row. A device that gains a mouse mid-session gets the behaviour back on reload, which is not worth a listener.
  - **Losing it costs nothing on touch**: the name is a link, so tapping it opens the whole stock page — a better answer on a phone than a floating card — and `/m` exists besides.
  - Verified: **32 checks** across desktop, iPad Pro landscape, iPad gen 7 and iPhone. Each touch context **asserts the emulation really reports a coarse pointer before testing anything**, or the rest would pass by testing a desktop. Both a real hover and a **synthesised `mouseover`** are checked, since the latter is how a tap actually arrives. **Proved by reverting**: without the one guard line, 6 checks fail.
  - **A fixture with only `qualityRating` cannot test the tooltip** — `scoreTip` returns `null` without `qualityBreakdown`, deliberately, so a caller skips showing rather than flashing an empty card. The desktop assertion failed on exactly that and it was the fixture, not the change.
- **`.rc-*` classes are unscoped in `app.css`**; only the floating container is tied to `#rowcard`. The hover card and `/stock/<SYMBOL>` render the same sections from the same `FIELD_SPEC` via `RowCard.buildSections()` — a third copy of the field list is exactly what the row card existed to prevent.
- **`GROUP_COLORS` / `GROUP_LABELS` now live in `rowcard.js`** and are exported. `index.html` and `analysis.html` keep their own copies because they also colour the table's group banners and the columns menu, so **all three must stay in step** — renaming the `rank` group's label to `Scores` in one of them left the stock page's card still saying `RANK`.
- **The Google Finance URL lives in `rowcard.js` (`RowCard.gfUrl`), moved there 2026-09-26 rather than copied** when the stock page wanted the same link. The MIC → venue table (`XNGS` → NASDAQ, `ARCX` → NYSEARCA, …) is a pile of venue trivia that would only ever be corrected in one of two copies; the MIC is authoritative and the free-text exchange is the fallback. **A row with no venue yet still gets a working link to the bare symbol** — exchange rides the profile, which rotates weekly, so "no link" would be the common case for a new ticker. The screener's ticker cell calls through it now, and the test asserts each venue mapping AND that index.html no longer carries its own.
- **`/stock/<SYMBOL>` says it out loud in the masthead** (owner, 2026-09-26): a blue `Google Finance` pill with an out-arrow, beside the sector chips and left of the price. The screener's four-letter ticker link is easy to miss, and on a page about ONE stock "go and look at it somewhere else" is the obvious next move. `align-self: center` because `.head` aligns on the baseline and a padded pill hangs low on one. Verified as drawn, inside the masthead, above the chart, not crowding the price, and a different colour from the chips — "very visible" was the request, so it is measured rather than asserted.
- **YAHOO FINANCE SITS BESIDE IT since 2026-09-27** (owner's request), from `RowCard.yfUrl`, and the pill class was renamed `.gfin` → `.olink` in the same commit — two links sharing a class named after one of them is a small wrongness the next reader trips on, and unlike a prefs key or a group id a class in one page has no stored data behind it. Both keep the accent: same kind of thing going to two places, so colouring them apart would be a distinction with nothing behind it.
  - **IT NEEDS NO VENUE — `https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MU/` is the whole URL** — which is the one way it is simpler than Google. What it does need is the share-class spelling: **Yahoo writes those with a HYPHEN**, and this universe holds `BRK.A`, `BRK.B` and `HEI.A`.
  - **THE FAILURE IS SILENT, NOT A 404.** Checked against the live site: `quote/BRK.B/` answers **200 with an empty company name** — a quote page with nothing on it — where `quote/BRK-B/` is Berkshire Hathaway. **A status-code check would have passed over a dead link**, which is why the rule is measured rather than assumed.
  - **Nothing else is translated, and that holds only BECAUSE the universe is US-listed only**: a foreign listing needs Yahoo's own market suffix (`005930.KS`, `VOD.L`). One more thing that rule quietly buys.
  - Verified: **56 checks** in the extended out-links suite — both pills drawn and measured in the masthead, on one line, clear of the price, styled as a pair, not underlined (the peers `vs` pill arrived underlined for exactly that reason), and **each selected BY WHAT IT SAYS rather than by position**, since with two pills an index passes just as happily with the hrefs swapped. The fixture carries a real dotted symbol and asserts **both spellings on the same page**: Yahoo hyphenated, Google still dotted, because they are not the same rule. **Proved by reverting**: dropping the one `replace` fails 4, including the end-to-end page check.
  - **THE PILLS ARE NEUTRAL, NOT A SECOND ACCENT** (owner, an hour later: *"all the pills are in blue, can you change the colour on google and yahoo to make it more distinct"*). They were accent-blue and so are the chips — the group chips became links the day before and were given the accent deliberately — so the masthead read as one blue row and **the two loudest things on it were the two that say least about the stock**.
    - **It is not another signal colour, and that is the point rather than a compromise.** Every coloured token on this page already MEANS something about the data: green and red are direction, amber is *notice this, it is old*, **violet is RSI in three places** (the toggle, the caption, the crosshair readout), and the accent is now *this chip opens its group*. An external link is not a reading about the stock, it is navigation — so it takes the treatment navigation already has here, the **`Back to screener` pill**: `--text` on `rgba(255,255,255,.075)` with a hairline, no hue. Distinct from every chip beside it **without spending the one unspent colour in the palette**.
    - Still louder than a chip, which was the original brief: filled at 33px against a 26px outline. The out-arrow drops to `--muted` — the same glyph twice at full strength is noise.
  - **THAT ASSERTION HAS NOW GONE STALE ONCE AND BEEN UNDER-WRITTEN ONCE, which is the lesson.** It first checked the pill was not the CHIP's colour; the chips went accent and it failed over a page working as asked, so I replaced it with **box-only** checks — and the owner then reported the real fault by eye, *"all the pills are in blue"*, which a box check cannot see. Colour is asserted again and now **against every meaning the palette carries** (not the chip's, not the accent, not violet) plus *no hue at all* (channel spread ≤ 12) and *still bright* — so it cannot rot the same way a third time. **Proved by reverting**: putting `--accent` back fails 4, reproducing the reported symptom exactly.
- The name cell links to `/stock/<SYMBOL>` on **both** the screener and the analysis page; the symbol cell still links out to Google Finance. All of them open in a new tab (`target="_blank" rel="noopener"`), so a click never loses your place in the list. `.namelink` lives in `app.css` because two pages use it; only the frozen-column truncation (`td.frz1 .namelink`) stays in index.html. `.namelink` inherits its colour and only underlines on hover — 69 rows of blue underlines would wreck the table.

## Bar archive
The `bars` table keeps one row per symbol per trading day (`open/high/low/close/volume`, keyed on `(symbol, d)`). **Currently 4,582,357 rows across 1,182 symbols, 1998-12-23 → today** (measured 2026-09-28, after the backfill below).

### 61% of the universe had fourteen months of history, and nothing would ever have fixed it (2026-09-28)
**Reported by the owner as "why does URI only go back to July 25 — this is a very old company".** United Rentals has been listed since 1997 and held **303 bars from 2025-07-14**. Everything else about it was fine: SEC facts back to 2009, 26 earnings quarters, a fresh profile and a fresh price. It was the archive alone.

- **The cause is `LIGHT_MIN_ARCHIVE`, and the shape of it is worth remembering.** A new ticker gets one ~300-bar pull; a live refresh is then deliberately shallow (12 bars) and only re-pulls deep when the archive is **under 300**. URI sat at **303 — three bars over the line that would have rescued it**, so it grew forward for ever and never backward. **A threshold that heals the symbols below it strands the ones that land just above it.**
- **It was not one stock.** Measured off `/api/data-quality`: **750 of 1,182 flagged *no 5Y*, and 722 of those sat in a 300-399 band with only ten distinct start dates clustered in July 2025** — the September 2026 bulk adds, each given one ~300-bar pull. The 2026-09-22 repair had covered only the 47 that were genuinely *under* 300, which is precisely the band the auto-deepening already handles.
- **`/quality` had the answer all along** — its `thin` list is every stock flagged `no 5Y` or `too short`, 781 of them, with a ready `--only` command. **Ignore its `--depth 1300`**: five years clears the flag and still discards twenty years, and the depth costs the same 1 credit either way.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| clean | 401 | **1,070** |
| no 5Y | 750 | **80** |
| 300-399 sessions | 722 | **10** |
| 1,260+ sessions | 401 | **1,071** |
| archive | ~1.85M rows | **4,582,357**, earliest bar 2003-01-09 → **1998-12-23** |

- **Every one of the 112 still flagged holds exactly what the provider serves** — checked symbol by symbol against the dry run, 0 short of it. The remaining shortfall is the market's, not the archive's, the same conclusion the 2026-09-19 pass reached.
- **WRITES ARE 8x FASTER THAN THIS FILE SAYS, and the old number would have talked you out of the job.** Measured: **2,934,059 bars in ~16 minutes across seven batches (~203,000 bars/min)**, against the 2026-09-19 reading of 24,259/min. Budgeting from the old figure predicted 2-3 hours and an overlap with the nightly, which is why it was batched at all. Re-measure before planning around either number.
- **Batched 130 symbols at a time, deepest first**, so an early stop leaves the most valuable symbols done rather than queued — and each batch is independently resumable, since a symbol is replaced wholesale.
- **`--rate 100`, not the default 580.** An intraday price round needs ~500 credits inside one minute against the plan's 610, so the default starves the live refresh. The fetch side is never the bottleneck here (writes are), so the throttle is free. As it happened the run was pre-market and contended with nothing — see the Git Bash timezone trap above, which is why I thought otherwise.
- **`FAILED: terminated` with an exit code of 1 does NOT mean the batch failed.** One batch reported `130 symbols ok, 0 failed, 307,264 bars written` and *then* exited 1: the closing `archiveStats()` is a whole-table `count(*)` over what is now 4.5M rows, and the socket was dropped. Spot-checking six of its symbols found all of them written. **Judge a batch by its row count, not its exit code** — the same lesson the `tech_history` build records about silence.

**What this invalidates, and none of it is rebuilt yet**: `tech_history` (the trend backtest's usable floor was 2008 with 278 symbols and could now reach much further), the local analysis copy (`analysis-db.js --full`), and the three derived files built from it — `single-closes.json`, `strategy-*.json`, `lab-grid.json`. Every backtest number on those surfaces still describes the shallow archive.

**It costs no API credits.** Every refresh already fetches ~300 daily bars per symbol and discards them; `persistBars()` writes them instead. Twelve Data charges **1 credit per symbol regardless of `outputsize`** — measured, `Api-Credits-Request: 1` for 5000 bars — which is why the deep backfill was affordable in the first place.

- **The backfill is PACED, and it had to be (2026-09-15).** One symbol is one credit and the plan allows 610 a minute; the unpaced script fetched at ~15 symbols a second (900/min) and only survived the 190-symbol run because the whole job was 190 credits in 13 seconds. `makePacer(limit, windowMs)` is a sliding-window meter shared by the workers — `take()` resolves only when one more credit keeps the last 60s under `--rate` (default **580**) — and a refusal (`/credit|rate limit|429|too many/i`) waits 62s and retries up to 3 times rather than writing the symbol off. The receipt prints symbols/min and how long was spent waiting. Verified: the pacer on a fake clock (8 checks — no 60s window over the limit across 1,000 symbols, a 190-symbol run never delayed, the window sliding, the refusal pattern) and a live 3-symbol dry run at `--rate 2` that waited exactly 60s.
- **Throughput is dominated by WRITES, and it degrades as the archive grows.** Two measurements, same script, same depth:
  - 2026-09-15: 190 symbols, **755,991 bars in 3 min 45 s** (~50 symbols/min), against an archive of ~1.08M rows.
  - 2026-09-19: 177 symbols, **640,433 bars in 26.4 min** (~7 symbols/min), against an archive of ~1.13M rows growing to 1.71M. Fetching was 0.1 min of that — the dry run over the identical list finished in six seconds.
  **Seven times slower per row for a comparable job**, with no pacing wait in either. So budget a backfill by the archive it is writing INTO, not by the symbol count, and do not quote the 2026-09-15 figure as the expectation.
- *(Superseded, kept for the comparison above)* **Measured throughput, 2026-09-15**: 190 symbols at depth 5000 took **3 min 45 s** and wrote **755,991 bars** — fetching was 13s of that, so writes are ~95% of the wall clock. Extrapolating to a 1,000-symbol universe: ~2.9M more rows, ~15-20 minutes, ~730 credits. **What actually costs at that size is profiles, not bars**: 730 new stocks is ~58,000 credits and ~1h45m of Fill missing.
- **The 2026-09-19 deep backfill, and what it bought.** Run as Phase 0 of the trend-only backtest: 177 symbols (the `/quality` page's own thin list, verified to contain none of the 196 deep ones), at the default depth 5000. **640,433 bars written, 0 failed, 0 retried.** The archive went **1,125,447 → 1,708,406 rows** and its earliest bar moved from 2006-10-12 to **2003-01-09** — three years further back than the file had ever recorded, because several long-listed names had only ever had one shallow price pull.

| reaches back | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 3 years | 260 | **406** |
| 5 years | 253 | **392** |
| 10 years | 211 | **332** |
| 15 years | 183 | **297** |
| 19 years | 169 | **276** |

  `/quality`'s own flags moved with it: `noFiveYear` **166 → 27**, clean **250 → 389**, thin **177 → 38**. **Only 12 stocks now hold under 320 sessions and every one is a genuine recent listing** (CBRS from 2026-05-14, SKHY 2026-07-10, GOOGM/GOOGN 2026-06-03…), so there is nothing left for a backfill to fix — the remaining shallowness is the market's, not the archive's.
  - **Use the default depth, not the page's command, for a deep study.** `/quality`'s fix command says `--depth 1300` — five years, which is what its own "no 5Y" flag is about. A nineteen-year study wants the default 5000.
  - **The dry run is the cheap way to find out what is actually available**, and it corrected a wrong inference: "164 stocks under 320 sessions were never backfilled" was only half right. CBRS returns 88 bars because it listed in May 2026, while VSAT returns the full 5000 back to 2006. One credit a symbol, six seconds for 177, and it reports the real first date per symbol before anything is written.
- **Never run a shallow `--depth` over symbols that already have deep history** — each symbol is replaced wholesale, so `--depth 1300` would truncate twenty years to five. Use `--only` with the shallow ones (2026-09-15: 190 of 271 had under 1,300 bars).
- **`backfill-bars.js` is a local script, not a route.** 5000 bars is ~580 KB per symbol and ~40 MB across the universe: fine locally, far past what a serverless function should hold. Same one-off pattern as `migrate-to-turso.js`, dry-run by default.
- **Writes are incremental, not wholesale.** `persistBars()` upserts only bars newer than the stored `max(d)` plus a `BAR_OVERLAP` of 5. Steady state is a handful of rows per symbol per refresh, not 300.
- **The overlap is not decoration.** Twelve Data returns a bar for *today* while the market is open, with the current price as its close, so a mid-session refresh stores a provisional value. Re-upserting the recent window replaces it with the settled close. Measured drift on a real pull: 0.003–0.007%.
- **Splits are detected, not ignored.** A split re-prices all of history, so a stored bar `SPLIT_PROBE_BARS` (60) back would silently disagree with the fetched one and leave a phantom cliff in any chart. `persistBars()` compares that one bar per symbol — one query for the whole universe, since US symbols share trading days — and rewrites the symbol in full when it differs by more than `SPLIT_TOLERANCE` (0.5%). Re-running `backfill-bars.js --only SYM` is the manual repair.
- **An as-of pull must never write.** `computeStocks(asOf)` fetches a truncated range; persisting from it would corrupt the archive. Guarded by `if (!asOf)`, the same rule the snapshot uses.
- **A failed archive write never fails the refresh** — it is caught and logged. The screener is the product; the archive is a by-product.
- `open` is stored although nothing reads it yet. `high`/`low` drive the 52-week range and `volume` the volume trend, so an archive without them could draw a chart but not reproduce the screener — which is the point of keeping it.

## The nightly job
**It runs from the laptop now, twice a weekday, at 07:30 and 19:30 ET — `nightly-ping.js` driven by `nightly-task.ps1` (2026-09-30, owner's request).** The GitHub workflow keeps its `workflow_dispatch` and has had **both `cron:` lines and its New-York hour gate removed**; a long comment in the file records that the crons and the guard belong together if a schedule ever returns there.

### Why it moved, and the objection that shaped it
**The owner's question was the right one: "why is GitHub better than my own laptop?"** I had listed the generic laptop caveats — battery, Modern Standby, a closed lid — **without checking that any of them applied to this machine**, which already runs the intraday schedule all day behind a mouse mover. They do not. Meanwhile GitHub's own scheduler had **missed 2026-09-21 outright** (one firing all day, two hours late, correctly refused by the hour gate) — the failure this file already records. So the reliability argument ran the other way and I reversed the recommendation.

- **"ONE BIG ISSUE WITH THE LAPTOP IS I CANNOT RE-RUN A JOB" — a better objection than any of mine, and it is why `workflow_dispatch` stays.** The workflow is now a **manual re-run button** rather than a schedule: the crons are gone, the dispatch path is untouched, and a missed or broken night is still one click from a full round loop with a job log. Nothing was deleted that a re-run needs.
- **TWO SHORTER RUNS, NOT ONE LONGER ONE.** A round is 7 profiles against the 610/minute ceiling, so refreshing N profiles takes N/7 minutes *whatever anyone builds* — the rotation cannot be made faster, only more frequent. Doubling the rotation by doubling the run length gives one ~2-hour job; two firings give two ~37-minute ones covering the same ground. The split wins on every axis that bites a laptop: a shorter window to sleep through, half the loss when one is missed, and the credit burst spread across the day.
- **WEEKDAYS FOR THE API RUNS, ALL SEVEN DAYS FOR NEWS** (the owner's call). Fundamentals do not move at a weekend — no filings, no earnings — so 2 × 5 re-covers the universe about **1.4 times a week** against the 7-day rotation it replaces. Headlines keep arriving, so the news task is separate and unchanged in cadence; its morning firing moved **08:00 → 09:00** so it clears the 07:30 rotation, which takes ~37 minutes. Not over credits — news costs none — but over this machine and the same Vercel instance: a long refresh makes every other call cold and a heavy call makes the refresh miss its deadline, which this file records in both directions.
  - **A `.ps1` THAT NO LONGER REPRODUCES THE TASK IT REGISTERED IS WORSE THAN A WRONG SCHEDULE, and `news-task.ps1` was in exactly that state for a day.** The live trigger had been moved to 09:00 and the script still said `08:00`, so **re-running it to change anything else would silently have moved the schedule back** — and nothing would have looked wrong. Found by asking Task Scheduler rather than by reading the file: `Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'TickrLab *'` with its `Triggers` expanded is the whole check, and `DaysOfWeek 62` is Mon-Fri. **After editing a time in one of these scripts, read the live trigger back** — and whenever a schedule is changed by hand, change the script in the same breath.
- **19:30 RATHER THAN 16:15 IS STRICTLY BETTER.** The old slot was fifteen minutes after the close and could store a provisional bar for the next run to heal; by 19:30 the close has settled. And the **07:30 run means a completed nightly is already on record for the day** by the time Vercel's watchdog fires (23:30 UTC, drifting up to an hour), so it can never mail a false "missed night" about a run that is only just starting.
- **`nightly-ping.js` IS AN HTTP CALL, NOT A REFRESH** — `intraday-ping.js`'s rule, and the one that matters most here. It reads `CRON_SECRET` and `APP_URL` out of `.env` (never the command line or the task XML) and asks the deployed app to do the work. **It must never become `node server.js`**: booting a local server against the production database to do the same job is the documented way to burn credits and fight the live instance for the same rows.
- **`--dry` uses `/api/cron/intraday?dry=1`**, which is non-mutating and takes the same secret, so the wiring can be proved end to end without starting anything.
- **THREE PHASES RUN AFTER THE ROUNDS, never in the refresh tail** — `secRotate()` (EDGAR filings, capped in batches), `shortRotate()` (FINRA short interest, one call that writes nothing on most nights) and `holdingsRotate()` (the index holdings import). All three are **non-fatal to the night** and all three read a 404 as an older server, so deploy order never matters. Anything added here follows that shape: work put in the refresh *tail* has surfaced as "the refresh failed" over perfectly good data three times on this project. **They are no longer gated on the rotation completing** — see the entry below.

#### ONE DEAD TICKER SWITCHED OFF THREE UNRELATED SUBSYSTEMS (2026-10-03, owner: "can you fix the subsystem refresh issue")
**All three phases sat inside the `if (j.done)` branch, so PROFILE COVERAGE decided whether they ran at all.** Measured 2026-10-02: the rotation stalled at **1225/1302** behind twenty tickers the provider cannot serve — a refused pull leaves `fetched_at` at 0, the retry sentinel, so the same twenty were re-picked every round and blocked the sixty good ones behind them. SEC filings, FINRA short interest and the holdings import were therefore skipped on **every night it happened, for days**, and *silently*: the night reports itself failed for the ROTATION's reason, and nothing anywhere says the other three never ran. The holdings import had shipped the day before and **would never have fired unattended**.

- **`tailPhases()` runs on the three exits that end a run which was actually underway** — gave up with no usable response, stalled with no progress, hit the `MAX_ROUNDS` ceiling — and still on the `done` path.
- **IT RUNS AFTER `finish()`, AND THE ORDERING IS WHAT MAKES IT SAFE.** That call clears the refresh flag and lets the server report what it gathered, so nothing is competing for the database by the time these start. **Proved by reverting**: moving it above `finish()` fails the order assertion.
- **TWO EXITS DELIBERATELY DO NOT RUN IT**, and both are cases where something else is, or was deliberately put, in charge: a **human Stop** from `/refreshes`, and a **skip because another refresh is in flight** — which is precisely the contention this whole phase ordering exists to avoid. **Proved by reverting**: running it on a skip fails 1.
- **THE NIGHT STILL REPORTS `FAILED` AND STILL EXITS 1.** The rotation really did fail and a green task would hide that; what changes is only that three unrelated subsystems no longer fail with it. There is a check on the exit code for exactly that, because "fix the failure" could so easily have meant "stop reporting it".
- **`GAP_MS` and `SEC_GAP_MS` became env-overridable**, following `SEC_MAX_BATCHES` in the same file. Without it this driver cannot be tested at all: a stall takes `STAGNANT_LIMIT` rounds, so at 65s the one thing worth asserting costs three and a half minutes a case — and the alternative is testing a **patched copy**, which proves something about a file nobody runs.
- Verified: **20 checks driving the driver in a REAL CHILD PROCESS**, because the question is what it does on its way out. The copy under test is **byte-compared against the real file** and runs in a temp directory, so it reads its own `.env` and **cannot append to the log that IS the evidence the schedule fired**. **Proved by reverting five times**: the original `j.done` gating fails 7, the tail before `finish()` 1, running it on a skip 1.
  - **Two guards fail 0 and are KEPT with that recorded in the code**: the per-phase `try/catch` (all three phases are internally defensive today, so nothing can escape them — but adding a FOURTH phase to that array is a one-line change and a new phase is exactly the thing likely to throw) and the run-once flag. The `CHAT_DAILY_LIMIT_MEMBER` rule — *keep what one guard flips back on*.
  - **A SPENT ONE-OFF PATCH SCRIPT IS A LOADED GUN, and one went off during this change.** Looking for the driver's own suite with `for t in $(ls *.js | grep -iE "nightly|...")` matched **`patch-nightly.js`**, a script from the holdings work the day before — it re-inserted a whole `holdingsRotate` function, reported `PATCH DID NOT APPLY` for the part that had moved, and then **wrote the file anyway**, leaving a duplicate declaration that would not parse. Repaired by `git checkout` and re-applying through a fresh idempotent script that refuses if already applied. **Never glob-run scratchpad scripts: a patch script and a test suite look identical from the outside.** The spent ones now live in `scratchpad/used-patches/`.
  - **The checkout rewrote the file from LF to CRLF**, which is the documented line-ending trap arriving in the middle of a repair — the re-apply script detects per file at the moment it runs, and printed `"\r\n"` where the original edit had seen `"\n"`.
- **`process.exitCode`, never `process.exit`, and this is the OPPOSITE of the rule the test suites follow.** Calling `process.exit` mid-socket crashes Node on Windows; the suites must call it, because `uni-boot.js` leaves a server listening and the event loop never drains. Two drivers, two rules, and each file says which it is.
- **The log is append-only** (`nightly-ping.log`, not committed). It is what caught the Git Bash timezone trap by disagreeing with a hand-computed New York time.

#### A LAP DIED WITH NO TRACE, AND THE LOG IS THE ONLY RECORD THESE JOBS LEAVE (2026-10-01)
**The 13:00 news lap stopped two thirds of the way through and nothing anywhere said why.** The task reported exit 1, the log's last line was `batch 11`, there was **no `FAILED` line and no Windows crash record** — and every deliberate failure path in all three drivers writes through `say()`. So it had reached no catch: it threw or rejected in a callback *outside* the try, and Node printed the reason to a stderr **Task Scheduler discards**.

- **The server is what settled the shape.** `/api/news-runs` held **twelve** completed batches against the log's eleven, so the driver died during or just after batch 12's response rather than before it. 480 of 1,192 covered; the remainder was independently confirmed by a dry run reading **`712 of 1192 stale past 3h`** — exactly 1192 − 12×40 — and the 17:00 slot collects them, so **nothing was lost but the diagnosis**. *When a driver's log and the server's own record disagree, the gap between them is where it died.*
- **`uncaughtException` and `unhandledRejection` are logged in all three drivers now.** They cannot prevent the death; they make it diagnosable, which is the whole difference between a lap that failed and one that merely stopped. The stack is logged, not the message — the cause is still unknown and a bare "socket hang up" would not name it.
- **THE FIRST CUT OF THAT GUARD WAS STRICTLY WORSE THAN NO GUARD, and the test caught it rather than a reading.** **Registering either handler SUPPRESSES Node's own exit**, so the process survived the fault, ran on to `DONE` and `throw new Stop(0)`, and **overwrote `exitCode` 1 with 0** — a green task with `DONE` logged underneath `FAILED`. The handler must therefore `process.exit(1)`, which is **the one place these files may**, against their own documented rule; the `appendFileSync` has already put the evidence on disk, so even the Windows `UV_HANDLE_CLOSING` assertion leaves a non-zero code and a complete log, which is all that is asked of a run that has already failed.
- Verified: **22 checks**, each shape driven in a **real child process** — the question is what a process does on its way out, and asserting it in-process would test a handler just called by hand. The load-bearing half is the **unguarded** case, which reproduces the production symptom in miniature: non-zero exit, the reason present on stderr, and **nothing in the log**. **Proved by reverting** to `exitCode = 1`: the guarded runs come back **exit 0**, the silent-success defect above.
  - **A test fault worth keeping**: the "clean run" case fell through a ternary's else branch and injected a rejection, so the one case asserting *no* `FAILED` line was not clean at all.
- `nightly-task.ps1` is **ASCII only** and sets the four settings that bit the intraday task first — `AllowStartIfOnBatteries` (Task Scheduler refuses to start on battery by default, so an unplugged laptop would skip every firing silently), `DontStopIfGoingOnBatteries`, `StartWhenAvailable`, `WakeToRun` (which does **not** work on Modern Standby machines; `powercfg /a` says which) — plus `MultipleInstances IgnoreNew` and a 2-hour `ExecutionTimeLimit`, a ceiling for a hung run rather than a budget.

### `?start=1` NO LONGER HIJACKS A RUN THAT IS ALREADY LIVE
**A second driver's start call used to expire the cache and raise the flag over whatever was in flight**, which with two scheduled firings and a manual re-run button is no longer a theoretical collision. `POST /api/cron/refresh?start=1` now reads `readRefreshState()` first and, finding one, answers `{ok: true, done: true, skipped: true}` naming the run it stood aside for and its progress — so the driver exits 0 and quiet, rather than either failing or trampling.

- **It answers `done: true`, deliberately.** A driver's whole contract is "stop when told done", and a start that cannot start has nothing for this driver to do. A failure here would turn a correctly-avoided collision into a red task, which teaches its owner to ignore the task.
- **The name comes from `live.mode`** (Fill missing / Fast refresh / Refresh prices / Refresh all), because "a refresh is already running" is not enough to act on when the answer might be a Fill missing somebody started by hand.
- The flag ages out on its own (`REFRESH_STALE_MS`), so a run that dies mid-flight cannot lock the schedule out — the same property that makes `standAside` safe.
- Verified: **11 checks**, and **proved by reverting**: without the guard 8 fail, a second start wiping the live run's own progress.

*What follows describes the GitHub schedule as it was, and the two-cron mechanism that would be needed again if one ever returns.*

`.github/workflows/nightly-refresh.yml` ran a Refresh all at **4:15 PM in New York** — fifteen minutes after the close (changed 2026-09-15; it was 00:00 UTC, which drifted between 8PM and 7PM Eastern).

**A local time needs two crons and a guard, because GitHub cron is UTC and has no timezone option.** Both UTC times are registered — **20:15 while EDT is in force and 21:15 while EST is** — and the first step of the job converts `now` to `America/New_York` and stops unless the hour is 16. Exactly one of the pair can be right on any given day. **The guard asks the tz database rather than hardcoding changeover dates**, because those move; the US has shifted them before. Verified by replaying 400 days through the real tz data: exactly one run fires per day, with clean handover on 2026-03-08 (21:15Z → 20:15Z) and 2026-11-01 (back again). A `workflow_dispatch` run is never gated.

**4:15 PM is close to the close, and that is a deliberate trade.** Twelve Data returns a bar for *today* while the market is open whose close is the current price, so a run this soon after the bell can store a value that is not yet the settled close. It self-heals: `persistBars()` re-upserts a `BAR_OVERLAP` window of 5 sessions, so the next day's run overwrites it with the final figure (measured drift on a real pull: 0.003-0.007%). What it costs is that the evening's snapshot may carry a provisional close. Moving to 4:30 or 5:00 PM is one digit in both cron lines if that ever matters.

**A runner, not a Vercel cron, because a full pass takes ~13 minutes** and no serverless function stays alive that long. The workflow drives exactly the loop the browser drives.

- **`POST /api/cron/refresh`** is the job's only endpoint, authenticated by `Authorization: Bearer $CRON_SECRET`. Deliberately **not** admin: the secret satisfies that one route, so a leak cannot delete a portfolio. Unset leaves the route closed, not open. `?start=1` expires the cache and raises the flag; every later call runs one round. `DELETE` on the same path ends a run early and reports what it got.
- **The 62-second gap between rounds is not conservatism — it is measured.** Two rounds inside one minute returned *"1128 API credits were used, with the current limit being 610"*. A round costs roughly **560 credits** — and the decomposition was re-measured off `Api-Credits-Request` on 2026-09-13: **profiles are 85% of it, not the prices.** Exact per-call costs: `time_series` **1 credit per symbol** (batched or single), `/statistics` **50**, `/profile` **10**, `/earnings` (8 quarters) **20** — a cold profile is **80 credits/symbol**, so 6 per round = 480, plus ~1/symbol for the batch. The plan ceiling of 610/minute allows at most **7 cold profiles a minute**; prices for even a 300-symbol universe would cost only ~300 credits. Don't lower `GAP` without measuring again.
- The job stops after 3 rounds without progress, same as the browser loop, and cleans up the flag on its way out.
- Repository secrets required: `APP_URL`, `CRON_SECRET`.

### The refresh report
**Both kinds of refresh email the owner** — a Refresh all and an ordinary price Refresh — **whoever started it**, the job or the button. The Refresh all path hangs off `endRefresh()` rather than the cron route, because both ways of finishing one converge there.

- **Which report goes out is decided by whether a run was live a moment earlier, not by what the `delete` returned.** `endRefresh()` runs either way so a flag left stale by an abandoned run gets cleared, but a *stalled* Refresh all still reports nothing, and the click that happens to complete the universe is reported as the ordinary Refresh it was.
- **An ordinary Refresh has no `refresh_state` row**, so `/api/stocks` passes its own `startedAt` and actor into `finishLiveRefresh()` as `ctx`. No `ctx`, no plain report — which is what keeps the nightly job's dozen rounds quiet.
- **The plain report says `Fundamentals: not re-pulled — prices only`.** A price Refresh reuses cached profiles, so presenting the fundamentals as fresh would make the mail actively misleading. It is judged on failed symbols alone; coverage is a Refresh all's measure, and "no profile yet" is omitted entirely.
- **A plain price Refresh no longer mails (2026-09-15)** — manual or scheduled. Intraday refreshes made it thirteen emails a trading day, burying the Refresh all report that matters. `sendRefreshReport(state, 'plain')` still builds the report and stores it on the run for `/refreshes`; only `kind !== 'plain'` resolves a recipient. Refresh all, Fill missing and the nightly job mail as before.

- **Receipt**: run time first and largest, then the start and finish clock times, actor, `n/total` coverage, failed symbols, symbols still without a profile, prices-as-of, fundamentals rows recorded, bar-archive size and through-date. The duration leads because it is the number that says whether the night went normally — a Refresh all that finishes in seconds did not really run.
- **Clock times are rendered in `REPORT_TZ`, defaulting to `America/New_York`** — the runner is UTC and the reader is not. `fmtClock()` uses explicit `month`/`day`/`hour` components rather than `dateStyle`/`timeStyle`, because ECMA-402 refuses to combine those with `timeZoneName` and the throw lands in the fallback, which would quietly print UTC instead of saying so.
- **The digest is gone, and "The run" replaced it (2026-09-16, owner's call).** The day's movers and the advice changes both restated a standing the screener shows live, and neither said anything about the job — which is what this mail is for. In their place, the figures from the Refresh runs page: **rounds** (and how many were refused), **profiles** pulled and refused, **credits** with a per-round average against the 610/min ceiling, whether **prices** were pulled live or read from the archive, **round time** (average and longest), **round spacing** (against the 62s floor), the **trigger**, a link to that run's page and, for a nightly, the Actions job log. `runFacts()` reads the run's own row and its rounds. Removing the advice section also took the per-symbol news read off the report path — it no longer touches the `news` table.
- **The final round is now recorded BEFORE the tail runs.** `finishLiveRefresh` is what closes the run and builds the report, so a round recorded after it was missing from the very summary it completed; the counts it needs are derived from the same rows a moment earlier.
- **A Fast refresh mails as "Fast refresh"** — subject and heading both, from `state.mode`, rather than borrowing Refresh all's name.
- Verified end to end with the provider and the mail API stubbed: a Refresh all and a Fast refresh each driven to completion, then the delivered body checked — no movers, no advice changes, the run section present with rounds/credits/profiles/timing, the run link, the receipt still leading with the duration, and each job named correctly in its own subject and heading (18 checks).
- *Removed:* the day's five best and worst movers. **The screens and the highest-rated list were removed in Sep 2026** — both restated a *standing* rather than reporting what happened, both are one click away on `/analysis` and the screener where they are current rather than frozen at whenever the refresh finished, and together they were most of the email. `Screens.run()` over the whole universe went with them, so the report costs less to build too. `REPORT_SCREEN_NAMES`, `rating()` and `symLink()` were deleted as dead code; `Screens` is still imported for `cleanWeights` and `PAST_PERIODS`.
- **"Fundamentals that moved" was REMOVED on 2026-10-03** (owner: *"Remove the section Fundamentals that moved from all refresh emails"*). It compared each symbol's `fundamentals_history` row against the previous recorded set and listed what had changed. Gone from both the text and the HTML body, along with `FUND_MOVES`, the four thresholds, `fmtBig` / `fmtPts` / `signed`, both builders, and `readFundamentalsPair` — which had exactly one caller and is the only accessor that went.
  - **THE TABLE STAYS, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE RISK OF THIS CHANGE.** The section was `fundamentals_history`'s only reader *in the report*, so the obvious over-removal is to take `store.writeFundamentals` with it — **silent** (the mail looks right) and **irrecoverable** (the provider only ever returns today's numbers, so a day not recorded is gone for good). `/backtest` and `/adjustedbacktest` both read it through `readFundamentalsAsOf`, and `/stock`'s own history reads it through `readFundamentalsRows`.
  - **A STATIC CHECK ON THE WRITE WAS NOT ENOUGH, and the revert harness is what said so.** `/store\.writeFundamentals\(/` **passed against the call commented out** — a regex cannot tell a call from the same text in a comment, which is the "a grep passes if the engine reads it under another name" trap in a new place. The check drives a real Refresh all and reads the row back; reverted, it fails 3.
  - **The measurement that justified the six exclusions is worth keeping even though the section is not**: price, market cap, forward P/E, PEG, FCF yield and net-cash % each move on **79-100% of consecutive nights with a median of about 2%**, because each is divided by, or is, the price — they restate the day's price move. The twelve fields that were tracked move on **1-5% of nights**, and when they move it is a step rather than a wobble (AVGO's revenue sat at 75.46B for five recorded days, went to 89.10B, and stayed). Anything that ever reports on this table again should start there.
  - **Two derived signals were tried and rejected, and the reason is not about this section** — it is about the data. Forward EPS revision backed out as `relΔ(price) − relΔ(forward P/E)`, and share-count change as `relΔ(market cap) − relΔ(price)`. Both look clever and both measure the wrong thing: SNOW threw a "+20.9% EPS revision" on a day its forward P/E was **byte-identical**, and the share-count signal oscillated −20.9% then +22.1% on consecutive days. The profile blob and the price are not sampled at the same instant, so the subtraction reads that staleness rather than the company.
  - **The `Fundamentals` RECEIPT LINE is a different thing and survives** — `Fundamentals  1 symbols recorded for 2026-02-04`, or `not re-pulled — prices only` on a plain Refresh. There is a check on it, because the two are one word apart and removing the wrong one would be easy.
  - **New record closes is now the only section reporting an EVENT**, and the comment that ordered the two was updated rather than left pointing at a sibling that is gone.
  - Verified: **16 checks** driving a real Refresh all with the provider and Resend stubbed — each dead phrase absent from BOTH bodies, the receipt / run section / Prices as of / Fundamentals line still present, no `undefined` or `[object Object]`, and the archive row read back **with its real figures**. **Proved by reverting four times**: the text heading fails 3, the html heading 3, the archive write 3, and dropping `readFundamentalsAsOf` **aborts the suite** — which the harness reports as `?? only 0 of 16 ran` rather than as 0 failed, since an aborted run is indistinguishable from a guard that never mattered.
    - **Two fixture traps, both of which made a working write look removed.** `uni-boot.js` leaves `TWELVE_DATA_API_KEY` empty, so the round is **refused** and records nothing; and the whole `/statistics` branch sits behind **`ENABLE_FUNDAMENTALS`**, so without it every fundamental is null and the archive row is an empty shell that passes a row-count check. Set both.
- A run that *stalls* sends nothing — nobody calls `endRefresh()` and the flag ages out on its own. The cron job covers that case, since it is the thing still awake.
- `REPORT_TO` overrides the destination; unset it falls back to the owner account's email, so it works before anything is configured.
- **Fundamentals rows are dated by `marketDay(rows)`** — the freshest bar in the universe, not the server clock. This mattered more at the old 8PM Eastern slot, where the server's UTC date was already tomorrow and dating by `new Date()` filed every automated run a day ahead of its own bars. At 4:15 PM Eastern the UTC date still agrees, but the rule stands: the bars decide the date, not the clock.

## Chatbot
`/chat` answers questions about the screener data. **ADMIN ONLY since 2026-09-26** (`requireAdmin` on the route and the page), at the owner's instruction, taken before opening registration. Two reasons, both measured: every question ships the whole table as the system prompt — **930KB of CSV at 1,185 stocks** — which makes it much the largest variable cost per user, and it is the feature nearest its own ceiling. It was open to any signed-in user before.

- **The claim had to leave with the feature.** The Intro carousel's five-things slide promised "Ask in plain English" and now offers alerts instead; `/about` no longer names an assistant; `/help` §6 carries the `.adm` owner-only badge rather than being deleted; and the bar's Ask button is `admin-only`. **A feature removed from members but still advertised to them is the "every feature live" error in a new place**, which this project made once already.
- `CHAT_DAILY_LIMIT_MEMBER` is now unreachable and is kept rather than deleted — one guard flips it back, unlike the analyst flag, which could never be switched on at all.
- **The context wall was re-measured and CLAUDE.md was WRONG about it.** This file said the prompt was "~250 tokens per stock" and "viable past 700 stocks", which predicts failure at 1,185. It does not fail: asked a real question on production it answered in 12s. The CSV is 929,954 bytes, so the true rate is nearer 4.8 bytes per token. **The honest reading is that it works with very little headroom** — on the order of 1,200–1,250 stocks — and a bulk add of the size done on 2026-09-22 (+117 in a day) would break it.

**The whole dataset goes in the system prompt — there is no retrieval layer, and adding one would make it worse.** Measured against the live API, not estimated: the system prompt was **~17,500 tokens** for 69 stocks, roughly 250 per stock — so at the current 93 it is around **23,000**, and worth re-measuring off `usage` rather than scaling this number if it ever matters. (A bytes/4 estimate said 7,400 — it underestimates dense numeric CSV by well over 2x, so trust `usage` in a real response, not arithmetic on the payload.) That still fits a 200k context about eleven times over and stays viable past 700 stocks, well beyond the 119-ticker ceiling the price API imposes. Embeddings are the wrong tool twice: the data is a numeric table where "margin above 15%" is an exact filter rather than a similarity, and retrieval could only drop rows the answer needs.

- **`cache_control` sits on the data block, which caches everything before it too** — so the rules block rides along and the whole system prompt is cached. A real call showed `cache_read_input_tokens: 17470` against `input_tokens: 31`: after the first question, all you pay for is the question and the answer.
- **`max_tokens` must cover the model's reasoning, not just the reply.** At 1200 a ranking question spent the entire budget thinking and came back with a single `thinking` block and no text at all — a silent empty answer. It is 6000 now. The reasoning is worth paying for: working through 69 rows is exactly where a model miscounts. `stop_reason === 'max_tokens'` is reported to the user as "ask something narrower" rather than a generic failure.
- **`CHAT_FIELDS` is the glossary and the column list at once.** Adding a column to the bot means adding one entry there — nothing else. Fields absent from older snapshots simply come through blank.
