  - **A consequence worth knowing**: the News column's 7-day count badge could only ever count what the last fetch returned, so it had been understating coverage since it shipped.
  - Verified: 23 checks. The load-bearing one is the SECOND FETCH — items from the first must survive a fetch that no longer carries them. Plus dedupe on a repeat, both trims, the newest kept rather than the first to arrive, and the page's fold measured by `getBoundingClientRect()` rather than by class.
  - **Harness trap**: `uni-boot.js` defaults `NEWS_PROVIDER` to `'off'` to keep tests off the network, and the server then short-circuits `/api/news` to an empty list **before it reads anything** — so a news page test silently sees no headlines however many are stored. Set it explicitly.
- **News is its own button and rides NOTHING (2026-09-18, owner's instruction: "don't mix the news refresh with any API data refresh").** `POST /api/news/refresh` does ONE batch of the stalest stocks and says how many remain; the page loops it, the same shape the price refreshes use, because a serverless function must not be asked to hold hundreds of network fetches in one request. The button is on `/news-runs`, and the console's **Refresh news** row deep-links `?do=refresh` — the `/refreshes?do=` pattern. `topUpNews()` is deleted.
  - **Why it was moved.** It was awaited inside the refresh (nothing may run after a response on this platform), which put a dozen network fetches inside the request that also priced the universe and wrote the snapshot. On 2026-09-18 a refresh recorded its round at 78s, wrote a correct snapshot at 10:10, and was then cut before `finishRun` — logged **`abandoned`, with no error**, while the data was perfectly fine. The owner reported it as "price refresh failed again"; it had not failed. A refresh is one request and the tail was most of it.
  - **Staleness is the CLOCK, and the same test decides both what is picked and what `remaining` counts.** The first cut let "holds no headlines" make a stock stale, which is fine as an ORDERING boost (an empty feed is retried ahead of the rotation) and fatal as a termination test: a stock the provider has nothing on would be re-picked forever while the run reported itself done. Caught by a test that looped to completion and then asked for one more batch.
  - Batches log `trigger: 'manual'` with no `refresh_run_id`, so `/news-runs` no longer shows them as riding a refresh round. The stock page's own stored-or-fetch on a six-hour TTL is unchanged — that one is user-driven and costs nothing.
- *Superseded:* **Coverage without a schedule**: `topUpNews()` rides every refresh (each cron round included), topping up the `NEWS_TOPUP_PER_REFRESH` (12) stalest symbols, never-fetched first — the nightly job's ~20 rounds cycle the whole universe in one night. Started early in the round and **awaited before the response** — it was fire-and-forget until 2026-09-15, and on Vercel a function is frozen the moment it responds: batches were suspended mid-fetch, then every 6-second abort timer fired on the next wake, so two batches logged 54s and 279s with all 24 fetches "aborted due to timeout" for refreshes that took 19s. **Nothing may run after a response on this platform.** The batch still never rejects, so a failed news write never fails a refresh (the bars rule). `GET /api/news?symbol=` is stored-or-fetch with a 6-hour TTL so a visited stock page stays fresh regardless; on a provider failure it serves the stored set, stale beating nothing.
- **Frontends (deliberately only two)**: a News card on `/stock/<SYMBOL>` between the chart and the fields (ten headlines, escaped, http(s)-vetted links out, `target=_blank rel=noopener`), and one `News` row in the hover card's Info group — injected onto the rows by `loadLatestNews()` after the table paints (`GET /api/news/latest`, stored-only, one query — the sparklines rule), never a table column. The analysis page shows nothing because its rows never get `newsLatest`; `CHAT_FIELDS` still excludes news.
- Verified: 18 checks in the news suite (RSS entities/CDATA, publisher-suffix strip, dedupe caps, stalest picker, renderer escaping incl. a `javascript:` url refused), plus a live boot fetching real MU headlines through the whole path.

### The News column (screener)
**A News column in the Info group, and a panel behind it (2026-09-16).** Until now the only per-stock way in was hovering a row or opening its page; this makes the whole thing one click from the table.

- **The cell is the age of the latest stored headline** (`2h`, `4d`) with a **count badge** when the stock has more than one from the last week, brightened when the latest is under a day old. **Blank means two different things and the cell separates them**: an em-dash is "checked, nothing stored" with the tooltip saying when it was last checked, a faint dot is "not looked at yet" — headlines are topped up a dozen stocks per refresh round, so the second case is common and must not read as "no news". The latest headline is the cell's tooltip.
- **Sorting is on the timestamp, not the age**, because a new column starts descending and descending has to mean freshest first. Stocks with nothing stored sort last.
- **`GET /api/news/latest` now returns `{items, counts, checked}`** — the latest per symbol as before, a 7-day count per symbol (`newsCountsSince`, one bounded group-by over the pruned table: 5,849 rows on 2026-09-16, allowlisted in the query-plan test with that number) and `news_state`'s fetch clock. All three are guest-filtered. The screener already loaded this after the table painted for the hover card, so the column costs one extra small query, not a new request.
- **Clicking a cell opens `#newsPop`**: up to ten headlines with source and age, each opening the publisher in a new tab, plus a link to the stock page. It reads `GET /api/news?symbol=`, which is stored-or-fetch on a six-hour rule — so **a stock nobody has looked at gets its headlines on the first click**, at no API cost (the provider is free and keyless). Escape, an outside click or a resize closes it.
- **`?force=1` checks now** rather than waiting out the six-hour rule — the stock page's **Check now** button, beside a line saying when that stock was last checked. The provider is free and keyless, so a forced check costs no API credits; the server keeps a **one-minute floor per symbol** so a held-down button cannot hammer anyone, and a refused force answers normally with `forced: false` rather than an error. The route now returns `checkedAt` so the page can say "checked just now". Verified with the provider stubbed: 12 checks (no call inside the TTL, a call when forced, the headlines stored, the clock moving, the second force inside a minute refused, the button's states).
- Verified in a browser over four seeded stocks (fresh / old / checked-but-empty / never-checked): 15 checks — the endpoint's three parts, each cell's shape and tooltip, the panel's list with sources and links, the stock-page link, Escape, the "nothing stored" wording, and the sort order.

### The news ticker (screener)
**A slow crawl of headlines published in the last 12 hours, under the table (2026-09-15, owner's spec: slow, hideable, 12h then stale).** **It follows the table** — the owner first chose the whole universe, then changed it the same day: the strip shows only stocks `visibleStocks()` leaves on screen (portfolio, sector, industry, advice, advice move, column filters), the label reads "last 12h · stocks in view" while narrowed, and a view with no recent news says so in the strip rather than hiding it (hiding would resize the table on every filter change; the strip hides only when nothing in the universe is recent). **`render()`'s empty-table branch returns early, so it calls `paintTicker()` itself** — missed on the first cut and caught by the test. `GET /api/news/recent` reads stored rows only (`readRecentNews`, published_at ≥ now − 12h — ISO strings, so the comparison is lexical), keeps at most 2 per stock and one row per URL, universe-filtered and guest-filtered, and sends **every stock's share** (147 items / 70 KB at the time) — a universe-wide top 60 would leave most filters empty; the page takes the first 60 of what is in view. Item: `SYM ▲2.3% · headline · source · 2h`; the symbol opens the stock page, the headline the article (http/https only), both in a new tab.

- **`#ticker` is `flex: none` inside the page column**, so showing it takes ~44px from the table rather than growing the page; every visibility change calls `paintWindow(true)` because the windowed table sizes itself from `.table-wrap`'s height and no resize event fires.
- **Two copies of the items crawl by exactly one copy's width** (`translateX(-50%)`), so the loop has no seam; `--tk-dur` is set from the measured width at **60px/s**. Hover, keyboard focus and the pause button stop it (`animation-play-state`) — pausing moving content is a WCAG requirement, not a nicety. **Reduced motion gets no crawl**: one headline at a time, swapped every 6s with an opacity fade.
- **Rebuilt only when its items or the prices change** (`tickerKey` = urls + `lastUpdated`): `paintTicker()` runs at the end of every `render()`, and rebuilding the track restarts the crawl, so a sort or a filter must not. Re-read every 10 minutes, and the 12-hour window is enforced client-side too, so an item ages out between reads.
- **On by default; hiding is stored** (`prefs.tickerOff`, boolean-only in the PUT whitelist). The × on the strip hides it; `News ticker` at the top of the ⋯ menu toggles it back. Hidden when the window holds nothing.
- **Fixed first, because a ticker would have advertised it: news was searched by the quoted LEGAL name**, which matches mostly old filings that fall outside the 21-day window — 36 of 271 stocks held no headlines. `newsNamesFor()` now searches the display name (override, else `deriveShortName`), measured on all 36: legal-name queries found anything for 28 and stored nothing that survived the window; short names found 22-25 results for all 36, and at least as many for the control group. A stock holding no headlines whose fetch is past the TTL is now picked ahead of the rotation in `topUpNews`. **The short-name rule gained whole `American Depositary Shares` / `Sponsored ADR` / `N.V.` / `S.A.` tails** — 8 of 271 display names changed, every one a fix (AstraZeneca PLC American → AstraZeneca, Toyota Motor Corporation Sponsored → Toyota Motor, Adyen N.V → Adyen, NXP, STMicroelectronics, Spotify Technology, Ericsson, Nano Dimension); 14 rule cases pass.
- **Cadence caveat**: headlines are only as fresh as their last fetch — 12 stocks per refresh round plus stock-page visits. A 12-hour window therefore shows mostly the stocks fetched recently; the News runs page's coverage tile says how many that is.
- Verified: the filtered strip headlessly (11 checks — a sector shows only its stocks and all of them, a sort keeps the crawl, an empty table and a newsless view keep the strip with its message, one stock shows only its headlines, clearing returns to everything); the endpoint on live data (≤2 each, none older than 12h, no duplicate URLs; a guest saw only preview symbols); TM and AZN fetched through the fixed search (25 new headlines each, from nothing); a headless run on the real page over those headlines — 15 checks normal, 10 under `--force-prefers-reduced-motion`.

### The news log (`/news-runs`)
**Every batch of headline fetches is logged (2026-09-15)** — `news_runs` (one per batch) and `news_run_items` (one per stock in it), read by `/news-runs` (admin, a `News runs` row in the console's Data section). Two triggers: `refresh` (a refresh round's top-up, linked to the refresh run it rode on via `refresh_run_id`, whose kind the page shows — "Nightly round", "Fill missing round") and `page` (a stock page fetching headlines older than `NEWS_TTL_MS`).

- **`runNewsBatch(picks, meta)`** is the one path both triggers take: it logs each stock's outcome as it lands (fetched, **new** — not already held — and stored after the write) and closes the batch `complete`, `partial` or `failed`. **`writeNews()` now returns `{added, stored}`**, reading the symbol's prior ids and its final count in the same batch as the write, so the log costs no extra round trip.
- **`topUpNews` is called after `finishLiveRefresh` reads the run state**, so the batch knows its refresh run; it was the first line of the function before.
- **`abandoned`** = still `running` three minutes after starting (`NEWS_RUN_ABANDON_MS`). The top-up is fire-and-forget, and on serverless an instance can be frozen once the response has gone — this is the status that would show it happening. Swept lazily by every read.
- **The page**: coverage (last fetch under a day / under a week / older / never, the stalest stock, rounds for a full pass at 12 a round, provider), headlines stored (total, stocks with at least one, **stocks fetched but holding nothing**), the last 7 days (batches, fetches, failure rate, new headlines, batches that never finished), fetches per day for 14 days with new headlines as a line, filterable history, and a per-stock dialog linking to the batch's refresh run (`/refreshes?run=<id>` opens that run).
- **Retention**: 30 days of batches, 14 of per-stock rows, pruned after each batch.
- **First real reading, 2026-09-15: 36 of 271 stocks have been fetched and hold no headlines** (MS, RBRK, SKHY, BABA, CMCSA among them). The Google query is the quoted legal name + "stock", and a quoted "SK hynix Inc. American Depositary Receipt" matches nothing — the short name is the likely fix.
- Verified end to end locally: a stale stock page (EBAY, 13h) logged one batch — 25 fetched, 4 new, 25 stored, 668ms — and a second open inside the TTL logged nothing; route walk (anon/guest 302 and 403, admin 200, unknown batch 404); headless page over synthetic history.

## Logos — built and removed the same day
**There are no company logos anywhere (owner's call, 2026-09-14): the provider's marks aged badly and sat on white boxes, and the whole pipeline came out the day it went in** — the `logos` table (dropped from Turso), the fetch/override/serving routes, the admin button, its receipt email, the LogoFX transparency module, and every `<img>`. Tickers render as **typographic monograms** (`.lg` on the promo cards) or plain text; the stock masthead is back to the symbol alone. What the episode measured, kept for the next time logos come up: Twelve Data `/logo` costs 1 credit/symbol and its image URL is keyless (~7KB 128px JPEG) but the marks lag rebrands by years; Wikimedia thumbnails moved to `thumb.wikimedia.org`, exist only at pre-rendered sizes, and require a User-Agent; ~11 of 93 symbols (ETFs mostly) had no mark at all. If logos ever return, the per-symbol URL override was the workable shape and the bulk provider was the problem.

## The basket page
**`/portfolio/<name>` — one portfolio aggregated, for shared portfolios and a member's own lists (`my:<Name>` in the URL), reached from a chart-arrow beside every row in the portfolio picker (2026-09-14).** A screener view, deliberately not a tracker: no positions exist anywhere in this product, and the owner ruled out P&L tracking explicitly. First cut is three cards; more modules (composition, movers, earnings, news) are the planned second pass.

- **The curve** (`GET /api/basket?name=&days=`, requireMember): equal dollars at the window start, held — `mean(close/start)` per session over the union-of-dates axis, symbols with no history at the window start sit out and are counted in the caption. **The benchmark is the whole universe on the same convention**, not SPY: the benchmark is deliberately never archived, and "did my list beat my own screener" is the better question anyway. One `readBarsFor(all, since)` covers both curves (basket ⊆ universe); measured 1.27s at 1Y × 93 symbols, cached per range client-side. Ranges 1M/3M/6M/1Y; the chart is a hand-rolled dual-line SVG (no `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, so SVG text labels are safe here).
- **Stance**: trend-state stacked bar + counts, % above the 200D, Balanced advice rollup, and today's advice changes within the list.
- **Returns next to the whole screen**: mean of each stock's own horizon return (1W→1Y), list vs all vs difference — an equal-weight reading, the caption says so. Verified live: Mag 7 +11.0% 1Y against the universe's +60.4%, both curves anchored at exactly 1.0.
- Personal lists resolve against the CALLER's own `user_portfolios` via `prefsKey`, so one member can never read another's; guests are refused by requireMember and the page redirects them.

### Sector, Industry and Size are groups too — one page, four scopes (2026-09-27, owner's request)
**"I don't think I have anything that summarizes data and charts for a sector, industry, theme or size."** A theme already had one; the other three had nothing (`/pivot` cross-tabs them as counts and total cap, which answers *where is the weight*, not *how is Semiconductors doing*). **`/sector/<name>`, `/industry/<name>` and `/size/<band>` are the SAME page as `/theme/<name>`**, because a group differs from a theme only in which stocks are in it.

- **The owner was offered a separate page and chose one.** The alternative was a second page for the three new dimensions, which is two copies of every card added afterwards — the drift `rowcard.js`, `action.js` and `cards.js` all exist to prevent. **The whole server change is ~18 lines of resolution**: `basketPayload` turns a name into a symbol list and everything downstream (the date axis, the equal-weight curve, the universe benchmark, the per-symbol series) was already scope-agnostic.
- **The wire name carries the dimension as a prefix** (`sector:Technology`), the way `my:` already did, and the payload reports `scope` so the page can word itself. `/theme/<name>` and `/portfolio/<name>` are untouched.
- **`groupIndex()` IS CACHED (60s), and that is not decoration.** Resolving a sector needs the snapshot, the page refetches per range click, and `readSnapshot()` is the ~1.3MB read that took `/quality` from 2.4s to 10.8s. One read a minute per instance instead of one per click; the `tile_config` pattern. Being a minute stale means a stock that changed sector overnight, which does not happen between two clicks.
- **`capBand` is STAMPED on the way out and never stored**, so the index derives it with `stampCapDerived` rather than reading it — otherwise `/size/<band>` is empty until something else happens to have stamped that snapshot.
- **A stock with no sector is in NO sector group**, rather than one called "null". The blank-bucket rule, and there is a check that it is still in `All`.
- **The 404 names the dimension** — "No such sector" is the whole diagnosis when a link carries a value the taxonomy has since renamed.

**Four cards were added, and they serve all four scopes at once** (the owner took every one when asked):

- **What it is made of.** The bar is **market cap**, the number beside it is **companies**, and *where those two disagree is the finding* — "Technology +18%" means something different if two names are 60% of it. What it breaks down BY follows the scope: a sector into industries, an industry into size bands (its sector is constant by construction), everything else into sectors. Each row opens that group.
- **Leaders and laggards**, over the window the range buttons chose — so the card and the curve above it cannot tell different stories. The verdict rides along, labelled as the Balanced rules' reading.
- **Fundamentals against the whole screen.** **MEDIANS, never means**: one 300x multiple drags a mean somewhere no company in the group sits. A **forward P/E at or below zero is excluded** (a multiple off a loss is arithmetic, not cheapness — the Size card's rule, the Bubble card's, and the peer table's), and **financials are dropped from gross margin only**, counted and said rather than silently. The gap is in the figure's own units — turns of a multiple, points of a percentage — never a percentage OF a ratio.
- **The stocks themselves**, 50 at a time, with the return column following the range — biggest first until 2026-10-02, **sortable on every column** since (below).

#### The comparison is the INDEX now, not your own universe (2026-09-27, owner: "remove All screened… you can add S&P 500 and Dow 30")
**The blue "All screened, same convention" line is gone from the chart and from the returns table; the S&P 500 (SPY) and the Dow 30 (DIA) are drawn in its place.** An equal-weight line over everything screened answered *did this group beat the rest of my list* — which **changes meaning every time a ticker is added** and means nothing to anyone the page is shown to. An index is fixed, public, and something a reader already has a feel for.

- **One symbol through the SAME `equalWeightIndex`** the basket uses, so both are rebased at the same point on the same date axis. A second code path is how the picture and the numbers would come to disagree — there is a check that every benchmark line starts at exactly 1.
- **`PAGE_BENCHMARKS` carries the labels in server.js**, so basket.html restates nothing. `stock.html` keeps its own list of four: those are toggles with their own colours, a different control.
- **The lines are accent and violet, never green and red** — those two already mean up and down on every chart here, and an index coloured by its own direction would make a different claim from the one the chart is for.
- **`notBenchmark` went with the line it existed to serve.** Nothing computes "your universe, equal weight" any more, and a predicate nothing calls is residue that reads as intent. **`BENCHMARKS` stays** — it is now the delete guard.
- **THE FUNDAMENTALS CARD DELIBERATELY STILL SAYS "ALL SCREENED", and says why on its own face**: the S&P 500 and the Dow are *ETFs* here, and a fund has no margin, no growth and no P/E to compare against. There was nothing to put in the column; removing it would have gutted the card rather than improved it.
- **THE FOUR BENCHMARKS CANNOT BE REMOVED FROM THE SCREENER** (the owner's instruction). Every group page draws their line, so dropping one would take the comparison off pages that have nothing to do with that row — **damage that surfaces somewhere else entirely**, which is exactly the kind a guard is for. `DELETE /api/tickers/:symbol` answers **409** naming the reason; the screener's × is `disabled` with the same sentence on it, because a control that looks live and then errors is worse than one that explains itself. Removing a benchmark from a *theme* is untouched — that purges nothing.
  - The page's `BENCH_LOCK` mirrors `BENCHMARKS`; **the refusal lives in the route**, and a stale copy in the page can at worst offer a click the server then declines in its own words.
- Their bars ARE archived — checked against production, all four hold the full window. This file's older note that "the benchmark is deliberately never archived" predates the Benchmarks theme and is stale.
- Verified: **+16 checks** — the `universe` field gone, two labelled lines in its place, each a real series the length of the axis, each rebased to 1, and **SPY's line differing from the group's** (a benchmark that silently averaged the group would pass everything else). Plus the legend, three drawn lines told apart by stroke width, the returns table's exact four rows with no screened row, the fundamentals card keeping its column AND carrying the reason, all four DELETEs refused at 409 with the symbol still in the universe, **an ordinary ticker still deleting** (or the guard has locked the route), and the disabled × beside a live one on the screener. **Proved by reverting**: dropping the delete guard fails 8.

- **Entry points**: the Sector, Industry and Size pickers in the screener's bar each gained **the chart-arrow the theme picker already carried**. "All" gets none — it is not a group. **And every masthead chip on `/stock/<SYMBOL>` is a door into its group** (owner, 2026-09-27) — the chips were the one place on that page already naming these cuts, and a chip that goes somewhere is worth more than one that does not. **Industry and Size were not drawn there at all before**: the masthead carried the sector and the themes only, so two of the four cuts were simply missing. Order is coarse to fine, then membership: sector, industry, size, themes.
  - **`text-decoration: none` is not optional on an `a.chip`** — nothing on that page resets it, and the peer table's `vs` pill arrived underlined for exactly that reason. The chip keeps its muted colour at rest (a row of tinted pills would shout); the pointer and a lift on hover are the whole affordance.
  - **A stock with no industry or no cap draws FEWER chips**, never `/industry/undefined` — the field arrives one profile at a time, so that is the common case rather than an edge one.
  - Verified: **22 checks** over a fixture where the five values are five distinct strings, so a chip wired to the wrong cut cannot pass by coincidence — the exact order, every href, a theme name with a space and an ampersand surviving encoding, no underline and a pointer measured as DRAWN, the unclassified stock drawing nothing, and **each of the four hrefs actually fetched: 200 and the group resolving to a list containing the stock**, because a chip pointing at a 404 is worse than no chip. **Proved by reverting**: plain spans fail 3 and then the suite cannot continue.
  - **Test trap worth keeping**: `waitForSelector('.head .meta')` hangs on the unclassified stock — an empty chip span is zero-size and therefore never "visible", so the one case the suite exists to check waits for itself. Wait on `.head .sympick`.
- **The masthead picker crosses all four dimensions and is searchable**, because the reason you are on a sector page is often that you want an industry inside it. 11 sectors and 6 bands are a list; ~100 industries is a wall; one flat list of 130 is neither. A heading left over an empty section is hidden — a heading over nothing reads as a list that lost its rows.
- **A GRID ITEM IS `min-width: auto`, and that is what broke the phone.** The stock table's 620px floor pushed the card wider than a 390px screen and `.tblwrap` never got the chance to scroll, so the right-hand columns were simply unreachable — `body` here is `overflow-x: clip`, so nothing could be panned to reach them. The zero has to be on **every** level between the grid and the scroller.
- Verified: **58 checks**. The fixture makes every cut a different set — Technology holds two industries, and one Healthcare name and one financial are Mega alongside two Technology names, so **`/size/Mega` crosses sectors** and nothing resolving it as a taxonomy cut could produce that list. Plus the four 404s each naming their dimension, the no-sector stock in no sector group, all five routes, the composition bars **measured as drawn** and proved to be cap rather than count (one industry's bar >6x another's while being 3 of 4 by count), the leaders following the range button both ways, the negative P/E changing the median from 27 to 30 (so the guard IS the number), the industry page naming its parent sector, the searchable picker, the legacy `/portfolio/` address, and the phone. **Proved by reverting**: dropping the scope branch fails 11.
  - **`portfolios` and `portfolio_tickers` ARE `themes` and `theme_tickers`** — the tables were renamed even though the accessors were not, and a fixture writing the old names dies with `no such table`. Several lines in this file still say the old ones.
  - `bench-test.js` and `sector-test.js` in the scratchpad both fail at HEAD, confirmed by stashing — pre-existing, not this.

#### How much they move together — is a group one bet or many? (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**A card on every group page: the average pairwise correlation of its members' daily returns, how many independent holdings would damp the swings as much, the member least like the rest, the closest and furthest pairs, and a matrix where the group is small enough to read one.** Asked for off a list of fifteen quant concepts — six of which are already in this app under other names, four of which are impossible here for want of an options chain or an order book. The other two that were worth building are [docs/backlog.md](docs/backlog.md) entries 23 and 24.

- **IT COSTS NO QUERY AND NO BYTES.** `basketPayload` already returns `series` — every member rebased on one shared date axis — for the chart, so this is a loop over data the page is holding. **Memoised on the window and the membership**, because `paint()` runs on every sort click and every Show-more, and at the 150-member cap that is 11,175 pairs.
- **RETURNS, NEVER LEVELS, and that is not a refinement — it is the difference between right and meaningless.** Measured over 72 real pairs BEFORE building: the rebased-levels figure lands between **−0.96 and +0.90** away from the returns figure and **flips sign** — AAPL/MSFT is **+0.12 on returns and −0.27 on levels**. Two shares that both drift upward look alike on their price lines whatever they do day to day. **Proved by reverting**: the fixture's average goes 0.52 → **1.00** and 12 checks fail.
- **THE 3dp ROUNDING IN `symbolSeries` IS IMMATERIAL — 0.0039 at worst over those same pairs**, and that is what makes computing in the browser off the rounded payload the right call rather than a compromise. The same rounding turns a very small move into an exactly flat one, which is also what a carried-forward price gives; neither is distinguishable from the other here, the date axis already drops the sessions where that would be common, and both are inside the 0.0039.
- **THE WINDOW MOVES THE ANSWER MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE** — AAPL/MSFT is **0.12 over 120 sessions and 0.44 over 1,000** — so the card follows the page's own range buttons and prints the session count it used. There is a check that the count really changes with the buttons.
- **A PAIR IS COMPLETED PAIRWISE**, so a ticker added last week is compared over the sessions it actually has rather than dropping the pair whole. Under `CORR_MIN_PAIR` (20) shared returns the pair is dropped and counted as thin. **Proved by reverting**: requiring both series complete fails 29.
- **A MEMBER NOBODY COULD BE COMPARED WITH IS OUT OF THE DENOMINATOR.** Leaving it in the N reports a basket as better spread than its pairs say, which is **the direction that flatters**. **Proved by reverting**: fails 2.
- **Effective N is `N / (1 + (N−1)·ρ̄)`** — exact for an equal-weight basket of equal-volatility members, and **both assumptions are stated on the card** rather than buried: this page's basket really is equal-weight, the volatilities really are not. It falls back to the plain count where ρ̄ ≤ 0, because the formula then returns something larger than N; **proved by reverting**, which prints *9.0 of 3*.
- **THE SIGN COMES FROM THE ROUNDED VALUE.** An exactly orthogonal pair computes to −1e-17 and printed **"−0.00"** while being marked as a diversifying cell — a minus sign in front of a zero, the `+0%` lesson from the earnings card in a second place. Caught by the suite's own first run.
- **ONE HUE, AND THE NUMBER IN EVERY CELL.** Correlation has no good end, so green and red — which mean up and down on every other surface here — would read a verdict into it. The shade is an aid and the figure is the data; **a negative cell is unfilled and outlined**, because unfilled at +0.01 and unfilled at −0.50 must not look identical.
- Capped at `CORR_MATRIX_MAX` (14) for the grid and `CORR_MEMBERS_MAX` (150, biggest first) for the computation, both said on the card when they bite.
- Verified: **42 checks** over a fixture whose every expected value is **exact by construction** — Hadamard rows, so the twins are 1.00, the mirror −1.00, the orthogonal pair 0.00 and `p+q` exactly 0.71 — plus two deliberately short histories for the pairwise and thin paths. **Proved by reverting eleven times**, every one load-bearing.
  - **TWO REVERTS CAME BACK NOT LOAD-BEARING AND BOTH WERE THE FIXTURE.** It had no short history, so the pairwise guard could not bite; and it had no MIDDLING positive pair, so "shaded by strength" could not be told from "shaded at all" — a zero cell is unfilled whatever the scale in between does. Three strengths in order is the honest check.
  - **A READ IN THE DETAIL ARGUMENT ENDS A RUN** just as surely as one in the assertion: with the card in its empty state `get(...).g.slice()` threw and a revert that fails 29 reported as 1. Every accessor is total now.
  - **`group-page-test.js` NEEDED CORRECTING, NOT WORKING AROUND**, twice over: a hardcoded *"seven cards"* that said nothing about WHICH seven (it names them now, which also catches a card going missing), and a bare `.tblwrap` selector that picks the **first** wrapper on the page — now the matrix, not the stock table it means.

##### IT FOUND A DEAD DUPLICATE TICKER ON ITS FIRST LIVE RUN
**`SQ / XYZ at 1.00`** in Technology. They are the same company — Block renamed its ticker — and **both are in the universe**: `SQ` "Block" at $45.4B and `XYZ` "Block" at $44.7B. The independent confirmation is the clock: **SQ's prices stopped on 2026-09-28** while XYZ runs to 2026-10-02.

- **Nine pairs of rows share a display name**, and seven are legitimate: BRK.A/BRK.B, FOXA/FOX, NWS/NWSA, HEI.A/HEI, LBTYA/LBTYK, Z/ZG are real dual share classes (the set `peers-test.js` already dedupes), and OWL/OBDC are two Blue Owl entities. The two that are not are the **renames**: SQ/XYZ and FI/FISV.
- **What a duplicate costs**: it inflates every correlation reading for its group, counts twice in the sector and size aggregates, and takes two of the slots on any ranked card.
- **Not acted on — removing a ticker is the owner's call**, the standing rule. Reported with the evidence instead.

#### The stock table sorts on every column (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**Click any heading in `THE N STOCKS` to re-sort; click it again to reverse.** It was market cap descending and nothing else, which is the right default and the wrong only option — the table carries price, today, the range return, the cap and the Balanced verdict, and on a 200-stock sector "which of these fell hardest today" had no answer on the page.

- **IT SORTS THE WHOLE GROUP, THEN TAKES THE FIRST 50 — never the other way round.** The list is capped at 50 with a Show 50 more button, so slicing before sorting reorders only the page you happen to be looking at: **plausible on a 24-stock industry and wrong on a sector**, and it looks perfectly well formed either way. **The fixture is what makes that provable — 60 stocks against the cap, with the winner of every sort planted DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE the first 50 by market cap**, so a sort that touched only the drawn rows could never surface it. **Proved by reverting**: slicing first fails 8. The note says so too, naming the number it ordered.
- **THE VERDICT SORTS ON THE ENGINE'S LADDER, NOT THE ALPHABET**, through `ActionRules.ACTIONS.indexOf` — the index IS the rank. **`ACTIONS` runs WORST-FIRST**, so the raw index already ranks Strong Buy highest on a descending sort and needs no reversal; the pivot's own advice-move measure records what happens when that list is read in display order. The fixture separates the two ladders at position two (Buy against the alphabet's "Sell Immediately") and at the tail, because descending they agree on the leader. **Proved by reverting**: sorting it as text fails 4.
- **A BLANK IS NOT A ZERO AND GOES LAST WHICHEVER WAY THE COLUMN IS SORTED.** No verdict is not the worst verdict and no price is not free. The blank row is given the LARGEST cap in the fixture so the default sort puts it FIRST, which is where a blank-as-zero bug is most visible. The note says it in one clause. **Proved by reverting**: fails 4, the priceless row leading an ascending price sort.
- **THE RETURN COLUMN FOLLOWS THE RANGE BUTTONS, so the comparator reads the field rather than freezing one.** A sort that stopped following 1M/3M/6M/1Y would still look sorted. One fixture stock leads on 1Y and sits mid-pack on 1M, so changing the range must re-sort. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- **A FIRST CLICK OPENS ON THE INTERESTING END** — descending for a number, ascending for a name. Nobody opens a price column to see the cheapest stock first. **Proved by reverting**: all-ascending fails 9.
- **THE ARROW BOX IS ALWAYS RENDERED and only the active column fills it.** An arrow that appears and disappears changes the header's width and jogs the whole column as you click between them; the screener positions its own arrow absolutely for the same reason. **Proved by reverting**: the conditional span moves the columns and fails 1.
- **Reachable by keyboard and announced to a screen reader** — `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, Enter and Space, and `aria-sort` on the live column. **Proved by reverting** twice: the click handler alone fails 17, the keydown handler 1.
- **Sorting does NOT collapse an expanded list** back to 50, and the second tiebreak is always market cap, so rows level on the sorted column keep the order the page opened in rather than shuffling.
- **Nothing is persisted.** A sort surviving a reload is a table in an order the reader did not choose on a page they have just arrived at — the filter row's rule.
- Verified: **43 checks** on the real page, plus `group-page-test.js` (58) re-run unchanged. **Proved by reverting ten times, every one load-bearing.** `consol-test.js` fails 12 at HEAD too, confirmed by stashing.
  - **A REVERT THAT ABORTS THE SUITE REPORTS "NOT LOAD-BEARING".** Slicing before the sort leaves 50 rows as the whole list, so `Show 50 more` is never drawn and a bare `page.click('#moreRows')` **throws** — 28 of 43 checks ran and the harness reported 6 failures where there are 8. Assert the button exists, then click the handle; the `page.selectOption` trap in a new shape.
  - **The glyphs in the source are LITERAL UTF-8, not `▾` escapes**, so a double-backslashed anchor looked for text the file does not contain — and the source line ends `` </span></th>` ``, so an anchor carrying that trailing backtick matched nothing either. Two separate ways for one anchor to miss.

## Cards, and the module behind them
**`private/cards.js` owns every card: its markup, its wording AND its styles** (2026-09-14). Its hosts are `/promo` and the phone’s saved posts, and a second copy of "Top gainers this week" would have drifted inside a week, the same reason `rowcard.js`, `screens.js` and `action.js` exist. The contract is one call: `Cards.build(id, ctx)` with `{stocks, myLists, size, opts, getBasket}` returning the card's inner HTML. **The module reads no DOM and issues no requests** — the host hands it control values by control id and a `getBasket(days)` that returns the archive payload or null while it loads, which is what makes all sixteen card variants testable off-page in a `vm`. Styles ride along in a template literal injected by `Cards.injectStyle()`, so a grammar added to one page cannot be styled only in the other.

**A card is dated by its DATA, not by the reader's clock (2026-09-16).** `dateStr()` stamped `new Date()`, so a card built on a Saturday — or after a refresh had failed — printed today's date over Thursday's prices, and that card goes on Instagram. It is the freshest `latestDate` across the rows now, derived in `build()`, parsed at **local noon** because `new Date('2026-09-16')` is UTC midnight and renders as the 15th west of Greenwich.

**The card prints the refresh TIME beside that date** (owner: "why can't you show the same on the visual itself") — `Sep 16, 2026 · 4:37 PM ET` in the header pill, from `ctx.updatedAt`, which the studio and the phone’s post endpoint both pass. **Always America/New_York, never the builder's own zone**: the card is a baked image, so whoever renders it would otherwise bake their clock into something other people read, and the market it describes keeps one timezone. A host that does not supply the time gets the date alone rather than an invented one.

**Both studio pages say when the prices were pulled** (`#freshLine`, owner's request — "this will give me confidence that it is latest data"): the refresh clock, how long ago, and the day the cards will carry, from the `updatedAt` that `/api/stocks` already returned and both pages were discarding. It goes **amber past 26 hours**, because the one thing worth noticing before posting is that the numbers are yesterday's. The phone's post sheet carries the same fact as "data as of …". Verified on fresh and week-old snapshots: the wording, the flag, and the card stamping Sep 9 rather than today.

**Cards label by NAME, not by ticker** (2026-09-14, owner's instruction). `nameOf(row)` is `shortName || name || symbol` and `symOf(sym)` looks a bare ticker up through it; every card's rows, tiles, tracks, rankings, verdict roll-calls, scatter labels and the Intro live-data slides run through them. A feed reads a company faster than a four-letter code, and the screener carries a Short name column now, so the string exists on every row. The columns were restyled with it — the mono face gives way to the sans one, widths roughly double, and every one truncates with an ellipsis rather than wrapping a post into two lines.

**The Movers time window has calendar windows beside the rolling ones (2026-09-15)**: *This week* (`wtd`) runs from the last close before the current week's Monday, *This month* (`mtd`) from the last close before the 1st — "current" being the week and month of the freshest bar, so a Saturday post shows the week just ended. *Week* and *Month* stay **rolling** (5 and 21 sessions — the last 7 and ~30 days) and are labelled so in the dropdown; the card text for Week changed from "this week" to "past week", since that phrase now belongs to week-to-date. **The snapshot carries no calendar anchors**, so `GET /api/period-anchors` (member, cached 10 minutes) reads each symbol's last close before each boundary (`closesBefore`, ~80ms a boundary) and the studio stamps `wtdPct` / `mtdPct` = price ÷ anchor on its rows; a row without an anchor is simply not ranked. **An anchor more than 7 days older than its boundary is dropped** — a symbol with a gap in its bars (AVB, no bars after 2026-08-24, at the time) would otherwise show a move spanning weeks under a "this week" label. Only `/promo` offers the two windows; `cards.js` supports them wherever a host stamps the fields. Verified: the endpoint against an independent query (NVDA −2.25% week, −3.36% month), and headlessly on real prices (10 checks — both windows rank their own leaders, Week still ranks the rolling 7 days, compare column, side by side).

#### …and year to date is the third of them (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**A `This year (since last year's close)` option in the Movers time window, and `This year` in the compare picker beside it.** The module already knew the key — `ytd: ['ytdPct', 'this year', 'year to date']` went into `MOV_PERIODS` with the screener's YTD column — so the window was reachable by a saved post and by nothing a reader could click. The whole change is two `<option>` lines.

- **IT NEEDS NO `/api/period-anchors` STAMPING, which is the one way it differs from its two calendar siblings.** `computeStocks` puts `ytdPct` on every row, so it rides the snapshot — and that is exactly why **it is the only calendar window that survives a saved post to the PHONE**: `/api/m/post` builds from the snapshot and never stamps the week- and month-to-date anchors, so a `wtd` or `mtd` post draws blank there. Worth knowing before that is read as a new fault.
- **Placed between 6 months and 1 year, where two conventions happen to agree**: calendar windows sit immediately before their rolling neighbour in this picker (*This week* before *Week*, *This month* before *Month*), and the screener's own columns run 6M, YTD, 1Y.
- **A STOCK THAT LISTED THIS YEAR IS ABSENT, NEVER RANKED AT 0.0%** — the blank-versus-zero rule, inherited free, because a row without the field is simply not ranked the way a row without an anchor is not. In the compare column it is an em-dash.
- **THE TWO PICKERS ARE A SECOND COPY OF ONE ANOTHER and nothing made them agree.** A window offered in the time picker and not in the compare one is a card that can rank by something it cannot compare against. The check is stronger than either list: **every key in `Cards.MOV_PERIODS` must appear in both, and neither may offer a key the module does not know** — so a window added to the module alone is caught without this suite restating the catalogue.
  - **The silent fallback is why that last half matters.** `MOV_PERIODS[perKey] || MOV_PERIODS.w1` means a picker sending a key the module has never heard of draws **last week's card under a heading nobody chose** — no error, no blank, just the wrong numbers. **Proved by reverting**: deleting the module's entry fails 12.
- Verified: **28 checks** in the real studio. **The fixture is the test** — each stock's YTD rank disagrees with its rank in *every* other window the picker offers, so a card still reading `oneWeekPct` comes out in a different order rather than coincidentally the same one; and the no-YTD stock is given the **best one-week return in the fixture**, so it tops the week card and its absence from the year card is a fact about the window rather than about a missing row. Plus the compare column, the losers direction, and a saved post round-tripped through the server and built by the phone's own route. **Proved by reverting five times**: the time picker's option fails 15, the compare picker's alone 3, the wrong slot 1, the module's entry 12, and wiring the key to `oneYearPct` instead of `ytdPct` fails 7 — a calendar window reading a rolling field being the whole reason YTD is not `oneYearPct` under another name.
  - **A `\n` IN A REVERT ANCHOR MATCHES NOTHING AND THE PATCH IS SILENTLY SKIPPED**, which reads exactly like a guard that never mattered — four of these five reverts reported that way on the first run for that reason alone. This file had named only `server.js` and `index.html` as CRLF; the files this change touches are CRLF too.
    - **AND THE LINE ENDING IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE FILE — IT IS A PROPERTY OF THE WORKING COPY AT THAT MOMENT (corrected 2026-10-02, hours after the line above it was written).** I generalised that measurement to *"every tracked source file in this repo is CRLF, all 124, not one LF-only or mixed"*, and it is **false**: measured the same day, **64 all-CRLF, 60 all-LF, 0 mixed**. What makes it worse than a wrong count is that **it moves under you**. `core.autocrlf` normalises on CHECKOUT, so a `git stash` and `pop` rewrote `private/basket.html` from LF back to CRLF **in the middle of this session** — while an Edit/Write tool had rewritten it the other way an hour earlier. Git stores LF either way, so **the difference never appears in a diff** and nothing warns you.
    - **So the rule is DETECT, NEVER ASSUME — per file, at the moment the harness runs**: `const NL = read().includes('\r\n') ? '\r\n' : '\n';`. A harness carrying a hardcoded `'\r\n'` is correct until the next checkout, stash or branch switch, and silently inert after it. Keep the assert-every-anchor-hits-once guard that caught it, which is what makes either mistake loud.
  - **`page.selectOption` ON A VALUE THE SELECT DOES NOT CARRY TIMES OUT AT 30s RATHER THAN FAILING**, so a revert that removes an option **aborts the suite**, and an aborted suite reports "0 failed". Two of these reverts ran 8 and 16 of 28 checks for that reason. Set `.value` and dispatch the page's own `change` event instead: a missing option leaves the select empty, the card falls back, and the assertions decide rather than the wait. The documented trap, met again in a new place.

#### …and on the Chart card, as a date-anchored slice (2026-10-02, owner's request)
**A `This year (since last year's close)` option in the Chart template's Window picker, between Past six months and Past year.** This is the entry the YTD column's own section listed as a deliberate omission, and **the reason it gave was right and is unchanged**: `CHART_WINDOWS` maps bar COUNTS, and a count of sessions is not a calendar boundary on any date but one. What changed is the mechanism — the count is now only the FETCH size and the boundary is found in the date axis the host returns.

- **THE ORIGIN IS 31 DECEMBER, NOT THE YEAR'S FIRST SESSION**, because that is the close `ytdPct` anchors on. Rebasing one session later silently drops the year's first day: on the fixture that is **+100.0% against +66.7%**, with nothing on the card to account for the difference. **Proved by reverting**: fails 6.
- **IT AGREES WITH THE SCREENER COLUMN TO THE PAYLOAD'S PRECISION, NOT EXACTLY, and that is measured rather than claimed.** My first code comment said "exactly" and was an overstatement. `symbolSeries` rounds every value to 3dp, so re-dividing two of them compounds it — against production over **1,169 symbols: median 0.03pt, worst 0.31pt** (AEHR, +429.95 against the column's +430.26), 27 symbols past 0.1pt, and **the error grows with the move**. Left alone deliberately: more decimals on the wire costs ~0.6MB on the studio's largest fetch, and taking the tag from the row's `ytdPct` would print a number disagreeing with the point it is drawn beside.
- **ONE SLICE, ABOVE ALL FOUR MODES.** The one-stock line, the pair, the leaders and the whole-screen average all read `d.dates` and `series`, so slicing once in `tplChart` reaches every one where four copies could only drift — and the 50-day average comes along free, since `maSeries` already rebases to the first window date the archive holds.
- **THE SERIES HAVE TO BE RE-REBASED, not only sliced.** The host rebases to the first session it FETCHED, so slicing alone draws a year-to-date window off a year-ago origin — the right dates with the wrong numbers, which looks perfectly well formed. **Proved by reverting**: fails 5, with the card reading +307.4% under a "this year" kicker.
- **ONLY THIS CARD CAN SLICE, so only this card may be offered the window.** Sparks and the Spotlight read the same `CHART_WINDOWS` map and draw the axis as fetched — handed `ytd` they would draw a FULL YEAR under a heading reading "this year". `barWin()` makes them fall back to six months, so the map cannot lie to two of its three consumers, and that is asserted through the exported `basketDays` rather than left to the markup (a saved post is hand-editable). **Proved by reverting**: fails 2.
- **`over the ${winLabel}` reads "over the this year"**, so the two-stock note takes its phrase from `winPhrase` — "ahead by 50.0 points **so far this year**". The `.replace(/^Past /, '')` that used to sit there **could never fire** (every label is lower case) and went with it: residue reading as intent.
- **THE CARD NAMES ITS OWN ORIGIN.** Every mode's note says "the start of the window", which a bar count's kicker already pins ("past six months") and this one does not — and a posted image has no picker beside it.
- **Before the year's first session it says so** rather than drawing a one-point "line". Without the guard `lineChart` falls through to its generic *No stored history*, which blames the archive for a calendar fact. One or two days a year, and **proved by reverting**: fails 2.
- Verified: **38 checks** in the real studio. **The fixture's load-bearing half is a +20% gap on the year's first session**, so the right origin and the wrong one cannot be confused; the same path makes six months **−50.0%** and a year **+300.0%**, so a card that ignored the key comes out at a different number rather than coincidentally the same one. **The axis is the proof the slice happened** — asserted as `dates[0] === '2025-12-31'` exactly, since a correct end tag could sit over a line drawn across a whole year. Plus the 50-day average on the sliced axis, both end tags, leaders and list, a saved post round-tripped and rebuilt by the phone's own route at the same +100.0%, and a 12-combination fit sweep (3 artboards × 4 modes, nothing overflowing) because the note gains a sentence. **Proved by reverting nine times**, every one load-bearing: no slice 7, no re-rebase 5, the wrong origin 6, the phrase 1, `barWin` 2, the year-not-opened guard 2, the origin sentence 1, the module's entry 13, the option 16.
  - **THE SILENT FALLBACK IS WHY THE MODULE'S ENTRY IS WORTH ITS OWN REVERT.** `CHART_WINDOWS[v] || CHART_WINDOWS.m6` means a picker sending a key the module has never heard of draws **six months under a kicker reading "this year"** — measured in that revert as −50.0%. No error, no blank, just the wrong window.
  - **A REVERT THAT READS `.ytd[0]` UNGUARDED ABORTS THE SUITE**, which reports "0 failed" — the documented trap, met again. The module probe reads `(CHART_WINDOWS.ytd || [0])[0]`.
  - **THE MOVERS PICKER CARRIES A BYTE-IDENTICAL OPTION** (shipped an hour earlier), so the option line alone hits twice in `promo.html` and the patch is refused. The anchor takes the comment above it. *An anchor that is unique today stops being unique the moment the same control is added twice.*
  - **A FIXTURE'S WINDOW IS N SESSIONS INCLUSIVE, so its first index is `LAST - (N-1)`.** Both the six-month and one-year anchors were off by one and reported 293% against a planned 300% — the code was right.
  - **`/api/basket` DERIVES `since` FROM THE CLOCK, so an archive rewound past the window is legitimately empty.** The check that a bar window still draws beside the year-not-opened refusal asked for six months against a ten-month-stale archive and got nothing — proving neither thing. It asks for a year, which reaches back far enough.
  - **The date-axis labels are classless `<text>` holding the ISO date** — read off `lineChart` rather than guessed at. My first selector (`.xlab, .cx`) matched nothing and reported an empty axis, the speculative-selector trap the Disclaimer card records.

**The Movers card can carry the verdict** (2026-09-14, `movAdv`): off by default, else a rule set from `ADV_PROFILES`, scored in the browser through `advScored()` — the same cached engine pass the Advice cards use, so it costs nothing beyond the first profile. **The word rides UNDER the name, not in a column of its own**: "Sell Immediately" would need ~170px, and with the comparison column on there is not that much left; stacked it costs no width and about 2px of row height. **The rule set is named in the KICKER, not in a paragraph** — the first cut put it in an `s-sub` and the five extra lines of prose were most of what pushed the card over its own masthead; the attribution still has to be there, so it moved somewhere free. A row the engine cannot score simply has no second line. **The side-by-side layout is excluded** — it already runs two rankings in half the width apiece — and the promo control hides itself when Direction is "Both, side by side". 

**A card is a fixed artboard and cannot scroll, so a list too tall does not clip — it sits on top of the masthead**, because `.s-body` centres its content. The ranked list therefore picks its rhythm from the row count, the artboard and whether a verdict line is on (`ROOM` / `RHYTHM` in `tplMovers`): default, then `tight`, then `tighter`, each shrinking the bar, the name and the number **together**, since a short bar beside a full-size number reads as a mistake rather than as a denser card. Past the tightest rhythm the list is **trimmed** rather than overflowed — the same per-shape cap the side-by-side card takes — and because the rows are sorted by the move it is always the smallest that go, with the title saying "Top gainers" rather than a count so nothing on the card becomes untrue. Square at Top 15 with a comparison column lands there (11 rows); it overflowed before the verdict feature existed too. **Verified by a harness that measures the artboard independently of the builder's own estimates** — 72 combinations of shape × count × advice × compare × direction, 0 overflowing, tightest fit 46px of slack.

**Side by side on a Story fills the frame (2026-09-15)** — it used to render the post layout, dense past ten rows (names cut at 92px), bunched at the top of a 1920px artboard. On `sz-story` each row is two lines (name and move above, the bar full width beneath), the rows sit in `.mlist` and spread with `space-evenly`, and **the shorter column is padded with invisible `.mpad` rows** so the nth gainer stays level with the nth loser. Six rows or fewer get `.few` (40px type, 30px bars), because five rows spread through a story read as lines floating in a frame. Post and square are unchanged. Verified by measuring the real page, 3 shapes × 3 scopes × Top 5/10/15 × two windows: no overflow anywhere, columns level everywhere, the list uses 94-98% of the story height, at most 2 names in 30 truncated on a story.

**Two places deliberately keep the ticker.** The **Chart** card: its legend chips and end tags sit in inches of space beside a drawn line, where only a short code fits — the owner excluded it by name. And the Intro **mock** slide, which draws a fake screener row beside its star: that column really does show the symbol, so naming it would make the illustration lie about the product. The fundamentals scatter compromises instead — it names its eight outlier dots, anchors a label back towards the middle when its dot sits in the right half, and clips past 22 characters, because a name is many times wider than a ticker and would otherwise run off the artboard.

**`/cards`, the member room, was REMOVED on 2026-09-23** (owner: "I dont need cards anymore as I have promo"). It offered three data cards — Movers, Chart, Advice — at one shape, with controls in a bar rather than a studio panel. **Nothing was lost by deleting it**: `/promo` carries the identical guard (signed-in, not guest), is linked from the screener bar for every member, and is a strict superset — every template the member room had, plus the other two artboard sizes, the crop guide and the owner-only Announcement card. Keeping two hosts for one module meant every card change had to be checked twice. The page, its route, its `GATED_PAGES` entry and its three links (the Research picker, and two rows on `/admin`) all went; **`cards.js` and `cardshot.js` stay** — they are the module and the rasteriser, and the studio and the phone both depend on them. Guests were refused by both pages and are unaffected.

## The public side: a landing page and a blog
**Three pages a stranger can read (2026-09-16, owner's request — "a home page like tastytrade.com, and a blog open to all visitors").** Until now the whole site was a door: anonymous `/` redirected to a password form that never said what the site was.

- **`/` serves `private/landing.html` when signed out**, the screener when signed in — the one-line change in the root route. Structure follows the reference site (nav → hero with two CTAs → stat strip → what it is → an illustrated table row → the research-honesty section → data/freshness → FAQ → closing CTA → footer with the not-advice disclaimer), in this app's own voice and palette. **The illustrated row is labelled as an illustration** with made-up names; the two real numbers come from `GET /api/public-stats` (universe count + snapshot timestamp, cached 10 min, deliberately cheap — no row counts).
- **`/blog` and `/blog/:slug` are PUBLIC and RENDERED ON THE SERVER.** The pages are templates in `private/` with `%PLACEHOLDERS%` filled by the route, so a post's words are in the HTML: a blog that needs JavaScript to show its text is one that search engines and bad connections cannot read. Each post page carries its own `<title>`, description, `og:` tags and canonical link. `/robots.txt` and `/sitemap.xml` list the published posts.
- **Posts live in `posts` (slug primary key, `status` draft|published)** and are written at **`/posts`** (admin) — title, address, summary, markdown body, Save draft / Publish / Preview / Delete. Publishing needs no deploy. `published_at` is stamped on the FIRST publish and never moves on an edit, so the index does not reshuffle when a typo is fixed; a rename carries the post to the new slug rather than leaving two. The editor's preview renders through the SERVER's markdown, because a second renderer in the page would drift from what readers see.
- **`renderMarkdown()` escapes first, then formats** — the chat renderer's rule, and it matters more here: `<script>` in a draft comes out as text, and a `javascript:` link keeps its words and loses its href. Supported: headings (`#` becomes an `h2`, since the page owns the `h1`), lists, quotes, fenced code, bold/italic/inline code, `---`, and http(s) or internal links.
- **Drafts are invisible to everyone but the owner** — enforced in the route (`publishedOnly`), not in the page: `/blog/<draft>` is a 404 and the public list and sitemap omit it.
- The login page gained **Read the blog** and **What is Tickr Lab?** links, and the landing page's Try it button uses `/login?guest=1`, which the login page acts on — the guest door stays in one place rather than being POSTed from a public page.
- **The admin API routes had to move below `requireAdmin`'s definition** — registered beside the public ones they threw `Cannot access 'requireAdmin' before initialization` at boot, exactly as the `/api/db-stats` note warns. `node --check` passes that; only running it catches it.
- Verified: 34 checks against the real server with a password set, so the public pages are tested as a stranger sees them (publish/draft/rename/delete, the publish date surviving an edit and a rename, the escaping and link rules, anonymous access to `/`, `/blog`, a post, the sitemap and robots, 404s for a draft and an unknown slug, 403s for the admin API, the editor's redirect) plus 20 browser checks at 1440px and 400px (no sideways scroll on any page, headings present, the live stock count, no console errors).

### Post to blog — a studio card becomes a draft (2026-09-25, owner's request)
**A second button beside Download PNG: the same shot, stored instead of downloaded, wrapped in a draft.** Three steps and **every piece already existed** — `CardShot.shoot()` rasterises the artboard, `POST /api/admin/posts/image` stores the bytes, `PUT /api/admin/posts` writes the post. The feature is the wiring and the words.

- **A DRAFT, never published.** The card is the finished half and the prose is not; nothing here may put a page reading "One sentence on…" in front of a reader. **The summary is left EMPTY for the same reason** — that one would reach the blog index.
- **The picture is the first block and carries NO width word**, which on the post page means the right-hand rail at its full width: the two-column shape, image on the right, prose running down the left. A `"wide"` there would span both columns, which is what the revert-proof uses.
- **Everything under it is a prompt**, under the headings `posts.html`'s own `TEMPLATES` already use, closing on the house caveat ("a card reports what the screen and the rules did; it is not a forecast") — the one line that should survive being edited.
- **THE CAPTION IS THE CARD'S HEADLINE, NOT THE POST TITLE.** The alt becomes the `figcaption`, printed under a picture printed under the `h1` — so captioning it with the title put the same words twice in 200px, **the duplication the owner already pulled this blog up on once**. It is `.s-title` now ("Top gainers past week") against a title of "Movers — Sep 22, 2026". **A screenshot caught it; all 31 assertions passed straight through it.**
- **Both are read off what the card DREW**, not computed a second time: `.s-date` for the date and `.s-title` for the headline. A card is dated by its DATA, so a title from `new Date()` would disagree with the picture directly beneath it — and **`innerText`, never `textContent`**, because a `<br>` contributes no whitespace and a two-line headline comes back as one run-on word.
- **A 409 makes the NEXT draft rather than overwriting the one there** (`-2`, `-3`, up to 9). `was` is what an EDIT sends and this is not an edit; silently replacing a draft somebody had started writing is the one outcome worth ruling out. The image is content-hashed, so clicking twice on an unchanged card stores **one** row.
- **`/posts?slug=` opens that draft**, added for this: a link that lands you in front of a list you then have to search is not a link to the thing. An unknown slug is ignored — the address bar is not a form.
- **A PNG, like the download**, for the reason the editor's own uploader states: re-encoding a picture that is mostly text as JPEG is how you get mush. ~550KB for a 4:5 card, against the route's 2MB cap.
- **NOTHING NAMED `post*` IN promo.html WAS TOUCHED** — on that page a "post" is a saved CARD PRESET, so the new ids are `blogBox` / `blogBtn` / `blogMsg`. A collision worth not walking into on a page that already has eight hardcoded listener lists.
- **Admin only in two places, and only one of them is security.** Both routes are `requireAdmin` and that is the boundary; the button is hidden so a member is never offered something that would be refused — a visible control that 403s is worse than none.
- Verified: **34 checks** driving the real studio and the real server, plus **13** on the roles. The fixture is dated **three days back**, so a clock-derived title fails rather than passing by coincidence, and the card is proved to have **drawn its companies** before it is shot — a blank artboard would make every later assertion vacuous. **Image on the right is MEASURED** off `getBoundingClientRect()` on the published page (a draft is a 404, so the test publishes one deliberately: the editor's preview box says of itself that its edges are a shape, not a measure). **Proved by reverting**: emitting a `"wide"` image spans both columns and fails six checks including both positional ones. The role walk has the member 403'd on both routes, the guest never reaching the studio at all, and **the owner seeing the button** — which is what stops that suite passing with the feature deleted.
- **Two test faults worth keeping**: the movers card's rows are `.row`, not `.mrow` (that is the side-by-side variant), so a class count is a statement about today's template — count the COMPANIES the card names instead; and `/api/me` nests the address under `user`, so reading `me.email` gives `undefined`, which is exactly what a signed-OUT answer looks like.

### The mailing list (2026-09-25, owner's request)
**The note left at `MAIL_POST_MAX` when email-a-post shipped said what this would need if it ever became a list — *confirmed opt-in and a one-click unsubscribe in every message* — and that is what this is.** A box at the foot of the blog index and every post, and a `Everyone subscribed (N)` option in the editor's send.

- **A SUBSCRIPTION IS NOT AN ACCOUNT.** `subscribers` is its own table, never a column on `users`: signing up to use the screener is not agreeing to a newsletter, the blog is public so most subscribers will never have an account, and a consent record needs somewhere to say WHEN and HOW it was given. **Nobody existing was imported** — the list started at zero and opt-in is the only way on.
- **TWO TOKENS, AND THEY FOLLOW OPPOSITE RULES.** Confirm is the password-reset shape (hashed at rest, single use, expires in a week) because it proves once that someone owns the address. **Unsubscribe is stored in the clear, never expires and is reused in every message**, because a link in a mail from a year ago must still work and the reader is not signed in. Copying the reset rules onto it would silently break unsubscribe for anyone who did not act at once, which is how you collect spam complaints instead of quiet exits. Deriving it from `ADMIN_PASSWORD` (the guest-cookie trick) was rejected: rotating the password would kill every link ever sent. Plaintext is right for the threat — the worst a leak buys is unsubscribing somebody.
- **A GET SHOWS A BUTTON; THE POST ACTS.** Corporate link scanners and inbox previewers follow every URL in a message, so a GET that unsubscribed would remove people who never clicked anything. The mail client's own button sends the POST, which is exactly what `List-Unsubscribe-Post` asks for, so one click really is one click there.
- **The headers are not decoration.** `List-Unsubscribe` + `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` are required of bulk senders by Gmail and Yahoo and largely decide inbox versus spam. `sendMail` gained a `headers` pass-through for them; **transactional mail passes none and must not** — a password reset is not something anyone can opt out of.
- **Topics from day one**, `SUB_TOPICS` with one entry (`posts`) and a JSON array on the row, so a second mailing costs no migration and no re-consent. The id is what a stored consent points at, so a topic may be renamed but **never re-keyed**. Dropping the last topic IS unsubscribing.
- **Non-enumeration, the `/api/forgot` rule.** Already on the list, brand new, or throttled all answer identically — otherwise the form is an oracle for whether an address is subscribed. One confirmation a minute per address.
- **An unsubscribed row is KEPT, never deleted**: the row is the record that the address asked to stop. `/subscribers` says so and the × is for junk and erasure requests only. **Re-subscribing goes back through confirmation and REISSUES the unsubscribe token**, so a link in old mail cannot kill the new subscription.
- **Sending is one batch of 20 per call with the editor looping** — the `/api/news/refresh` shape, because a serverless function cannot hold hundreds of sends and nothing may run after the response. A **`post_sends` ledger is claimed BEFORE each attempt**, so a function killed mid-batch loses a send rather than doubling one: the right way round for a newsletter. The editor confirms with the number first, since a broadcast cannot be taken back.
- **Person-to-person mail is untouched and carries NO unsubscribe link** — offering to remove someone from a list they were never on is a lie. The two audiences are decided once in the route and **never share a send path**.
- **Both blog pages post a plain HTML form** and load no JavaScript, which is that page's own standing rule (the carousel is CSS-only for the same reason). `doSubscribe` / `doUnsubscribe` each serve an HTML door and a JSON one from one body; **content negotiation is deliberately not how they are told apart** — a browser's `fetch` sends the same Accept header as a navigation, which this codebase has been bitten by once.
- **The postal address is a SITE SETTING, edited on `/subscribers`.** CAN-SPAM wants a real one in commercial bulk mail; unset, the list still works and the page flags it in amber rather than the server inventing one. It lives in `app_meta` (`mail_postal`) beside `hidden_columns` and the rest, because **it is content the owner writes and the one legal requirement of this feature should not be reachable only from a hosting dashboard**. `MAIL_POSTAL_ADDRESS` still wins if an operator prefers config, and the page says so instead of offering a field that would do nothing. The one-minute cache is cleared on save, or the first broadcast after setting it would go out without the line it was set for.

#### A SECOND DOOR: the tick on the sign-up form (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**A checkbox on `/login`'s register tab — *"Email me when there is a new post"* — writing a `subscribers` row sourced `signup`.** Asked as *"on user sign-on page, need to give an option if the user wants to subscribe to emails and record the same in the Subscribers table"*.

- **PENDING AND A CONFIRMATION, NEVER AN ACTIVE ROW, and the reason is that REGISTRATION DOES NOT VERIFY THE ADDRESS.** With `REQUIRE_APPROVAL=false` anyone holding the invite code can type anyone's address and be let straight in, so a tick here is an **intent, not a proof**. Recording it confirmed would mail a newsletter to a person who never asked — the spam-complaint path confirmed opt-in exists to close, and the domain it would damage is the one password resets depend on.
  - **It does NOT contradict the welcome email being off.** That one was turned off for volume, being *"the least necessary mail here"*; a confirmation is the one message that **protects** the domain, and it goes only to somebody who asked for it seconds earlier — which is the best engagement signal a young sender can have.
- **ONE DEFINITION OF SUBSCRIBING.** `beginSubscription({email, topics, source, ip, base})` is extracted out of `doSubscribe`, which becomes a thin wrapper over it; the blog box and the sign-up tick share the path, the store call and the confirmation mail. A second copy of that mail would drift the first time either was edited — the reason `rowcard.js`, `action.js`, `filters.js` and `cards.js` all exist. **Proved by reverting**: a hand-rolled store call in its place writes the row and sends nothing, failing 5.
- **`req.body?.subscribe !== true`, STRICTLY.** Every non-empty string is truthy, so a loose test subscribes a hand-rolled POST carrying `"false"`. **Proved by reverting**: fails 5, on `"false"`, `1`, `"yes"`, `"true"` and `{}`.
- **AWAITED, unlike the welcome and the operator notice beside it in the same route.** Nothing may run after a response on this platform, so a detached send is simply lost — and `startSubscribe` writes the row **before** the mail, so losing it leaves a pending subscription with no link and the one-a-minute throttle blocking the obvious retry. `/api/forgot` and `/contact` both await a send on a request path for the same reason. Its rejection is swallowed, so the route's own rule still holds: **a failing mail provider can never fail a sign-up**, and there is a check that drives exactly that.
- **ONE CALL SITE, BEFORE THE PENDING/ACTIVE BRANCH.** The newsletter does not wait on an admin letting somebody in — the blog is public and most subscribers will never have an account at all. **Proved by reverting**: skipping a pending registrant fails 4.
- **`source: 'signup'`** is the point of that column: the consent record says WHEN and HOW it was given, which is the stated reason the table is separate from `users`.
- **Gated on `mailReady`, new on `/api/me`** beside `googleReady` and for its rule: with no provider configured nothing can be confirmed, so the box would be a control that does nothing. With mail off a hand-rolled POST leaves **no row that nobody could ever confirm**.
- **UNTICKED, and the fine print is beside it rather than after the fact.** A pre-ticked box is not consent; it is the one thing the regulators name outright. **Proved by reverting**: shipping it `checked` fails 4 — including the registration that was supposed to subscribe nobody.
- **The page says a confirmation is coming, and holds 1.8s before navigating** — only where one was really sent. It is the one moment anybody can be told: the next thing that happens is a navigation to the screener, and an address already on the list gets no second email, so saying otherwise would promise mail that is not coming.

##### TWO UNSCOPED RULES ON THAT PAGE CAPTURED THE CHECKBOX, and a third hazard was the browser's own
The **ninth** time an unscoped rule on this project has captured later markup, after `.warn`, `.card`, `input[type=text]`, `.mk`, `.sub`, `.news-when`, `.fav` and `.bezel > .core`. Both are undone **by name**, because neither ties on specificity by accident:
- **`input { width: 100% }`** turns a checkbox into a **350px bar**. **Proved by reverting**: the drawn box goes 16px → 350px.
- **`label`** is a 10px uppercase caption with 0.2em tracking — right for a field name, unreadable for a sentence. **Proved by reverting**: `uppercase 10px 2px`.
- **AND AN EMPTY BOX MUST LOOK EMPTY.** Left to the browser it renders as a **pale FILLED square on a black card**, which on a consent control reads as *already ticked* — the one impression it must not give. `accent-color` does not help, since it paints the ticked state only, and **`color-scheme: dark` was tried and changed nothing**. It is drawn instead, with the same hairline and inset the text fields have; `appearance: none` would throw keyboard focus away, so `:focus-visible` keeps a ring. The check measures **both states as drawn** and demands they differ, because a control whose states look alike is worse than an ugly one.
- **Found by looking at the rendered page**, as every layout fault on this project has been.

- Verified: **68 checks over three boots**, because `REQUIRE_APPROVAL` and `MAIL_READY` are read at module scope and one process cannot hold both settings — mail on (53), approval on (7), no mail at all (8). **Every claim is read out of `subscribers`, never off the route's 200**, which looks identical whether the row landed active, pending or not at all. **Proved by reverting twelve times, every one load-bearing.**
  - **THE PER-IP SIGN-UP THROTTLE IS 5 A DAY AND IT MADE THREE CHECKS VACUOUS.** A suite registering a dozen accounts from one address gets 429 from the sixth on — and every check asserting **no subscriber row** then passes because the registration never happened. `SIGNUP_PER_IP_DAY` is raised in the fixture, and each of those cases now asserts the account was really created **first**. *An absence is satisfied just as well by the action not happening.*
  - **A SECOND PAGE IN THE SAME BROWSER CONTEXT INHERITS THE FIRST ONE'S SESSION**, and `/login` sends a signed-in visitor straight to `/` — so the register tab never exists and the click **times out** rather than failing. A fresh context, which is also what a second person is.
  - **A SUITE THAT THROWS REPORTS A HANDFUL OF FAILURES WHERE THERE ARE TWENTY.** Two reverts stop the confirmation going, which makes `confirms(addr)[0]` undefined; both aborted at 8 of 53 and read as marginal guards. Every mail read is total now, and they fail 12 and 5.
  - **A `git stash` / `pop` rewrote `public/login.html` from LF to CRLF mid-session**, the documented hazard met again — in the same session that recorded it. The revert harness detects per file at the moment it runs, and `anchor-check.js` re-confirms all twelve anchors still hit exactly once rather than assuming it.
  - **`login-busy-test.js` fails 1 and `subs-ui-test.js` throws, both PRE-EXISTING** — confirmed by stashing. `subs-test.js` (43), `subbox-test.js` (22), `subs-batch-test.js` (14), `subs-limit-test.js` (14), `email-log-test.js` (57), `google-auth-test.js` (57) and `posts-test.js` (42) all re-run clean, which is what holds the `doSubscribe` extraction down.
- **THE GOOGLE PATH HAS NO SUCH OPTION, and that is a named gap rather than an oversight.** A Google signup never sees the register tab — it lands on `/join`, which asks the invite code — so those accounts cannot subscribe at sign-up. Worth knowing that it is also the one path where an **active** row would be defensible, since Google asserts `email_verified`; that is a second decision and the owner's.
- **Not verified end to end on production, deliberately.** Submitting the form there would create a real account and send real mail to a made-up address, and a bounce is exactly the deliverability harm this feature exists to avoid. Live checks are read-only: `mailReady` on `/api/me`, and the box drawn, gated and unticked at 1200px and 390px.

#### A RATE LIMIT MUST COST NOBODY THEIR COPY (2026-09-25, found before it shipped a send)
**Resend refuses at 2 requests a second by default, and the first cut sent a batch of 20 back-to-back.** A 429 came back as a plain `false`, the address was already claimed in `post_sends`, and it was never retried — so on any real list most of a broadcast would have been recorded as tried and silently skipped, with no way to re-send. **Proved by reverting: the un-fixed version reports `0 sent, 0 left`** — the loop believing it finished while nobody got the post.
