  - **It is REBUILDABLE**, unlike `fundamentals_history`: every field derives from bars. Delete the table and re-run `build-tech-history.js`.
  - **The nightly top-up is self-pacing** (`noteTechMark`): write a mark when the newest one is seven days old. No weekday arithmetic, no holiday list, and it heals after a missed week — where "write it on Fridays" would silently skip whenever a Friday was a holiday. It rides the Refresh-all gate beside `fundamentals_history` and `noteAdvice`, and costs nothing: every technical it stores was already computed for that row. **It stores the ALL-TECHNICAL verdict, deliberately not `row.action`** — mixing the two would make the column mean one thing before today and another after it.
  - **Multi-row inserts, and the measurement that forced them.** `writeTechHistory` first sent one statement per row in batches of 500, the shape every other writer here uses. Against production that measured **~1,000 rows a minute — five hours for the table.** The cost is per STATEMENT, not per row: 200 rows in one `values (...),(...)` runs at **23,525 rows a minute, a 23x speedup**, and the same 333k rows in about thirteen minutes. Worth remembering before any other bulk write here.
  - **REBUILT ON THE DEEPENED ARCHIVE, 2026-09-28: 891,537 rows, 1,152 symbols, 2001-03-21 → 2026-09-28**, against 332,883 / 421 / 2004-01-14 before it. **571,519 rows written in 9.6 minutes — ~59,500 rows/min, against the 23,525/min this file records** — so the multi-row insert scales better than the first measurement suggested. 0 failures, 0 retries, no deadline fired.
    - **The usable floor is what actually moved. 733 symbols priceable in 2008 against 278**, rising to 1,152 in 2026. The 2.9M-bar deepening that morning is what bought it, and this is the surface it was bought for.
    - **The sub-cent floor landed in `techrow.js` FIRST** — see the bar-archive section. Verified afterwards on the rebuilt table rather than assumed: **all 112 of APLD's sub-cent-close marks in 2013-2015 read `Hold`, none carries a `vs200` or `m1`, and none reads `Buy`.** The first version of that check counted `vs200` across the whole window and proved nothing, because APLD oscillated around a penny and a mark at or above a cent may legitimately have one — **the test has to be the sub-cent marks alone.**
    - **THE RESUME CAN NEVER CONVERGE, and it is not a fault in the rebuild.** `have[sym] === n` is an exact COUNT test against the builder's own canonical calendar — the last trading day of each week — while `noteTechMark` adds nightly marks dated by the market day, which land on whatever weekday the Refresh all ran. Measured: MU holds Wednesday marks (09-02, 09-09, 09-16) beside the canonical Fridays. Both are legitimate readings and they coexist; the cost is that **749 of 1,152 symbols mismatch for ever and every full rebuild rewrites ~570k rows** (0.8 min on a no-op pass). Worth knowing before reading a resume line as damage.
  - *(superseded by the rebuild above)* **The table was COMPLETE as of 2026-09-20: 332,883 rows, 421 symbols, 2004-01-14 → 2026-09-18.** The final resumed pass wrote 104,960 rows in 278 minutes.
  - **A dropped socket does not throw for HOURS, and the retry only fires on a throw.** That same run lost **159 minutes — 2h39m of its 4h38m — to one chunk**: the write at 60,000 stalled at the 72-minute mark and the `terminated` error did not surface until 231 minutes. `writeTechHistory` awaits `db.batch` with no deadline, so between the socket dying and libSQL noticing there is nothing to catch and nothing printed. From the outside it is indistinguishable from a hang: **the process stays alive, CPU sits near zero, stdout says nothing** — and that is exactly what it looks like when it is working normally too, because the job is network-bound. **So do not judge this build by CPU or by silence; judge it by the row count.** I called a healthy run dead on those signals and was wrong.
    - **Fixed the same day: `withDeadline(label, ms, run)` in db.js, and every `writeTechHistory` batch now runs under one.** It races the request against a clock, so silence becomes an ordinary throw — which `noteTechMark`'s caller already catches and logs, the rule that a history write never fails a refresh. `DB_BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (60s) is the default, chosen to suit a REQUEST path; the two real callers each say why they differ: **`noteTechMark` passes 30s** (optional work in the tail, and a missed mark self-heals because the writer is self-pacing) and **the offline builder passes 15 minutes**, because a *healthy* batch there takes 3-6 minutes against an archive this size. That still turns 159 minutes of silence into one retry.
      - **The request is NOT cancelled** — libSQL offers no handle for that — so this is only safe because every caller is an idempotent upsert. A caller that is not must not use it. The abandoned request settles minutes later and `withDeadline` attaches its own `catch`, or that late rejection arrives unhandled and takes the process down long after the code that started it gave up.
      - **`timer.unref()` was in the first cut and is a trap: never add it back.** An unref'd timer does not hold the event loop open, so in a CLI script — the builder, the one place this most has to work — a hung request leaves nothing else pending and **Node exits 0 mid-write instead of throwing**, turning the hang into a silent success. Caught by the test, which is itself a bare script; an assertion names the cause.
      - Verified: 13 checks, and the fixture is the point — **every hang is a promise that never settles**, not a rejection, because that is what actually happened. A stubbed throw would have proved nothing.
  - **`Buy with Risk` never appears** — `etfRules` has no path to it. The trend-only backtest has five usable tiers, not six.
  - **What the archive actually supports**: marks span 2004 → today, but 2004-2007 carry ONE symbol (the 5,000-bar API ceiling puts most deep symbols at 2006-11, plus 252 sessions of run-up). **The usable floor is 2008 with 278 symbols**, rising to 421 today — which does cover the financial crisis, the one stretch where a trend rule should prove itself.
  - Verified: the extraction (10 checks, identical to the last commit's function), the store round trip (18 checks — the round trip, replace-not-duplicate, windowing, purge, blanks staying null, and that **every rule set re-derives from a stored row**), the nightly mark through the REAL refresh path (11 checks — a Refresh all writes, a second the same day does not, a week later does, a plain Refresh never does, and the stored verdict re-derives), and the query plans against 344,000 rows (every read SEEKS; a one-year window is 22,360 rows in 60ms).
  - **Two fixture traps, both caught by an assertion passing on an empty set.** The refresh test stubbed the provider to refuse everything, so the refresh produced no rows and "every mark re-derives" passed over zero marks; it needs a price stub serving the fixture's own bars, **including the benchmark** — SPY is fetched on every refresh and is deliberately never archived, so returning an error for it failed the whole round. And the store test hand-wrote `action: 'Buy'` beside technicals that genuinely read Strong Buy; the fixture now derives the verdict the way the builder does.
- **Phase 2 — the sweep and the page, done.** `GET /api/trend-backtest` and **`/trend-backtest`** (admin, a row in the console's Research section beside the advice one).
  - **A FIXED forward horizon** (1M/3M/6M/1Y as 1/3/6/12 MONTHLY marks), never "carry to today" — that would give a 2008 window eighteen years and a 2026 one a fortnight, and averaging those compares nothing. *It was 4/13/26/52 weekly marks until 2026-09-20; see the read cost below for why whole months, and note the page had always said "held three months" while the code meant 91 days.*
  - **The benchmark is the equal-weight universe over the same window**, so the question is whether the rules SELECTED. Excess is basket − market, per window.
  - **A window with no picks is CASH, not a missing observation** — it returns 0 and its excess is minus the market. Dropping those would delete exactly the 2008-shaped windows a trend rule exists for, and would flatter every remaining one. **Thin windows (under 3 picks) are flagged, never filtered**: a filter there is a thumb on the scale.
  - **The two honesty numbers are computed and printed, not left to the reader.** The **effective sample** — monthly starts at a 3-month horizon overlap ~3:1, so ~220 windows is ~74 independent readings — is a CARD, not a footnote. And the **pool per window**, since it grows from 89 to 129 (and will grow further) across the span, so an early window is a narrower claim.
  - **`Buy with Risk` is shown struck through and disabled**: `etfRules` has no path to it, so the trend backtest has five usable tiers. Hiding it would read as an oversight.
  - **THE FIRST FULL-UNIVERSE READING (2026-09-20, the complete 332,883-row table — this is the number the module was built to produce).** 3M horizon, Strong Buy + Buy, Balanced, from 2008: **222 windows spanning 2008-01-02 → 2026-06-03, on a pool growing 268 → 417**, and **74 independent readings** after the 3x overlap discount.

| | median excess | hit rate | avg picks |
|---|---|---|---|
| all years (222 windows) | **−0.32%** | **44.6%** | 108 of 336 |
| pre-2020 (144) | −0.27% | 47.2% | 106 |
| post-2020 (78) | −0.89% | 39.7% | 112 |

    Mean excess −1.14%, p10/p90 −4.4/+2.7, worst −36.8%, best +6.7%.

##### RE-MEASURED ON THE REBUILT TABLE (2026-09-28) — 2.7x the rows, and it got WORSE
**891,537 rows across 1,152 symbols, 733 of them priceable in 2008 against 278.** Same question, same settings: 3M horizon, Strong Buy + Buy, Balanced, from 2008.

| | median excess | hit rate | avg picks |
|---|---|---|---|
| all years (222 windows) | **−0.51%** | **35.6%** | 288 |
| pre-2020 (144) | −0.38% | 36.1% | 279 |
| post-2020 (78) | −0.92% | 34.6% | 304 |

Mean −2.17%, p10/p90 −5.5/+1.6, worst −85.8%, best +6.2%. **Against the 421-symbol reading of −0.32% and 44.6%, the hit rate fell by nine points in both eras.** That is the direction the universe section predicts and the reassuring one: *if a result improves after the universe shrinks, suspect the universe* — here the pool grew and got deeper history, and the verdicts looked worse. The standing conclusion is unchanged and now rests on far more data: **the model orders downside and does not pick winners.** The "barely a selection" caveat also stands — 288 picks is still about a third of the pool.
 **The verdicts do not select: the basket loses to its own universe by a small margin, in both eras, and beats it less than half the time.** That is the research log's standing conclusion — the model orders downside and does not pick winners — now measured on twenty years rather than inferred from two months, and it agrees with the 18-year `action-backtest.js` re-measurement taken the same day on 1,588,936 stock-days.
    - **The likeliest reason is that this is barely a selection at all**: Strong Buy + Buy qualifies **108 of 336 stocks**, about a third of the universe, so the basket is close to being the benchmark with a third of the names dropped. A test with more discrimination (a top-N cut inside the tier, or Strong Buy alone) is the obvious next question and has not been run.
    - **The distribution is narrow and left-skewed** — p10 −4.4 against p90 +2.7, worst −36.8 against best +6.7. The big negative tail is the 2009 whipsaw the partial reading already showed, and it is what a trend rule does at a violent bottom, not a defect.
  - *(superseded by the reading above)* **First real reading (partial table, 89→129 symbols, 3M horizon, Strong Buy + Buy)**: median excess **−0.65%**, hit rate 42%, and the crisis behaves exactly as a trend rule should — picks fall 22 → 2 through the 2008 fall while beating equal weight by 3–15 points, then **1 pick through the March 2009 snap-back** for −28% and −40% excess. That whipsaw is also what the −132% worst window at 1Y is, and it is not a bug. Across all windows the rules slightly underperform, at every horizon, which is the research log's standing verdict now measurable from a page.
  - Verified: 31 checks on the sweep (basket, benchmark, excess, horizon and the overlap discount all against hand-computed values; a symbol with no end price excluded from BOTH legs; cash windows; theme scoping; the rule set re-evaluated from the stored inputs) and 31 on the page (both charts drawn and actually distributions, the table agreeing row-for-row with the API, sorting, the URL round trip, and **the honesty prose asserted as text** — a page that reports a median over overlapping windows without saying how few are independent is the exact failure this module exists to avoid).
  - **`#cards > .card`, not `#cards .card`** — the double-bezel puts the class on the shell AND the core, so the descendant selector counts every card twice. The `/quality` trap, met again in a test rather than in the page.
  - **The sweep read the WHOLE table, and that was three minutes (2026-09-20).** Measured against production: **181.8 seconds cold**, 0.4s warm, for a sweep whose arithmetic is **154ms** — so essentially all of it was moving 232,000 rows out of Turso, on a table still growing toward 333,000, against a documented response wall of about three minutes. The page was days from simply failing, and nothing on it would have said why. Three narrowings, in the order they mattered:
    - **The DATES.** The sweep starts on month-firsts, and with WHOLE-MONTH horizons it ends on one too — so one cached read of **273 marks out of 1,185** serves all four horizons. In weekly marks the end dates were arbitrary weeks, which meant reading the other three weeks of every month for the sake of them. This is the reason the horizon is months now; the statistics are if anything better, since "started in March 2012 and held three months" is what the page always claimed.
    - **The COLUMNS.** Balanced reads the stored verdict and the close and nothing else, so it asks for **four of fourteen**; a non-default rule set re-runs the engine and gets its own cached copy with the inputs. **The trap that buys is handing the slim row to a rule set that evaluates** — every input would be undefined, "No trend data" would fire on every row, and every window would quietly go to cash, which looks like a result. There is a test that runs a non-Balanced sweep with the slim copy warm in the cache and asserts it still finds picks.
  - **MEASURE ON AN IDLE DATABASE, or you will design around the wrong number.** Every figure in the bullet above was first taken while the `tech_history` bulk build was writing to the same database, and contention inflated them by 3-70x. Re-measured idle, at the table's full 332,883 rows:

| read | contended | idle |
|---|---|---|
| the whole table, 14 columns (the old path) | 181.8s *(at 232k rows)* | **126.2s / 106.7MB — and `terminated` on another run** |
| month-first marks, 4 columns (Balanced) | 64.6s | **5.7-7.7s** |
| month-first marks, 14 columns (other rule sets) | 166.8s | **23-25s** |
| `select distinct d` for the mark calendar | 429.9s | **~250ms** |

    **The old path is MARGINAL rather than merely slow, and that is the real finding.** Two idle runs minutes apart: one carried all 332,883 rows in 126.2s, the next answered `terminated`. 106.7MB is past the 83MB at which this file's own wall table records a failure, so the page worked or failed by luck on every cold instance — the hardest kind of fault to diagnose, because reproducing it is a coin toss. The narrowing takes the Balanced path to **5.7-7.7s and 13.4MB**, roughly **17-22x**, and puts it nowhere near the wall. **A third change was built on the bad number and then reverted the same day**: a `tech_marks` table holding nothing but the ~1,200 mark dates, justified by that 429.9s. Idle, the query it replaced is ~250ms against the table's ~100ms — 150ms inside a six-second operation, which does not buy a second copy of derivable state plus a write to keep in step. Production still holds the now-unused table; it is harmless and empty of consequence. The lesson is the measurement discipline, not the table.
  - **`readTechMarks` (a whole range, every column) is kept for offline work and nothing on a request path may call it.** It is the shape that cost the 181.8 seconds.
- *(superseded)* **Phase 2 — the sweep and the page: not built yet.** Planned: every month-start across the archive with a FIXED forward horizon (1M/3M/6M/12M) rather than "carry to today", measured benchmark-relative against the universe's own equal-weight return, reporting the distribution — median excess, hit rate, p10, worst window, and the pre/post-2020 split. Two numbers it must print or it misleads: the **effective sample** (monthly starts at a 3-month horizon overlap ~3:1, so ~230 windows is ~75 independent observations — the research log's own discount rule) and the **symbol count per window**, since the pool shrinks going back.

### A card can be pointed at a SCREEN (2026-09-24, owner's request)
**"How do I put a popular screen from the screener on the promo, but as a visual?"** Every scoped template gained a `Screen` picker offering the 22 starter screens, and pointing one at **Bouncing off the lows** is the card the request was really about.

- **ONE CHANGE, every scoped template.** `Cards.scopeOf()` is where every card answers "which stocks?", so the screen reads off the same prefix as the other three cuts (`movSector` → `movScreen`) and all eight templates gained it at once — exactly what the size band cost. The definition is evaluated by **`Filters.screenRows`**, the module the server `require`s and the screener loads, so a card and the Screens menu cannot disagree about who is in a screen. It applies the screen's sector / industry / advice / move as well as its filters, so a card gets the whole question rather than its numeric half.
- **ANDed, not substituted** — a screen is orthogonal to a sector the way a size band is, and the kicker names both.
- **`ctx.screens` is how the module gets them**; it reads no DOM and issues no requests. The studio hands over `/api/screens`, the phone's post endpoint hands over `store.readScreens()`. A host that passes neither offers no screen cut and is unchanged — the rule `/cards` followed for the industry control it did not have.
- **The picker is filled from what the endpoint returned**, grouped as the Screens menu groups them, so a screen the owner adds, renames or deletes appears with no edit here.

**The Range card's track now shows the TURN as well as the depth.** A position alone says how far a stock fell; it cannot say whether it is still falling, and "bouncing off the lows" is a claim about both. A lighter leg behind each marker is the past month — green where it rose, red where it fell — with a tick where it started.

- **ANCHORED TO THE DRAWN MARKER, not computed from the band independently.** The dot sits at the stored `range52Pos`; deriving the month-ago position from `price`/`pctFromLow`/`pctFromHigh` on its own puts the two marks on different footings the moment those three do not perfectly reconcile, and the leg between them then measures nothing. Taking the **travel** and subtracting it from the dot keeps them on one ruler whatever the row says. Found by a fixture whose three range fields disagreed — which is also how a real row could disagree.
- **Measured on TODAY'S range, and the caption says so.** A month ago the 52-week window was a different window with a different low and high; placing the old price on the ruler in front of you is the only way the two marks are comparable at all.
- **A chosen screen TITLES the card**, split over two lines at the word boundary nearest the middle. "Down at their lows" over the bouncing screen is true and discards the half that matters, and the screen's own name is what the reader knows the question by. The kicker then drops the screen — printing the same words one line above the headline reads as a mistake.
- **The footnote runs the full width** (owner, from a screenshot). `.s-sub` is capped at **40ch**, which is right for the templates that set a sentence BESIDE a chart and wrong for one that runs UNDER full-width content: measured, the track note was at **50.1% of the body**, stranded in a column with empty space to its right. The cap is lifted per card by `.s-sub.wide` — compounded with `.s-sub` on purpose, because a bare `.wide` in a stylesheet injected into whatever page hosts a card would be the seventh unscoped class here to capture later markup. That class was `.zsub`, named off the Size card’s own prefix; it is shared by two cards now, so it is named for what it does. All three Range modes take it. Proved by reverting: the note drops back to 50% and three checks fail.
- **The 40ch cap was stranding FOUR MORE notes, not one** (owner, reporting the Bubble card after the Range one). Rather than fix the reported card and wait for a third, every template was measured: note width against the widest content above it, on the 4:5. **Bubble 47%, Fund 50%, Advice board 53%** against full-width plots and boards — Range and Size were already `wide`. Fifteen notes across seven templates take `.s-sub.wide` now: Movers, Chart, Sparks, Advice board, Fund, Bubble and Stock, all of which put a note under FULL-WIDTH VISUAL content. **Intro, Announcement and Avatar keep the 40ch measure** — those are prose slides, where a reading measure is the feature rather than the bug. **One exception since 2026-09-26: the Intro CLOSE slide takes `wide`**, because it is the one Intro slide that puts its note under a full-width block (the "Try it free" card) — the criterion, applied per slide rather than per template.
  - **The survey metric over-reports and the intro line is the proof**: a block-level `<h2>` is 100% wide on every card, so "content=100%" alone never meant a chart. The decision is whether the card draws a full-width VISUAL, which is a judgement the measurement informs rather than makes.
  - Widening can only ever make a note SHORTER (fewer lines), so it cannot overflow a fixed artboard — but the 33-combination sweep was re-run anyway, along with the Size card’s own 135.
- **A STORY NOTE HAD BEEN PRINTING AT POST SIZE ON EVERY CARD** (owner, from a screenshot of the 9:16). `.sz-story .s-sub { font-size: 25px }` existed and was DEAD: **20 of the 23 notes set `style="font-size:18px"` inline**, and an inline declaration beats a class rule, so the story override never applied to any of them. The size is `--fs` now and the rule is `calc(var(--fs, 20px) * 1.25)` — each card keeps its own relative choice (17 / 18 / 19 / 26) and the artboard scales the lot, at the same 1.25 the 20px-to-25px rule had already chosen. One CSS line plus a mechanical substitution; no per-card judgement, no new class names.
  - **Bigger type on a fixed artboard is exactly what overflows**, and a card cannot scroll, so `note-fit-test.js` sweeps **every template on every artboard** — 33 combinations, measuring the body’s own overflow and the kicker-to-tagline gap the way `size-fit-test.js` does. Zero overflowing, tightest gap 11px. **Proved by reverting**: every one of the six cards with a note goes back to x1.00.
  - **Two measurement traps in the sweep itself.** `getComputedStyle().fontSize` reports AUTHORED px — a transform does not touch it — so dividing by the artboard scale reported 45px for an 18px note and a ratio of 2.22, which is the ratio of the two artboards’ scale factors and nothing the card did. And the fallback branch of `var(--fs, 20px)` is used by only 3 notes, none on a template the sweep happened to render, so it is probed directly rather than asserted over nothing.
- **An empty screen is a different sentence from missing data.** "Nothing passed Overextended today" is a fact about today and is postable; "nothing has a 52-week range stored yet" blames the data and would be wrong. `scopeOf` returns `screen` so a card can tell them apart.

**First real reading (2026-09-24, 940 stocks):** the screen catches **20** — AppLovin, AeroVironment, Symbotic, Ubiquiti, Roblox, Virgin Galactic, Quantum Computing, Watsco, Cerebras, Arqit — each 4-22% into its own 52-week range and up 4-45% of that band over the month. Ten tracks, ten legs, zero overflow on the 4:5 artboard.

- Verified: **26 checks** driving the real studio. The fixture is four stocks that separate every clause of the screen from every other — near the low but still falling, turning but nowhere near its low, and one that fails the two-week clause alone — so a filter that dropped any single clause still fails. **Every assertion that matters changes the control and diffs the card**, because the eight hardcoded listener lists in promo.html are a second copy of `CONTROL_IDS` and a control missing from one exists, saves, is read by the builder, and does nothing. Control ids **81 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 100**, counted rather than assumed.
- **Three fixture traps, all this project's own, all met again**: `#stage` IS the artboard (`#stage .s-art` matched nothing, the `#tplSelect` lesson); a `<br>` contributes no whitespace to `textContent`, so a two-line headline reads as one word; and the first cut wired the new ids into the list that fills the **Cap** pickers, which would have offered market-cap bands as screens — caught by asserting the Size picker still offers sizes.

### The S&P 500 cut — eight promo templates and the pivot (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**"Can you add s&p filter to all promo and pivot."** A `S&P 500` picker on every scoped studio template — All stocks / In the index / Not in the index — and an `S&P 500` dimension on `/pivot`, which gives that page a row axis, a column axis and a page filter at once. *(The pivot half was replaced on 2026-10-04 by a filter of its own — see the entry under **The pivot view**. Everything below about the studio still holds.)*

**It cost one change on each side, and that is the point of both mechanisms.** `Cards.scopeOf()` is the one place every scoped card answers "which stocks?", reading `xxSector` / `xxIndustry` / `xxCap` / `xxScreen` off a per-template prefix — so `xxSp500` reached all eight templates at once, exactly as the size band and the screen cut each did. On the pivot the Filter picker is built from `DIMS` rather than from a list of its own, so one entry there became three controls.

- **NO SERVER CHANGE AT ALL.** `spMember` is one of the read-path stamps and **both** hosts already apply it — `/api/stocks` through `serveStamps`, and `/api/m/post` through its own line — so a saved post carrying the cut draws correctly on the phone without anything being wired. That was checked rather than assumed; the stamps are a set, and the set has been incomplete twice.
- **The cut is ORTHOGONAL, not narrower**: ANDed with the sector, the industry, the band and the screen, and named in the kicker *alongside* them (`Technology · S&P 500 · past week`) rather than replacing any of them. A posted card has no picker beside it, so the kicker is the only thing that can say which cut emptied it.

#### `=== true` AND `=== false`, NEVER TRUTHY — the whole guard in one line
`spMember` is **three-state**: null until a holdings file has been imported, and **null is not No**. A truthy/falsy test puts every unchecked stock in the "Not in the index" cut — which on an instance that has never run the import is the card stating that **all 1,278 of these are outside the S&P 500**, with confidence, in a picture somebody posts. The screener's own column refuses to give that answer and so does this.

- So on a no-file instance **both** cuts are empty rather than one of them being everything, and that reads correctly because the kicker names the cut.
- **An ABSENT field behaves like a null one**, which is not the same case: `serveStamps` catches per stamp, so a stamp that threw leaves the key off every row rather than setting it null. Both are checked.
- **Proved by reverting**: the truthy version fails exactly the two checks that matter, naming all ten fixture stocks in a cut that must hold none of them.
- The pivot takes the same guard from the other end: its getter is **`Filters.filterValue(s, 'spMember')`**, the one function that already knows the field is three-state and returns `''` for unknown — which `valuesOf` then buckets as the blank the page already draws and counts in its note. **Proved by reverting**: a `s.spMember ? 'Yes' : 'No'` ternary there labels a whole unchecked universe `No`.

#### Membership only — the weight never leaves `/holdings`
That page is `requireAdmin` because a reconstructed constituent list *with its weights* is the issuer's dataset, where a Yes/No for the stocks we happen to track is derivable from any financial website. The same line holds here: there is no weight on a card, no weight measure on the pivot, and a check that no card prints one.

#### The catalogue is the module's, so a host cannot offer a word the card ignores
`Cards.spCuts()` returns the three `[value, label]` pairs and the studio builds all eight pickers from it. A copy in the markup sending `yes` where `scopeOf` means `in` would filter **nothing and say nothing** — the silent-fallback class this module exists to keep out, and the reason `basketDays`, `evolutionNeed` and `themeClass` are exported too. **Proved by reverting**: hardcoding the options with `yes`/`no` fails 21 checks.

- Three values and no fourth. **"Unknown" is deliberately not offered as a cut**: it is a gap in our own data rather than a fact about a company, and a card captioned "stocks we have not checked" is not a card.
- A post saved before this existed carries no key, which filters nothing — checked, because that is every existing post.
- **No fourteenth listener list was needed and eight existing ones were.** A control in the markup and in `CONTROL_IDS` but not in its template's list saves with a post, is read by the builder, and **does nothing when you touch it**. Reverting the eight list entries fails 10 checks and reverting the eight `CONTROL_IDS` entries fails 13. The warning comment above them said "THESE EIGHT LISTS" while there were thirteen; it says "THESE LISTS" now, since a count in a warning is the thing that rots.
- Control ids **100 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**, counted rather than assumed.

#### On the pivot: a dimension on an axis is not offered as a filter
That is existing behaviour and worth knowing before reading it as a fault — filtering rows by the thing the rows ARE leaves one row. **Yes sorts before No**, which the alphabet and a count-ordered list both get backwards; reverting the order puts No first, because there are more of them. **No tint**: membership is not a severity ladder and has no good end.

> **SUPERSEDED ON THE PIVOT, 2026-10-04 — it is no longer a dimension there at all.** The two paragraphs above describe the DIMS entry, which is gone; the ordering and the no-tint reasoning went with it. The studio half is unchanged. See **Include S&P — a filter of its own, not a dimension** under **The pivot view**.

#### The first live reading, and it is the argument for the feature
**1,278 stocks: 498 in the index, 780 out, 0 unknown, as of 2026-10-01.** The index is **$70.0T of market value against $23.4T** outside it — 75% of the screen's weight on 39% of its names. Members by sector: Technology 84, Industrials 76, Financial Services 68, Healthcare 60, Consumer Cyclical 54, Utilities 31, Consumer Defensive 31, Real Estate 30, Communication Services 22, Energy 21, Basic Materials 20.

**The top five movers of the whole screen that week were ALL outside the index** (PACB +56.8%, ACLS, SYNA, MTRN, VIAV) against CCL / LITE / SNPS / RCL / COHR inside it — so "top gainers" unfiltered is a small-cap list, and the cut is what makes it a list of companies a reader recognises. That is also why the test fixture puts the best mover, the biggest company and the widest margin all OUTSIDE the index: a card that ignored the cut leads with a stock the `in` cut must not contain, rather than passing by coincidence.

- Verified: **68 checks** over four parts — the module with no server and no browser (all eight templates, the three states, the kicker, the AND with a sector), the real studio (each picker present, filled from the catalogue and redrawing its own card, and a saved post round-tripped with every control moved away first), the phone building that post from the same module, and the pivot (both axes, reconciliation, the filter's counts, and the no-file state reached by **rewriting the response**, since a database with a holdings file in it cannot produce a null row). **Proved by reverting ten times, every one load-bearing**: the cut unapplied 19, the pickers unfilled 21, a hardcoded catalogue 21, `CONTROL_IDS` 13, the listener lists 10, the pivot dimension 6, the kicker 5, truthy/falsy 2, the pivot's ternary 2, the Yes-first order 1.
  - **THE FIXTURE ARCHIVE HAS TO REACH TODAY.** `/api/basket` derives `since` from the clock and the chart card's default window is six months, so a fixture dated to a fixed year in the past comes back empty, the chart and sparks cards fall through to their *Reading the archive* placeholder, and "changing the control redraws the card" then compares **one placeholder with another** and passes whatever the listener does. Both read as failures until the bars were re-dated — which is the honest direction for that mistake to point.
  - **Two scratchpad suites hardcoded `POST_OPT_MAX` as 100 and were CORRECTED, not worked around.** The cap became 200 on 2026-09-30, so both were failing against a ceiling that is not the ceiling. They read it out of server.js now, which is strictly stronger and cannot date. `promo-ind-test.js` dies with `window is not defined` at HEAD too, and `pivot-test.js` fails 1 at HEAD — it asserts the drill carries FOURTEEN fields and YTD made it fifteen. Both confirmed by stashing.
  - **`page.selectOption` on a value a revert can remove waits 30s and THROWS**, so the suite stops short and reports fewer failures than there are — indistinguishable from a guard that never mattered. The pivot half sets `.value` and dispatches the page's own `change` event instead. The documented trap, and it cost one run here before the harness's own `?? only N of 68 ran` line caught it.

### The day card — the whole session on one artboard (2026-09-29, owner's request)
**"One card that summarizes the day: how the indexes performed, top 10, bottom 10, how each sector performed, all in one card."** A twelfth template, `day`, first in the studio's picker because it is the one that needs no setting up to be worth posting.

**THE DENSITY IS THE DESIGN PROBLEM AND THE LAYOUT SOLVES IT, NOT THE FONT SIZE.** Four indexes, eleven sectors and two lists of ten is 35 data rows, and a 1080px card renders about 400px wide in a feed — so 19px on the artboard is ~7px to the reader and "font can be smaller" has a floor set by where the card is read. The indexes are a strip of four chips rather than four rows, the sectors a two-column bar chart rather than eleven rows, the movers two columns rather than twenty. 35 rows becomes ~17 lines.

- **SECTORS ARE ALWAYS CAP-WEIGHTED** (the owner's instruction, given before the code existed), so there is no weighting control — the toggle `/consolidated` carries would make the same card mean two things. Two exclusions, and they are different rules: a **missing move is ABSENT, never a zero** (`Number(null)` is 0 and finite, and a fabricated flat stock drags a mean), and a stock with **no market cap carries no weight at all**, since a fund reports AUM rather than capitalisation — `w > 0` rejects null and zero in one test.
- **THE INDEXES ARE THE HEADLINE, SO THEY ARE NOT THE MARKET.** SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA are ordinary rows in the universe and are classified into Technology; left in the pool the S&P's own ETF inflates that sector and takes a mover slot — the trap `/consolidated` already records. Removed once, from both the sector aggregate and the movers.
  - **`cards.js` restates the list and exports it** (`Cards.benchmarks()`). It cannot read server.js's `BENCHMARKS`: the module has no requires and no DOM, which is what lets a card render identically in Node and the browser. The export exists so the suite asserts the two are the same set rather than hoping — the treatment `BRAND_IG` already gets.
- **THE CAP FLOOR'S OWN ARGUMENT DID NOT SURVIVE BEING MEASURED.** I wrote "without one the leaders are ten names nobody has heard of"; measured against the live snapshot (1,177 stocks, an ordinary session) the unfiltered top ten is **nine recognisable companies and one $0.2B name**. So the floor is not rescuing the list — it keeps the ten comparable in scale and guards against a junk bar, the class that once printed **+56,000,000%** on the screener itself. The default is **$1B, which keeps 97.5% of the pool** (1,147 of 1,177) and drops exactly that one name; $10B keeps 67.2%, $50B 24.6%. It narrows the **movers only**, and the kicker says so.
- **The metric picker ranks the movers by percent or by value added, and the title's second line names which** — not the card, because the sectors stay cap-weighted percentages either way, so "by value added" over the whole card would describe two of its three blocks wrongly. `fmtMoney` carries neither a sign nor a `$`, so the card adds both: a CHANGE takes a sign whichever unit it is in, the Value added column's rule.

#### A step-down that could never fire, and a nowrap that fixed nothing
**Both were written, both were proved worthless by reverting them, and both were deleted rather than kept unproven.** This is the half worth remembering.

- The card shipped with **tplMovers' ROOM/RHYTHM machinery** — default, then tight, then tighter, then trimming the lists. Measured on the real artboards the body has **958px on the 4:5, 688 on the square and ~1460 on the story**, and the tallest card the controls can reach — a story at fifteen a side — draws **993px**. It was selecting `tight` on the square alone, and only because the estimate I had written put that artboard's room **108px too low**. **Proved by reverting: forcing the default rhythm on all 54 swept combinations overflows nothing.**
- `white-space: nowrap` on the block heads, which I had commented as load-bearing, **wrapped nothing when reverted**: every head this card writes is short by construction ("Sectors · cap-weighted", "Top 10"). The sweep asserts no head wraps, which is the guard that can actually fail.
- **What IS load-bearing is the per-artboard CAP** — ten a side on the 4:5, five on the square, fifteen on the story. Reverting it fails 8 checks and reproduces the symptom exactly: **16 of 54 combinations overflow, worst 144px, and the kicker prints 140px past the tagline**, i.e. over the masthead.
- **A guideline this leaves: a step-down copied from the card that needs one is not free.** It reads as care and it hid a wrong constant.

#### Three faults found by SCREENSHOT with every assertion passing
- **The story used half its frame** — 993px of content in 1920 — which is the fault tplMovers already records for its own story layout ("five rows spread through a story read as lines floating in a frame"). Fixed its way: taller rows AND the three blocks spread with `space-evenly`. **That fix was scoped to the story and should not have been** — see the entry below, which the owner reported the same day on the 4:5.
- **Two of eleven sector names truncated** ("Communication ...", "Consumer Defen..."). There are exactly eleven and the set is fixed, so an ellipsis there is a width bug rather than the unavoidable thing it is on a company name — the width is scoped to `.dy-grid .dy-lab`. **An off-page probe said the longest needed 156px and was wrong: copying a computed `cssText` onto a bare span does not carry the font.** The honest measure is the element's own `scrollWidth`, which says **197px on a post and 243 on a story**; the story labels therefore stay a size behind the movers' rather than eat a 459px column's bar down to 91px.
- **A BACKTICK IN A CSS COMMENT TOOK THE WHOLE MODULE DOWN AGAIN.** `Cards.STYLE` is itself a template literal, so one inside it ends the string: `ReferenceError: story is not defined`, nowhere near the cause, and **`node --check` passes** — it is valid syntax, just an interpolation. The Size card records this and it cost a round of debugging here anyway.

#### Two empty bands, and they were ONE piece of slack (2026-09-29, owner, from a screenshot with both marked in red)
**The 4:5 left 164px unused — 82px above the kicker and 81 under the last mover row — and the square 74px.** The two are not separate faults: `.s-body` is a flex column with `justify-content: center`, so a block whose height is its content gets the leftover room split evenly at its ends. **Neither band can be fixed on its own**, and trimming a margin would only move the slack to the other end.

- **THE FIX IS THE ONE THE STORY ALREADY HAD, applied to all three shapes.** The wrapper fills what the body leaves (`.dy-in` is a full-height flex column, `.dy-wrap` takes `flex: 1`) and the three blocks spread through it with `space-evenly`. The story's copy of those two rules is deleted — it is the general behaviour now rather than a special case, which is what it should have been when it was written an hour earlier.
- **The `gap` is a FLOOR, not the spacing.** Free space is distributed *after* gaps are allocated, so a full card keeps 22px between blocks and a sparse one opens up, instead of a sparse card stranding the room at its ends again. **A card sitting ON the floor has nothing left and the next row overflows**, which makes the gap the honest capacity reading now that "slack" is zero by construction.
- **Part of the room goes into the ROWS rather than all of it into the gaps**, on the 4:5 only: a 1080px card renders about 400px wide in a feed, so a 36px row is ~13px to the reader. **40px, not the 42 that also fit** — measured, the worst reachable card (the 4:5 at ten a side, sixteen rows) leaves a 29px gap at 42 against the 22 floor, and 37px at 40. Seven pixels is not headroom. **The square keeps 36**: it had 74px of slack against the post's 164, and its eleven rows would have eaten 66 of it.
- **The taller row came with a bigger label and broke something the suite caught**: "Communication Services" stopped fitting the 202px sector column at 18px. That is the no-truncation check earning its place — the same fault was found by eye the first time.
- **`getClientRects`-style measures were useless here and the test had to change with the fix.** With the wrapper filling, "slack at the ends" is zero on every shape whatever the card does, so the old margin assertion would have passed for ever. It is two checks now: **the band under the movers is ≤2px on every artboard** (the owner's report, as an assertion) and **the tightest inter-block gap stays ≥30px** (the capacity reading). **Proved by reverting**: putting the centred block back gives a **618px band on the story** and fails both.

#### THE SECTORS ARE THE FUNDS' OWN RETURNS NOW (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**The block used to aggregate our own stocks cap-weighted; it reads the eleven Select Sector SPDRs instead, and the head says `Sectors · sector funds`.** The fund is the better source and it is not close: **it needs no weighting choice**, it is the published tradeable number, and it sidesteps the two things that made the computed version disagree with it — measured the same day, our Technology ran **44.9 points above XLK over a year**, because this pool is 214 names against the fund's ~70 and because our cap weighting is uncapped where a RIC-diversified fund holds nothing near the **52.2% Alphabet reached in Communication Services** here.

- **THE FUNDS LEFT THE MOVERS POOL IN THE SAME CHANGE, and that is not tidying.** They carry a real market cap (a fund reports AUM) and clear the $1B floor, so nothing else excluded them — a fund listed among the day's movers directly beneath a block that already reports it as its sector is the index-in-its-own-market error twice over. This is also the day-card half of the exposure recorded under the Sector Benchmark theme; the size bands are still open.
- **THE COMPUTED AGGREGATE STAYS AS THE FALLBACK** for an instance that does not hold the funds, and **the head names which basis is on screen** — two different numbers looking like one thing is the thing worth preventing. All of the cap-weighting rules (a missing return absent rather than zero, `w > 0` rejecting a null cap, the index funds out) still live there and are still asserted, in the fallback section of the suite rather than deleted.
- **`SECTOR_ETF` is restated in `cards.js` and exported** as `Cards.sectorEtfs()`, the `benchmarks()` bargain: the module has no requires and no DOM, which is what lets a card render identically in Node and the browser, so a test asserts the two lists agree rather than hoping.
- **Eleven is the whole set**; fewer means a fund is not held and the head says `(9 of 11)` rather than quietly showing nine sectors as though that were all of them.

#### The three grounds, and why the theme key became per-template
**`dayTheme` — Dark / Light / Navy, the spotlight's own themes on this card.** The generalisation that section predicted (*"when this generalises it becomes one `cardTheme`"*) went a different way and the reason is worth keeping: **each themed template keeps its ground under its OWN control id**, because one shared key means setting the spotlight to navy silently changes the day card too. `THEME_KEY = { spotlight: 'spotTheme', day: 'dayTheme' }`, asked of the module — the `basketDays` shape.

- **`Cards.themeClass` takes the TEMPLATE now** (`themeClass(tpl, opts)`), since which control holds the ground depends on which card is drawn. Three call sites, all updated: the studio's stage, and `/api/m/post`, which is what carries the ground to the phone.
- **The day card's own white-alpha furniture needed overriding** — `.dy-head`'s rule, `.dy-chip`, `.dy-rail`, and both `.dy-bar` gradients, whose soft end had to become the LIGHT green and red or the bar fades into the page instead of into its own colour. On a light ground an un-overridden surface is **invisible rather than wrong**, which is the failure that reads as an empty card. Navy needed nothing: the dark palette clears 4.5:1 on `#0d1a2d`, which is what made that theme an hour's work against the light theme's day.
- Control ids **89 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**.
- Verified: the day suite is **81 checks**, and the fixture is the test — **every fund's value is far from what this pool computes for that sector** (XLK +9.1% against a cap-weighted +1.3%), so a card still aggregating its members fails rather than coincides, and XLK would sit THIRD in the top ten if the funds were not excluded from the movers. Plus the head's wording, all eleven matched to their own fund, both grounds measured as DRAWN with every text role over 4.5:1, the two surfaces proved to be dark-on-light rather than white-on-white, and **the two cards proved independent in both directions**. **Proved by reverting five times**: the previous always-aggregate behaviour fails 4 and prints +1.3% where the fund says +9.1%; the funds back in the pool fails 1 with `SPDR Technology` in the top ten; one shared theme key fails 2; dropping the light overrides fails 1; and `dayTheme` missing from the day's listener list fails 6 — the control saves, is read by the builder, and does nothing.
  - **A REVERT HAS TO SIMULATE THE PREVIOUS BEHAVIOUR, not an impossible state.** Forcing `byEtf = false` alone left the aggregate uncomputed behind its own guard, so the block vanished, the suite threw, and it "proved" the wrong thing. The honest revert flips the guard as well.

#### Wiring
`promo.html` gained a `dayBox` and **a NINTH hardcoded listener list**, which is a second copy of `CONTROL_IDS`: a control in the markup and in that array but not in one of these lists is saved with a post, is read by the builder, and **does nothing when you touch it**. Control ids **84 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 100**, counted rather than assumed. The card has **no scope pickers at all** — every other data template answers "which stocks?", and this one answers "what did the market do"; a sector breakdown of one sector is not a breakdown — so `INDUSTRY_PREFIXES` is untouched.

**The phone needed no server change**: `/api/m/post` already calls `stampCapDerived`, so a saved day post draws its value-added column there rather than a row of dashes.

Verified: **54 checks** driving the real studio. The fixture separates all three mechanisms — every sector holds one giant and one small name moving the other way, so **equal weighting reverses the order and two signs**; percent and dollars **rank differently** by construction; and the four indexes carry a sector and a trillion-dollar cap, so leaving them in the pool is visible. Plus the sweep (54 combinations: no overflow, tightest kicker-to-tagline gap 32px, no dead band on any artboard, 31px between blocks on the tightest card, no head wrapped, no sector name clipped), each control changed and the card **diffed**, and a saved post round-tripped through the server and drawn by the phone's own route. **Proved by reverting five times**: equal weighting fails 5, leaving the benchmarks in fails 2, dropping the cap fails 6 (including 18 of the 54 combinations overflowing and the block gap landing exactly on its floor), un-filling the wrapper fails 2, and deleting the listener list fails 9.

#### …and an S&P cut on it, which narrows the MOVERS and nothing else (2026-10-05, owner's request)
**A `S&P 500` picker on the day card's panel: All stocks / In the index / Not in the index.** Asked as *"In Promo, Template The day, can you include s&p filter"* — and this card is the one data template the cut shipped to eight others on 2026-10-04 could not reach, because **it has no scope pickers at all** and so never calls `scopeOf`, where that cut lives.

##### THE OTHER TWO BLOCKS ARE ALREADY INDEX READINGS, which is a measurement rather than a judgement
The card draws three things and only one of them is a question about which stocks. **The chips ARE the benchmarks.** And the sector block is the eleven **Select Sector SPDRs**, which divide the S&P 500 between them — the provider's own stored names say so outright (`State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF`, and the same for all eleven), so cutting that block would be filtering the index out of itself. Measured off the stored names, rather than inferred from the tickers.

- **So the cut narrows the movers only, which is the FLOOR's own documented rule** — the panel has said *"The floor narrows the movers only"* since the card shipped, and the two controls now sit together under one hint.
- **The computed fallback is deliberately not cut either.** Cutting one path and not the other would make the sectors mean one thing with the funds held and another without, invisibly — the *"two different numbers looking like one thing"* the head wording already exists to stop.
- **The check is BYTE-IDENTICAL markup, not eleven rows.** This pool holds exactly eleven sectors of its own, so a revert that cut the fund block and fell through to the computed aggregate still draws 11 rows — with different numbers under a different head. **Proved by reverting**: cutting the sector block fails 1 on the byte comparison, and a row count alone would have passed over it.

##### The three-state guard is SHARED with `scopeOf`, not restated
`spFilter(rows, cut)` was lifted out of `scopeOf` and is called by both, so the day card and the eight scoped templates cannot disagree about what a null membership means. `=== true` / `=== false`, never truthy: `spMember` is null until a holdings file has been imported, and **null is not No** — on an instance with no file both cuts are empty, which reads correctly because the kicker names the cut that emptied the card.

###### THE NULL CHECK WAS VACUOUS, AND ONLY THE REVERT SAID SO
The third state is unreachable once a file exists — `stampSpMember` writes true or false on every row — so it is driven by **rewriting the response** (`page.route` + `route.fetch()` + `route.fulfill`), the technique the rebalance-axis suite uses. The first version nulled ONE member and asserted it was absent from the top of each cut. **It passed with the bug in place: `NOT LOAD-BEARING — 0 failed (113 ran)`.**

- **A truthy read drops a null from the `in` cut exactly as the correct read does**, so that side cannot tell the bug from the fix at all. Only `out` can — and only where the nulled stock would otherwise be **visible** there. BIGTECH at +1.0% is placed in `in` (two members move up) and **buried past the tenth row of `out`**, whose fillers reach +2.1%. So the one assertion that could fail was reading a list the symptom could never appear in.
- **The fixture nulls a SECOND member chosen for its rank**, MIDCARE at −6.0%, which lands **second** in the `out` bottom list — and both lists of both cuts are searched rather than the top of each. **Proved by reverting**: it now fails 1, printing `out … Tinycare,Midcare,…`, which is the production symptom in miniature.
- **The general rule: an absence is satisfied just as well by the row never being eligible.** Before asserting that something does not appear, check it WOULD have, under the bug, in the list being read.

##### Worth knowing
- **NO SERVER CHANGE.** `spMember` is a read-path stamp and `/api/m/post` applies it on its own line, so a saved day post carries the cut to the phone with nothing wired — **checked rather than assumed**, because the stamps are a set and the set has been incomplete twice. There is an end-to-end check that a post saved with the cut draws it there.
- **THE KICKER NAMES THE CUT**, because a posted card has no picker beside it: `49 stocks · S&P 500 movers over $1.0B`. It degrades to exactly the old string when the cut is off, and carries the floor **alongside** the cut rather than instead of it.
- **No new listener list — the id joined the DAY's existing one**, which is the ninth of thirteen. A control in the markup and in `CONTROL_IDS` but missing from its template's list exists, is saved with a post, is read by the builder — and **does nothing when you touch it**. Control ids **104 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**, counted rather than assumed (this file's own previous reading of 100 was stale).
- **With the cut `in` the floor is inert**, measured: all 504 members clear $1B. The two controls sit together and only one of them is doing anything on that setting.

##### What it does to today's card, which is the argument for it
Measured against the live snapshot (1,284 rows, the 2026-10-02 holdings file, **504 in / 780 out / 0 unknown**), at the default $1B floor:

| | the top ten |
|---|---|
| **All stocks** | Vaxcyte, PTC, XP, Banco Bradesco, Itau Unibanco, Sabesp, Nu, Ambev, Petrobras, Bentley |
| **In the index** | PTC, Western Digital, Autodesk, Seagate, AppLovin, Coinbase, Corteva, Intuit, Synopsys, DoorDash |

**Six of the unfiltered ten are Brazilian ADRs** — one country's session dominating a card captioned "The day". The cut replaces **18 of the 20 names** across both columns; only PTC survives at the top and only C.H. Robinson at the bottom. The bottom end also narrows from −9.8%…−4.7% to −9.1%…−2.7%, the index being less volatile than the tail.

- Verified: the day suite went **89 → 113 checks**. The fixture's load-bearing property is that **the biggest riser and the biggest faller are both OUTSIDE the index**, so a card ignoring the cut leads with a name the `in` list must not contain rather than coinciding with it; inside, exactly four rows carry a move, so the COUNT is evidence as well as the names (`Top 2` / `Bottom 2`). Membership is then checked per name against the fixture's own list in both directions. **Proved by reverting seven times, every one load-bearing**: the cut unapplied 10, the picker unfilled 12, `CONTROL_IDS` 10, the day's listener list 10, and the sector block, the kicker and the three-state read 1 each.
  - **THE FIXTURE'S SANITY CHECK EARNED ITS PLACE FIRST.** `fund_holdings` and `fund_state` are keyed **`'spy'` lowercase** — both accessors fold the key — so a `'SPY'` seed matches nothing, every row stamps null, both cuts come back empty, and every assertion below then passes for the wrong reason. One check comparing the two cuts' sizes against zero says so in one line.
  - **NEVER `page.selectOption` ON A PICKER A REVERT CAN EMPTY.** On a value the select does not carry it waits 30 seconds and **throws**, so the suite aborts and reports a load-bearing guard as one that never mattered. The new checks set `.value` and dispatch the page's own `change` event; the existing three controls were moved onto the same helper. The documented trap, met for the fourth time on this project.
  - **A TEST FAULT WORTH KEEPING: the phone's HTML is RAW, so the ampersand is escaped.** `/S&P 500 movers/` fails over a card that is correct; it is `S&amp;P`, because `esc()` is what writes the kicker.
  - **A dollar-figure count was weakened to `>= 2` mid-debug and then put back to the exact `=== 4`** the `in` cut produces, so the stamp cannot silently go missing from half the rows while the check still passes.
  - **A python heredoc wrote the literal characters `“` into a comment** in the suite — the escape survived as text rather than becoming the glyph. Harmless where it landed and the sixth instance of that trap; the repair patch is ASCII-only for that reason.

#### The day card became the Snapshot, over five windows (2026-10-05, owner's request)
**"Expand it to other time periods namely week, Month, YTD and Year. Maybe rename the template to Snapshot."** A `Period` picker on the panel — Today, Past week, Past month, This year, Past year — read by **all three blocks**, so the chips, the sector bars and the movers always describe one window.

- **THE LABEL CHANGED AND THE ID DID NOT.** `day` is a stored key: every saved post names it and `cleanPosts` checks it against `Cards.ids`. The Scale rename's own rule — renaming a label is free, re-keying is not — so existing posts keep working and the picker reads Snapshot.
- **A SUBSET OF `MOV_PERIODS`, never a second mapping.** `SNAP_PERIODS` names five keys from the catalogue the Movers card already uses, so the two cannot disagree about what *past week* reads.
- **WHY THOSE FIVE, and the odd-looking mix is the house convention.** 1W and 1M are **rolling** (five and 21 sessions), YTD is **calendar** (since last year's close), 1Y is rolling again — which is exactly the screener's own column family, so the card reads in the same words as the table it is made from.
- **`wtd` and `mtd` are deliberately NOT offered**, though the catalogue has them: they need the host to stamp anchors from `/api/period-anchors`, which **`/api/m/post` does not do** — so a saved Snapshot on one of those would draw blank on the phone. YTD needs no stamping, because `computeStocks` puts `ytdPct` on the row.

##### VALUE ADDED IS TODAY-ONLY, and that is arithmetic rather than a restriction
`capChangeToday` is `cap × todayPct / 100`, and it is right **because the stored market cap predates today** — measured when that column was built, the gap between `price × shares` and the stored cap regresses on today's move at a slope of **0.795**. Over a week or a year the cap **already contains** the move, so the same formula double-counts it; the correct one would be `cap × r/(1+r)`, which further assumes a share count that has not changed — false over a year, with buybacks and issuance.

- So rather than print an invented figure the metric **falls back to percent**, the title stops claiming it, and **the studio greys the option and says why** (`Value added, $ (today only)`). A control that looks live and does nothing when you touch it is this page's own documented hazard. **Proved by reverting**: offering it on every window fails 2.

##### THE PERIOD IS THE SUBTITLE, because the template no longer says it
`The day` carried the window in its name; `Snapshot` does not, so **a YTD card reading as today would be the worst thing this template could do**. The subtitle is the period for the whole card, with the metric clause appended only when it applies.

- **`movers by` was dropped from that clause, and the reason is a measurement.** With it the subtitle wraps at story/value/15 and the gap between blocks falls to **27px against the sweep's own 30px floor** — the card still fits, but it would be sitting on its limit. Something had to give once the period had to be stated, and this clause is the half the columns below already carry: the movers are the only ranked thing on the card and their heads say *Top 10*.
- Caught by the day card's existing 54-combination fit sweep, not by eye.

- Verified: **28 checks** on the real studio and the real phone route. **The fixture is the test**: every company leads exactly one window and every index and sector fund carries a different value per period, so a block still reading `todayPct` names a different company and prints a number belonging to another window. Plus the picker built from the module, the greyed metric, and a saved post round-tripped through `/api/m/post`. **Proved by reverting ten times, every one load-bearing**: the picker unfilled fails 19, the listener list 15, `CONTROL_IDS` 14, the movers 5, the chips and the sector funds 4 each, the old title 3, the subtitle 2, and value-added everywhere and the old label 1 each.
  - **ONE REVERT FIRST ABORTED THE SUITE and read as a guard that never mattered.** The hardcoded picker left `lab` referenced by an arrow body that no longer bound it, so the page threw at load and 0 of 28 checks ran. *A revert has to simulate the bug, not an impossible state* — with a valid hardcoded list it fails 19.
  - **A PRESENCE CHECK WAS VACUOUS and reported a working card as broken.** The phone check asked whether `Ytdco` appeared in the HTML — and it appears in the *day* window's top ten too, just not first, so it was true whatever period the card drew. It reads the FIRST name in the first column now. The failure it masked was real and in the test: the opts were collected by sweeping `#panel select`, which matched nothing, so the post saved without its period and the phone correctly drew Today. **Collect by name, and assert the key is there before saving.**
  - **A FIXTURE'S OWN SORT ORDER, not the fixture's first row.** The sector block sorts by value, so the leader is the fund with the largest value in that period — XLC, not XLK. Asserting XLK reported five failures on a block that was working perfectly.
  - `/api/promo-posts` is a **PUT**, not a POST; a POST answers 404 and the save silently does nothing.

### The Stock spotlight — one company, the whole picture (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**"One card for a single stock — use your judgement."** A thirteenth template, `spotlight`, second in the studio's picker. Three templates already answered ONE question about one company — the Chart card in `stock` mode draws its line, the Advice card in `profiles` mode reads the five rule sets against it, the Fundamentals card in `one` mode lists its figures — so the whole picture took three posts.

**IT IS NOT `stock` (tplStock), which already existed and is not this.** That one is the STOCK PAGE's chart export, fed by `ctx.chart` — a host that already holds one symbol's closes — which is why it is deliberately absent from the studio's picker. This reads the basket like every other studio card. Checked before building rather than after.

**What is on it**, in order: the sector and industry as the kicker; the company NAME as the headline with the ticker, the price and today's move under it as a label; a rebased line over the chosen window; **twelve figures in three rows — what it did, where it stands, what it is**; and the verdict with the rule that fired. Three controls (`spotSym`, `spotWin`, `spotProf`) and **no scope pickers at all** — the card IS its scope — so `INDUSTRY_PREFIXES` is untouched.

#### The decisions worth keeping
- **REVENUE IS DELIBERATELY NOT ON IT**, though it is the obvious size number beside the cap. An absolute is in the company's OWN reporting currency (Samsung's is in won, Ericsson's in krona), so a card printing it with a `$` would be confidently wrong. Margins and growth are ratios and carry the same story with none of that exposure. **Market cap is the one absolute that is always USD**, verified across eighteen foreign reporters, which is why it alone gets a dollar sign — and the PRICE is in the trading currency, which for a US-listed universe is USD, one more thing that rule quietly buys. **Proved by reverting**: adding a Revenue cell fails 10.
- **A multiple off a loss is a dash**, through `thirdReader('fpe')` — the reader the Size and Bubble cards already share, so the rule is stated once. The two kinds of blank are counted apart, as they are there: *losing money* and *does not report it* are different facts, and drawing them the same is how a card quietly lies. **Proved by reverting**: printing the raw ratio fails 3 and puts **-41.7** on the card.
- **A RETURN takes a sign and a MARGIN does not.** "+25.9%" as a profit margin reads as a change rather than a level; a negative one still takes the red, because loss-making is the reading.
- **Gross margin is meaningless for a lender**, so the margin shown is the PROFIT margin — true for a bank and a manufacturer alike, which is what lets this card skip the sector exclusions the ranking cards need.
- **The verdict always travels with the rule that fired AND the rule set's name.** That is the whole difference between this and a tip sheet, and it is why the attribution is not a setting. The test asserts the drawn word against **`ActionRules.apply`** rather than a literal, so a card that had stopped scoring and started guessing would fail.
- **The 52-week track is the Range card's own markup and `recoveryLeg`**, not a second drawing, so the two surfaces cannot disagree about what a marker means. **It is labelled with the POSITION, not the company name** — printing the name again on a card whose headline is that name is the repetition the blog's own image caption was pulled up for.
- **Three cases must not empty the card**, and each is common rather than an edge: no industry yet (the kicker falls back to the sector), no 52-week range (the track is simply absent), and **no stored bars** — where the Chart card correctly returns a bare "no stored history" card, here the figures, the range and the verdict are all still worth posting, so the plot alone stands aside and says why.

#### `Cards.basketDays(tpl, opts)` — one pairing, two hosts
**The card shipped internally with a chart that never arrived, and the cause is worth the export.** Three templates draw a price line and each keeps its window under its own control id, so both hosts knew the pairing: server.js listed `chart -> chtWin, sparks -> spkWin` inline, and **promo.html repeated the template names again in the repaint its fetch triggers**. A third such card made that a list rather than a pair — the basket landed, nothing repainted, and the spotlight kept its *Drawing the chart…* placeholder for ever. It is asked of the module now, the way `chartHistoryNeed` already is. **Proved by reverting**: the hardcoded list stops the suite dead on its second assertion.

#### A card cannot scroll, and the first cut ran the 4:5 body 67px past the foot
The note printed under the tagline. Three things were changed and **only after each was proved to bite on its own**:

- **The headline steps down by the LENGTH of the name** (58 / 46 / 38px on a post). It is set alone on a line and a company name is arbitrarily long: "Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings Limited" wraps at the full size and the second line is 59px the card does not have. Deterministic from the string, which is the only measurement the module can take — it reads no DOM. **Reverting fails 2**, worst 23px over.
- **`lineChart` takes an `mt` option and the spotlight passes 0.** Its 26px top margin is spacing for the cards that put a chart under a title; here it is the first item of a flex column that already spaces its children, so it was that spacing charged twice. A parameter rather than `!important`, because the CALLER is what knows which case it is in. **Reverting fails 1**, 12 of 90 combinations over.
- **The chart height is the free parameter** (318 / 176 / 624) and is where the remaining room came from.

**I OVER-CORRECTED FIRST, AND THE REVERT PROOFS ARE WHAT CAUGHT IT.** With all three in place plus a chart shaved twice, **two of the six reverts came back 0 failed** — which reads exactly like a guard that was never load-bearing. The chart was given the room back until each one bites alone. *Three fixes for one 61px problem is two fixes too many, and only running the reverts says which.*

- **HEADROOM IS NOT VISIBLE IN A POSITION on this card**, because `.sp-wrap` is `flex: 1` and absorbs every spare pixel into its own gaps — the note sits on the foot whether the card is full or half empty. **Nor is it the wrap's box minus its children**: a child's own margin is inside the wrap and outside every one of those rects, which is exactly how the first version of that metric reported **80px of room on a card that was full to the pixel**. `space-evenly` splits the free space into n+1 equal spaces, so one of those spaces multiplied back up IS the free space, measured from the drawn positions where a margin cannot hide.
- **The worst case for height is not the one that looks worst**: a SHORT name (so the headline stays at full size) on a company that LOSES money (so the note carries the extra sentence about the multiple). The long-named stock has the headline problem and the loss-maker has the note problem; neither is the pair, and the pair is what has to fit.

#### Wiring
`promo.html` gained a `spotBox` and **a TENTH hardcoded listener list**, which is a second copy of `CONTROL_IDS`: a control in the markup and in that array but not in one of these lists is saved with a post, is read by the builder, and **does nothing when you touch it**. **Proved by reverting: 19 checks fail.**

**`POST_OPT_MAX` went 100 -> 200.** The real list reached **87**, four controls from breaching a cap whose entire failure mode is silence — it once ate every control past the fortieth, all seven of the Size card's among them. It is a guard against a page being used as free storage, not a budget, so the headroom costs nothing.

Verified: **57 checks** driving the real studio, over a fixture where **every stock separates one mechanism from the others** (a loss-maker whose row really carries -41.7, a company reporting no multiple at all, one with no industry and no 52-week range, one with no bars, a 38-character name, and the short-named loss-maker above). Plus the sweep — **90 combinations, 3 artboards x 5 stocks x 3 windows x verdict on/off: nothing overflows, tightest kicker-to-tagline gap 32px, 11px of headroom left on the tightest card** — each control changed and the card **diffed**, and a saved post round-tripped through the server and built by the phone's own route with its chart drawn. **Proved by reverting six times.**

#### Three grounds — dark, light and navy, on the spotlight only (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**"Is it possible to have some other colour theme just for the promo studio"**, then, seeing the light prototype, *"only keep this variant — commit this only on the spotlight"* and *"is it possible to create a third navy blue background"*. A `Ground` picker on the spotlight's panel: Dark (the default, unchanged), Light, Navy.

**A THEME IS THE GROUND AND THE FURNITURE, NOT THE SIGNALS — except on light, where that line cannot be held.** Green is up, red is down, amber is *notice this*, and the six-tier ladder is the screener's own; a palette that moved any of them would make the card say something it does not mean. **Measured against `#f7f8fa`, every one of them fails outright**: green **1.9:1**, red 2.7, amber 1.7, `--text` **1.2**. So the light theme keeps each HUE and darkens it to clear 4.5:1 — *same semantics, second value* — which is what doubles its token surface. **Navy needs none of that**: on `#0d1a2d` the whole dark palette still clears the floor (green 9.1, red 6.5, amber 10.5, faint 4.8), so it is a ground, an aura and a one-token lift on `--faint`, and it cost an hour against the light theme's day.

- **The token block is most of the card for free.** ~35 `var()` uses in `Cards.STYLE` resolve against whatever `.s-art.th-light` declares, so the chrome, the type and every hairline follow from one block.
- **WHAT A TOKEN CANNOT REACH IS THE 34 `rgba(255,255,255,.0x)` SITES**, and on a light ground they are invisible rather than wrong — the failure that reads as an *empty* card rather than a broken one, which is much harder to spot. Each one the spotlight draws is overridden explicitly; the other twelve templates keep their dark ground until they are done one at a time.
- **`ADV_TINT` is deliberately NOT touched.** The spotlight reads its verdict colour from `pal.tints`; the other eight cards that read that map are untouched, so this really is the spotlight's theme rather than the module's. A Proxy over `ADV_TINT` was written first and thrown away — all nine call sites are key reads today, so it worked, and it would return `[]` the day somebody wrote `Object.keys` on it.

##### `Cards.themeClass(opts)` — one pairing, THREE hosts
The builder returns inner HTML only, so the ground lives on a class the HOST puts on `.s-art` — and there are **three** such places: the studio's stage, the phone's post sheet, and the phone's off-screen rasterise stage. **The phone does not hold the post's controls**, so left to each host to derive, a saved light post draws a **light chart on a black card**, silently. The module is asked instead, exactly as `basketDays` is, and the ground travels on the `/api/m/post` payload beside the html. An unknown value falls back to dark, which is the injection guard as well as the fallback — only known class names ever reach the DOM.

##### THE CHECK IS CONTRAST, MEASURED OFF WHAT IS DRAWN
**The prototype's first render put "Sell Immediately" at 2.7:1 on white** — the verdict ladder was a hardcoded map nobody had routed through the palette — and **the card did not look broken, it looked WEAK**, beside a perfectly crisp `-2.71%` that came through the token. No assertion on a class name or a hex could catch that. So the suite reads **every drawn colour** — 18 text roles by computed style, plus the chart stroke and every distinct `<text>` fill by ATTRIBUTE, since that markup travels through the PNG export — and ratios each against the artboard's own rendered background. Written as a sweep, so a fourth ground or a new coloured element is covered with no new check. Measured: **21 colours, worst 4.74 on light, 5.61 dark, 5.77 navy.**
- **Colour moves no box**, so the fit sweep should be free — asserted anyway across 18 combinations, so a future theme that touches type or spacing cannot land unnoticed.
- Verified: **35 checks**, including the phone's OWN sheet measured end to end (the light post really is light there, which is the bug `themeClass` exists to prevent). **Proved by reverting seven times**: the ladder fails 3 (verdict at 1.81), the chart line 3, the axis labels 2, the studio's class 5, the listener list 4, the ground not travelling to the phone 4, the phone's own class 3.
  - **ONE REVERT REPORTED 0 AND IT WAS THE TEST, NOT RESIDUE.** The colour sweep read `querySelector('svg text')` — the FIRST one, a gridline label routed through the palette by a different line — so reverting the *date* labels at the foot was never looked at. `#7d8797` on white is **3.42:1**, a real failure the check walked straight past. It reads every distinct fill now, and the revert then fails 2. *An assertion that samples one of several sibling elements passes over the others.*


##### The 52-week track became four figures (2026-09-30, owner's request)
**The rail went and `% from the 52-week high`, `% from the low`, `RSI` and `vs the 200-day` took its place**, making the grid three rows of four: four windows of its own price, four readings of where it stands, four of the business.

- **TWO OF THEM ARE LEVELS, SO THEY TAKE THE SIGN AND NOT THE COLOUR.** "From the high" is always negative and "from the low" always positive, so green and red there would read as good and bad — when **-3.1% off the high is as good as it gets**. It is the margin rule one step on: a margin drops the sign because zero is not a boundary it crosses; these keep it because the sign IS the label's direction. **Proved by reverting**: colouring them by sign fails the check.
- **RSI IS AN INDEX, NOT A PERCENTAGE** — no `%`, no `+`. 55 is not 55%. Deliberately uncoloured too: 70 and 30 mean overbought and oversold, but that is a reading this card does not otherwise make and the verdict below already carries it. The stock page paints RSI violet; violet is not in play here and spending it on one cell would make it mean something new on this surface alone. **Proved by reverting**: `pct(v)` prints `+55.0%`.
- **`vs 200-day` DOES take the colour**, because it is a direction — the trend gate every rule set reads first.
- **A null is not a zero.** A listing too young for a 200-day average, or with no stored range, dashes rather than printing `0.0%`. The fixture's range-less stock is what holds that down.
- **WHAT IS LOST IS THE RECOVERY LEG** — the faint month-ago segment behind the marker, which showed whether a stock near its low was still falling. Nothing here replaces it; it is a shape rather than a figure. Worth knowing before it is missed. `recoveryLeg` stays, because the Range card draws it.
- **`pal.mid` and `pal.wash` went with the track**, along with the light theme's `.trk` override — each had exactly one consumer and residue reads as intent.

**Net it GAINED room**: the track cost more than the extra row, and the tightest card went from 11px of headroom to 36.

##### THE FIXTURE'S "LONG NAME" WAS 38 CHARACTERS AND THE REAL ONE IS 99
When the track's height came back, the headline step-down's revert proof stopped biting and read as residue. **It is not residue — the fixture was gentle.** Measured against the live universe: **58 display names pass 28 characters, 16 pass 40, 8 pass 60, and the longest is 99** (`Brookfield Renewable Corporation Brookfield Renewable Corporation Class A Subordinate Voting Shares`). On the real string the step-down fails 9 of 90 combinations when reverted, worst **181px** over.

- A **fourth step** (`t4`, 30px on a post) was added for names past 60, because at three steps that name still took three lines and left the 4:5 card **4px**.
- **4px is luck, not headroom**, so the sweep's floor is **20px** now — roughly half a text line, the standard the kicker-to-tagline gap already holds. That is what makes `t4` and the chart's `mt: 0` load-bearing rather than merely correct.
- **THE HEADROOM METRIC WAS WRONG TWICE, AND THE SECOND WAY IS THE SUBTLE ONE.** Box-minus-children's-rects misses margins (it once said 80px on a card full to the pixel). Its replacement — one `space-evenly` space multiplied back up — is fooled in the OPPOSITE direction: a top margin on the first child sits inside that space, so **adding** a margin made measured headroom go UP while real headroom went down, which is exactly why the doubled chart margin kept reporting as a guard that does not bite. It reads each child's margins explicitly now: with the margin restored it reports 9px against 36, and the guard bites.
