- **The multiple was coloured green and red.** A P/E rising is good for a holder and bad for a buyer, so colour there is an implied verdict — the one thing this card must not make. Revenue, earnings and market value keep theirs: those are facts with a direction.

#### THE VALUE PANEL RUNS TO TODAY (2026-10-04, owner: "report upto today instead of last filed making the same assumptions you made on /adjusted")
**Reported as a discrepancy first: MSFT read `$2.77T` on this card and `$3.85T` on `/adjusted`, with P/Es of 20.7× and 28.8×.** Decomposed against production, neither was wrong — they were struck at **different dates**: 7.427B shares × **$373.02** (the close on 2026-06-30, MSFT's last filed quarter) against 7.445B × **$517.53** (the latest close). The cap gap is **+39.1%** and the price move over exactly that span is **+38.7%**; the 0.24% remainder is two slightly different filed share-count vintages. Same earnings both sides, so the multiple inherits all of it.

- **ONLY THE MARKET HALF COULD MOVE, and that asymmetry is the feature.** Prices exist for every session; there is no filing after the last filed quarter. So the value panel gains **one more point at the latest close** and revenue and earnings stop where the record does — carrying them forward would be inventing a figure. **The two panels now end on different dates**, which is honest and is itself the finding: the gap between the lines' right edges IS how stale the filings are.
- **THE LIVE P/E IS /adjusted's OWN ASSUMPTION**, stated as arithmetic: today's cap over the **last filed** trailing year. That is what a trailing P/E is everywhere in this app, and it is why the two pages now agree rather than differing by a quarter's price action.
- **BOUNDED AT 200 DAYS, because an unbounded extension draws a straight line across years of unfiled history.** Measured over 1,183 symbols: the newest statement filing is a median **61 days** old, p90 151, **98.4% inside 180**, then a thin tail of 19 reaching **5,661 days** — and **JPM's own trail stops in 2014**, so one segment would span twelve years of price action it never touched. 200 days on the period end is about two quarters, so the new segment is never more than twice the length of any other. **Proved by reverting**: the bound removed fails 2.
- **THE BOUNDARY PROBE FOUND A REAL BUG IN MY OWN CODE, which is what probing both sides is for.** The gap was computed from `Date.parse(d + 'T12:00:00')` — **local** time — so a span crossing the daylight-saving change gains an hour and a gap of exactly 200 days measured **200.04** and failed its own bound. It is `T00:00:00Z` on both ends now. **This is the one place local noon is wrong**: that rule exists for RENDERING a date (the card-dating lesson), and a *difference* must be taken in UTC. A one-sided check would have passed. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- **THE FIGURES ROW NOW NAMES TWO DATES, and that is the half that answers the original question.** It carried none, so `MARKET VALUE $2.50T → $2.77T` read as *now* when it was end-of-June — the same cause as the owner's earlier question about why the chart ends on 30 June. The line reads *"Revenue and earnings to 2026-06-30 · market value and P/E at the 2026-09-30 close"*, or *"All four as of …, the last filed quarter"* where the filings are too stale to extend. **Proved by reverting**: dropping it fails 4.
  - **IT IS ONE FLEX CHILD WITH THE FIGURES, NOT TWO.** `.evo-wrap` is a `space-evenly` column, so a second child buys a **whole extra gap** on top of its own height — measured, the line alone cost **70px** on the square and overflowed the artboard. Wrapped in `.evo-foot` it costs its own ~30px.
  - **THE NOTE WAS NOT ALSO EXTENDED, and the first cut's was.** A sentence there repeating the as-of line is the duplication this project has been pulled up on before — and because the note sits inside `.evo-in` above a `flex: 1` wrap, it squeezed the charts: with it the story overflowed by **63px** and the budget script disagreed with the suite, which is what exposed it.
- **The chart heights were re-measured, not re-guessed**: square **194/136 → 180/127** and story **545/380 → 537/374**; the portrait is unchanged. The suite's floor is **20px, half a text line** (the how-to deck's standard, because 4px of room is luck), and the tightest of 36 combinations now reads **24px**.
- Verified: **14 checks** on the module with no server, no browser and no database — `evolutionSeries` touches only two SecFacts functions, so they are stubbed and the test is about the live point alone — plus **84** driving the real studio (72 before). The module fixture gives **every quarter a different net income**, so a live P/E computed off the wrong one comes out visibly different rather than coincidentally the same; the page fixture is **production's own shape**, filings to 2026-06-30 against bars to 2026-09-30. **Proved by reverting six times**, every one load-bearing: the live point never computed fails 8, the as-of line 4, the bound 2, the value chart left on the filed axis 2, the figures left on `Z` 2, and the local-time gap 1.
  - **NOSHRE CARRIES THE NON-LIVE BRANCH** — it has no share count, so `live` is null and the as-of line must say all four are as filed rather than naming a price date it does not have. A branch nothing reaches is a branch nobody has checked.
  - **A REVERT MUST NEUTER THE OUTPUT, NEVER THE SYNTAX.** The as-of case first left an unbalanced paren; the suite would not parse and the harness reported `?? only 0 of 84 ran` rather than "0 failed" — which is the guard that stops an aborted run reading as residue. Changing the class name instead gives the honest 4.
  - **A QUOTED HEREDOC ATE A BACKSLASH LEVEL AGAIN** (`'\n-- …'` became a real newline inside a JS string). Write the block to a file with the Write tool and splice it; this is the sixth time.

#### THE FILL'S STRENGTH FOLLOWS THE BASELINE (2026-10-04, owner: "an area chart will be more impactful")
**The card already drew an area** — a vertical gradient from 0.26 to transparent — so the request is about its weight, and strengthening it is not a style change. **A filled area is read as a QUANTITY measured from the baseline; a bare line is read as a shape.** This project settled that once already on the short-interest strip, where the note records that *truncating a bar axis is the classic misleading chart* while a line *carries no such claim*. So a solid fill is only honest where zero genuinely sits on the axis, and the fill is solid exactly there: **0.42 → 0.05 where it does, the old 0.26 → 0 wash where it does not.**

- **THE OTHER WAY ROUND WAS MEASURED AND REFUSED.** Forcing zero onto every axis would let every card take the solid fill, at a cost taken over 99 real series (12 symbols × 3 windows): **62 are already zero-based and 11 cross zero**, so only 26 would move — and those are the mature companies the chart is least able to lose, with **PG's five-year revenue down to the top 10% of the panel**, AAPL's 19%, KO's and WMT's 22%. A flat strip at the top of a panel says nothing about the one company type whose revenue genuinely creeps.
- **THE READER IS NEVER LEFT GUESSING WHICH THEY HAVE, which is what makes two treatments safe rather than arbitrary.** The bottom gridline is LABELLED, so a solid fill always sits above a `$0` and a wash always sits above a real number. The fill's weight and the axis label say the same thing, and the check asserts exactly that correspondence rather than either alone.
- **ZERO IS ON THE AXIS WHEREVER THE RANGE REACHES IT, which is three cases and not one** — and the old `lo < 0 && hi > 0` test caught only the middle one. A series whose FLOOR the rule pulled to zero was closing `PADPX` (14px) below its own zero gridline; and **an all-negative series, whose CEILING the rule pulls to zero, was closing to the plot FLOOR** — so a company loss-making across the whole window had its mass drawn piling up from the bottom of the panel while zero sat at the top. **Upside down, and invisible at 0.26 alpha**, which is why strengthening the fill is what exposed it. It hangs from zero now.
- **THE BUSINESS PANEL CHARTS EARNINGS AND MARGIN AS WELL AS REVENUE, so both of those branches are live** — the revenue default can reach neither, and the first version of this check tested revenue alone. Measured on production: **SNAP and RIVN are all-negative over five years**, and PTON, UBER, TSLA, PLTR, ROKU and SOFI cross zero.
- **The gridlines survive it, and only a screenshot could say so.** The fill is painted UNDER them (`area + grid + path`), so too strong a peak washes the guides out — an attribute check cannot see that, and 0.42 was confirmed by eye on all three grounds. The **gutter labels are never at risk**: they sit at `PL − 14`, outside the plot box entirely.
- Verified: **22 checks** over production's own series, plus the ground sweep (155 over 114 combinations) and the width sweep re-run unchanged. **Each case asserts the drawn fill against the drawn baseline**, so a treatment wired to the wrong test fails rather than passing on a sample that happens to agree — and the sample is deliberately mixed, **13 solid against 7 wash**.
  - **THE AXIS IS READ, NEVER INTERPOLATED, and the first version of the check reported a working fill as broken.** Fitting zero through the end labels puts it ~2px out, because the labels are ROUNDED for display: TSLA's margin axis reads `-20..15` against a true `-19.9..15.5`. Zero is taken from the thick zero rule where the series crosses, else from the gridline whose own label IS zero. *A value read off a rounded label is not the value the chart used.*

#### Wiring, and the boundary
`evolutionNeed(tpl, opts)` is asked of the module by **both** hosts — the studio and `/api/m/post` — for the reason `basketDays` exists: that pairing was a hardcoded list in each of them once, and it is how the spotlight shipped drawing nothing. `evolutionFor(symbol, years)` is one assembly with two callers, cached ten minutes. **`readBars` returns NEWEST FIRST and names the date `datetime`, not `d`** — read off db.js rather than guessed at, which cost a probe that reported zero points on perfectly good data. A **THIRTEENTH** hardcoded listener list in promo.html; control ids **92 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**.

**THE BOUNDARY IS UNCHANGED**: nothing is stamped onto a snapshot row, so this cannot become a screener column, then a filter, then a screen. Asserted against the real `/api/stocks` payload and the real row keys, not by grep.

- Verified: **72 checks**, over a fixture where each company separates one mechanism — SPLITR's filed share counts jump 4× mid-trail (so the naive formulation comes out at a visibly different number rather than coincidentally the same one), LOSSCO crosses zero, THINCO has five filed quarters, NOSHRE has no share count, and MIDNAM/LONGNM exist for their 57- and 99-character names alone. Plus a 36-combination fit sweep, the second host round-tripped through `/api/m/post`, and the ground and width sweeps re-run with the template registered (**155 and 97 checks over 114 combinations each, 0 failed**). **Proved by reverting thirteen times, every one load-bearing**: the listener list fails 17, `CONTROL_IDS` 11, the split formulation 5, the filed-count fallback 4, the step classes 4 (including 6 of 36 combinations overflowing and −211px of headroom), the phone's fetch 3, a shared gradient id 3, and the short-trail refusal, the unmeasured heights, the multiple's colour, the zero label, the 25px figure and the window-end anchoring 1 each.
  - **A QUOTED HEREDOC STILL ATE ONE BACKSLASH LEVEL**, so `\\u2192` in a patch script arrived as the arrow itself and the anchor matched nothing. This file already records the trap for CLAUDE.md prose; it applies to `<<'EOF'` too. Use Write for anything carrying an escape.
  - **A PATCH SCRIPT THAT WRITES AT THE END DISCARDS THE EDITS THAT ALREADY SUCCEEDED.** One failing anchor threw after three `~ applied` lines had printed, the file was never written, and the three were silently lost — and the clipping check then passed because it happened to run on a card whose figures all fit.
  - **`#stage` IS `.s-art`, not its parent**, so `#stage .s-art` matched nothing and **both** sweep assertions were vacuous — "0 of 27 combinations" over 27 cases that had all bailed at the first line. An identical or absent number across cases that should differ is the tell.
  - **`cards.js` assigns to `globalThis`, not `module.exports`** — `const Cards = require(...)` returns `{}` and every call on it throws.
  - **`size-scope-test.js`'s `NO_SCOPE` list was stale and failed at HEAD too** (confirmed by stashing): `howto` had been missing since it shipped on 2026-10-02. Corrected with `evolution` rather than worked around — neither template has a scope picker.

### Flow — where the value sits, and how each sector has done (2026-10-05, owner's request)
**An eighteenth template, `flow`, fourth in the studio's picker: a one-step alluvial with the eleven sectors down the left sized by market value, three performance bands down the right, and a ribbon per sector flowing between.** The owner asked for *"composition (Market cap, Number of Stocks) of s&p by Industry and the performance of those industry"* with a Sankey attached as the reference, then narrowed it twice — *"I like the Sankey, Ignore the time, This is as of today always, Left side show the Composition of S&P by Industry, Right side show the YTD Performance"*, and then **"Just sector at the moment"**.

#### PERFORMANCE IS THE DESTINATION, NEVER THE WIDTH — the one decision the whole design rests on
The tempting version starts a ribbon at share of value and ends it at share of the GAIN, fanning wider or narrower. **It cannot be drawn, and the measurement is decisive**: at industry grain **50 of 112 industries have a NEGATIVE contribution this year**, the positives sum to **+17.0% against a basket of +13.7%**, and a ribbon has no negative width — so **3.3 points would have to be hidden**. Market cap flows (always positive) and the return only decides WHERE it lands, which makes the chart conserved by construction: every band is exactly the sum of the ribbons entering it.

- **TIME IS DROPPED, and the data could not have supplied it anyway.** The reference is a two-date Sankey; `fund_holdings` holds **two days**, so a composition-over-time chart has nothing to flow between. The owner dropped it independently.
- **SECTOR, NOT INDUSTRY, and the owner chose that after the measurement.** At industry grain the **top twelve are 63% of the index**, so the "Other" ribbon would be **37%** — the biggest element on the chart and the one that says least. Eleven sectors cover 100% with nothing pooled. (Industries per sector is median 10 / max 19, so a drill WOULD work; it is deferred, not refused.)

#### BEGINNING WEIGHTS, or the parts do not sum to the whole
Today's weight times the window's return is not the basket's return, and not by a rounding margin: measured on the index's own members, **the end-weighted parts overstate the basket by 24.6 points over the year and 15.7 points this year**, while the begin-weighted ones land on it EXACTLY at every horizon (gap 0.00 at a week, a month, YTD and a year), because a winner has already grown into the weight being applied to it. The start weight is reconstructed as `cap / (1 + r/100)` — which assumes an unchanged share count, the only approximation available since no share count is stored per date, and the note says so.
- **MY FIRST PROBE REPORTED THIS RECONCILING TO 0.0000pt AND WAS MEASURING ITSELF.** It computed the "whole" the same (ending-weight) way as the parts, so of course they agreed. **The claim a contribution makes is that the parts sum to the BASKET'S OWN RETURN** — `sum(cap_end)/sum(cap_begin) − 1` — and only the second probe, which computed that independently, showed the 24.6-point gap.
- **Proved by reverting**: end weights fail the suite outright, drawing +23.0% where the truth is +6.9%.

#### A BLANK SECTOR HAS TO LEAVE BEFORE THE INDEX IS STRUCK, not after
A stock whose profile has not been pulled yet belongs in no band — the rule `/pivot` and `/consolidated` both keep — but if it still counted toward the reference return the card would be measuring eleven sectors against a basket holding twelve things. **Measured: a gap of up to 0.10pt** (13.210 against 13.313 on the `out` cut), and **exactly 0.00000pt** once the index is struck over the sectored rows alone. The dropped rows are named in the note rather than disappearing; live, that is 1 of 504 inside the index and 3 of 738 outside.

#### THE BANDS ARE INDEX-RELATIVE, AND THE ORDER OF THE THREE TESTS IS WHAT KEEPS THE PALETTE HONEST
`r < 0 → down`, else `r > index → ahead`, else `behind`. **`r < 0` is asked FIRST**, so every sector in Ahead or Behind is non-negative **by construction** — which is what makes green always mark a sector that rose and red always one that fell, exactly the meanings those two colours carry on every other surface here. Ask "ahead" first instead and a year with a negative index paints a sector that lost money green. **Proved by reverting**: the other order fails 2, and the second names the harm — `drawn: #fb7185 #34d399` on a card where every sector fell.

- **FIXED BANDS COLLAPSE, measured over all five windows the picker offers.** Cuts at >30 / 15-30 / 0-15 / down put **TEN OF ELEVEN sectors in one band holding 98% of the value** on a single-day window — a chart that says nothing. The index-relative split never degenerates (3 bands today, 3 over a week, 2 over a month, 3 this year, 3 over a year) and needs no threshold that goes stale. **Proved by reverting.**
- The degenerate case is honest rather than broken: in a falling month every sector is Down, the card draws **one band at 100% of value**, and nothing is green.

#### THE RETURNS ARE OUR OWN AGGREGATE, NOT THE SECTOR FUNDS — deliberately unlike the Snapshot
`tplDay` reads the eleven Select Sector SPDRs and records why. **This card cannot**: its left column is the members' own market cap, so a right half taken from the fund would join two ends of one ribbon that describe different baskets. The gap is real and material — measured on YTD, **mean 2.84pt, and Communication Services reads +5.7% ours against −5.3% for XLC, a 10.9-point difference that puts it in a different BAND**; Technology is −6.3pt and Basic Materials −3.9pt.
- **Corroborated rather than asserted**: Energy reads **+41.0% ours against XLE's +41.9%**, a 1.0pt gap on the most extreme sector on the screen (refiners — MPC +168%, VLO +158%, PSX +109%). So the aggregate is right and the disagreements are basket composition, not arithmetic.
- The index funds and the eleven sector funds are removed from the pool first — a fund that IS a sector, inside that sector's own aggregate, double-counts it. **Proved by reverting** both ways.

#### A SMALL SECTOR STILL HAS TO BE VISIBLE
Basic Materials is **1.4% of the index**, which on the portrait's column is **seven pixels** — thinner than the label beside it and too thin for a ribbon to be followed. `FLOW_MIN` is 18px and the shortfall is taken back **from the slack above the floor in proportion**, so the distortion lands on the big nodes where it is a few percent rather than on the small ones where it would be everything. **The note says how many were floored**, the Size card's rule that a thing drawn at the floor says so.

#### EVERY DIMENSION IS MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN
- **The heights.** `.s-body`'s own `clientHeight` is **1128 / 858 / 1695** (portrait / square / story). That is NOT the day card's recorded 958 / 688 / ~1460 and neither is wrong — those are the room left BELOW its kicker and title, which on this card is 172px of the 1128. **The probe that first disagreed with both had divided `clientHeight` by the artboard's scale, and a CSS transform does not change layout pixels** — only `getBoundingClientRect` readings need converting, which is what made the body look 1600px tall and the slack impossible to reconcile. `FLOW_H` is 660 / 402 / 1120, leaving **32px of slack on all three** — the note takes `margin-top: auto`, so all the free space collects in ONE band between the drawing and the footnote instead of splitting at both ends, which is the fault the day card had to be rebuilt for.
- **The tracks.** `FLOW_TRACKS` is per artboard because the longest sector name is fixed and known: **"Communication Services" draws 197px at the label's own 17px**, so an ellipsis here is a width bug rather than the unavoidable thing it is on a company name. The binding width turned out to be the BAND SUB, not the name — **248px against a 220px box**, so it wrapped mid-phrase ("of the / value") on two artboards and the story's band name wrapped too. Dropping one article ("of value") took it to 213 and fixed all three.
- **`scrollWidth` ON AN ALREADY-WRAPPED ELEMENT REPORTS ITS OWN BOX, NOT WHAT IT WANTED**, so the first measurement said "needs 232" against a 232px box and looked satisfied. The honest reading is taken with `white-space: nowrap` forced on and then put back.
- **A wrapped label is now a suite check**, and the honest line count is a **Range over the contents** — `getClientRects` on the element returns ONE border box however the text flows inside it, and these are blockified flex items. The documented trap, met again.

#### THE SUBTITLE INHERITS 66px, AND THAT COST THE CARD 86 PIXELS
Inside `.s-title` a `.dim` span takes the display size, which is right for the Snapshot's one-word period and wrong for "and how each sector has done this year" — it **wrapped, so the heading took three lines and 202px** of a card whose whole content is a drawing. Scoped to 32 / 29 / 40px it is one line and 116px.

#### THE EMPTY STATE NAMES THE CAUSE, NOT THE CUT — found by screenshot
There are three different reasons to be empty and the first draft branched on the **cut**, so a card with a perfectly good holdings file and no readings over the chosen window announced that *no holdings file has been imported*. **A posted picture has no picker beside it, so that sentence is the reader's only explanation.** It now distinguishes a cut that matched nothing (and says which cut) from a window with no readings (and names the window) from rows with no sector recorded. Every assertion had passed over it; the navy/month shot is what showed it.

#### THE PAGE AND THE MODULE DISAGREED ABOUT THE DEFAULT, SILENTLY
`flowSp500` was filled by the shared S&P loop, which reads `keep` **before the options exist** — on a first paint that is the empty string, which is in no option list, so the select stays on its FIRST option, `All`. The module's own fallback is `in`. So the card opened on the whole screen while every internal default said the index, and the only symptom was numbers that were quietly the wrong basket. It has its own fill with `selected`, mirroring `flowPeriod`'s. **Proved by reverting**, which is also the first thing the suite caught.

#### …and the industry drill, with the sector mandatory (2026-10-05, owner's request)
**A `Break down` picker on the Flow card: *All sectors — the eleven* (the default, unchanged) or one sector, which draws that sector's INDUSTRIES instead.** The owner's words were *"do the industry drill down, Sector has to be mandatory selection"*, which is one control rather than two: there is no invalid state to guard, because the industry view is simply unreachable without naming a sector.

- **A FLAT INDUSTRY VIEW IS NOT OFFERED AND COULD NOT BE DRAWN** — the measurement that deferred the drill in the first place. 138 industries, of which the top twelve are **63% of the index**, so a pooled tail would be **37%** and the biggest element on the chart. Inside ONE sector the same pooling is a genuine tail (below). Re-measured the same day: **0 of 138 industries span more than one sector**, which is the property the drill rests on, and it has held as the count grew from the 99 recorded for the pivot.
- **Industries per sector, measured**: S&P members **max 19 (Industrials), median 10, min 5**, 112 slots across the eleven; whole screen **max 23, median 12, min 6**, 138 slots. Industrials 19 and Consumer Cyclical 18 are the long tail — every other sector is 12 or fewer.

##### THE REFERENCE BECOMES THE SECTOR, because the left column has
Drilled, the left column is share of **Technology's** value, so a right half measured against the S&P would join two ends of one ribbon describing different wholes — the same objection that rules out reading the sector funds. The bands read *Ahead of the sector* / *Behind the sector*, and the identity is preserved: the industries' begin-weighted returns sum to the sector's own return exactly, as the sectors' sum to the index's. **Proved by reverting**: leaving `refWord` as the index fails 2; not renaming the band labels fails 1.

##### FOURTEEN ROWS, and both halves of the number are measured
- **THE SQUARE CANNOT DRAW 19 ROWS AT ALL.** Its column is 402px, so 19 nodes at the 18px floor is **342 against 294 available** — the nodes would have run past the bottom of their own svg, which CLIPS rather than overflows, so the card would have quietly lost its last rows with nothing on screen or in the body-overflow check saying so.
- **At 14, nine of the eleven sectors show every industry they have.** The two that do not pool **4.1% over 6 industries** (Industrials) and **1.7% over 5** (Consumer Cyclical). At 10 those tails are 14.6% and 6.8%, which is a chart hiding its own content.
- **The pooled row is a real basket, so it is banded like any other** — a cap-weighted return over the industries it holds — and conservation still holds exactly. It is italic, named *"N smaller industries"*, and stays LAST even where its combined cap exceeds a named row above it: it is the tail, and sorting it into the middle would read as an industry. The note names it **the way the row names itself**, so the sentence and the ribbon can be connected.
- **Proved by reverting**: dropping the tail rather than pooling it fails 11; removing the cap fails 11.

##### THE FLOOR NEEDED A CEILING, and only one check can see it
`n × FLOW_MIN` can exceed the column, and the svg clips what runs past — so the body-overflow check, which is what every other fit question here is answered with, is blind to it. `floor = Math.min(FLOW_MIN, avail / n)`. **The suite gained the only check that catches it**: the last node's bottom against the svg's own height. The cap makes the state unreachable today, so the revert is run **together with** the cap — one guard flipping the other back on, which is what that rule means in practice.

##### The drill gets its own tracks, and the story does NOT grow its type
Industry names run to **40 characters** ("Drug Manufacturers - Specialty & Generic", "Utilities - Independent Power Producers") against a sector's 22, and the band sub is four characters longer because "industries" is. Measured at the story's own larger sizes, the two label columns need **417 + 292 = 709 of the body's 952**, leaving **243px of horizontal run for a 1120px-tall drawing** — ribbons so steep the chart stops reading. Nothing requires the type to grow with the height, and the drawing is the card. One track set for all three artboards: **lw 380, rw 268, svg 304**, measured at 376 and 259 needed.
- **THE DRILL CLASS IS ON THE WRAP, NOT THE LEFT SIDE.** `.fl-r` is a SIBLING of that side, so a class there cannot reach the band labels — and the drill's longer sub is exactly what needs them. **Proved by reverting**: fails 1.
- The `.sz-story .fl-drill` rules are **undoing** that artboard's own bumps rather than adding any, so they have to sit at (0,3,1) and (0,4,1) to beat the `.sz-story` rules further down, which a bare `.fl-drill` only ties with.

##### `Cards.sectors` ALREADY EXISTED, and a duplicate key is silently the last one
The picker was first built from a new `sectors: () => SECTOR_NAMES.slice()` export — and `Cards.sectors(rows)` already existed **22 lines below it**, returning the sectors actually present. A duplicate key in an object literal is the LAST one, so the new export never existed; the picker came back empty and **`node --check` passes it**. The same family as the backtick-in-`STYLE` trap: valid syntax, wrong program.
- The existing accessor is the better one anyway — it offers only sectors with stocks behind them, and it is what every other sector picker on the page already uses. The fixed list went with it. **Proved by reverting**: calling it bare again fails 22, the most of any revert here.
- **A SECTOR NAME IS NOT AN ENUM THIS MODULE OWNS**, which is why the card's own guard is `!== 'All'` rather than a membership test: it is the provider's taxonomy arriving as free text on the row, so eleven hardcoded names would refuse a twelfth the day one was added. A name that matches no row reaches the empty state, **which says so by name** — better than silently drawing the eleven-sector card.

##### Worth knowing
- **"A industry that fell"** — caught by eye on the drilled card, not by an assertion. The article follows the word it precedes now, and there is a check on both forms.
- **The empty state has four branches, not three**: a sector with no rows in the cut names the sector.
- The kicker gains the sector, the subtitle says *industry*, and the note's every "sector" becomes "industry" from one `partWord`.
- **No new endpoint, no query, no basket** — `industry` is already on the snapshot row, so the drill is a second `groupBy` over data the studio is holding.
- **The global sweeps were pointed at the drill too**, and their fixture gained varied industries so a drill there is a real split rather than one ribbon restating its parent. Their `flow` entry walks the SECTOR rather than the period now: the drill brings its own tracks, type sizes and band labels, which is the bigger structural difference, and the falling-window colour case is covered by the card's own suite, which reads the drawn fills.
- Verified: the suite went **82 → 134 checks**, and its artboard sweep now walks **both modes**, because an artboard that fits the sector view says nothing about the drill. **Proved by reverting fourteen times, every one load-bearing**: the picker called bare 22, `flowSector` out of `CONTROL_IDS` 21, the drill ignored 20, the listener list 16, the floor's ceiling 12 (with the cap), the group key 12, the pool not narrowed 12, the cap 11, the tail dropped 11, the drill's own tracks 9, the reference 2, and the drill class, the band labels and the article 1 each.
  - **TWO REVERTS CAME BACK 0 ON THE FIRST PASS AND BOTH WERE THE HARNESS.** One was a no-op — it dropped the pooled row and concatenated it straight back — and the other guards a state the cap makes unreachable. *A revert has to simulate the bug, and a guard that another guard hides has to be reverted together with it.*
  - **A HARDCODED SECTOR COUNT WENT STALE THE MOMENT THE DRILL'S OWN SECTOR WAS ADDED to the fixture.** It is derived from the rows now, which cannot rot the same way.
  - **A fixture fault worth keeping**: the drill sector is deliberately priced CLOSE to the index, so that adding it could not move the Healthcare/Energy band split the suite already asserts — which makes it the one sector that cannot demonstrate the reference changing. That check drills into Communication Services (+20% against +8.5%) instead.

#### Worth knowing
- **It costs no endpoint, no query and no basket.** Every field it reads is on the snapshot row, so there is no `basketDays` entry and no fetch; the whole card is a reduction over `/api/stocks`, which the studio already holds.
- **NO SCOPE PICKERS, which is not the same thing as no sector picker** — `tplDay`'s reasoning: this answers *what is the market made of and how has each part done*, so it takes no list, no screen and no size band. `flowSector` is the DRILL (above), which narrows what the card divides up rather than scoping a ranking, so there is still no `flowIndustry`/`flowCap`/`flowScreen` and `INDUSTRY_PREFIXES` is left alone.
- **A FOURTEENTH hardcoded listener list** in promo.html. A control in the markup and in `CONTROL_IDS` but not in one of these saves with a post, is read by the builder, and **does nothing when you touch it**. Control ids **108 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**.
- **HTML labels over the drawing, never SVG text** — the module's standing rule, since the artboard is scaled to the window and a glyph inside a stretched svg is distorted with it.
- **Ribbons are drawn biggest first** so a thin one is never buried under a thick one it crosses, and at `fill-opacity 0.32` so a crossing can be read. The band's own sectors keep the LEFT column's order, which is what holds the crossings down to what the data actually makes.
- **The note makes no claim a reader cannot check.** It explains the begin-weighting rather than asserting that the parts sum to the whole — that identity needs the START weights, and the percentages drawn are today's share. The SEC ratio card's rule.
- **A `min-width: 0` ON THE TRACKS REVERTED TO NOTHING, AND IS DELETED.** It was a second mechanism for one thing: each track takes its width INLINE from the same map the svg's own width comes from, and with `flex: none` beside it the item never shrinks, so the `min-width: auto` content floor cannot bind at all. The floor HAS bitten the trade log, the sparks grid and the saved-name field — it is disarmed here by the explicit width rather than by luck, and the comment says so, because anything that makes these tracks flexible has to put it back.
- **THE RIGHT COLUMN'S INTERNAL ORDER IS NOT A GUARD and is not claimed as one.** `b.mine` is `secs.filter(...)`, so a band holds its sectors in the LEFT column's order by construction; reversing it costs nothing measurable, because conservation and every count hold either way. It is what keeps the crossings down to what the data actually makes, and there is no code to delete.
- Verified: **82 checks** over a fixture whose six properties each make a different wrong implementation come out at a different answer — Technology holds a giant up 40% and a tiddler down 45% so begin- and end-weighting are **sixteen points** apart; Healthcare +6.0% and Energy +14.0% sit inside one fixed bucket and in different index-relative bands; a falling window makes the index negative; four kinds of absence (no sector, no return, no cap, a −99.5% wipeout that would weigh 200x its own cap); the cut crosses every sector; and the real longest sector name is on the card. Plus the ground sweep (**164 checks over 120 combinations**) and the width sweep (**103 over 120**) with the template registered.
- **Proved by reverting eighteen times, every one load-bearing**: the eleven sector funds left in the pool fails 18, flowPeriod/flowSp500 out of `CONTROL_IDS` 13, the S&P picker back on the shared fill 13, the blank sector left in until after the index is struck 10, the fourteenth listener list 9, the period picker unfilled 9, the −99 floor 6, end weights 5, the four index funds left in 5, a null return coerced to zero 4, the subtitle at the title's own size 4, the note not pinned to the foot 3, fixed bands 2, a null market cap given a weight 2, "of the value" 2, the band tests in the other order 2, and the minimum node height and the empty state branching on the cut 1 each.
  - **THE BAND-ORDER GUARD FIRST FAILED ONLY ONE CHECK, AND THE HARM IS A COLOUR.** The label beside each sector is coloured by the SIGN, which is right whichever order the bands are tested in, so the only thing that moved was a band count. The suite now reads the **drawn fill** and asserts that in a window where every sector fell, nothing on the card carries the rise colour — reverted, it reports `drawn: #fb7185 #34d399`, which is the whole objection in one line. **The rise colour is taken from the AHEAD BAND'S OWN NODE**, not from a riser's: a sector can rise and still be Behind, in which case its node is the neutral grey and the assertion would be about the wrong colour.
  - **A ROUND-TRIP WRITTEN AGAINST THE API IS NOT A TEST OF THE CONTROL THAT WRITES IT** — the pivot preset's lesson, met again. The saved-post check built its `opts` from the DOM and PUT them itself, so it exercised the server and never `controlOpts()`, which is what reads `CONTROL_IDS`. It goes through the page's own **Save this card as a post** button now, and the `CONTROL_IDS` revert then fails 13 rather than nothing.
  - **THE HARNESS CRASHED ON ITS SEVENTEENTH CASE** (four of the twenty were written as 4-tuples against a 5-tuple loop) — the `finally` restored both files, which is the only reason that was a nuisance rather than a working copy left patched. A spent patch script is a loaded gun on this project; the four ran in a harness of their own.
  - **EVERY ONE OF THESE HARNESSES BOOTS A SERVER ON PORT 3999, SO TWO CANNOT OVERLAP.** Starting the shot script while a sweep was still running gave `EADDRINUSE` and a run that exited 0 having drawn nothing — a green exit over no work, which is the `| tail` exit-code trap in a second shape. Judge a harness by its own summary line, never by how it exited, and run them one at a time.

## The pivot view
**`/pivot` — the screen counted by two dimensions at once (2026-09-20, owner's request), a button in the screener bar beside Promo Studio.** Member page, guests refused like the studio: a preview of five stocks has no shape to show. Rows and columns are chosen from Sector, Industry, Theme, Today’s move, Size by market cap, Balanced advice, Advice move, Trend state, Entry state, Company type, Exchange and S&P 500, plus the two time axes (which are columns only); every cell is a count, and clicking one expands the stocks in it underneath the row.

- **No endpoint, no query, nothing on the rows-read meter.** Every dimension is already on a snapshot row, so the page reads `/api/stocks` once and cross-tabulates in the browser — measured 2.1MB and 11.6s cold, then every change of dimension is instant. Exploration means changing the axes constantly, which is exactly when a round trip per change is the wrong shape.
- **THE CARDINALITIES WERE MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS DESIGNED**, and they decided the design: sector 11, industry **87**, advice 6, trend 6, type 3, exchange 4, theme 26 — over 430 stocks. Sector × advice is 66 cells at ~6.5 stocks each and reads well; **industry × anything is 522 cells for 430 stocks and is mostly empty**, with the average industry holding five companies. So a dimension past `WIDE_CAP` (24) values **folds its tail into one "Other" bucket**, and the test proves the fold loses nobody — the totals still reconcile.
- **Reconciliation is the assertion that matters.** A pivot whose totals do not add up is worse than no pivot: it looks authoritative and is wrong. Every cell is summed against its row total, the row totals against the grand total, and the grand total against the stock count.
- **A THEME IS MULTI-VALUED, and that breaks the arithmetic everyone expects.** 33 stocks sit in more than one theme and **189 in none**, so with Theme on an axis the cells add up to more than the universe. The page says so in words — "the cells add up to 9, not 8 — 1 stock is counted in more than one bucket" — rather than printing a total that quietly disagrees with itself. `multi` is a property of the dimension, not a special case buried in the sum.
- **A blank is a BUCKET, never a dropped row.** 20 stocks have no sector yet, because profiles arrive on rotation; omitting them would make every total wrong while looking tidy. Shown as `—`, sorted last, and counted in the note.
- *(superseded 2026-09-21 — see **Total market cap as a measure** below; the rule it states still holds for every other money field.)* **No money measures, deliberately.** Summing revenue would add SEK to USD: `currency` reads USD for all 430 because it is the TRADING currency, while revenue and net income are in the company's **reporting** currency, which is not stored. Counts cannot lie that way. Market cap would be safe and is left for when it is missed.
- **A ladder is not the alphabet.** Advice, trend, entry and type order by their own ladders; everything else orders by size, because "where is the weight" is what a pivot is opened to answer.
- **A FOOTNOTE UNDER THE GRID SAYS THE CELLS ARE CLICKABLE** (2026-09-27, owner's request). The drill is the page's main control and the only things announcing it were a tooltip — which speaks after the pointer has already arrived — and one clause of the intro paragraph, a screen away by the time anyone is reading numbers. `#ghint`, written by `render()`.
  - **The instruction LEFT the intro in the same commit.** Stating it twice inside one screen is the duplication this project has been pulled up on before; the paragraph says what the numbers ARE, the footnote says what to do with them, where the doing happens.
  - **Built from what was DRAWN, not from what the measure ought to produce.** A time axis has row averages and no column totals, and an empty grid has neither — so the "a total opens the same way" half is appended only when a `td.drill` exists, and the whole line is hidden when no `td.cell` does. Promising a control that is not there is worse than silence.
  - **IT IS HIDDEN WHILE A SELECTION IS OPEN, and that is load-bearing rather than tidiness.** `sizePanes()` budgets the two panes from the grid's TOP and the child caption, so **anything unaccounted for between them comes straight off the bottom of the window** — and with both panes capped the budget lands the child table exactly on the foot of the viewport, so there is no slack to absorb it. Measured: **−1px of slack hidden, −27px visible**, the footnote's own 26px box. It is also spent by then: the child table carries its own crumb and a Clear selection button.
  - **`ghint`, never `hint`.** An unscoped class here would be the sixth on this project to capture later markup, and `.sub` already did it on this very page.
  - Verified: **20 checks** — drawn, measured as sitting between the two tables, the wording, the totals clause against a grid that really has drillable totals, the intro no longer saying it, hidden on a pick and back on Clear, and the phone. **The pane check needs BOTH panes at their caps or it proves nothing**: a first fixture of nine stocks left 222px of slack and passed with the footnote deliberately left showing, so it is twenty sector rows and sixty stocks, and the assertion first checks `scrollHeight > clientHeight` on each pane. **Proved by reverting**: dropping the one hide clause fails 2, the child table hanging 27px off the bottom of the window.
- **THE SNAPSHOT'S `action` IS IGNORED ON READ** — `scoreActionInto` re-derives the verdict, company type, trend and entry from each row's technicals every time. A fixture that writes `action: 'Strong Buy'` therefore tests nothing: the first version of this test did exactly that, got one verdict for all eight stocks, and its ladder assertion passed on a **single column**. The fixture carries real technicals now, checked against `Action.apply` beforehand to confirm they produce five different verdicts.
- Verified: 30 checks on the real page — reconciliation in both the single- and multi-valued cases, the blank bucket, the ladder order, drill-down (expanding, the count matching the list, each row linking to its stock page, closing again), swap, the same-dimension-twice guard, the wide fold keeping every stock, and no sideways scroll at 390px.

### Total market cap as a measure (2026-09-21, owner's request)
**A `Measure` picker beside the two dimensions: Number of stocks (the default) or Total market cap.** This file had left the door open — *"Market cap would be safe and is left for when it is missed"* — and it is safe for the reason recorded under the Size column: **the cap comes back in USD even when the rest of the row does not**, verified across 18 foreign reporters. **It is still the ONLY money measure this page may have**: revenue and net income are in the company's reporting currency, which is not stored, so summing them would add SEK to USD and produce a confident, meaningless number.

- **A measure is one number per stock** (`MEASURES[k].each`), and the ordering, the wide fold, the row and column totals, the child rows and the drill all reduce over it — so adding one is an entry in that map rather than a parallel path through `build()`.
- **The totals are now REDUCED OUT OF THE CELLS** rather than accumulated beside them. They were a correct parallel running count that could have drifted from what the grid draws; derived this way **a row total cannot disagree with the row above it, whatever the measure**. The grid is walked as rows × columns rather than by splitting cell keys on `|`, because sector and industry names are the provider's, not ours.
- **THE EMPTINESS TEST IS THE STOCK LIST, NOT THE VALUE.** A cell holding two funds sums to zero and is still a cell with two stocks in it: it reads `$0`, stays clickable, and the note says **how many stocks have no cap and that "a count and a total need not agree"**. Drawing it as the empty dot would hide them, and a sum that silently omits rows is the quietest kind of lie.
- **Ordering follows the MEASURE, deliberately** — showing money while ordering by count would put the biggest number halfway down the table. The test pins it: two sectors tied at 3 stocks fall back to the alphabet under counts and reorder by size under money.
- **The double-counting warning is judged on PLACEMENTS, never on the measure.** With money on screen `placements` is dollars, and "adds up to $4.1T, not 573" would be nonsense — so `placeCount` is kept separately. The count wording is kept **word for word** ("the cells add up to 9, not 8"), because a rephrasing lost the directness; money gets its own sentence saying a cap is added once per placement.
- **Changing the measure keeps both axes and the open sector** — it is the same table answering a different question, and dropping the reader's place would make comparing the two answers a chore. Changing an *axis* still clears them, since their keys name values that are leaving the screen.
- **The drill names the total** (`2 stocks, $125.0B in total`), or the number in the cell above cannot be checked against the list under it. The child-row reconciliation is compared with a **relative epsilon**: summing dollars leaves a floating-point residue that a strict equality would report as a mismatch over two numbers identical to the penny.
- Verified: 26 checks — every row's cells summing to its own total and the rows to the grand, each column footer against its own column, hand-computed totals ($175B / $8B / $183B), the `$0` cell staying clickable with its explanation, the drill's total, the hierarchy reconciling **in dollars**, the reorder-by-money, the expansion surviving a measure change, and counts coming back unchanged. The two earlier pivot suites still pass.

### Balanced advice moves, as a measure AND a dimension (2026-09-23, owner's request)
**"Analyse Balanced advice moves from the previous trading day to today… so I can slice by Sector, Theme."** Both halves shipped, because they answer different questions and the pivot expresses them differently:

- **`moves` — a MEASURE, "Advice moves"**: how many stocks in each cell changed verdict since the previous close. Deliberately UNSIGNED. The page orders, shades and totals on the measure, and a signed one would shade only its positive half and draw a −20 cell the same as an empty one.
- **`advmove` — a DIMENSION, "Advice move"**: Upgraded / Unchanged / Downgraded. Direction belongs on an AXIS: "Technology 27" says where the churn is, crossing it says what happened. Cross the two and the grid says both at once.

Both read fields already stamped on every snapshot row — `action` and `advicePrev` — so this costs a comparison and no fetch. Measured on the live screen the day it shipped: **136 of 942 moved, 63 up and 73 down**.

- **`ActionRules.ACTIONS` RUNS WORST-FIRST** (Sell Immediately → Strong Buy), so an upgrade is an INCREASE in index. The page reverses that list for display, and using the display order here would label every upgrade a downgrade. The test's two sectors have the same number of movers in opposite directions precisely so that inversion cannot pass.
- **A stock with no previous verdict is a BLANK, not "Unchanged".** New to the screener is a different fact from held its verdict, and the measure counts it as neither — the two-kinds-of-blank rule this project keeps re-learning.
- **The note carries the up/down split**, because it is not derivable from the grid unless the dimension is on an axis, and it names the dimension that would show it per cell.
- **The drill gained a "Was" column**, filled only where the verdict moved: a column repeating today's verdict on 800 unchanged rows is noise, and the blank then means "held". **REMOVED 2026-09-28 (owner), with Trend and Cushion, replaced by the 3M and 6M returns** — see the drill's own note below. `advicePrev` is still on the row and the Advice move measure still reads it; only the column went.
- **THE DRILL'S COLUMNS ARE FOURTEEN, AND WHICH FOURTEEN CHANGED ON 2026-09-28 (owner).** Out went **Was, Trend and Cushion**; in came **3M and 6M**, placed between 1M and 1Y so the row reads left to right as time passing. All three that left were readings of the advice engine, and the Advice column beside them already gives the verdict — a drill opened from a cell is read for *which stocks are in here and how have they done*, so the two missing horizons earn the width more than a second and third opinion on the same row. **Two suites had to be corrected rather than the change worked around**: `pivot-test.js` asserted “the FIFTEEN fields” and named Cushion, and `pivot-advmove-test.js` asserted the Was column was present and filled. Both now assert the new set **in both directions** — the horizons present AND the three readings absent — so neither half can quietly revert.

**THE NOTE'S WORDING WAS HARDCODED AROUND MARKET CAP and had to move onto the measures first.** `const money = measure !== 'count'` meant any new measure inherited the sentence about funds reporting AUM. Each measure now owns `everyStock`, `missingNote`, `placeNote` and an optional `summary`; only `count` sets `everyStock`, because it is the one whose total IS the stock count.

**`tint: 1` IS A DEAD FLAG UNTIL THE VALUES ARE IN `LADDER_TINT` — and this project has now shipped that wrong twice.** The first time was the move bands. This time a screenshot showed Unchanged carrying a dot while Upgraded and Downgraded did not, and only because the band ladder already defines that same word and means the same by it. There is a check now that reads the rendered dot colours and asserts the two ends differ.

- Verified: 20 checks — the measure's per-row counts and a grand total of the movers rather than the universe, a 0 cell still clickable, the note's split and its absence of fund wording, the dimension's three columns reconciling, the blank bucket, the drill's Was column opened on an UPGRADED cell (opening whichever cell held a number landed on Unchanged, where the column is correctly blank and the assertion tested that a blank is blank), and a saved preset carrying both new keys.
- **The fixture had to supply real technicals AND a `prevTech` overlay.** The server re-derives both verdicts on read, so hand-written `action` / `advicePrev` values are discarded — the first cut did that and every stock came back with no previous verdict at all. The documented trap, met again.

### Time as a column axis — the last 12 months, or the last 12 years (2026-09-27, owner's request)
**"One column per month… it will help to see how stocks perform over time."** `Last 12 months` and `Last 12 years` are column dimensions; the cell is the group's **equal-weight return** for that period, newest first. Rows stay any dimension, so it answers *how did each sector do each month* in one grid.

- **THE REQUEST SAID BOTH** — "Last 12 Month" and "one column per last 12 years" — and the answer was to build both, because **they are the same query**: thirteen boundaries and the last close before each. The owner confirmed.
- **THIRTEEN ANCHORS, NOT A BAR WINDOW.** Twelve years of daily bars for the universe is millions of rows and past the ~83MB wall this file records. `closesBefore` is one indexed seek per (symbol, boundary) on the `(symbol, d)` primary key — ~15,000 single-row reads, the shape it was rewritten into when the 5Y anchor went from 748,859 rows to 254. `GET /api/pivot-periods?kind=`, cached ten minutes per kind.
- **A RETURN IS A MEAN AND DEPENDS ON THE COLUMN**, where every other measure is a per-stock number summed. `cellVal(list, c)` is the one place that aggregates, so the grid, the row totals, the child rows and the drill cannot do it three different ways. **A mean cannot be summed out of the cells**, so the row total is the *average of that row's own periods* ("Avg", not "Total") — still reduced from the cells the grid draws, so it cannot disagree with the row above it.
- **THE FOOTER IS THE S&P 500, not a column total.** Averaging group means down a column would weight a two-stock sector like a two-hundred-stock one. It is deliberately **not drillable**: one ETF's own return has no list of stocks behind it.
- **COLOURED BY SIGN, never shaded by size.** The heat ramp says *bigger*, and a −8% month is not smaller than a +2% one; the shading control disables itself for a signed measure.
- **A STOCK ABSENT FROM A PERIOD IS ABSENT, NEVER A FLAT ZERO.** No opening anchor, no return — inventing one from a stock's first trade would print a return for a period it did not live through. So an earlier column is an average over fewer companies, and **the note says how many have all twelve**: the survivorship point, in the one feature most able to hide it.
- **ALL TWELVE PERIODS ARE DRAWN even when nothing has data for one** — the Size picker's rule. "2015: nothing reaches back that far" is an answer; silently drawing four columns after asking for twelve looks broken. Found by the test, not by reading.
- **The newest period is PARTIAL** (month- or year-to-date) and the header says *so far*, because that is what "the last twelve months" means to a reader on the 20th.
- **A time axis is NOT double-counting** (`noDouble`): a stock sits in every period it has a return for, which is the same stock measured twelve times. The "counted in more than one bucket" warning would be true arithmetic and a false alarm.
- **Columns only, and the measure is forced.** Twelve periods down the side with a taxonomy across the top is the same grid read the wrong way round; and a count of stocks per month is the same number twelve times, a market cap per month is today's cap printed twelve times — so the picker locks to the return and shows what it is locked to rather than vanishing.
#### ONE JUNK BAR DESTROYED A WHOLE COLUMN, and only the live screenshot showed it
**The first deploy drew Technology 2025 at +411,732% and its Avg at +34,337%.** `SOLS` holds closes of about **$0.0001** at the head of its archive, so its 2025 anchor pair gave **+48,579,901%** and the sector's equal-weight mean went with it. `a.close > 0` was not a sufficient test of "is this a price".

- **`MIN_CLOSE` is a cent**, and deliberately far below any real value rather than tuned: the lowest legitimate close in this archive is **NVDA's split-adjusted $0.16 from 2007**, sixteen times clear of it. Below a cent is a delisted shell or a bad bar. The same shape as `MIN_VOL` in the strategy backtest, where a zero-volatility hole produced a **3,227,535× position** — *a near-zero divisor makes the failure impossible rather than merely unlikely*.
- **A MEAN HAS NO DEFENCE AGAINST AN OUTLIER THAT SIZE**, which is exactly why the fundamentals card uses medians. The owner chose equal-weight here (rightly — it matches the group pages), so the guard has to be on the input.
- **`junk` is returned by the endpoint**, so a rising count is visible rather than silent.
- **SOLS LEFT THE UNIVERSE on 2026-09-28 (owner), which is the right ending and not a substitute for the guard below.** The `BBX` / `PXD` / `BF` precedent: a ticker whose data is permanently wrong at the PROVIDER is a gap every future run re-attempts for ever. Universe 1,182 → 1,181, its bars, profile and name purged. **The floor stays**, because it was never about this one stock — the next reused ticker or unadjusted reverse split arrives unannounced, and without it the first warning is a six-figure percentage on a page somebody happens to screenshot.
- **THAT REPAIR WAS WRONG, and this line used to state it as the fix (corrected 2026-09-28).** It said to run `backfill-bars.js --commit --only SOLS`. **Re-pulling changes nothing: the PROVIDER itself serves `$0.000099999997`** for every session from 2024 to 2025-04-10, then a gap, then $56 — an unadjusted reverse split or a reused ticker, measured by asking Twelve Data directly. A backfill replaces our copy with the same numbers. **Before assuming a bad bar is ours, ask the provider what it holds.**
- **So the floor moved to where returns are COMPUTED** — `MIN_CLOSE` now guards `pctChange` and the 5Y anchor in server.js, not just this page's anchors. Until then SOLS reported a **1Y of +56,129,902%** on the screener itself, which dragged the Semiconductor Equipment & Materials row on `/consolidated` to **+4,677,721%** — that is how it was finally noticed, by the owner, from a screenshot. One definition of the constant now, beside `pctChange`.
  - **It is a bad-bar guard, NOT a plausibility filter, and the test holds that line**: NVDA's split-adjusted $0.16 from 2007 and AXTI's genuine +1,447% both still compute. Only sub-cent readings are refused, at either end of the window.
  - **A stored snapshot keeps the old number until something recomputes it**, so the screener still showed +56M% until the next refresh — worth knowing before concluding a fix did not land.
- **Only a screenshot of the live page found it.** Every check passed on a fixture of clean prices; the test now carries `JNK` — a real price now, a fraction of a cent then — and `PNY` at $0.16, so the guard is proved to reject the one and keep the other. **Proved by reverting**: `close > 0` gives **+39,999,900%** and a Technology cell of **+7,999,980%**, the production symptom in miniature, failing 4.

- Verified: **41 checks** over a fixture whose prices sit exactly on month boundaries, so every return is hand-checkable, with the two Technology names at **+10% and +30% in the same month** — a cell returning one member's number instead of the mean fails. Plus a **late lister** absent from the months it did not trade, both kinds, the locked measure and disabled shading, the sign colours measured as DRAWN, the S&P footer carrying SPY's own +4%, and the note. **Proved by reverting**: the off-by-one in the boundary loop fails 5.
  - **Two bugs the suite caught that reading did not**: the loop made THIRTEEN boundaries for twelve periods, and `DIMS` referenced `periodLabel` by name — a **TDZ throw at load**, because the object literal is evaluated before the helpers below it exist. The fix is an arrow (`fmtKey: (k) => periodLabel(k)`), and it is the `/api/db-stats` ordering trap in a new place.
  - **`pivot-expand-test.js` asserted `rows === cols - 1`**, which encoded "industry is the only column-only dimension". It names them now (`industry,months,years`), so a fourth fails loudly instead of arithmetically.

### Include S&P — a filter of its own, not a dimension (2026-10-04, owner's request)
**`Include S&P`: All stocks / In the S&P 500 / Not in the S&P 500, always on screen, between Shading and Filter.** The owner's words: *"I don't want s&p filter on Rows and Column filter like this, I want to create a separate filter called Include s&p."*

- **IT WAS ONE `DIMS` ENTRY, WHICH IS EXACTLY THE PROBLEM.** The Filter picker is built from DIMS rather than from a list of its own, so a single entry bought a row axis, a column axis and a page filter at once — which read as economical when it shipped and is the reason it turned up in two places nobody wanted it. **On an axis it is a two-row grid whose interesting half is always the other dimension.** The entry is deleted, so it is gone from Rows, Columns *and* the generic Filter together.
- **DELIBERATELY NOT LEFT IN THE GENERIC FILTER AS WELL.** Two controls for one cut can be set to different things, and nothing on the page would say which won. There is a check that no axis menu so much as says the words.
- **ANDed with the generic Filter, applied in `pageRows()`** — the one place everything downstream starts, so the cells, both sets of totals, the shading denominators, the drill-downs and the note all describe the same population without any of them knowing the filter exists. **Proved by reverting**: making the cut *replace* the other filter fails 1, the intersection coming out at 3 where it should be 2.
- **UNKNOWN IS NOT OUTSIDE, and that is the whole reason the read did not change.** `spMember` is null until a holdings file has been imported, so the value still comes from **`Filters.filterValue(s, 'spMember')`** — the one function that knows the field is three-state. `out` means **known to be outside**, not "not known to be inside", so an unchecked stock is in **neither** cut and the note says how many and why; otherwise the two cuts quietly fail to add up to the screen. **Proved by reverting twice**: `spOf(s) !== 'Yes'` fails 2, and a `s.spMember ? 'Yes' : 'No'` ternary fails 5 — on an instance that has never run the import that one would put all 1,278 stocks in the `out` cut.
- **Counted over the WHOLE universe in the menu**, like the Filter's own values and for the same reason: a menu describing the table you have already narrowed to cannot tell you what you would get back.
- **`cleanPivots` REBUILDS A PRESET FROM AN EXPLICIT FIELD LIST**, so `sp` had to be named there or every saved pivot would open on the default cut with nothing saying why — a key it does not know is dropped. A preset saved before this reads as `all`, in `samePreset` as well, or an old one would read "(edited)" the moment it was opened. **Proved by reverting**: the server drop fails 4, `samePreset` 2, `applyPreset` 3.
- **Checked production before deleting the dimension**: neither of the two saved pivots used it, so nothing was stranded. Live afterwards: **498 in, 780 out, 1,278 all**, both presets still listed, no page errors.
- **The values are spelled as `Cards.spCuts()` spells them (`all` / `in` / `out`) and are NOT shared with it.** That catalogue lives in `cards.js`, which this page does not load; a third home for three labels would be worse than two, and matching the spelling means a later unification is a deletion rather than a translation. **The part that genuinely must not be duplicated — the three-state read — already is shared.**
- Verified: **39 checks**. The fixture's load-bearing property is that **the cut CROSSES the sector** — each sector holds members and non-members — so a cut wired to the wrong field comes out at a different grid rather than coincidentally the same one, and every state sums the grid back up. **Proved by reverting eleven times**, every one load-bearing: the cut unapplied 9, replacing instead of ANDing 1, unknown-as-outside 2, the raw-field ternary 5, the dimension restored 4, the note 5, the menu counts 2, `currentPreset` 2, `samePreset` 2, `applyPreset` 3, the server key 6.
  - **THE FIXTURE SANITY CHECK EARNED ITS PLACE ON THE FIRST RUN.** `fund_holdings` and `fund_state` were seeded as `'SPY'`, and **both accessors fold the key** (`String(fund).toLowerCase()`, against `SP_FUND = 'spy'`), so nothing matched, every stock stamped null, and the page correctly called them all unchecked — twelve failures that looked like the feature and were the fixture. One check comparing the route's own stamp against the intended members said so in one line.
  - **A GUARD CAME BACK "NOT LOAD-BEARING" BECAUSE THE TEST NEVER TOOK THE PAGE'S OWN PATH.** Dropping `sp` from `currentPreset()` failed nothing, because the suite wrote its presets with a hand-built PUT — which exercises the server and never the page. It now saves through the **Save this pivot** button (handling the `prompt`), and the revert then fails 2. *A round-trip written against the API is not a test of the control that writes it.*
  - **FOUR FAILURES WERE MY OWN ARITHMETIC** — the fixture has three non-members and the comment above it said two. Worth stating because the run also surfaced a real copy bug while they were being fixed: the note read *"1 stock has not been checked … and **are** in neither cut"*, and there is now a check that the sentence agrees with its own count.
  - **`io.open(path, encoding='utf-8')` IN PYTHON TRANSLATES CRLF ON READ**, so writing back with `newline=''` silently converts the whole file — `pivot.html` went from CRLF to LF mid-session this way. Invisible here only because git normalises on commit, so the diff stayed at 87 lines rather than 1,875. Pass `newline=''` to the READ as well.
  - **`pivot-test.js` fails 1 and it is PRE-EXISTING** (the drill carries fifteen fields since YTD; the suite still says fourteen). The other eight pivot suites re-run clean — 24, 28, 47, 29, 28, 46, 19 and 21 — which is what holds the DIMS deletion down.

### Saved pivots (2026-09-23, owner's request: "something similar" to the promo presets)
**The promo-preset model applied to /pivot, and the owner chose that scope explicitly when asked**: ONE site-wide list in `app_meta` under `pivot_presets`, every member reads it, only the owner writes. `GET /api/pivot-presets` is `requireMember` (so guests are refused, matching the page, which redirects them); `PUT` is `requireAdmin`. `cleanPivots()` rebuilds from scratch, `PIVOTS_MAX` 20, cached 60s per instance.

- **A preset is the QUESTION, never the answer** — both axes, the measure, the shading and the page filter. Opening one tomorrow cross-tabulates tomorrow's screen, which is the whole point and the same reason a saved promo post stores controls rather than a picture.
- **The open sector and the drill selection are deliberately NOT stored.** They are where you happened to be looking, not what you wanted to keep, and restoring yesterday's stock list into today's counts is the one thing a saved pivot must not do.
- **Keys are SHAPE-checked, not listed against DIMS/MEASURES.** Those live in pivot.html, and restating them server-side would drift the first time a dimension was added — the rule `cleanViews` follows for the screener's columns and `cleanPosts` for the studio's controls. `applyPreset()` falls back rather than throwing, so a preset naming a dimension that has since been renamed opens to a working grid.
- **`pageVal` takes any printable text, deliberately.** It is a sector, a theme or a band name that came out of the data, not an identifier. Narrowing it is exactly how every screen silently lost its `<` and `>` filters on 2026-09-15; the page escapes it where it is shown.
- **A saved filter value that no longer exists says so.** fillPicks already falls back to the first value rather than filtering to nothing; the preset path adds a line naming what it could not find, because silently showing a different cut is worse than admitting the saved one is gone.

**THE ONE DESIGN BUG, caught by the test rather than by reading it.** The first cut derived the picker's selection from whether the screen still MATCHED a preset, so the moment an axis moved the picker deselected and **Replace vanished — at exactly the moment it becomes useful**, since you change the pivot and then want to point the preset at it. `chosenId` is kept apart from `samePreset()` now: the selection survives divergence and the option reads "(edited)", the idiom the screener's Screens menu already uses. An exact match still adopts the selection, so arriving at a saved pivot by hand names it rather than reading "Not saved".

- Verified: 26 checks against the real page and the real server. **The round trip moves EVERY control away before reopening** — the promo suite passed for weeks without doing that, reading values that had never left the page while 23 controls were being silently dropped. Plus the grand total matching what it was when saved, the stored shape carrying no drill state, Replace keeping the name, validation (no axes, an unsafe key, duplicate ids, punctuation in a value), and the member seeing the list with no write buttons.
- `.psaid` and the whole row are scoped under `#presetBar`. Five unscoped class names have captured later markup on this project, one of them (`.sub`) on this very page.

### Sector expands into its industries (2026-09-21, owner's request)
**Industry is a DRILL of Sector, not a peer dimension, and the data says so:** measured on the live screen, **0 of 99 industries span two sectors** — every one belongs to exactly one. So as a row dimension it drew 99 rows of which each was a single sector's slice, and crossed with Sector it was a block-diagonal grid with one non-empty cell per column. `DIMS.industry` carries **`childOf: 'sector'`** now, `ROW_DIMS` filters those out, and a sector row carries a caret that opens its industries underneath it.

- **It stays a COLUMN dimension.** Advice × Industry is still a real question; only the Rows entry went. **The caret is switched off when the columns are already Industry** — the child rows would restate the grid — and the page says that rather than leaving a dead control.
- **One sector open at a time (the owner's call).** Two hierarchies on screen and the eye stops knowing which child rows belong to which parent.
- **A caret is drawn only where a sector holds TWO or more industries.** One child row is a copy of its parent, which is a control that does nothing — and it is exactly the blank-sector bucket's shape, so the rule handles that case without naming it.
- **THE RECONCILIATION IS THE FEATURE.** The children are counted through the *same* `cFold.map` and de-duplicated multi-value list as the grid above, so they add up to their parent's own total — and the note **says so on the page**, printing the sum. The hard case is a multi-valued column: a stock in two themes inflates its sector's total, and the industry rows have to be counted the same way or they disagree with the row directly above them. A hierarchy whose children do not sum to their parent is a pivot that lies while looking authoritative.
- **No fold on the child rows**, measured: the widest sector holds **16** industries against a `WIDE_CAP` of 24, so a child list is always a list rather than a wall.
- **Child cells drill to stocks like their parents do**, keyed `sub:<industry>|<column>` — the prefix is what keeps the two sets of keys apart, so a sector and an industry that happened to share a name could never share a drill. Expanding or collapsing drops every child drill, or a key left in `open` silently re-opens a stock list the next time any sector is expanded.
- **The same-dimension "step aside" now avoids child dimensions.** It took the first key in `DIMS` — which is `industry` — so setting rows to whatever the columns already were silently landed on Industry-as-columns and the caret vanished from a state the reader chose nothing to get into. Found by the test walking into it.
- **`.sub` was already taken on this page** — the intro PARAGRAPH eleven rules up the stylesheet (font-size 13px, max-width 78ch, its own colour) — and `<tr class="sub">` inherited all of it. **The FIFTH unscoped class on this project to capture later markup**, after `.warn`, `.card`, `input[type="text"]` and `.mk`. It is `tr.kid` now. **A screenshot found it; all 38 assertions passed straight through it, because the numbers were right.** There is now a check comparing a child row's *computed* type size and column width against its parent's.
- **The caret was `--faint` at 10px and read as a bullet**, not a control — it is `--muted` at 12px, and the test asserts the rendered box rather than the markup (the `/quality` lesson).
- Verified: 42 checks on the real page — the pickers, carets only where they earn their place, the reconciliation in the total AND column by column AND with a multi-valued column, the blank child bucket sorting last, one-open-at-a-time, a child drill holding only stocks in that sector *and* that industry, the columns-are-Industry guard with Swap disabled and a reason on it, the expansion not outliving its axis, and the computed-style checks above. The original 30-check suite still passes with its wide-fold case moved to the columns axis.

### The Histogram — the shape of the whole screen on one measure (2026-10-06, owner's request)

**A nineteenth template, `histogram`, fifth in the studio's picker, with two modes: the distribution on its own, and the same distribution with one stock pinned to it.** Asked as *"One chart we do not have is Histogram, can you give me some ideas"*, answered with a measurement of which distributions actually have a shape, and the owner took **both** of the two concepts offered.

#### IT IS THE ONE SHAPE THE STUDIO COULD NOT DRAW
Every other data card is a **ranking** (movers), a **relationship** (bubble, fund), a **time series** (chart, evolution) or a **composition** (flow, size). None of them answers *what does the whole screen look like on this measure* — which is also the thing that makes a single stock's reading mean anything. `stock` is `screen` plus a pin, so they are two MODES of one template rather than two templates; the `fund` and `chart` pattern.

#### THE MEASURES WERE CHOSEN BY DRAWING THEM, not by sounding interesting
Twelve, each binned against the live distribution rather than guessed. The three with a genuinely striking shape:

| | what it looks like |
|---|---|
| **% below its own record** | a broad body with a long left tail — median **−30.5%**, p10 −72.4, and 27 companies more than 90% below |
| **a bad day** | sharply peaked: **376 companies at −3 to −4** and a thin tail to −14, so "normal bad" is 3-4% |
| **position in the 52-week range** | **not** the U-shape anyone would predict — a pile at the bottom (133 + 108 in the lowest two bins), a flat middle, a small lift at the top |

**Value added today was measured and REFUSED**: 1,141 of 1,262 fall in two bins, because dollar amounts spanning orders of magnitude do not make a histogram.

#### THE BINNING IS PER MEASURE AND FIXED, never derived from the data
A range taken from today's own percentiles moves every time the card is drawn, so two posts a week apart would not be comparable — and **the range is most of what a histogram asserts**.

- **AN OPEN END BIN IS THE TRAP SPECIFIC TO THIS CHART.** Drawn without saying so, everything beyond the range piles against the edge and reads as a real mode. Measured on the live screen: **forward P/E has 125 values outside a 0-60 window and revenue growth 81**. An open end is labelled with a sign (`≤−90`) and counted in the note.
- **THE AXIS LABELS ARE BIN EDGES, not midpoints.** The bins were chosen to land on round numbers and a midpoint label throws that away — the first render read `−77, −62, −47` where the bins start at −75, −60, −45.
- **THE AXIS IS ZERO-BASED, AND THAT IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE EVOLUTION CARD'S RULE.** A bar is read as a quantity measured from the baseline, so a truncated one is the classic misleading chart; a LINE carries no such claim, which is why that card may use its data's own range and this one may not. **Do not "fix" this to match it** — the comment in the builder says so.

#### COLOUR ONLY WHERE ZERO IS A DIRECTION
`signed` is true for returns, margins and growth, where a reader already reads red as down. It is false for everything whose values are all one sign — *a column negative on every row says nothing by being red*, the Bad day rule — and **false for `peerPe`, which is a measurement rather than a style choice**: this project found the cheapest third of each industry has the worse growth, margin, ROE and Quality, so a green bar there would be the card asserting the opposite of its own data.

#### Worth knowing
- **FUNDS ARE OUT.** A fund has no fundamentals and reports AUM as a market cap, so it does not belong in a distribution OF companies — the rule `/consolidated`, the Snapshot card and the flow card all keep. The fixture gives both funds a value in a bin the data otherwise leaves **empty**, so including them would be visible rather than a rounding difference.
- **THE PERCENTILE IS THE PAYLOAD of the subject mode**, not the value — the row already carries the value. Worded neutrally (*higher than 18% of them*), because whether higher is better is the reader's to decide.
- **A FLOOR OF 30 READINGS.** Below it the card says so rather than drawing a row of single-count spikes, and it names how many it found.
- **The flag anchors to whichever side has room.** Centred is right in the middle and runs off the artboard at either end — measured on the story, where a subject at its own record pins at 100%.
- **A null is counted and named, never binned at the left edge**, which is what `Number(null)` would do.

#### IT FOUND A REAL GAP IN THE CONTRAST SWEEP
**`groundBehind` starts at `el.parentElement`** — exactly right for the SURFACE check (a background compared with itself would always pass) and **wrong for the INK check: text sits on its OWN background when it has one.** The subject's flag is ground-coloured text on an accent pill, so it measured **1:1 against the artboard**, a failure that is not there. The two checks now take two different grounds, which is what they always meant. *Same class as the text/graphic floor fix the day before: a sweep gets the wrong answer when one model is asked to serve two questions.*

#### A SCOPED TEMPLATE HAS TO JOIN SIX LISTS, NOT TWO
This page documents the hardcoded **listener** lists (now sixteen) and `CONTROL_IDS`. There are **four more that FILL the pickers** — sector, size, screen, S&P — plus a line that copies the scope options. Missing from a fill list, a picker exists carrying only its placeholder: **the control is there, it is in `CONTROL_IDS`, it is wired to a listener, and it still cannot be changed to anything.** Caught by the suite asking whether changing `histSector` redrew the card, not by reading.

- Control ids **117 against `POST_OPT_MAX` 200**, counted rather than assumed.
- Verified: **41 checks**, plus the ground sweep (**229 over 168 combinations**) and the width sweep (**109 over 126**) with the template registered and **both modes swept** — a template with no `MODES` entry is visited on its default mode only, the coverage hole the Intro's step slides sat in for weeks.
  - **THE FIXTURE IS THE TEST.** Every value is planted in a KNOWN bin, the counts per bin are all different, and **the median is deliberately not the midpoint of the range** (−3.5 on a −14..0 axis is 75%), so a card that bins wrongly, or that splits the difference, comes out at a different picture rather than coincidentally the right one. **A histogram that mis-bins looks perfectly well formed.**
  - **THE ZERO BASELINE IS PROVED BY PROPORTION** rather than asserted: if the drawn heights are proportional to the counts then the baseline is zero, and if it were lifted they would not be.
  - **THE PHONE IS THE SECOND HOST** and is round-tripped through the page's own Save button — a round-trip written against the API exercises the server and never `controlOpts()`, which is what reads `CONTROL_IDS`.
